title: CaseWeaver: A Multi-Agent Framework for Multimodal Virtual Clinical Case Generation
summary: Clinical diagnosis relies on consistent multimodal data collected from the same patient throughout the disease course, yet such data are difficult to acquire at scale because of collection costs, missing modalities, fragmented systems, and longitudinal follow-ups. Existing synthetic-data approaches largely focus on individual modalities or vision-language dual modalities at report-level generation. Little work has been done to construct synthetic data with consistent patient backgrounds, coherent disease trajectories, and interrelated modality-specific evidence at a complete clinical case level. We introduce CaseWeaver, a multi-agent framework built around a timeline-anchored Latent Clinical Case Graph (LCCG). The LCCG organizes patient context, latent disease states, clinical events, and expected observations in a shared patient-level representation. Modality-agents use scoped observation subgraphs and clinical protocols to generate evidence including clinical records, laboratory results, physiological signals, and medical images. We evaluate clinical inferability using a calibrated AgentClinic protocol and case diversity using Virtual Case Diversity (VCD) score. CaseWeaver outperformed general-model and agentic-workflow baselines on both metrics, producing more diverse and coherent multimodal virtual clinical cases.

AI.tldr: CaseWeaver: A multi-agent framework for generating synthetic multimodal clinical cases with consistent patient backgrounds, disease trajectories, and interrelated evidence.
AI.motivation: Real clinical data is difficult to acquire at scale due to collection costs, missing modalities, fragmented systems, and longitudinal follow-ups. Existing synthetic-data approaches focus on individual modalities or vision-language at report-level, lacking comprehensive patient-level consistency.
AI.method: CaseWeaver uses a timeline-anchored Latent Clinical Case Graph (LCCG) that organizes patient context, latent disease states, clinical events, and expected observations. Modality-agents use scoped observation subgraphs and clinical protocols to generate evidence including clinical records, lab results, physiological signals, and medical images.
AI.result: CaseWeaver outperformed general-model and agentic-workflow baselines on clinical inferability (using calibrated AgentClinic protocol) and case diversity (using Virtual Case Diversity score), producing more diverse and coherent multimodal virtual clinical cases.
AI.conclusion: CaseWeaver represents a significant advancement in synthetic clinical data generation by creating comprehensive, patient-level consistent multimodal cases that address limitations of existing approaches.

title: DART: A DAG-Based Reputation and Incentive Framework via Blockchain-Enabled Governance for Trustworthy LLM Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) predominantly rely on centralized orchestration and lack formal verification mechanisms for agent reliability, participation, and system-level behavioral alignment. These shortcomings leave open environments severely vulnerable to uncooperative or malicious agents. This work proposes DART, a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)-based reputation and incentive regulation framework for trustworthy multi-agent collaboration, combining centralized operational orchestration with blockchain-enabled decentralized governance and accountability. DART unifies DAG workflow orchestration, capability and reputation-aware task allocation, dynamic behavior updates, multi-factor incentives, and smart contract accountability paired with IPFS storage. Under this paradigm, agent selection dynamically balances task alignment, historical reputation, and workload, while post-execution behavioral evidence continuously calibrates agent trust and the probability of future participation. Evaluated across four axes, DART achieves 93.6% Pass@1 on GSM8K and builds a full-stack application in 142 s using two agents, outperforming centralized baselines. Across five independent 150-round longitudinal trials, Full DART achieves a mean task success rate of 93.33 +/- 2.26%, output quality of 0.9357 +/- 0.0117, retry rate of 0.2307 +/- 0.0816, and allocation delay of 1.1153 +/- 0.0408 s, consistently outperforming its ablated configurations DART isolates persistent and intermittent malicious agents, obtaining a 99.3% output containment rate and restoring system success to 99.8%. These results demonstrate the potential of coupling reputation, incentives, DAG-based coordination, and verifiable blockchain-enabled governance to support adaptive and accountable multi-agent collaboration.

AI.tldr: DART: A DAG-based reputation and incentive regulation framework that combines centralized orchestration with blockchain-enabled decentralized governance to ensure trustworthy multi-agent collaboration through dynamic reputation management, smart contracts, and IPFS storage.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based multi-agent systems lack formal verification for agent reliability and participation, and rely solely on centralized orchestration, making them vulnerable to uncooperative or malicious agents in open environments.
AI.method: Proposes DART framework that integrates: DAG workflow orchestration, capability and reputation-aware task allocation, dynamic behavior updates, multi-factor incentives, and smart contract accountability paired with IPFS storage for decentralized governance.
AI.result: Achieved 93.6% Pass@1 on GSM8K, built full-stack application in 142s with two agents, and in longitudinal trials: 93.33% mean task success rate, 0.9357 output quality, 99.3% output containment rate for malicious agents, and restored system success to 99.8%.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that coupling reputation, incentives, DAG-based coordination, and verifiable blockchain-enabled governance can support adaptive and accountable multi-agent collaboration, effectively addressing vulnerabilities in current LLM-based multi-agent systems.

title: SimTIO: A Simulation-Grounded Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Compositional Traffic Intervention Optimization
summary: Traffic analysts must translate diagnosed bottlenecks into executable interventions without allowing local improvements to degrade network-wide performance. This study presents SimTIO, a simulation-grounded multi-agent large language model framework for composing and selecting traffic interventions under explicit operational constraints. SimTIO first simulates an unmodified SUMO scenario to identify a baseline-frozen set of ten bottleneck edges. A grounded sampler then initializes signal-control, corridor-speed, and demand-preserving routing actions, while three specialist agents use measured simulation feedback to select one-parameter refinements from validator-confirmed mutation catalogs. Compatible actions are combined and re-simulated so that their interaction effects are measured rather than inferred. Final selection minimizes bottleneck time loss while constraining network-wide delay, neighboring-road spillover, throughput loss, and teleport events, with the unmodified scenario retained as a no-operation guard. Across 15 cases covering five U.S. urban networks, three synthetic-demand seeds, and 2,400 origin-destination trips per scenario, SimTIO reduced Top-10 bottleneck time loss by an average of 9.18 percent and network-wide delay by 2.78 percent. It found a feasible improving plan in 86.7 percent of cases, compared with 73.3 percent for grounded random search and 80.0 percent for a deterministic heuristic under the same seven-simulation budget, although the differences in Top-10 improvement were not statistically significant. These results support using LLMs as constrained, feedback-guided local search operators while reserving final decision authority for executable tools, microscopic simulation, and explicit safety constraints.

AI.tldr: SimTIO is a simulation-grounded multi-agent LLM framework that generates and selects traffic interventions to reduce bottlenecks while maintaining network-wide performance through iterative simulation feedback and explicit constraints.
AI.motivation: Traffic analysts need to translate diagnosed bottlenecks into effective interventions without causing network-wide degradation. There's a need for automated systems that can generate executable traffic control actions while respecting operational constraints.
AI.method: Multi-agent LLM framework using simulation feedback: 1) Simulates baseline SUMO scenario to identify top 10 bottlenecks, 2) Grounded sampler initializes signal control, speed, and routing actions, 3) Three specialist agents use simulation feedback to refine single-parameter changes, 4) Compatible actions are combined and re-simulated to measure interaction effects, 5) Final selection optimizes for bottleneck reduction while constraining network-wide delay, spillover, throughput loss, and teleport events.
AI.result: Across 15 cases in 5 US urban networks, SimTIO reduced Top-10 bottleneck time loss by 9.18% and network-wide delay by 2.78%. Found feasible improving plans in 86.7% of cases, outperforming random search (73.3%) and deterministic heuristic (80.0%) under same simulation budget.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can serve as effective constrained, feedback-guided local search operators for traffic intervention planning, but final decision authority should remain with executable tools, microscopic simulation, and explicit safety constraints.

title: Adaptive stabilization of a leaderless bearing-constrained formation with disturbances
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, preprint, submitted to a journal
summary: In this paper, we consider the problem of regulating and maintaining a target formation characterized by a set of bidirectional bearing constraints under disturbances. The agents in the formation are modeled by single integrators with bounded continuous disturbances of which the upper bound is unavailable for the control design. Due to the time-varying disturbances, the target formation is time-varying. We propose adaptive sliding mode control laws to uniformly globally asymptotically stabilizes the moving target formation and reject the matched disturbances. In addition, to alleviate chattering phenomena from sliding mode control, smooth adaptive control laws are then designed to guarantee uniform global boundedness of the desired formation. Finally, simulation results are given to support the analysis.

AI.tldr: Adaptive sliding mode and smooth control laws are proposed to regulate multi-agent formations with bidirectional bearing constraints under unknown bounded disturbances, achieving asymptotic stability while reducing chattering effects.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of maintaining target formations under unknown bounded disturbances. The key problems are: 1) agents are subject to continuous bounded disturbances with unknown upper bounds, 2) these disturbances make the target formation time-varying, and 3) standard sliding mode control causes undesirable chattering phenomena.
AI.method: The authors propose two main approaches: 1) Adaptive sliding mode control laws that achieve uniform global asymptotic stabilization of the moving target formation while rejecting matched disturbances, and 2) Smooth adaptive control laws designed specifically to alleviate chattering phenomena from sliding mode control, ensuring uniform global boundedness of the desired formation.
AI.result: The proposed adaptive sliding mode control achieves uniform global asymptotic stability of the target formation despite unknown bounded disturbances. The smooth adaptive control version provides uniform global boundedness while successfully reducing chattering effects. Simulation results validate the theoretical analysis.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully addresses formation control under unknown bounded disturbances by developing both adaptive sliding mode and smooth adaptive control approaches that guarantee stability while mitigating practical implementation issues like chattering.

title: Beyond Right and Wrong: Evaluating Second-order Social Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Previous AI alignment efforts have focused primarily on first-order social norms -- teaching models what is socially acceptable or unacceptable (e.g., `do not steal'). However, social intelligence depends not only on norm recognition, but also on anticipating who will enforce it and how (e.g., public shame or even imprisonment). These second-order expectations, known as metanorms, govern how people respond when social rules are broken. We introduce a novel framework for evaluating metanorm reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs) along two dimensions: emotional appraisal and behavioral response, and propose new classification tasks, namely, predicting self-regulation in violators, and other-regulation in observers. We release a multi-perspective dataset, NormReact, of 450 norm violation scenarios, hand-annotated for emotions and behavioral responses across norm violators' gender and observers' social closeness. Current LLMs portray a harsher social world: across six models, they overpredict negative sanctions where humans would expect inaction, and alignment with human judgments deteriorates as social distance increases. These findings suggest that AI systems in norm-sensitive domains from conflict mediation to policy simulation, may risk producing a distorted picture of social regulation: one that over-represents punishment and under-represents the tolerance, restraint, and relational calibration that characterize actual norm enforcement in real world.

AI.tldr: LLMs show poor metanorm reasoning, overpredicting negative sanctions and failing to understand social dynamics in norm enforcement.
AI.motivation: Current AI alignment focuses only on first-order social norms (what is acceptable/unacceptable), but real social intelligence requires understanding second-order expectations (metanorms) about who enforces norms and how, which is crucial for applications in norm-sensitive domains.
AI.method: Introduces a framework evaluating metanorm reasoning along emotional appraisal and behavioral response dimensions. Creates NormReact dataset with 450 norm violation scenarios hand-annotated for emotions and behaviors across violator gender and observer social closeness. Tests six LLMs on predicting self-regulation (violator responses) and other-regulation (observer responses).
AI.result: LLMs portray a harsher social world than humans, consistently overpredicting negative sanctions where humans expect inaction. Alignment with human judgments deteriorates as social distance increases between observer and violator. Models fail to capture the relational calibration and tolerance seen in actual human norm enforcement.
AI.conclusion: AI systems in norm-sensitive domains risk producing distorted views of social regulation, over-representing punishment and under-representing the nuanced tolerance, restraint, and relational factors that characterize real-world norm enforcement. Current LLMs lack sophisticated metanorm reasoning.

title: AhaBench: Do Agents Learn from Prior Experience? A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Continual Learning
summary: Modern language agents are expected to operate over long horizons: they ask follow-up questions, reuse worked examples, handle tool feedback, and adapt to delayed consequences. Most evaluations still reset the agent after a prompt or score only the final state of one trajectory. AhaBench asks a more operational question: when a fixed model receives useful experience, does its later behavior improve under a related evaluation condition where the obvious support has been removed, changed, or delayed? The suite contains three components. Aha-Puzzle tests no-hint exploration after solved hidden-state puzzles; Aha-Euler turns Project-Euler-style mathematical ideas into generated taught/held-out tasks with exact validators; and Aha-Vending, an open-source implementation inspired by Vending-Bench, tests whether a simulated vending agent remains profitable while handling delayed feedback and operational incidents. AhaBench reports a three-part scorecard: Initial Score measures starting competence, Post-Experience Score measures the later empirical outcome, and Learning Lift is their difference. This decomposition is the main empirical message: models that use visible support well, models that reach high post-experience scores, and models that improve most during a run are not always the same. On the common eight-model panel, Claude Opus 4.6 leads aggregate Post-Experience Score at 64.3 and aggregate Learning Lift at +25.8, with Gemini 3.1 Pro close behind at 63.4. The component results explain the split: puzzle traces raise supported scores but often fail to become no-hint exploration behavior; Aha-Euler full teaching reaches 78.6-100.0% while answer-only transfer ranges from 0.0 to 73.9%; and Aha-Vending separates profitable incident handling from bankruptcy and no-order failure. We release benchmark tasks, rubrics, validators, simulator code, and interfaces for evaluating new agents.

AI.tldr: AhaBench is a benchmark suite that evaluates how language agents improve their performance after receiving useful experience, testing whether they can maintain or enhance capabilities when support is removed, changed, or delayed.
AI.motivation: Most language agent evaluations reset agents after each prompt or only score final states, failing to assess whether agents can learn from experience and maintain improved performance when obvious support is removed or conditions change. The benchmark aims to answer whether fixed models show behavioral improvement after receiving useful experience.
AI.method: The suite has three components: Aha-Puzzle tests no-hint exploration after solving hidden-state puzzles; Aha-Euler transforms mathematical concepts into taught/held-out tasks with exact validators; and Aha-Vending, inspired by Vending-Bench, tests simulated vending agents handling delayed feedback and operational incidents. It uses a three-part scorecard: Initial Score, Post-Experience Score, and Learning Lift (their difference).
AI.result: Claude Opus 4.6 leads with aggregate Post-Experience Score of 64.3 and Learning Lift of +25.8, followed closely by Gemini 3.1 Pro at 63.4. Key findings: puzzle traces raise supported scores but often don't translate to no-hint exploration; Aha-Euler full teaching achieves 78.6-100.0% while answer-only transfer ranges from 0.0 to 73.9%; Aha-Vending separates profitable incident handling from bankruptcy/no-order failure.
AI.conclusion: The main empirical message is that models that use visible support well, those that achieve high post-experience scores, and those that show greatest improvement during a run are not always the same. The benchmark reveals important distinctions in how language agents leverage experience across different challenge types, with full teaching generally outperforming answer-only transfer.

title: CAPMAS: Capability-Based Delegation of Privileges in Multi-Agent Systems
summary:
Agentic systems require secure and efficient delegation of privileges across multiple collaborating agents. Existing approaches fall into two categories. Some propagate user identities directly to agents, obscuring accountability and creating persistent over-privilege risks that are amplified by the non-deterministic behaviour of AI agents. Others rely on continuous synchronization with a central Identity and Access Management (IAM) provider, introducing additional latency and communication overhead.
  We present CAPMAS, a novel architecture for secure end-to-end query execution in multi-agent systems. CAPMAS newly combines a contrastive learning-based semantic scoping pipeline that maps natural-language queries to bounded privilege sets before execution with expressive Macaroon-based tokens that enable offline, tamper-evident delegation with monotonic privilege reduction across agents. By decoupling authentication and delegation enforcement from agent reasoning, CAPMAS enables practical agentic execution while enforcing strict least-privilege guarantees.
  By eliminating synchronous delegation exchanges with the IAM, CAPMAS yields 30 times faster delegation operations, 2 times less delegation-oriented latency and up to 3 times lower bandwidth usage than the OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693). Its semantic scoping pipeline achieves over 90% perfect privilege-bundle retrieval within 17 milliseconds on enterprise-scale API schemas containing over 3,100 endpoints, while reducing unnecessary privileges by 99.5% when compared to systems that propagate all the user's privileges to agents.

AI.tldr: CAPMAS is a secure architecture for multi-agent systems that combines semantic scoping with Macaroon-based tokens to enable efficient, offline privilege delegation with strict least-privilege enforcement.
AI.motivation: Current approaches for privilege delegation in agentic systems have significant flaws: identity propagation creates accountability and over-privilege risks, while continuous IAM synchronization introduces latency and overhead, especially problematic with AI agents' non-deterministic behavior.
AI.method: CAPMAS combines a contrastive learning-based semantic scoping pipeline that maps natural-language queries to bounded privilege sets, with expressive Macaroon-based tokens that enable offline, tamper-evident delegation with monotonic privilege reduction across agents. It decouples authentication/delegation enforcement from agent reasoning.
AI.result: CAPMAS achieves 30x faster delegation operations, 2x lower delegation latency, and up to 3x lower bandwidth than OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange. Its semantic scoping achieves over 90% perfect privilege-bundle retrieval within 17ms on large-scale API schemas while reducing unnecessary privileges by 99.5% compared to systems propagating all user privileges.
AI.conclusion: CAPMAS provides a practical solution for secure agentic execution with strict least-privilege guarantees, addressing key challenges in multi-agent privilege delegation through efficient offline delegation and precise semantic scoping.

title: CriticGen: Generation-Aware Evaluation as Actionable Feedback
summary: Current evaluation methods for large language models are coarse-grained and decoupled from generation, producing generic explanations that fail to provide actionable feedback for model improvement. We propose CriticGen, a fine-grained, generation-aware evaluation framework that turns evaluation into actionable control for answer improvement. CriticGen first generates sample-specific evaluation dimensions and scoring criteria under high-level categories such as subjective, objective, and self-derived constraints. These criteria then serve as a dynamic rubric for jointly producing a score, a reason, an executable refinement suggestion, and a refined answer. This rubric-conditioned refinement process enables models to diagnose flaws and perform targeted answer improvement. Experimental results show that fine-grained evaluation should be both instance-specific and actionable. CriticGen induces higher-quality rubrics, improving relevance/coverage from 3.33/4.03 to 3.97/4.24. CriticGen also achieves the best score correlations, with 0.9556 Pearson and 0.9560 Spearman, and raises the F1 of criterion-grounded reasons and executable suggestions from 0.6369/0.5994 to 0.7554/0.7900. Crucially, its feedback translates into reliable answer improvement, improving 73.17% of answers with a 93.28% non-degradation rate.

AI.tldr: CriticGen is a fine-grained evaluation framework that generates instance-specific evaluation rubrics to produce actionable feedback for improving LLM answers, outperforming coarse-grained methods.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation methods are coarse-grained and decoupled from generation, producing generic explanations that don't provide actionable feedback for model improvement.
AI.method: CriticGen first generates sample-specific evaluation dimensions and scoring criteria under categories like subjective, objective, and self-derived constraints. These criteria serve as a dynamic rubric for jointly producing scores, reasons, executable refinement suggestions, and refined answers.
AI.result: CriticGen improves rubric relevance/coverage from 3.33/4.03 to 3.97/4.24, achieves best score correlations (0.9556 Pearson, 0.9560 Spearman), raises F1 of criterion-grounded reasons/executable suggestions from 0.6369/0.5994 to 0.7554/0.7900, and improves 73.17% of answers with 93.28% non-degradation rate.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained evaluation should be both instance-specific and actionable, with CriticGen demonstrating that turning evaluation into actionable control enables models to diagnose flaws and perform targeted answer improvement effectively.

title: When Do Options Help? Policy Necrosis and Redundant Coverage in Option-Critic
summary: Option-critic learns options: sub-policies together with a learned rule for when each one hands control back. Its headline result is that performance improves as options are added. We explain that result, with theory and experiment. First, the termination rule option-critic learns by maximising return contributes nothing. When the termination test and the policy that picks options read the same values, the test fires at every step, so the learned rule is identical to always terminating. When that policy explores and the test does not, as in option-critic itself, the rule can block the exploration; there are instances where it suffers $Ω(T)$ regret while always terminating holds to $O(\log T)$. Forcing termination at every step leaves the option-count curve intact. Second, the policy inside an option barely explores at all, so a state locks onto the first action that looked good and never updates again. We name this policy necrosis, give a state-level test for it, and find three fifths of states necrotic in a typical option. Restoring exploration repairs those states, and one option then solves the task. Third, extra options improve no option; what falls is the chance that all of them fail in the same state, from $59\\%$ to $4\\%$, and performance follows that joint quantity.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes Option-Critic learning framework, showing that its performance improvements come from reduced probability of all options failing simultaneously rather than from learned termination rules, and identifies policy necrosis as a major issue where states lock onto suboptimal actions.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand why Option-Critic shows performance improvements as more options are added, and to critically analyze the actual contributions of its learned termination rules versus other factors in the framework.
AI.method: The authors use theoretical analysis and experimental validation to examine Option-Critic. They analyze the learned termination rules, show they contribute nothing to performance, demonstrate policy necrosis where states lock onto initial actions, and measure the probability of all options failing in the same state across different option counts.
AI.result: Three key findings: 1) Learned termination rules are identical to always terminating when policies and termination tests read the same values, and can block exploration causing Ω(T) regret vs O(log T) for always-terminating. 2) Policy necrosis occurs where 3/5 of states in a typical option lock onto initial good-looking actions and never update. 3) Performance improvements come from reduced probability (59% to 4%) of all options failing in same state with more options, not from better individual options.
AI.conclusion: Option-Critic's performance improvements stem from statistical coverage (reducing chance all options fail) rather than from meaningful learned termination rules or improved individual options. The framework suffers from policy necrosis that prevents exploration within options, suggesting the need for exploration restoration mechanisms.

title: Certifying cooperation: a novel approach to cooperative multi-agent task generation
summary: A shared reward gives agents a common objective, but leaves open when, how and even whether they must cooperate to succeed. We address these questions in the Laser Learning Environment, a multi-agent path-finding environment where cooperation materializes as one agent blocking a laser to let a teammate pass safely. We represent these interactions through temporal cooperation graphs whose timed edges connect helpers to beneficiaries, define six cooperation profiles as overlapping graph predicates, and prove that every cooperative trajectory satisfies at least one. By encoding the environment dynamics and profile predicates as propositional formulae, we distinguish tasks that admit}a profile in some winning trajectory from those that require it in every winning trajectory within a specified horizon. Used as filters, these queries turn a random layout sampler into a generator of tasks with certified cooperation requirements. Experiments with five multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms show that training diversity improves joint success on unseen tasks when cooperation-free solutions exist. When cooperation is required, greater diversity improves individual-agent exits, but joint success remains near zero. Across five profile-certified pools, final exit rates averaged over algorithms separate the pools into four statistically distinguishable levels but this ordering primarily reflects partial completion: policies collect rewards for individual exits but rarely exhibit the profile required for joint success. Our framework exposes this gap between rewarded partial completion and realized cooperation by certifying what cooperation successful completion requires and using temporal cooperation graphs to reveal what policies exhibit.

AI.tldr: A framework using temporal cooperation graphs to analyze and certify cooperation requirements in multi-agent tasks, revealing gaps between partial rewards and true cooperation in reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Shared rewards in multi-agent systems define common objectives but don't specify when, how, or whether cooperation is actually required for success. The paper aims to address these questions by developing methods to analyze and certify cooperation requirements.
AI.method: 1. Use Laser Learning Environment where cooperation involves blocking lasers for teammates. 2. Define temporal cooperation graphs with timed edges connecting helpers to beneficiaries. 3. Identify six cooperation profiles as overlapping graph predicates. 4. Encode environment dynamics and profile predicates as propositional formulae. 5. Distinguish tasks that admit a profile in some winning trajectory vs require it in all winning trajectories. 6. Use queries as filters to generate tasks with certified cooperation requirements.
AI.result: 1. Training diversity improves joint success when cooperation-free solutions exist. 2. When cooperation is required, diversity improves individual exits but joint success remains near zero. 3. Across five profile-certified pools, exit rates separate pools into four statistically distinguishable levels, but this primarily reflects partial completion rather than true cooperation.
AI.conclusion: The framework exposes gaps between rewarded partial completion and realized cooperation by certifying what cooperation successful completion requires and using temporal cooperation graphs to reveal what policies actually exhibit. Policies tend to collect rewards for individual exits without achieving the cooperation needed for joint success.

title: When Does Memory Help? A Cost-Aware Evaluation of Long-Term Memory in Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Long-term memory for LLM agents is evaluated today by conversational recall benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval), which measure question answering over dialogue history, not whether remembered facts change what a tool-using agent does. We present MERIT (Memory Evaluation for Realistic Instrumented Tasks), a benchmark and harness that measures the marginal utility of memory for task-executing agents under explicit cost accounting. MERIT provides episodic tool-use tasks in three domains whose dependence on earlier-episode facts is verified by an automated leak check; a difficulty ladder ending in updated-fact recall; controlled memory corruption; and full token and dollar metering of every memory operation. Across 23,440 scored episodes ($42.57), a two-generation pilot on gpt-4.1-mini and a preregistered 3-model x 3-seed grid (GPT-4.1, Claude Haiku 4.5; memory side held fixed), memory lifts dependent-task success from a leak-verified floor of 0.00 to 0.55-1.00. On updated facts, embedding retrieval collapses unpredictably (0.30-0.95 across models; max seed gap 0.45), and agents act on a correctly retrieved value only 55% of the time, while update-on-write stores (a structured fact store and, notably, LLM summarization) remain at 0.70-1.00; the hybrid is worse than the fact store alone. A latest-generation spot-check (Claude Sonnet 5, gated on a clean full-replay control) reproduces the pattern. Swapping a memory's implementation moves task success by up to 60 points, and full replay is never economical: the best condition per domain delivers 2.7-3.9x its marginal utility per dollar. We release the benchmark, harness, and all traces.

AI.tldr: MERIT is a new benchmark for evaluating long-term memory in LLM agents that measures actual task performance improvement with cost accounting, rather than just conversational recall.
AI.motivation: Existing memory benchmarks only test conversational recall in dialogues, not whether remembered facts actually change what tool-using agents do in task execution. There's need for realistic evaluation with explicit cost accounting.
AI.method: Created MERIT benchmark with episodic tool-use tasks across three domains, featuring: automated leak checks to verify task dependence on earlier-episode facts; difficulty ladder ending in updated-fact recall; controlled memory corruption; and full token/dollar metering of all memory operations.
AI.result: Memory improved dependent-task success from 0.00 to 0.55-1.00. Embedding retrieval collapsed unpredictably on updated facts (0.30-0.95 across models), while update-on-write stores remained at 0.70-1.00. Swapping memory implementation moved task success by up to 60 points, and full replay was never economical - best condition delivered 2.7-3.9x marginal utility per dollar.
AI.conclusion: Memory implementation choice dramatically affects agent task performance and cost efficiency. Update-on-write memory stores outperform embedding retrieval for fact updates, and careful memory design is crucial for practical agent deployment.

title: Multi-granularity Adaptive Hypergraph Representation Learning via Granular-ball
summary: Hypergraph representation learning aims to capture high-order information in graphs by constructing hyperedges that simultaneously connect multiple nodes. These hyperedges adapt to the graph's topological features, facilitating the extraction of high-order relationships at multiple granularities. Most prior work relies on predefined definitions to generate hyperedges, overlooking the diversity in graph topological structures and the multi-granularity characteristics of hyperedges. As a result, this limits their ability to effectively and adaptively discover high-order relationships and efficiently process complex structural information. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework called \underline{M}ulti-\underline{G}ranularity \underline{H}ypergraph \underline{R}epresentation \underline{L}earning (MGHRL). MGHRL introduces an Adaptive Granular Hypergraph Generation strategy, which generates hyperedges at multiple levels of granularity through the adaptive splitting of granular-ball, effectively capturing high-order relationships based on the graph's topological structure. Additionally, we propose a Multi-Granularity Hypergraph Network with multiple sub-networks, capturing features from hyperedges at different granularities and integrating them via hierarchical reversible connections. Experimental results show that MGHRL significantly outperforms baseline models on benchmark datasets.

AI.tldr: MGHRL introduces a multi-granularity hypergraph learning framework with adaptive hyperedge generation and hierarchical networks to capture high-order relationships in graphs.
AI.motivation: Most existing hypergraph representation learning methods rely on predefined hyperedge definitions, which overlook the diversity in graph topological structures and the multi-granularity characteristics of hyperedges. This limits their ability to effectively and adaptively discover high-order relationships and efficiently process complex structural information.
AI.method: Proposes MGHRL framework with two key components: 1) Adaptive Granular Hypergraph Generation strategy that generates hyperedges at multiple levels of granularity through adaptive splitting of granular-ball, and 2) Multi-Granularity Hypergraph Network with multiple sub-networks that capture features from hyperedges at different granularities and integrate them via hierarchical reversible connections.
AI.result: Experimental results show that MGHRL significantly outperforms baseline models on benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MGHRL framework successfully addresses the limitations of prior hypergraph learning methods by enabling adaptive, multi-granularity representation learning that effectively captures high-order relationships based on graph topological structures.

title: Audit Without Verification: When LLM Accountability Layers Relay Rather Than Check
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures. Pre-registration: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/GBR3V. Code: https://github.com/Polpii/FaultLine
summary:
Multi-agent LLM pipelines increasingly span organisational boundaries; when a fault surfaces, someone must determine where it entered. The artifact available is rarely a full execution trace: it is the reports each agent filed, and a filed report can state a conclusion alongside its observations. Using a pre-registered, institutionally partitioned pipeline of six agents with process-level information boundaries, balanced defect injection and matched clean twins (345,600 requests per chain model, two models), we first report that our pre-registered hypothesis -- that collective responsibility framing degrades escalation with chain length -- is not supported.
  The layer nevertheless fails asymmetrically. It originates almost nothing: zero allegations across 7,996 clean episodes where every agent stayed silent. It filters upstream error poorly, naming an innocent party in 34.4% and 62.6% of clean episodes where an agent raised a false alarm. Conditional on no agent proposing the true origin (59.5% of episodes on one chain model), an auditor reading the reports recovers it in 4.1% of cases -- below a uniform guess (20%) and the best fixed-link accuser (31.0%) -- while reaching 60.3% from the raw documentation of the same episodes.
  Deleting one clause, the field carrying the agents' own conclusion, isolates the cause at constant observations: accuracy rises to 45.2% (+41.2 pp, 95% CI +35.3 to +46.9) and adherence collapses from 94.4% to 3.4%; where the suggestion was correct the same deletion instead costs accuracy, 70.5% to 55.7%. The harm replicates on two frontier auditors in four conditions out of four (+8.5 to +39.0 pp) and in a second domain (+47.7 and +61.1 pp), where the cost disappears. The net effect is governed by upstream reliability together with both conditional magnitudes. An accountability layer needs evidence sufficiently independent of the conclusions it verifies.

AI.tldr: When multi-agent LLM pipelines span organizations and faults occur, auditors must identify fault origins using agents' reports. The study finds that auditors overly rely on agents' own conclusions rather than their observations, harming fault attribution accuracy.
AI.motivation: As multi-agent LLM systems cross organizational boundaries, fault diagnosis becomes challenging. Auditors typically have only agents' reports (containing both observations and conclusions) rather than full execution traces. There's a need to understand how accountability mechanisms work in such partitioned systems and whether collective responsibility framing affects fault escalation.
AI.method: Used a pre-registered, institutionally partitioned pipeline of six agents with process-level information boundaries. Employed balanced defect injection and matched clean twins (345,600 requests per chain model across two models). Tested pre-registered hypothesis about collective responsibility framing. Then analyzed performance of accountability layer in identifying fault origins, examining both raw documentation and agents' conclusions.
AI.result: Collective responsibility framing hypothesis was not supported. Accountability layer performed poorly: originated almost nothing (zero allegations across 7,996 clean episodes), filtered upstream error poorly (34.4%-62.6% false accusations). When no agent identified true origin (59.5% of episodes), auditor recovered it in only 4.1% of cases vs 20% uniform guess. Removing agents' conclusions from reports increased accuracy by +41.2 percentage points while collapsing adherence from 94.4% to 3.4%. This pattern replicated across different auditors and domains.
AI.conclusion: Accountability layers in multi-agent systems need evidence sufficiently independent of the conclusions they verify. Auditors overweight agents' conclusions rather than relying on observations, leading to poor fault attribution. The net performance depends on upstream reliability and the magnitude of both beneficial and harmful effects of agents' conclusions.

title: AutoFyn Technical Report: Non-Parametric Expert Iteration for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: We introduce AutoFyn, an agent harness inspired by the Expert Iteration algorithm, adapting a frozen model across many rounds by updating persistent state from verified reward signals rather than model weights. Each round begins from a fresh model session, and durable information is reintroduced only through explicit interfaces such as persistent memory files, reports, and repository state. Within a round, an orchestrator explores, plans and builds many alternative approaches with specialized agents, while a task-grounded verifier verifies the work and supplies an objective reward for measuring progress. This reward is distilled back into the persistent state, which updates the effective policy for the next round. In this technical report, we formalize this loop and describe its persistent state and verification interfaces. We then demonstrate its use in three domains, namely olympiad mathematics, data science, and cybersecurity. On the six fresh problems of the 2026 International Mathematical Olympiad, every model with room to improve scores higher under AutoFyn than in its provider's own coding agent. AutoFyn also built the top-ranked agent on the Spider 2.0 dbt benchmark, and has produced $16$ maintainer-confirmed vulnerability advisories in Next.js, MetaMask, pnpm, Warp, LiteLLM, Langflow, and Open WebUI.

AI.tldr: AutoFyn is an Expert Iteration-inspired agent system that adapts frozen models through persistent state updates from verified rewards, achieving strong performance on mathematical, data science, and cybersecurity tasks.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to create an agent system that can effectively adapt and improve over multiple rounds of problem-solving without modifying the underlying model weights, enabling better utilization of frozen language models.
AI.method: AutoFyn implements an Expert Iteration-inspired loop where each round starts fresh with a frozen model, uses an orchestrator to explore multiple approaches with specialized agents, verifies work with a task-grounded verifier, and distills rewards into persistent state (memory files, reports, repository state) that updates the effective policy for subsequent rounds.
AI.result: AutoFyn outperformed providers' own coding agents on 2026 IMO problems, achieved top rank on Spider 2.0 dbt benchmark, and produced 16 confirmed vulnerability advisories in major open-source projects including Next.js, MetaMask, pnpm, Warp, LiteLLM, Langflow, and Open WebUI.
AI.conclusion: The AutoFyn framework demonstrates that persistent state adaptation through verified reward signals provides an effective way to enhance frozen model performance across diverse domains including mathematics, data science, and cybersecurity.

title: Capsule Lens: Locating and Tracking Concept Geometry in Model Representations
summary: Understanding how concepts are encoded in the internal representations of machine learning models is a central problem in mechanistic interpretability, essential both for the science of deep learning and for the trustworthy deployment of increasingly capable models. Existing approaches to interpret model representations mainly map representations onto more interpretable spaces and do not directly characterize how concepts occupy representation space; various hypotheses have been proposed, but often lack of rigorous validation and largely focus on static representations. In this work, we introduce Capsule Lens, a framework that matches the region a concept occupies with a simple, trackable geometric form, a capsule, defined by several interpretable parameters, fitted in closed form to each concept's geometry and validated on held-out samples. We apply Capsule Lens in two major settings: static and dynamic representations. On static representations, we demonstrate how to locate concept geometry across various models, and how the span and norm curves uncover important geometric characteristics. On dynamic representations, we present three case studies tracking representation drifts induced by distinct training settings, CLIP pretraining, RL post-training on visual question answering, and RL post-training on mathematical reasoning. These analyses reveal qualitatively different geometric dynamics, ranging from broad network-wide restructuring in CLIP pretraining to localized and concept-specific changes in RL post-training. Our results include findings aligned with existing literature as well as novel observations. We believe Capsule Lens stands as a promising tool for locating, analyzing, and tracking concept geometry in both static and dynamic representations.

AI.tldr: Capsule Lens is a framework that identifies concept geometry in ML models using interpretable capsule parameters, enabling analysis of both static representations and dynamic representation drifts during training.
AI.motivation: Existing interpretability methods mainly map representations to interpretable spaces but don't directly characterize how concepts occupy representation space. Current approaches lack rigorous validation and focus mostly on static representations, leaving a gap in understanding concept geometry and its dynamics.
AI.method: Capsule Lens matches concept regions with simple geometric forms called capsules, defined by interpretable parameters (span, norm curves, etc.). These capsules are fitted in closed form to each concept's geometry and validated on held-out samples.
AI.result: Applied to static representations: located concept geometry across models and uncovered important geometric characteristics via span and norm curves. Applied to dynamic representations: tracked representation drifts in three settings - CLIP pretraining (broad network-wide restructuring), RL post-training on visual QA (localized changes), and RL post-training on mathematical reasoning (concept-specific changes).
AI.conclusion: Capsule Lens is a promising tool for locating, analyzing, and tracking concept geometry in both static and dynamic representations, revealing qualitatively different geometric dynamics across training settings and providing novel observations alongside confirming existing literature.

title: Scaling Multi-Agent Systems with Prospect-State Propagation
summary: Current LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) periodically compress intermediate states to reduce inference-time token consumption, thereby attempting to incorporate more agents. However, naive scaling strategies face challenges. For example, in economic simulations, large-scale MAS typically discard semantically rich economic states, i.e., agent behavioral trajectories, which are key drivers of macroeconomic fluctuations. In this paper, we reveal a phenomenon in which agent heterogeneity gradually decreases during simulation, and propose Prospect-State Propagation for Multi-Agent Systems (PspMAS). Inspired by prospect theory, PspMAS decouples each agent's micro state into a compact Prospect State and an expressive Semantic State. The former records psychological traces through a lightweight, parallelizable propagator and continuously injects heterogeneity into the system. The latter leverages the strong perception, reasoning, planning, and decision-making abilities of LLMs. These two components work complementarily, providing a scalable LLM-based multi-agent simulation solution.

AI.tldr: Proposes PspMAS, a method using prospect theory to maintain agent heterogeneity in large-scale LLM-based multi-agent systems by decoupling micro states into Prospect and Semantic components.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based multi-agent systems discard semantically rich states (like economic behavioral trajectories) during state compression, losing key drivers of system dynamics like macroeconomic fluctuations. There's also a problem where agent heterogeneity decreases during simulation, limiting scalability and realism.
AI.method: PspMAS decouples each agent's micro state into: 1) Compact Prospect State - records psychological traces via lightweight, parallelizable propagator that continuously injects heterogeneity; 2) Expressive Semantic State - leverages LLMs' perception, reasoning, planning, and decision-making capabilities. Inspired by prospect theory, the two components work complementarily.
AI.result: The proposed approach provides a scalable solution for LLM-based multi-agent simulations by maintaining agent heterogeneity throughout the simulation while managing token consumption efficiently.
AI.conclusion: PspMAS addresses the limitation of decreasing agent heterogeneity in current MAS by separating psychological and semantic states, enabling more realistic and scalable multi-agent simulations that preserve the rich dynamics needed for applications like economic modeling.

title: Damage-Aware Bandit Pruning for Vision and Language Transformers
summary: Structured post-training pruning of transformers requires selecting complete functional units whose suppression causes limited degradation. We formulate structured-unit selection for language and vision transformers as a damage-aware multi-armed bandit problem under a fixed candidate-evaluation budget. Attention heads and MLP channel groups are temporarily masked on calibration batches. Paired damage is the masked loss minus the base loss on the same batch, reducing batch-to-batch variation. A smooth bounded reward drives either a UCB-style policy or fractional-Beta Thompson Sampling, and the final mask is constructed sequentially by adding one unit at each step. The selected units are functionally zeroed in the original dense checkpoint; therefore, the reported parameter effects represent effective structural suppression rather than physical compression or measured speedup. Experiments on WikiText-2, LAMBADA, and Imagenette cover GPT-2, OPT, Pythia, Qwen2.5, SmolLM2, ViT-B/16, DeiT-Tiny, and Swin-Tiny, with comparisons against random, magnitude, static-saliency, and budgeted-greedy selection. Across five seeds, the bandit methods usually reduce degradation relative to budgeted greedy in the paired language-model comparisons. Of 28 comparisons highlighted in the paper, 23 bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero and 11 paired tests have p < 0.05; six have q < 0.05 after Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the full family of 116 dataset-wise tests. Matched-evaluation results for ViT-B/16 and Swin-Tiny indicate that their gains are not explained solely by a larger candidate-evaluation budget.

AI.tldr: A multi-armed bandit approach for structured pruning of transformers that selects attention heads and MLP channel groups by temporarily masking them on calibration batches and measuring damage to loss.
AI.motivation: Structured post-training pruning of transformers requires selecting complete functional units (like attention heads and MLP channel groups) whose suppression causes minimal degradation. Existing methods may not optimally handle the selection process under limited evaluation budgets.
AI.method: Formulates structured-unit selection as a damage-aware multi-armed bandit problem with fixed candidate-evaluation budget. Temporarily masks attention heads and MLP channel groups on calibration batches, measures paired damage (masked loss minus base loss), uses smooth bounded reward to drive either UCB-style policy or fractional-Beta Thompson Sampling, and constructs final mask sequentially by adding one unit at each step.
AI.result: Experiments on WikiText-2, LAMBADA, and Imagenette with various transformer models show bandit methods usually reduce degradation relative to budgeted greedy selection. Of 28 comparisons, 23 bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero and 11 paired tests have p < 0.05 (6 have q < 0.05 after correction). Gains are not explained solely by larger evaluation budgets.
AI.conclusion: The damage-aware multi-armed bandit formulation provides an effective approach for structured post-training pruning of transformers, outperforming alternative selection methods while maintaining functional integrity through structural suppression rather than physical compression.

title: HB-PVI: A Hierarchical Bayesian Personalization and Value-of-Information Framework for Complex Activity Recognition
comment: Manuscript submitted to IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
summary: Personalization can improve activity-recognition performance, but participant-specific gains are heterogeneous, and every additional calibration label has an acquisition cost. This study presents HB-PVI, a hierarchical Bayesian personalization and value-of-information framework jointly modeling participant heterogeneity, the benefit and harm of four personalization mechanisms, and the economic value of an additional label, for the 47-participant MUSIC-CAR complex-activity cohort. A leakage-safe, leave-one-participant-out evaluation combines a sequential-Monte-Carlo participant-effect updater with a Student-$t$ hierarchical gain model and a one-step expected-value-of-sample-information (EVSI) stopping rule. Adapter personalization produced small positive mean F1 gains, growing from 0.00099 at one label to 0.00198 at ten, while adapter-plus-head and prototype-residual personalization were negative on average. Under the primary practical-benefit threshold ($Δ_{\min}=0.01$) and cost setting, one-step EVSI was zero at every decision state, so the policy purchased no labels and retained population inference for all 47 participants, matching always-stop exactly (region-of-practical-equivalence probability $=1$). Relative to fixed ten-shot adapter personalization, this reduced labeling by 100\% while keeping the posterior mean F1 loss at 0.00217 (95\% credible interval, 0.00048 to 0.00389), with posterior probability 0.9992 of remaining below the 0.005 tolerance. HB-PVI was utility-optimal in 199 of 216 cost-threshold settings and in every setting at or above the primary label cost. These results argue for a population-first deployment policy whenever personalization gains are small relative to labeling, computation, and harm costs, and show that value-of-information reasoning, not raw predictive accuracy, should drive personalization decisions in health-sensing applications.

AI.tldr: HB-PVI framework evaluates when activity-recognition personalization is economically worthwhile using hierarchical Bayesian modeling and value-of-information analysis, finding population inference often preferable to personalized models when gains are small relative to costs.
AI.motivation: Personalization can improve activity-recognition performance but has heterogeneous benefits across participants and incurs acquisition costs for calibration labels. The study aims to determine when personalization is economically justified versus using population inference.
AI.method: HB-PVI combines hierarchical Bayesian modeling of participant heterogeneity with value-of-information analysis. Uses sequential-Monte-Carlo participant-effect updater, Student-t hierarchical gain model, and one-step expected-value-of-sample-information stopping rule with leakage-safe leave-one-participant-out evaluation on 47-participant MUSIC-CAR dataset.
AI.result: Adapter personalization showed small positive mean F1 gains (0.00099-0.00198 with 1-10 labels), while adapter-plus-head and prototype-residual personalization were negative on average. EVSI was zero at all decision states, recommending no label purchases and population inference for all participants, matching always-stop policy. This reduced labeling by 100% versus fixed ten-shot personalization while keeping F1 loss minimal.
AI.conclusion: Population-first deployment policies are recommended when personalization gains are small relative to labeling, computation, and harm costs. Value-of-information reasoning, not raw predictive accuracy, should drive personalization decisions in health-sensing applications.

title: Rank Without an Oracle: Deviation-Aware Interaction-Rank Selection from Offline Multi-Agent Logs
summary: Offline multi-agent payoff models are estimated under a logging distribution but used on distributions induced by learned solutions and unilateral deviations. Standard held-out loss can therefore favor an interaction class that predicts logged play well while distorting strategic incentives. We introduce Selective Interaction-Rank Validation (SIRV) for finite games with known logging distributions. A training split fits nested payoff models and constructs a common union of all candidate deployment and unilateral-replacement distributions; an independent calibration split evaluates every candidate on this same union. SIRV returns the smallest rank whose simultaneous upper worst-target risk is within tolerance of the best upper score, and abstains when a declared target is unsupported or too imprecisely estimated. A common coverage event yields a finite-candidate target-risk bound and a candidate-specific coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) gap certificate. We also isolate an exact two-point off-support non-identifiability result. In a controlled factorial study with 2,048 independent games per family, empirical-Bernstein bounds reduce the median CCE-gap certificate by 42.5% relative to Hoeffding bounds on common returns, with a 1.36-point reduction in supported return. Under paired rank misspecification and in a separately generated congestion family, the SIRV-EB fallback rule lowers mean true candidate-selection CCE regret relative to ID-Mean, while retaining game-level losses. Across 384 games at $N=3,5,8$, ID-Mean-relative mean CCE-regret effects stay positive while certified return falls sharply under weak coverage. These results separate certifiable model selection from universal strategic improvement.

AI.tldr: SIRV method validates offline multi-agent payoff models to ensure they maintain strategic incentives when deployed, using selective interaction-rank validation with worst-target risk bounds and CCE gap certificates.
AI.motivation: Offline multi-agent payoff models are trained on logging distributions but deployed on different distributions induced by learned solutions and unilateral deviations. Standard held-out loss may predict logged play well but distort strategic incentives, failing to maintain proper strategic behavior in deployment.
AI.method: Selective Interaction-Rank Validation (SIRV) for finite games with known logging distributions. Uses training split to fit nested payoff models and construct union of all candidate deployment distributions; independent calibration split evaluates candidates on same union. Returns smallest rank with upper worst-target risk within tolerance, abstains when target unsupported or poorly estimated. Provides coverage event for target-risk bounds and CCE gap certificates.
AI.result: Empirical-Bernstein bounds reduce median CCE-gap certificate by 42.5% vs Hoeffding bounds. SIRV-EB lowers mean true candidate-selection CCE regret relative to ID-Mean while retaining game-level losses. Positive CCE-regret effects across 384 games at N=3,5,8 despite falling certified return under weak coverage. Separates certifiable model selection from universal strategic improvement.
AI.conclusion: SIRV provides principled validation for offline multi-agent payoff models, ensuring strategic incentives are preserved through finite-candidate target-risk bounds and CCE gap certificates. The approach successfully separates reliable model selection from strategic performance improvement while handling the distribution shift between logging and deployment.

title: Compiling VGDL into Causal Models
comment: To be published at IEEE Conference on Games 2026
summary: Reinforcement learning and large language models often struggle to accurately capture the causal mechanics of game environments. Standard reinforcement learning agents tend to rely on spurious correlations, while large language models are prone to hallucinating game rules. Although causal reinforcement learning improves interpretability, there is currently no formal methodology to map complex game mechanics directly into causal models. To address this, we propose a deterministic framework that compiles games specified in the Video Game Description Language into Dynamic Structural Causal Models. Rather than inferring causal structures from gameplay traces or noisy large language models' outputs, our methodology directly translates game components, including sprite dynamics, interaction rules, and termination conditions, into explicit structural equations. Each game tick represents a causal transition from state variables at time $t$ to $t+1$. By establishing this grounded mapping, the approach guarantees absolute causal fidelity to the ground-truth game mechanics. The resulting models offer transparent causal pathways that support counterfactual reasoning, causal reinforcement learning agent training, and procedural content validation. This framework provides a principled bridge between symbolic game descriptions and causally grounded game AI.

AI.tldr: A deterministic framework that automatically compiles video game specifications into Dynamic Structural Causal Models, ensuring causal fidelity to ground-truth game mechanics for better interpretability and agent training.
AI.motivation: Current reinforcement learning agents rely on spurious correlations, large language models hallucinate game rules, and there's no formal methodology to directly map complex game mechanics into causal models from game specifications.
AI.method: Proposes a deterministic framework that compiles games specified in Video Game Description Language into Dynamic Structural Causal Models, directly translating game components (sprite dynamics, interaction rules, termination conditions) into explicit structural equations with each game tick representing a causal transition.
AI.result: The approach guarantees absolute causal fidelity to ground-truth game mechanics and produces transparent causal pathways that support counterfactual reasoning, causal reinforcement learning agent training, and procedural content validation.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a principled bridge between symbolic game descriptions and causally grounded game AI, offering a formal methodology for deterministic causal modeling of game environments.

title: Endogenous Exploration in Reinforcement Learning with Intrinsic Curiosity
summary: We propose a reinforcement learning framework in which exploration is driven by intrinsic curiosity, designed for scenarios where environments are non-stationary and rewards are sparse, delayed, uninformative, or absent. In our model, action selection is guided by a combination of external rewards and an epistemic motivation mechanism that biases the agent toward structured exploratory directions. The central hypothesis is that effective exploration emerges at intermediate levels of incoherence, while performance degrades under both overly rigid and overly disordered dynamics. To test this idea, we implement the framework on top of a Liquid State Machine (LSM) substrate and evaluate it on two standard benchmarks: the discrete-action LunarLanderv2 and the continuous-control BipedalWalkerv3. The proposed method achieves competitive performance on both tasks relative to established deep RL algorithms, including Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Intrinsic Curiosity Module (ICM). We further show that the curiosity window is not recovered in Active Inference agents under the same analysis, suggesting that the proposed dynamics capture a distinct exploration regime

AI.tldr: A reinforcement learning framework uses intrinsic curiosity for exploration in sparse/non-stationary environments, implemented on a Liquid State Machine and achieving competitive performance on benchmark tasks against PPO and ICM.
AI.motivation: Addressing the challenge of reinforcement learning in environments with non-stationary dynamics and sparse, delayed, uninformative, or absent rewards, where effective exploration strategies are crucial but difficult to design.
AI.method: Proposes a reinforcement learning framework with intrinsic curiosity-driven exploration, using an epistemic motivation mechanism that biases agents toward structured exploratory directions. The method is implemented on a Liquid State Machine (LSM) substrate and tested on LunarLanderv2 (discrete-action) and BipedalWalkerv3 (continuous-control) benchmarks.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves competitive performance relative to established deep RL algorithms including Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Intrinsic Curiosity Module (ICM). The curiosity window is not recovered in Active Inference agents under the same analysis, suggesting the framework captures a distinct exploration regime.
AI.conclusion: Effective exploration emerges at intermediate levels of incoherence, with performance degrading under both overly rigid and overly disordered dynamics. The framework successfully addresses exploration challenges in difficult RL environments through intrinsic curiosity mechanisms.

title: Reachability-Certified Subteam Decomposition for Locally Interacting Multi-Agent MDPs
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, including references and appendices
summary: Persistent communication limits force a multi-agent system to decide which agents may coordinate throughout a rollout. Current proximity alone is insufficient: separated agents may interact later, whereas a large pair reward may remain unreachable until it is heavily discounted. We introduce Reachability-Certified Subteam Decomposition (RCSD) for finite multi-agent Markov decision processes with factorized physical dynamics, finite-range ordered pair rewards, and almost-sure motion bounds. RCSD combines a speed-limit lower bound on pairwise contact time with a reward envelope to form a current-state affinity. For any capacity-valid persistent partition, the sum of cut affinities bounds the reward-deletion error of every unchanged stationary Markov state-feedback policy. A product of team-optimal policies for the resulting cut MDP incurs at most twice this certificate in regret against the centralized optimum. Both bounds are worst-case tight. On a controlled five-agent family, RCSD-Exact reduces aggregate normalized execution regret by 56.0%, 28.8%, and 25.3% relative to uniform, distance-only, and envelope-only partitions. A separate stochastic two-dimensional study finds no bound violation over 384 exact-partition and 1,440 restricted-controller evaluations. Exact four-agent evidence favors RCSD over uniform and distance-only grouping; raw evidence for current contact is borderline and envelope-only is unresolved. Across balanced 8-20-agent strata, controller-library utility is mixed: pointwise paired intervals favor RCSD over distance and current contact, include zero for uniform, and favor envelope-only and Value-MIP over RCSD. Partition construction remains subsecond in median up to 100 agents; this last result does not include affinity formation or MDP planning.

AI.tldr: RCSD is a method for decomposing multi-agent systems into subteams using reachability analysis to bound coordination loss, outperforming simpler partitioning approaches in regret reduction.
AI.motivation: Current proximity-based team decomposition is insufficient for multi-agent systems because agents separated now may need to interact later, and important pair rewards may become heavily discounted before being achievable. There's a need for methods that account for future interaction potential and reward envelopes.
AI.method: RCSD (Reachability-Certified Subteam Decomposition) combines speed-limit lower bounds on pairwise contact time with reward envelopes to compute current-state affinities. It certifies any persistent partition's coordination loss, then solves cut MDPs for each subteam, with the product of team-optimal policies incurring at most twice the certificate's regret.
AI.result: On a five-agent system, RCSD-Exact reduced aggregate normalized execution regret by 56.0%, 28.8%, and 25.3% relative to uniform, distance-only, and envelope-only partitions. Extensive evaluations found no bound violations, and RCSD performed better than simpler approaches in various agent configurations, with partition construction remaining subsecond up to 100 agents.
AI.conclusion: RCSD provides provable performance guarantees for multi-agent coordination under communication limits, significantly outperforming naive partitioning methods while maintaining computational efficiency. The method offers theoretical tightness and practical effectiveness across different agent scales.

title: ARC-Bench: Closed-Loop Replanning Masks Broken Action Ranking in Frozen JEPA World Models
summary: Reward-free latent world models plan by scoring candidate actions with distances in a frozen latent space: an action is preferred if its predicted future embedding lands closer to the goal embedding. This silently assumes that latent closeness is action-rankable, i.e., that ordering candidates by latent distance agrees with ordering them by true cost. We audit this assumption directly. We introduce ARC-Bench, a no-leak, fixed-candidate protocol that measures whether frozen JEPA-style objectives rank candidate actions correctly, and apply it to official released JEPA-WM checkpoints across navigation and manipulation-style control. The assumption fails, severely and structurally: on the official manipulation audits the top-scored candidate is almost always suboptimal, and the same inversion appears in the maze domains. A controlled visual-backbone extension shows that the defect persists when DINOv2 is replaced by video-pretrained V-JEPA 1 and V-JEPA 2 encoders at ViT-L/ViT-G scale. Provenance, undertraining, matched-budget backbone controls, and metric-circularity controls rule out trivial explanations. We then explain why this defect has stayed invisible: closed-loop replanning masks it. When we reduce the planner's replanning frequency, success collapses in both a navigation and a manipulation domain, and the episodes rescued by frequent replanning are enriched for severe first-plan ranking failures in the PointMaze first-plan diagnostic. Closed-loop success rates therefore systematically overstate the rankability of frozen latent representations. ARC-Bench supplies the measurement, and the masking mechanism the explanation, for methods that adapt, amortize, or replan around latent-space planners without directly auditing released JEPA-WM action rankability.

AI.tldr: ARC-Bench reveals that frozen JEPA-style world models fail to correctly rank candidate actions by distance in latent space, and closed-loop replanning masks this fundamental defect in latent-space planners.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a critical unexamined assumption in reward-free latent world models: that latent space closeness (distance) reliably ranks candidate actions according to their true cost. This assumption underlies many latent-space planning methods but has never been directly audited.
AI.method: The authors introduce ARC-Bench, a no-leakage, fixed-candidate protocol that measures whether frozen JEPA-style objectives correctly rank candidate actions. They apply it to official released JEPA-WM checkpoints across navigation and manipulation domains, with controlled experiments using different visual backbones (DINOv2, V-JEPA 1, V-JEPA 2) at different scales.
AI.result: The assumption fails severely and structurally: on official manipulation audits, top-scored candidates are almost always suboptimal, with the same inversion appearing in maze domains. The defect persists across different visual backbones and scales. Provenance and various controls rule out trivial explanations. The paper also reveals that closed-loop replanning masks this defect - when replanning frequency is reduced, success collapses in both navigation and manipulation domains.
AI.conclusion: Latent-space closeness is not action-rankable in current frozen JEPA-style world models, and closed-loop success rates systematically overstate their rankability. ARC-Bench provides the measurement tool to audit this fundamental issue, while the masking mechanism explains why it has remained invisible in previous work.

title: Robustness of LLM-Generated SystemVerilog Assertions to Semantics-Preserving RTL Transformations
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for automating SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) generation, yet most evaluations report correctness on a single syntactic representation of an input. Such point accuracy does not reveal whether a model's correct output is stable when the same RTL behavior is written differently. This paper presents a controlled metamorphic evaluation of LLM-based SVA generation under semantics-preserving RTL transformations. Starting from the VERT dataset, we construct a quality-filtered conditional-control pool and a stratified 40-program evaluation set containing 295 assignment behaviors. We evaluate two open code models, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite, with an identical evaluation prompt and greedy decoding. Three transformations are studied: operand reordering, deterministic identifier renaming, and redundant parenthesization. Beyond baseline and transformed accuracy, we measure conditional robustness, invariance failure, and any-flip rate, with 10,000-sample clustered bootstrap intervals at the RTL-program level. Across all six model-transformation conditions, 9.7%-27.0% of behaviors that were correct on the original RTL become incorrect after a semantics-preserving transformation. Aggregate accuracy can therefore hide substantial instability: under identifier renaming, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite improves from 53.9% to 63.7% accuracy while 19.5% of its originally correct behaviors fail. Manual review of 30 sampled correct-to-wrong transitions identifies dropped path predicates, branch-polarity errors, Boolean-structure corruption, and output-contract violations. The results show that point accuracy alone is insufficient for characterizing LLM reliability in assertion generation and motivate robustness-aware evaluation for AI-assisted hardware verification.

AI.tldr: LLM-based SystemVerilog Assertion generation shows significant instability under semantics-preserving RTL transformations, with 9.7%-27.0% of correct behaviors becoming incorrect after transformations, revealing that point accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating LLM reliability.
AI.motivation: Most evaluations of LLMs for SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) generation only report correctness on single syntactic representations, failing to reveal whether models produce stable outputs when the same RTL behavior is expressed differently. This creates a gap in understanding LLM robustness for practical hardware verification applications.
AI.method: Controlled metamorphic evaluation of LLM-based SVA generation using semantics-preserving RTL transformations. The study uses the VERT dataset, constructs quality-filtered conditional-control pool and stratified 40-program evaluation set (295 assignment behaviors). Evaluates two open code models (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite) with identical prompts and greedy decoding. Tests three transformations: operand reordering, deterministic identifier renaming, and redundant parenthesization. Measures multiple robustness metrics with 10,000-sample clustered bootstrap intervals at RTL-program level.
AI.result: Across all six model-transformation conditions, 9.7%-27.0% of behaviors that were correct on original RTL become incorrect after semantics-preserving transformations. Aggregate accuracy can hide substantial instability - for example, under identifier renaming, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite improves from 53.9% to 63.7% accuracy while 19.5% of its originally correct behaviors fail. Manual analysis identified specific failure patterns including dropped path predicates, branch-polarity errors, Boolean-structure corruption, and output-contract violations.
AI.conclusion: Point accuracy alone is insufficient for characterizing LLM reliability in assertion generation. The significant instability revealed by metamorphic testing motivates the need for robustness-aware evaluation methodologies in AI-assisted hardware verification tools.

title: Beyond Agent Harnesses: Cross-Substrate Authority for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Agentic systems persist model-visible memory while mutating workspaces, while a runtime, registry, or approval service may hold authority state outside both. Identical final files can then require opposite safe actions. We call this the cross-substrate authority gap: decision- relevant authorization information resides outside the planner-visible workspace or memory state. Across two controlled mini-benchmark families, three experiments compare planner-observation augmentation with an execution-time authority check using real Git lineage, durably recorded agent execution attempts, deterministic oracles, and two model routes. Experiment 1 is a 128-cell controlled evidence ablation: authority-blind candidate evidence obtains 0/32 final semantic success, while raw receipts and a typed relation both obtain 32/32. The missing authority fact accounts for the gain; typed packaging provides no observed planning-accuracy gain over equal raw information. Experiment 2 uses 96 planning calls: workspace-visible evidence yields 12/16 unsafe publication decisions, and planning with the typed relation remains unreliable (15/32 first actions correct; 11/32 invalid or absent).
