AI.result: Method is accurate and efficient, provides continuous and differentiable representation of cell response over macroscopic state and gradient, significantly expedites macroscale solutions compared to traditional FE² scheme.
AI.conclusion: Parametric Deep Ritz method offers effective computational framework for nonlinear homogenization problems, enabling faster macroscale solutions through differentiable neural network representations of cell response.

title: Time-Varying Data as Sheaves: an Invitation to Narratives
summary: Modern science and engineering increasingly rely on time-varying data, yet the mathematical tools used to model temporal phenomena are often developed within separate disciplines, obscuring common principles and limiting the transfer of ideas across fields. This chapter presents the theory of narratives, an abstract framework for time-varying objects of any mathematical kind that supports both theoretical investigations and applications. To illustrate this perspective, the chapter develops three vignettes, each illustrating a different research direction. The first addresses a general concern: What information loss can occur when switching between different representations of temporal data? The second concerns structural and algorithmic approaches: How can we systematically decompose time-varying data into simple pieces and obtain invariants describing its structural complexity? The third is an application to control theory: How can we model multi-agent systems with switching communication topologies? More important than any individual vignette, the central message of this invitation is that a suitable abstract perspective can organize and guide research across remarkably diverse mathematical and scientific domains.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the "theory of narratives" - an abstract framework for modeling time-varying data across disciplines, demonstrating its utility through three research vignettes: information loss between temporal representations, decomposition of time-varying data, and modeling multi-agent systems with switching topologies.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from the fragmentation of mathematical tools for temporal phenomena across different disciplines, which obscures common principles and limits idea transfer. There's a need for unified abstract frameworks that can organize research across diverse domains dealing with time-varying data.
AI.method: The method involves proposing the "theory of narratives" as an abstract framework for time-varying objects of any mathematical kind. The framework is illustrated through three concrete vignettes: 1) analyzing information loss between different temporal representations, 2) systematic decomposition of time-varying data into simple components with structural invariants, and 3) application to control theory for multi-agent systems with switching communication topologies.
AI.result: The paper presents a new theoretical framework (theory of narratives) that successfully organizes research across diverse mathematical and scientific domains dealing with temporal data. Through three illustrative vignettes, it demonstrates how this abstract perspective can address varied concerns from information theory to algorithmic decomposition to control applications.
AI.conclusion: The central conclusion is that abstract perspectives like the theory of narratives are valuable for unifying research across diverse fields dealing with temporal phenomena. The framework not only supports theoretical investigations but also enables practical applications, demonstrating that unified mathematical approaches can bridge disciplinary divides and advance multiple domains simultaneously.

title: Deep belief networks are exact
summary: We prove that every strictly positive probability distribution on \(\{-1,1\}^n\) is represented exactly by a sigmoid belief network with finite parameters. This answers a question of Sutskever and Hinton. The proof upgrades their probability-sharing approximation to exact representation using Brouwer's fixed-point theorem.

AI.tldr: Every positive probability distribution on binary vectors can be exactly represented by a finite-parameter sigmoid belief network, resolving Sutskever and Hinton's open question.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses an open question posed by Sutskever and Hinton about whether sigmoid belief networks with finite parameters can exactly represent all strictly positive probability distributions on binary vectors {-1,1}^n.
AI.method: The proof extends Sutskever and Hinton's probability-sharing approximation approach to exact representation using Brouwer's fixed-point theorem to establish the existence of finite parameters achieving exact representation.
AI.result: The paper proves that indeed every strictly positive probability distribution on {-1,1}^n can be exactly represented by a sigmoid belief network with finite parameters.
AI.conclusion: This resolves Sutskever and Hinton's open question affirmatively, demonstrating the complete representational power of finite-parameter sigmoid belief networks for positive binary distributions.

title: Online Learning with LLM Experts from Limited Feedback
summary: We study adaptive routing of prompts to large language model (LLM) experts to maximize response quality in an online setting with limited feedback. We formulate it as a bandit problem with $K$ actions that represent experts and $d$ features that encode prompts, over a horizon of $T$ rounds. We propose algorithms that strategically select and observe rewards to minimize regret. In the full-information setting, we achieve a regret of $\tilde{O}(d T / \sqrt{m})$, while in the bandit setting we achieve $\tilde{O}(d T \sqrt{K / m})$, where $m \ll T$ is a budget on feedback. Our experiments show that we efficiently learn high-quality routing strategies across diverse LLMs from limited feedback.

AI.tldr: Online adaptive routing of prompts to LLM experts formulated as a bandit problem with limited feedback budget, achieving sublinear regret bounds in both full-information and bandit settings.
AI.motivation: To maximize response quality when routing prompts to large language model experts in an online setting with limited feedback. Addresses the practical challenge of efficiently learning optimal routing strategies when only partial feedback can be obtained due to cost constraints.
AI.method: Formulate prompt routing as a bandit problem with K experts and d prompt features. Propose algorithms that strategically select experts and observe rewards to minimize regret. Two settings: full-information (with limited observations) and bandit feedback. Use a feedback budget m that's much smaller than total rounds T.
AI.result: Achieve regret bounds of Õ(dT/√m) in full-information setting and Õ(dT√(K/m)) in bandit setting. Experimental results show efficient learning of high-quality routing strategies across diverse LLMs from limited feedback.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully addresses the challenge of learning optimal routing strategies to LLM experts under feedback constraints, providing both theoretical guarantees and practical effectiveness for real-world applications where obtaining full feedback is prohibitively expensive.

title: Procedural Graphs: Self-Evolving Execution Structures for LLM Agents
comment: 36 pages including references and appendices, 6 figures, 11 tables
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as agents that plan over long horizons and act through external tools. Most agents select actions through unconstrained generation over an accumulating history, leaving implicit the procedural knowledge of what to do, in what order, and under which conditions. As trajectories lengthen, agents can lose track of their objectives, invoke tools out of order, and repeat unproductive actions. We introduce the Procedural Graph: just as a knowledge graph organizes factual knowledge into (entity, relation, entity) triplets for what-is questions, a Procedural Graph organizes procedural knowledge into (procedure, relation, procedure) triplets for what-to-do questions. At each decision step, the framework localizes the agent's active node, and a guidance model translates the surrounding subgraph into step-level situational guidance that biases the solver's next action without dictating it. The graph is self-evolving: an LLM refiner contrasts failed trajectories with successful ones and edits the graph's topology and attributes, committing edits that preserve or improve held-out validation performance while retaining rejected ones to discourage repetition. Starting from a minimal skeleton, the loop builds graphs that match or surpass hand-designed ones. It can also repair a flawed expert prior. Across multiple datasets, task types, and LLMs, the Procedural Graph delivers consistent gains over memory-based baselines, and self-evolution further improves performance without manual engineering.

AI.tldr: Procedural Graph framework organizes procedural knowledge like knowledge graphs organize facts, enabling agents to maintain focus during long-horizon tasks through self-evolving graphs that guide action selection without dictating it.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents often lose track of objectives, invoke tools out of order, and repeat unproductive actions during long-horizon planning due to implicit procedural knowledge and unconstrained generation over accumulating history.
AI.method: Procedural Graph organizes procedural knowledge into (procedure, relation, procedure) triplets. At each step, a guidance model localizes active node and translates surrounding subgraph into situational guidance that biases action selection. The graph self-evolves through an LLM refiner that edits topology and attributes based on trajectory comparisons.
AI.result: Procedural Graph delivers consistent gains over memory-based baselines across multiple datasets, task types, and LLMs. Self-evolution further improves performance without manual engineering, and the framework can build graphs matching/surpassing hand-designed ones or repair flawed expert priors.
AI.conclusion: Procedural Graph provides an effective framework for organizing and evolving procedural knowledge in LLM agents, addressing key challenges in long-horizon planning and tool use while enabling systematic improvement through automated refinement.

title: EnvCraft: Synthesizing Executable Environments in Agentic RL for Claw-like Agent
summary: The paradigm of LLMs has rapidly shifted from passive language interfaces to autonomous Claw-like agents that execute long-horizon tasks across stateful workspaces. While Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL) provides a promising path to optimize these agents, its scaling is heavily bottlenecked by the severe scarcity of interactive training environments. Existing synthetic environments are strictly limited to tool-calling endpoints, rendering them insufficient for accommodating the end-to-end real-world demands of claw-like agents. To bridge this gap, we introduce EnvCraft, an automated framework for synthesizing executable environments and scalable training data. Specifically, EnvCraft employs an environment synthesis engine to build sandbox-isolated workspaces, alongside a topology-aware data generation engine to produce coherent task trajectories. Overall, we synthesize 139 interactive environments comprising approximately 20K complex tasks for Agentic RL training. Experiments on Qwen3/3.5 models (8B-32B) show that our method yields gains of up to +11.9% on Claw-style benchmarks and +8.0% on general tool-use benchmarks, with concurrent reductions in inference token cost. The results confirm that synthesized executable environments provide robust and generalizable learning signals for training.

AI.tldr: EnvCraft is an automated framework that synthesizes executable environments and scalable training data to address the scarcity of interactive training environments for LLM-based autonomous agents, achieving significant performance improvements on agent benchmarks.
AI.motivation: There's a severe scarcity of interactive training environments for optimizing autonomous LLM agents (Claw-like agents) through Agentic Reinforcement Learning. Existing synthetic environments are limited to tool-calling endpoints and can't accommodate the end-to-end real-world demands of these agents.
AI.method: EnvCraft uses an environment synthesis engine to build sandbox-isolated workspaces and a topology-aware data generation engine to produce coherent task trajectories. The framework automatically synthesizes executable environments and scalable training data.
AI.result: The authors synthesized 139 interactive environments comprising approximately 20K complex tasks. Experiments on Qwen3/3.5 models (8B-32B) showed gains of up to +11.9% on Claw-style benchmarks and +8.0% on general tool-use benchmarks, with concurrent reductions in inference token cost.
AI.conclusion: Synthesized executable environments provide robust and generalizable learning signals for training autonomous LLM agents, effectively bridging the gap between limited synthetic environments and real-world agent demands.

title: Generalizing HVAC Control With Domain Randomized Reinforcement Learning
comment: 4 pages, 5 figures. Short paper published in ACM Sustainability Week Companion '26
summary:
Deploying advanced HVAC (Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning) controllers at scale remains difficult because performance often depends on accurate building models or per-site retuning. We propose NOMAD-RL (Neural Online Meta-Adaptation for Dynamics), a general-purpose Reinforcement Learning (RL) controller designed to transfer across heterogeneous thermal zones through a universal, non-invasive thermostat interface. The controller acts on temperature setpoints from zone measurements and forecasts, while a recurrent policy supports online adaptation under partial observability.
  Our main contribution is an adaptive domain randomization scheme based on physics-informed normalizing flows, which models correlated and multimodal distributions of thermal-zone parameters while maintaining physical plausibility and controllability. This produces a realistic and progressively adaptive training curriculum that improves transfer across buildings. We evaluate NOMAD-RL against a constant-setpoint PID controller, RL without domain randomization, and MPC in single- and multi-zone settings. NOMAD-RL consistently outperforms the PID and non-randomized RL baselines, and approaches the performance of a well-tuned MPC, especially in the more challenging multi-zone case. These results highlight the potential of adaptive, physics-informed domain randomization for robust and transferable HVAC control.

AI.tldr: NOMAD-RL: A reinforcement learning HVAC controller that uses adaptive domain randomization with physics-informed normalizing flows for transferable control across heterogeneous thermal zones.
AI.motivation: Deploying advanced HVAC controllers at scale is difficult because performance depends on accurate building models or per-site retuning. There's a need for general-purpose controllers that can transfer across heterogeneous thermal zones without invasive installation or extensive retuning.
AI.method: Proposes NOMAD-RL with adaptive domain randomization using physics-informed normalizing flows to model correlated, multimodal distributions of thermal-zone parameters while maintaining physical plausibility. Uses recurrent policy for online adaptation under partial observability, acting on temperature setpoints from zone measurements and forecasts through universal thermostat interface.
AI.result: NOMAD-RL consistently outperforms constant-setpoint PID controllers and RL without domain randomization. Approaches performance of well-tuned MPC, especially in challenging multi-zone settings. Demonstrates improved transfer across buildings compared to non-randomized approaches.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, physics-informed domain randomization enables robust and transferable HVAC control, offering potential for scalable deployment of RL controllers across diverse building environments without extensive per-site tuning.

title: Planning and Scheduling Business Processes under Control-Flow Uncertainty
summary: Scheduling activities in business processes can improve efficiency (e.g., reduce makespan), but is challenging because the exact sequence of activities required to complete a case is often uncertain due to decisions based on data that emerges during execution. Nevertheless, probabilistic information regarding such decisions can often be estimated or derived from historical execution logs, and can help anticipate which execution paths are likely to lead to successful completion. Planning with particular execution paths affects feasibility, i.e., the probability of successful completion, and the expected number of superfluous activities that are planned but never executed. We frame the problem as a chance-constrained optimization problem and present two formulations: A decomposed approach with two stages, a planning stage that minimizes the expected number of superfluous activities subject to a feasibility constraint, and a scheduling stage that minimizes the makespan over the planned activities; and an integrated approach that combines planning and scheduling into a single formulation. Evaluation on two real-world and one synthetic dataset shows that the integrated approach yields superior makespans but is intractable at scale, while the decomposed approach scales to large settings.

AI.tldr: Business process scheduling with uncertain activity sequences: A chance-constrained optimization approach with decomposed vs integrated formulations.
AI.motivation: Business process scheduling can improve efficiency but is challenging due to uncertainty in activity sequences based on runtime data decisions. However, probabilistic information from historical logs can help anticipate likely execution paths.
AI.method: Frame the problem as a chance-constrained optimization problem. Two approaches: 1) Decomposed two-stage approach with planning stage minimizing expected superfluous activities subject to feasibility constraint, and scheduling stage minimizing makespan; 2) Integrated approach combining planning and scheduling into single formulation.
AI.result: Evaluation on two real-world and one synthetic dataset shows the integrated approach yields superior makespans but is intractable at scale, while the decomposed approach scales to large settings.
AI.conclusion: For business process scheduling under uncertainty, the integrated approach provides better performance but scalability limitations, while the decomposed approach offers practical scalability for large-scale applications with acceptable trade-offs.

title: Scaling Optimal Classification Trees via Adaptive Feature and Sample Reduction
summary: Dynamic programming for optimal classification trees becomes computationally expensive as the numbers of features and training samples increase. We develop a joint feature- and sample-space reduction framework based on STreeD. Weighted STreeD merges duplicate records created after projection onto a fixed candidate set into weighted representatives. This reduces sample-dependent computation without changing the fixed-candidate optimization problem. Adaptive STreeD repeatedly refines a bounded candidate set, retains features used by the incumbent tree, rebuilds the weighted representation, and solves the resulting reduced problems. Each certified Weighted STreeD solution is optimal for its current candidate set, while the outer feature search remains heuristic over the full feature space. Experiments on five data sets show that Weighted STreeD achieves speedups of up to 121.41 times over standard STreeD. Adaptive STreeD reduces runtime in matched comparisons at depths 2 to 4 and continues to return feasible trees at greater depths where full-feature methods are limited by time or memory. Under the same computational budget, its predictive performance remains comparable to the evaluated optimal classification tree baselines and is higher in some comparisons. These results show how joint feature- and sample-space reduction can scale dynamic-programming-based optimal-tree learning to more demanding instances.

AI.tldr: Weighted STreeD and Adaptive STreeD accelerate optimal classification tree learning by reducing feature and sample space, achieving up to 121x speedup while maintaining solution quality.
AI.motivation: Dynamic programming for optimal classification trees becomes computationally expensive with increasing features and training samples, limiting scalability to demanding instances.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: 1) Weighted STreeD merges duplicate records after projection onto fixed candidate features into weighted representatives; 2) Adaptive STreeD refines bounded candidate sets, retains features used by incumbent trees, rebuilds weighted representations, and solves reduced problems iteratively.
AI.result: Weighted STreeD achieves up to 121.41x speedup over standard STreeD. Adaptive STreeD reduces runtime at depths 2-4 and returns feasible trees at greater depths where full methods fail. Predictive performance remains comparable or better than baseline optimal trees under same computational budget.
AI.conclusion: Joint feature- and sample-space reduction enables scaling dynamic-programming-based optimal-tree learning to more demanding instances while maintaining solution quality.

title: Agents Trust Tools Too Much: Measuring Reliance on Unreliable Tools
summary: Existing evaluations of tool-using agents primarily measure whether an agent can successfully complete diverse tasks with tools. These evaluations generally assume that tools return reliable information. However, tool returns in real-world systems can be plausible yet incorrect. We investigate how agents respond to unreliable tool returns by evaluating fourteen LLMs using three tools-web search, LLM sub-agent delegation, and code execution. For each tool, we corrupt its returns and measure whether agents adopt the corrupted content in their final answers. Agents exhibit high levels of overtrust across all three settings: the mean adoption rate exceeds one third for every tool and reaches 68.0% for web search. Analysis of reasoning traces reveals a particularly concerning failure mode: agents often recognize conflicts and even recover the correct answer internally, yet present only the corrupted answer without warning the user. To mitigate agents' overtrust in tool returns, we intervene at three levels: prompting by the user, metadata from the tool provider, and post-training by the agent builder. Although some interventions help for particular models or tools, none consistently mitigates overtrust across tools. These findings identify overtrust in unreliable tools as a serious and persistent failure mode, motivating evaluations and interventions that enable agents to validate tool outputs and transparently communicate unresolved conflicts.

AI.tldr: LLM agents show dangerous overtrust in unreliable tools, often adopting corrupted information even when they recognize conflicts internally, with existing interventions failing to consistently solve this problem.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of tool-using agents assume reliable tool returns, but real-world tools can provide plausible yet incorrect information. The paper investigates how agents respond to such unreliable tool outputs, which is a critical safety concern for deploying AI agents in practical applications.
AI.method: Evaluated 14 LLMs using three tools (web search, LLM sub-agent delegation, and code execution) with corrupted returns. Measured adoption rates of corrupted content in final answers. Analyzed reasoning traces to identify failure modes. Tested interventions at three levels: user prompting, tool provider metadata, and post-training by agent builder.
AI.result: Agents exhibited high overtrust across all settings (mean adoption rates exceeded one third for every tool, reaching 68.0% for web search). Agents often recognized conflicts and recovered correct answers internally but presented only corrupted answers without warning. No intervention consistently mitigated overtrust across tools, though some helped for specific models or tools.
AI.conclusion: Overtrust in unreliable tools is a serious and persistent failure mode in LLM agents. This highlights the need for new evaluations and interventions that enable agents to validate tool outputs and transparently communicate unresolved conflicts to users, rather than silently adopting incorrect information.

title: SAFEGuard: Detect Optimization-Based Jailbreak Attacks Through Harmful Semantic Analysis and Fluency Measurement
comment: Published as a conference paper at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026). Our project page is available at https://vietvo89.github.io/SAFEGuard_project/
summary: Despite the significant efforts devoted to aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values and ensuring safe deployment, recent work has revealed that LLMs remain vulnerable to adversarial jailbreak attacks that can bypass safety guardrails and elicit harmful responses. Many defense methods are proposed to detect jailbreaks but they are limited in their effectiveness to counter wide-range optimization-based jailbreak mechanisms that can yield highly fluency-optimized or harmful semantic obfuscated prompts. To tackle this challenge, we propose a unified detection framework SAFEGuard which incorporates a hybrid fluency measurement based on cross-layer distribution distance and perplexity, and the analysis of harmful semantics through gradient matching. Our method is grounded in a paramount observation: high fluency prompts maintain their malicious intention close to harmful prompts while harmful semantic obfuscated prompts often inject gibberish token sequences. Our evaluation demonstrates that SAFEGuard consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and achieves significant improvement in accuracy across different optimization-based jailbreaks. This underscores the effectiveness of SAFEGuard against evolving jailbreak attacks.

AI.tldr: SAFEGuard: A unified detection framework that combines fluency measurement and harmful semantic analysis to defend against optimization-based jailbreak attacks on LLMs.
AI.motivation: Despite efforts to align LLMs with human values, they remain vulnerable to adversarial jailbreak attacks that bypass safety guardrails. Existing defense methods are limited in effectively countering wide-range optimization-based jailbreak mechanisms that produce fluency-optimized or harmful semantic obfuscated prompts.
AI.method: SAFEGuard incorporates: 1) A hybrid fluency measurement based on cross-layer distribution distance and perplexity, and 2) Analysis of harmful semantics through gradient matching. The approach is grounded in the observation that high fluency prompts maintain malicious intent close to harmful prompts, while harmful semantic obfuscated prompts inject gibberish token sequences.
AI.result: SAFEGuard consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and achieves significant improvement in accuracy across different optimization-based jailbreak attacks. The evaluation demonstrates its effectiveness against evolving jailbreak threats.
AI.conclusion: SAFEGuard represents an effective unified detection framework that addresses the limitations of existing defenses against optimization-based jailbreak attacks, providing robust protection for LLM safety deployments.

title: The convergent laboratory: when AI reasoning, autonomous experiments, high performance and quantum computing reshape chemistry
summary: This Comment emerges from TPC26 (https://tpc26.org), a conference convening leaders from academia, national laboratories, and industry who are reshaping materials science discovery. The meeting explored how AI, autonomous agents, self-driving labs, higher performance and quantum computing converge to amplify their individual impact on materials science discovery. The perspectives here reflect the firsthand experiences of researchers at these frontiers and capture the essence of this global endeavor. As AI-driven reasoning, autonomous agentic frameworks, self-driving laboratories, and fault-tolerant quantum processors mature simultaneously, we offer this Comment as a reference at what we believe is a tipping point of transformative advances and productive disruption in the chemical sciences.

AI.tldr: AI, autonomous agents, self-driving labs, high-performance computing, and quantum computing are converging to transform materials science discovery at a critical tipping point.
AI.motivation: To document and share perspectives from TPC26 conference about how multiple disruptive technologies are converging to reshape materials science discovery, capturing insights from leaders across academia, national labs, and industry.
AI.method: Commentary based on discussions and experiences shared at the TPC26 conference, synthesizing firsthand perspectives from researchers working at the frontiers of these converging technologies.
AI.result: The paper presents a collective view that the simultaneous maturation of AI-driven reasoning, autonomous agent frameworks, self-driving laboratories, and fault-tolerant quantum computing creates a convergence that amplifies their individual impacts on materials science.
AI.conclusion: We are at a tipping point where these converging technologies will lead to transformative advances and productive disruption in the chemical sciences, warranting this commentary as a reference for this critical moment.

title: Selective Posterior Margin Regularization for Forward-Corrected Classification
summary: Learning with class-conditional label noise often relies on a transition model from latent clean classes to observed annotations. Forward correction embeds this transition in the likelihood, yet finite-sample networks may still memorize corrupted labels. The corrected likelihood also induces a reverse posterior over the clean classes that could explain each annotation. When its leading class differs from the annotation, the model and transition matrix provide evidence against that annotation, but the leading alternatives can remain nearly tied. We introduce Selective Posterior Margin Regularization (SPMR), which preserves the Forward objective and converts this disagreement into a graded update on the clean classifier. SPMR selects the leading reverse-posterior class, scales a detached pairwise margin by the separation between the two leading posterior classes, and assigns correspondingly little influence to diffuse conflicts. The gap factorizes into transition- adjusted pairwise separation and the posterior mass carried by the leading pair. The active margin follows the locally minimum-norm logit direction that enlarges the selected pairwise margin. Across five known-transition benchmarks, SPMR improves full-length Forward by 2.5-7.0 percentage points and remains 0.7-2.5 percentage points above Forward with Mixup and early stopping. Matched interventions support distinct gains from the posterior-space coefficient, transition-adjusted target, and pairwise action. The same design transfers to estimated transitions, human annotations, architectural changes, and stronger Forward recipes. The formulation uses latent-class evidence already available inside Forward correction without promoting every posterior conflict to a corrected label.

AI.tldr: SPMR improves robust learning under label noise by selectively regularizing based on posterior disagreement between model predictions and annotations, without discarding Forward correction.
AI.motivation: Forward correction with known transition matrices still suffers from networks memorizing corrupted labels, and when the model's posterior over clean classes disagrees with the given annotation, this disagreement isn't effectively utilized to improve learning.
AI.method: Selective Posterior Margin Regularization (SPMR) preserves Forward correction but adds regularization that: 1) selects the leading reverse-posterior class when it differs from annotation, 2) scales a detached pairwise margin by the separation between the two leading posterior classes, 3) assigns little influence to diffuse conflicts, 4) follows the minimum-norm logit direction to enlarge selected pairwise margin.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks with known transitions, SPMR improves full-length Forward by 2.5-7.0 percentage points and remains 0.7-2.5 percentage points above Forward with Mixup and early stopping. Gains persist with estimated transitions, human annotations, architectural changes, and stronger Forward recipes.
AI.conclusion: SPMR effectively leverages posterior-space evidence already available in Forward correction to combat memorization of corrupted labels, providing systematic improvements over standard approaches without requiring additional labels or fundamentally changing the correction framework.

title: Beyond Arbitrary Geometry: Topology Generalization In neural PDE Operators
summary: Neural operators that accept arbitrary meshes are often treated as geometry-general, but unseen domain topology changes both the invariant and decaying subspaces of a PDE operator. We use Hodge heat flow as a controlled lens on this distinction and introduce TopoBox-3D, where tunnels and cavities vary Betti support while the exact Hodge decomposition separates the harmonic kernel from the positive spectrum. Across six architectures, models that infer topology implicitly suffer excess matched degradation in 37 of 45 model--task topology-OOD cells, yet cases that change harmonic dimension are not more strongly penalized on average. The dominant difficulty is instead spectral: the initial Rayleigh quotient is the most stable predictor of error, and spectral broadening adds information for edge and face cochains. Most strikingly, controlled probes show that explicit incidence and harmonic coordinates do not yield the best kernel-identity accuracy; nevertheless, TNO ranks first in mixed-input nonharmonic accuracy on all six tasks with nontrivial harmonic support. Together, these results establish topology as a distinct generalization axis beyond arbitrary-geometry compatibility and show that its influence extends across the Hodge spectrum rather than remaining confined to the harmonic kernel. More broadly, they suggest that global, low-frequency structural priors may help organize predictions in the faster-decaying complementary component, offering a new perspective on how neural operators may generalize across topology as well as geometry.

AI.tldr: Topological changes in PDE domains affect neural operator generalization, with spectral properties rather than harmonic components being the dominant difficulty factor. Models struggle with topological OOD generalization, and explicit topological features don't necessarily improve kernel accuracy.
AI.motivation: Neural operators are considered geometry-general but their generalization across different topological domains (with varying tunnels and cavities) remains unexplored. The paper investigates how unseen topological changes affect PDE operator subspaces and neural operator performance.
AI.method: The authors introduce TopoBox-3D, a controlled testbed using Hodge heat flow where Betti numbers vary. They analyze six neural operator architectures across tasks with varying harmonic support, using Hodge decomposition to separate harmonic kernels from positive spectra. They measure performance degradation in topology-OOD settings and analyze spectral properties via Rayleigh quotients.
AI.result: Models suffer excess degradation in 37 of 45 model-task topology-OOD cells. Changes in harmonic dimension aren't more penalized on average. The dominant difficulty is spectral: initial Rayleigh quotient is the most stable error predictor, and spectral broadening adds information for edge/face cochains. Surprisingly, explicit incidence and harmonic coordinates don't yield best kernel-identity accuracy, though TNO ranks first in mixed-input nonharmonic accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Topology represents a distinct generalization axis beyond geometry compatibility, with influence extending across the entire Hodge spectrum rather than just harmonic kernels. Global, low-frequency structural priors may help organize predictions in faster-decaying complementary components, offering new perspectives for neural operator generalization across topology.

title: Budgeted Task-Aware Acquisition of Dynamic Networks
summary: Learning on dynamic graphs is difficult when changes in the underlying network are only partially observed. Acquiring current graph information incurs observation and computational costs, making complete updates impractical under limited resources. This paper focuses on budgeted task-aware acquisition on dynamic networks, where a model needs to decide which stale graph information to refresh for a downstream task. We propose Scout, a lightweight framework that learns the task value of querying each node from the maintained graph and observation history. Our evaluation covers one synthetic and four real-world dynamic networks, two downstream tasks, nine acquisition baselines, and several query budgets. Scout achieves the highest mean downstream performance in 19 of the 21 benchmark-budget settings. Task-utility supervision also outperforms structural-change supervision in 13 of the 16 real-world settings. On the same dynamic network, task-matched acquisition improves link-prediction AUC by 0.012-0.016 and node-classification accuracy by 0.064-0.09 over task-mismatched acquisition. These results show that useful graph observations depend on the downstream task and that limited observation budgets can be allocated more effectively by learning directly from downstream utility.

AI.tldr: Scout is a lightweight framework that learns which nodes to query for graph updates based on downstream task utility, outperforming various baselines across multiple dynamic network scenarios.
AI.motivation: Learning on dynamic graphs is challenging when network changes are only partially observed due to observation and computational costs. Complete graph updates are impractical under limited resources, requiring intelligent decisions about which stale information to refresh.
AI.method: Proposes Scout, a lightweight framework that learns the task value of querying each node from the maintained graph and observation history. It focuses on budgeted task-aware acquisition on dynamic networks, determining which nodes to update based on their potential downstream utility.
AI.result: Scout achieves highest mean downstream performance in 19 of 21 benchmark-budget settings across one synthetic and four real-world dynamic networks. Task-utility supervision outperforms structural-change supervision in 13 of 16 real-world settings. Task-matched acquisition improves link-prediction AUC by 0.012-0.016 and node-classification accuracy by 0.064-0.09 over task-mismatched acquisition.
AI.conclusion: Useful graph observations depend on the downstream task, and limited observation budgets can be allocated more effectively by learning directly from downstream utility rather than focusing solely on structural changes.

title: Recovering Temporal and Geographic Signals from Language Model Embeddings
summary: Understanding whether language-model embeddings encode structured real-world information is important for both representation analysis and information retrieval. We study this question for temporal and geographic signals using a simple projection-based method that operates directly on output embeddings. Given a small set of seed examples, the method defines an axis in embedding space and ranks texts or entities by their projection onto that axis. Our approach is fully black-box and model-agnostic: it requires only embeddings, without access to model weights, internal activations, auxiliary probes, or additional training. This makes it applicable to modern embedding models available only through APIs and provides a lightweight way to analyze whether temporal and spatial dimensions are present in their representation spaces. We apply the method to temporal and geographic datasets and find that embedding projections recover meaningful chronological and spatial structure. These results provide evidence that output embeddings encode signals relevant to time and space, while also offering a practical tool for interpretability and for downstream temporal and geographic information retrieval tasks, such as temporal ordering, geographic ranking, and tagging.

AI.tldr: A simple projection-based method shows that language model output embeddings encode meaningful temporal and geographic information without requiring access to model internals or additional training.
AI.motivation: To understand whether language model embeddings encode structured real-world temporal and geographic information, which is important for both representation analysis and information retrieval tasks.
AI.method: A projection-based method that operates directly on output embeddings using a small set of seed examples. The method defines an axis in embedding space and ranks texts/entities by their projection onto that axis. It's fully black-box and model-agnostic, requiring only embeddings without access to weights, activations, probes, or training.
AI.result: The method successfully recovers meaningful chronological and spatial structure when applied to temporal and geographic datasets, demonstrating that embedding projections encode relevant time and space signals.
AI.conclusion: Output embeddings indeed encode temporal and spatial information, providing evidence for structured real-world knowledge in language model representations. The method offers a practical tool for interpretability and downstream applications like temporal ordering, geographic ranking, and tagging.

title: A budget-dependent crossover between coverage- and response-based training-set selection for machine-learned interatomic potentials
summary: Selecting compact training sets for machine-learned interatomic potentials requires deciding whether to preserve structural diversity or target configurations on which models disagree. The better choice can depend on how much data is retained, making a comparison at one training-set size insufficient. Here we link selection criteria to prediction accuracy through a budget-resolved comparison of retrained MACE models on GAP-20 Carbon and pooled revised MD17. Structural coverage is compared with a response-guided selector that targets disagreement between a coverage-trained model and a full-data reference. This retrospective response witness tests the value of model disagreement for compressing an already labelled pool. At 5\%, coverage gives smaller absolute deviations from the full-data error than random sampling across four force endpoints in both datasets. The witness has larger deviations than coverage at 1\% and 5\%, but the ordering reverses at 20\%. At 20\%, witness-selected models also lower direct held-out force errors by 0.46--5.89\% relative to coverage, with all eight paired training-seed intervals favouring the witness. Six errors fall below the full-data reference. Mean force-error reductions are 0.164--0.167~meV~$\textÅ^{-1}$, with larger gains for tail and masked endpoints. Complementary analyses show that learned similarity preserves the coverage ranking, while selecting by frozen-model error gives higher error than embedding coverage. These findings establish retained-data budget as a deciding variable in atomistic training-set selection and provide a direct test of when response-guided compression improves on structural coverage.

AI.tldr: Selecting compact training sets for interatomic potentials requires choosing between structural diversity and targeting model disagreements; the optimal choice depends on training-set size, with structural coverage better for small sets and response-guided selection better for larger sets.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the fundamental trade-off in machine-learned interatomic potentials: whether to prioritize structural diversity or target configurations where models disagree when selecting compact training sets. The optimal selection strategy likely depends on how much data is retained, making single-size comparisons insufficient for practical guidance.
AI.method: The authors conduct a budget-resolved comparison by retraining MACE models on GAP-20 Carbon and pooled revised MD17 datasets. They compare structural coverage selection with a response-guided selector that targets disagreement between a coverage-trained model and a full-data reference model. This "retrospective response witness" approach tests the value of model disagreement for compressing an already labeled data pool across different retention percentages (1%, 5%, 20%).
AI.result: At small data budgets (1% and 5%), structural coverage selection gives smaller absolute deviations from full-data error than random sampling and outperforms response-guided selection. However, at 20% retention, response-guided selection reverses this ordering, outperforming coverage selection by 0.46-5.89% in held-out force errors across all eight paired training-seed intervals, with six errors falling below the full-data reference. Mean force-error reductions range 0.164-0.167 meV·Å⁻¹, with larger gains for tail and masked endpoints.
AI.conclusion: Retained-data budget is a critical deciding variable in atomistic training-set selection. Response-guided compression becomes superior to structural coverage at larger training-set sizes (20% retention), while coverage remains better for very small budgets (1-5%). The work provides a direct test framework for determining when different selection strategies are optimal.

title: Beyond Prompts: Measuring and Optimizing LLM Tool-Agent Harnesses
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026. 18 pages, 9 figures, 10 tables
summary: LLM tool agents can be improved without retraining by modifying the runtime harness around a fixed model: prompts, tool interfaces, middleware, state handling, and recovery logic. We study this setting as resource-bounded harness selection for fixed-model multi-turn tool agents, with the search surface scoped to prompts and tool-boundary middleware: edits are guarded intercepts at the tool boundary, not arbitrary rewriting of agent execution logic. Our optimizer-agnostic protocol reports mean held-out lift, worst-condition lift, repeatability, logged cost diagnostics, and RelLift95(B), a conservative estimate of the held-out gain of the harness selected under budget B. We instantiate the protocol with prompt-only and prompt-plus-middleware optimizers, including PRISM, which clusters failures and routes repairs to prompt, tool-boundary middleware, or joint edit surfaces within a Pareto search. On BFCL multi-round, tau2-Retail, and tau2-Telecom, PRISM obtains mean held-out lifts of 14.2, 14.9, and 10.1 percentage points and positive empirical RelLift95 on all three benchmarks, and a component ablation attributes the margin chiefly to failure-surface routing and the edit-pattern constraint. Across optimizers, the results show that some search procedures can occasionally find large gains but still choose brittle updates, so the reliability of the chosen harness should be reported alongside average held-out lift.

AI.tldr: Researchers propose a framework for improving LLM tool agents without retraining by optimizing the runtime harness (prompts, middleware, state handling), introducing a protocol to evaluate harness reliability, and demonstrating that routing failure recovery strategies is key to performance gains.
AI.motivation: Current methods for improving LLM tool agents often require expensive retraining, but performance can be enhanced through better runtime infrastructure (harness optimization) - this approach is more resource-efficient and avoids model retraining costs.
AI.method: Proposed resource-bounded harness selection for fixed-model tool agents, focusing on prompts and tool-boundary middleware. Introduces optimizer-agnostic evaluation protocol with metrics including held-out lift, worst-condition lift, repeatability, and RelLift95(B). Developed PRISM optimizer that clusters failures and routes repairs to appropriate surfaces (prompt, middleware, or joint) within Pareto search.
AI.result: PRISM achieved mean held-out lifts of 14.2, 14.9, and 10.1 percentage points on BFCL multi-round, tau2-Retail, and tau2-Telecom benchmarks with positive empirical RelLift95 on all three. Component analysis shows failure-surface routing and edit-pattern constraints drive improvements. Key finding: some optimizers find large gains but produce brittle updates, so reliability metrics are crucial alongside average lift.
AI.conclusion: Harness optimization without model retraining is effective for improving LLM tool agents, but evaluation must include reliability metrics like RelLift95 to avoid selecting brittle improvements. The PRISM approach demonstrates significant gains through intelligent failure routing, suggesting runtime infrastructure improvements are a viable alternative to model retraining.

title: Grounded and Faithful P&ID Reasoning: Constraining Vision-Language Models with Recovered Evidence Graphs
summary: Piping and Instrumentation Diagrams (P&IDs) are the authoritative maps of process plants: isolation, maintenance, and HAZOP decisions depend on what connects to what. Vision-language models describe these sheets fluently, yet they often invent or miss process connections---and an invented or missed link can reverse an isolation or reachability call, so a plant decision cannot trust a fluent answer that was never checked against the linework. We instead recover an explicit graph of the drawing---its symbols, the process connections between them, and the tags that name them---and then require the model to answer only by querying that graph through seven read-only operators, so a topology claim is returned only when it cites the query results that support it. On TopoPID-VQA, a new suite of 3000 topology questions over these sheets, Graph-Grounded Harness (Ours) raises exact match accuracy from 36.7--41.3% under image-only prompting to 74.3--76.0% for Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen3-VL-8B, and Gemma-4-E4B. It does so on an imperfect substrate: on Digitize-PID dataset the recovered graph scores F1 0.742 on exact process connections, and 0.801 once symbols and tags are pooled in. The residual errors track that gap---grounding pays off where the recovered graph is right, and perception error still breaks topology questions where it is not.

AI.tldr: A novel graph-grounded approach for P&ID analysis that extracts explicit connection graphs from drawings and uses read-only graph queries to answer topology questions, dramatically improving accuracy over vision-language models.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language models struggle with accurate topology analysis of P&IDs because they can invent or miss critical process connections, which could lead to dangerous errors in plant decisions like isolation or maintenance planning.
AI.method: Extract explicit graph representation from P&IDs (symbols, process connections, tags) and ground model answers by requiring them to query this graph through seven read-only operators, ensuring topology claims are supported by actual drawing linework.
AI.result: On TopoPID-VQA dataset (3000 topology questions), accuracy improved from 36.7-41.3% with image-only prompting to 74.3-76.0% across three models. Even with imperfect graph extraction (F1=0.742 for exact connections), graph grounding dramatically reduces errors.
AI.conclusion: Explicit graph grounding effectively bridges the gap between fluent language generation and accurate topology reasoning for P&IDs, showing that structured querying of recovered drawings outperforms direct vision-language approaches, though perception errors in graph extraction remain a limitation.

title: The Normalization of Deviance in AI Development
summary: Work on the risks of artificial intelligence has focused predominantly on capability risk: the danger that systems become too powerful, too autonomous, or too misaligned with human values. Far less attention has been paid to the organizational level---to whether the institutions building these systems are themselves predisposed to drift toward failure. This paper argues that they are. Regardless of how capable AI systems become, the organizations building them face the same structural dynamics that preceded past major technological disasters. Drawing on case studies of the Space Shuttle Challenger, the Three Mile Island accident, and the Boeing 737 MAX crashes, this paper identifies the common structural mechanisms preceding each failure and maps them onto contemporary AI development. The findings suggest that existing safety infrastructure may provide less protection than it appears, as organizations can complete safety processes in full compliance and still produce catastrophic outcomes. The pre-disaster period of AI development is still underway; the purpose of this paper is to make these dynamics legible while they can still be interrupted.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI organizations are structurally predisposed to technological disasters similar to past failures like Challenger and 737 MAX, despite current safety processes.
AI.motivation: Current AI risk research focuses too much on capability risk (systems becoming too powerful/misaligned) and not enough on organizational-level risks - whether the institutions building AI systems themselves have structural predispositions to failure.
AI.method: Draws on case studies of major technological disasters (Space Shuttle Challenger, Three Mile Island accident, Boeing 737 MAX crashes) to identify common structural failure mechanisms, then maps these onto contemporary AI development organizations.
AI.result: Finds that existing AI safety infrastructure may provide less protection than it appears, as organizations can fully comply with safety processes yet still produce catastrophic outcomes. Identifies common structural mechanisms preceding each historical failure that are present in AI development.
AI.conclusion: AI organizations face the same structural dynamics that preceded past technological disasters. The pre-disaster period of AI development is still ongoing, and the paper aims to make these failure dynamics visible while they can still be interrupted.

title: CALM: Class-wise Agreement and Label-gated Disagreement Modulation for Decentralized Federated Learning
summary: Conventional federated learning relies on parameter averaging, which forces clients to be doubly homogeneous: all must run an identical architecture, and accuracy degrades when local data are non-IID. Decentralized federated distillation sidesteps both: each client runs its peers' model snapshots as teachers on its own local data and distills from their soft predictions, with no server, no public data, and no shared architecture. Under severe non-IID skew, however, the trustworthiness of the aggregated teacher target is a matter of degree, yet existing pipelines make hard, all-or-nothing decisions: outlier teachers are discarded by threshold, and whatever target survives is trusted in full. We propose CALM, which replaces every hard decision with a smooth trust gate at three levels: per class, teachers are weighted by agreement with the peer consensus; per sample, distillation is scaled by the teachers' divergence from that target; and a label gate scales it by how strongly the target supports the sample's true label. None of this adds communication or auxiliary data. On CIFAR-10, SVHN, OrganAMNIST, and Google Speech Commands with heterogeneous client architectures under Dirichlet label skew, CALM consistently outperforms uniform and hard-filtered distillation and matches or exceeds competing heterogeneous-FL methods.

AI.tldr: CALM (Consensus-Aware Learning with Multi-gate distillation) replaces hard thresholding in federated distillation with smooth trust gating at multiple levels to handle severe non-IID data skew, outperforming existing methods without adding communication or auxiliary data requirements.
AI.motivation: Conventional federated learning requires homogeneous architectures and suffers from accuracy degradation with non-IID data. While decentralized federated distillation addresses architecture heterogeneity and privacy concerns, existing methods make hard, all-or-nothing decisions when aggregating teacher predictions, which is problematic under severe non-IID label skew where teacher trustworthiness varies.
AI.method: CALM introduces smooth trust gating at three levels: 1) Per-class teacher weighting based on agreement with peer consensus, 2) Per-sample distillation scaling by teacher divergence from the target, and 3) Label gate scaling by how strongly the target supports the sample's true label. This replaces hard thresholding and filtering without adding communication or auxiliary data requirements.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10, SVHN, OrganAMNIST, and Google Speech Commands datasets with heterogeneous client architectures under Dirichlet label skew, CALM consistently outperforms both uniform distillation and hard-filtered distillation methods, and matches or exceeds competing heterogeneous federated learning methods.
AI.conclusion: Smooth trust gating at multiple granularity levels provides a more nuanced approach to handling teacher unreliability in federated distillation under severe non-IID conditions, outperforming hard-decision methods while maintaining communication and privacy advantages of decentralized federated distillation.

title: From Monolithic Blending to Agentic Orchestration: Dynamic Response for Conversational Assistants at Scale
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Industry Track. 16 pages, 1 figure, 21 tables
summary: Conversational assistants can blend retrieval, action selection, escalation, and wording in a single model path, or separate those roles. We report a production migration of a customer-support assistant at a large accommodation marketplace (millions of conversations per month, 11 languages, 10-second P90). Dynamic Response (DR) replaces a single Qwen3-235B-A22B blended responder with a bounded ReAct orchestrator over typed tools plus a smaller generator that writes from a backend-validated context contract. Because the migration also changed prompts, alignment, and serving, we attribute each effect to its cause and claim as architecture effects only those measured on identical replayed turns: typed entity selection moves the reservation selector to a precision-first operating point (precision 8.3% to 89.1%, recall 75.2% to 67.3%), and typed action IDs with a membership check remove observed structured-action hallucination (2.14% to 0.0%). A low-ramp A/B test reproduces the replay escalation reductions: hard-escalation responses fall from 5.60% to 3.08% and soft-escalation responses from 9.56% to 2.49%, while production handoff volume holds roughly steady; self-solve is directional (+5.1 points, 95% CI [-2, +12]). Serving optimizations cut orchestrator P90 latency from 3.87s to 2.24s on a GPU footprint reduced by roughly one-third, and self-hosting reduces estimated annual model-serving cost by more than an order of magnitude.

AI.tldr: Dynamic Response (DR) architecture replaces a single large blended conversational assistant with a bounded ReAct orchestrator over typed tools plus smaller generator, improving precision, eliminating hallucinations, reducing escalations, cutting latency by 42%, and reducing model-serving costs by over 10x in production.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses challenges in production conversational assistants at scale: improving precision of entity selection, eliminating structured-action hallucinations, reducing escalation rates, and reducing latency and infrastructure costs while maintaining performance.
AI.method: Migrated from single Qwen3-235B-A22B blended responder to a bounded ReAct orchestrator with typed tools plus a smaller generator that writes from backend-validated context contracts. Used typed entity selection, typed action IDs with membership checks, and comprehensive serving optimizations.
AI.result: Typed entity selection improved precision from 8.3% to 89.1% (recall 75.2% to 67.3%); eliminated structured-action hallucinations (2.14% to 0.0%); reduced hard-escalation from 5.60% to 3.08% and soft-escalation from 9.56% to 2.49%; cut orchestrator latency from 3.87s to 2.24s P90; reduced GPU footprint by ~1/3 and model-serving costs by >10x.
AI.conclusion: The bounded ReAct orchestrator with typed tools architecture significantly improves production conversational assistant performance across multiple dimensions while dramatically reducing infrastructure costs, demonstrating the effectiveness of separating concerns in large-scale customer support systems.

title: One Rate Is Not Enough: Adaptive Anisotropic Learning Rates for LoRA Fine-Tuning
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models. Most LoRA variants follow a uniform-LR convention, applying a single global learning rate across every rank-one component of every adapter. We show that this convention overlooks substantial within-module heterogeneity, where the rank-one components of a LoRA adapter update at highly uneven rates and low-velocity modules converge to concentrated singular spectra that underutilize the nominal rank budget. To address this, we propose an adaptive anisotropic learning-rate model that assigns each rank-one component its own effective learning rate, computed online from training-time signals and mean-normalized per module to preserve the global LR budget. AnLR-LoRA instantiates this model with two signals available during AdamW optimization, namely function-space velocity and Adam SNR, as a lightweight scheme with no extra trainable parameters. Across commonsense reasoning, natural language generation and visual instruction-tuning benchmarks, AnLR-LoRA consistently improves over LoRA while encouraging broader use of rank capacity, with gains that remain robust across a wide range of global learning rates and transfer cleanly to other LoRA variants.

AI.tldr: AnLR-LoRA introduces adaptive anisotropic learning rates for LoRA fine-tuning, assigning each rank-one component its own learning rate based on training signals, leading to better rank utilization and improved performance across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current LoRA variants use a single global learning rate for all rank-one components, overlooking substantial within-module heterogeneity where components update at uneven rates, and low-velocity modules converge to concentrated singular spectra that underutilize the nominal rank budget.
AI.method: Proposes an adaptive anisotropic learning-rate model that assigns each rank-one component its own effective learning rate, computed online from training-time signals (function-space velocity and Adam SNR) and mean-normalized per module to preserve the global LR budget. AnLR-LoRA implements this as a lightweight scheme with no extra trainable parameters.
AI.result: Across commonsense reasoning, natural language generation and visual instruction-tuning benchmarks, AnLR-LoRA consistently improves over standard LoRA while encouraging broader use of rank capacity. Gains remain robust across a wide range of global learning rates and transfer cleanly to other LoRA variants.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropic learning rate adaptation addresses the limitations of uniform-LR LoRA by better utilizing rank capacity through component-specific learning rates, offering improved fine-tuning performance without additional parameters.

title: Inference-Time Graph Engineering for Multi-Agent LLM Workflows
summary: Recent multi-agent LLM systems increasingly rely on graph-structured communication to coordinate specialized agents. We revisit multi-agent orchestration from a graph-engineering perspective: rather than optimizing a static topology, we synthesize a task-conditioned temporal workflow graph that jointly specifies agent connectivity and edge-level communication semantics. We introduce ReActNet, a training-free framework that compiles a query and a set of role-specialized agents into a sequence of directed communication graphs. Each graph snapshot corresponds to one reasoning stage, and each edge carries a natural-language instruction specifying the message that a source agent should provide to a target agent. The compiled temporal graph is then executed through structured message passing: agents update their reasoning states by integrating their previous states with messages from controller-assigned neighbors, and a final aggregator synthesizes the resulting states into the answer. This design separates graph compilation from graph execution, making multi-agent coordination explicit, inspectable, and task-conditioned without requiring reinforcement learning or gradient-based topology optimization. Across knowledge reasoning, mathematical problem solving, code generation, and GAIA-style assistant tasks, ReActNet consistently improves over fixed-topology and learned-topology baselines while maintaining competitive inference cost. These results suggest that effective multi-agent orchestration depends not only on which agents communicate, but also on engineering executable workflow graphs that encode when, why, and how information should flow during reasoning.

AI.tldr: ReActNet is a training-free framework that compiles task-specific temporal communication graphs for multi-agent LLM systems, enabling explicit and inspectable coordination between specialized agents without requiring reinforcement learning or gradient optimization.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent LLM systems rely on static graph topologies for agent coordination, which limits their ability to adapt to specific tasks and makes coordination implicit and hard to inspect. There's a need for more flexible, task-conditioned orchestration that specifies not just which agents communicate, but when, why, and how information should flow during reasoning.
AI.method: ReActNet separates graph compilation from execution: 1) Compiles a query and role-specialized agents into a temporal workflow graph with directed communication edges, where each graph snapshot corresponds to one reasoning stage and each edge carries a natural-language instruction, 2) Executes through structured message passing where agents update reasoning states by integrating previous states with neighbor messages, 3) Uses a final aggregator to synthesize resulting states into the final answer.
AI.result: Across knowledge reasoning, mathematical problem solving, code generation, and GAIA-style assistant tasks, ReActNet consistently outperforms fixed-topology and learned-topology baselines while maintaining competitive inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Effective multi-agent orchestration requires engineering executable workflow graphs that explicitly encode when, why, and how information should flow during reasoning, not just which agents communicate. ReActNet demonstrates that task-conditioned temporal graphs provide inspectable, explicit coordination without needing reinforcement learning or gradient-based optimization.

title: A First-Order Learning Algorithm for Online Resource Allocation with Constant Regret
summary: We study a finite-horizon online resource allocation problem with initial resource capacities proportional to the horizon. In each period, a request type is observed and one action is chosen from a finite menu. Each action earns a reward and consumes a vector of resources. The arrival types are independent and identically distributed, but their probabilities are unknown. We present a primal first-order learning policy that, in each period, performs one gradient ascent update of the action coordinates associated with the current request type. The policy achieves $O(1)$ expected additive regret relative to the hindsight optimum, with a bound independent of the horizon $T$. It does not solve any linear program, and the regret bound does not require a nondegeneracy assumption on the fluid linear program.

AI.tldr: A primal first-order learning policy achieves O(1) expected additive regret for finite-horizon online resource allocation problems without solving linear programs or requiring nondegeneracy assumptions.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses finite-horizon online resource allocation problems where resource capacities scale with horizon, arrival probabilities are unknown, and existing methods often require solving complex linear programs or impose restrictive nondegeneracy assumptions.
AI.method: The authors develop a primal first-order learning policy that performs one gradient ascent update of action coordinates associated with the current request type in each period, without solving any linear programs.
AI.result: The policy achieves O(1) expected additive regret relative to the hindsight optimum, with a bound independent of the horizon T, and does not require nondegeneracy assumptions on the fluid linear program.
AI.conclusion: The proposed primal first-order learning approach provides an efficient, practical solution for online resource allocation problems with unknown arrival distributions, achieving constant regret without solving complex optimization problems or requiring restrictive assumptions.

title: DI-Bench: Systematically Generating In-Domain Data Intelligence Benchmarks for Enterprise Agents
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures, 13 tables. Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Industry Track
summary: Evaluating enterprise agents on domain-specific benchmarks is critical, yet public benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents can integrate business knowledge with analytical computation, and constructing such benchmarks manually is costly. We present DI-Bench, a pipeline for generating realistic benchmarks for data intelligence (DI), the practice of extracting insights from large volumes of enterprise data. To emulate realistic DI tasks that require both computation and knowledge retrieval, DI-Bench builds an artifact linkage graph over data tables, dimensions, metrics, and documents to form questions involving structured data and associated knowledge. Ground truth answers are derived via query execution, followed by LLM question generation and validation. Applied to two public datasets, the pipeline produces a 731-task benchmark covering knowledge retrieval, analytical computation, and rule-grounded reasoning. To show the discriminatory capability and difficulty of the benchmark, we evaluate four models, revealing a substantial finding: models achieve only 32% accuracy when doing computational tasks where retrieved business rules modify the computation.

AI.tldr: DI-Bench is an automated pipeline for generating realistic data intelligence benchmarks that test agents on enterprise data analysis tasks requiring both computational and knowledge retrieval capabilities.
AI.motivation: Current public benchmarks fail to evaluate whether AI agents can effectively integrate business knowledge with analytical computation. Manual construction of such benchmarks is expensive and time-consuming, creating a gap in evaluating enterprise agents for real-world data intelligence tasks.
AI.method: The pipeline builds an artifact linkage graph connecting data tables, dimensions, metrics, and documents to form realistic questions. It generates ground truth answers via query execution, followed by LLM question generation and validation. Applied to two public datasets, it produces comprehensive benchmarks covering multiple task types.
AI.result: The pipeline generated a 731-task benchmark covering knowledge retrieval, analytical computation, and rule-grounded reasoning. Evaluation of four models revealed a significant finding: models achieve only 32% accuracy on computational tasks where retrieved business rules need to modify the computation, showing the benchmark's discriminatory capability.
AI.conclusion: DI-Bench provides an effective automated solution for generating realistic enterprise data intelligence benchmarks, revealing significant gaps in current models' ability to integrate business knowledge with computational reasoning. The benchmark successfully discriminates model capabilities and highlights the challenge of rule-grounded computation tasks.

title: A dictionary learning framework for graphs via filters and optimal transport
summary: We propose a graph dictionary learning (GDL) framework where each graph is represented as a zero-mean Gaussian distribution derived from its filtered Laplacian. Each observed graph is approximated by a barycenter over learned atom graphs, computed under the filter graph distance (fGOT), a graph comparison metric sensitive to global structural properties. The reconstruction error between the observed graph and its barycenter is measured by the surrogate fGOT (sfGOT) distance, a tractable approximation of fGOT that handles graphs without known node correspondence, and is minimized end-to-end via backpropagation. We further provide a novel interpretation of sfGOT through the lens of the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, showing that minimizing the sfGOT distance between two graphs is equivalent to maximizing statistical dependence between the spectral embedding of their nodes. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate competitive performance over existing GDL methods on graph clustering and classification tasks.

AI.tldr: Proposes a graph dictionary learning framework where graphs are represented as Gaussian distributions, approximated by barycenters of learned atom graphs using a novel filter graph distance metric, optimized end-to-end via backpropagation.
AI.motivation: Existing graph representation learning methods may not adequately capture global structural properties of graphs or handle graphs without known node correspondence effectively.
AI.method: Represent graphs as zero-mean Gaussian distributions derived from filtered Laplacians. Approximate observed graphs via barycenters over learned atom graphs using filter graph distance (fGOT), minimize reconstruction error via surrogate fGOT distance that handles graphs without node correspondence, optimized end-to-end with backpropagation.
AI.result: The framework shows competitive performance on graph clustering and classification tasks across benchmark datasets compared to existing graph dictionary learning methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed GDL framework provides an effective approach for learning graph representations that capture global structural properties while handling graphs without node correspondence, with theoretical interpretation linking distance minimization to maximizing statistical dependence between node embeddings.

title: Distilling Vision-Language Models for On-Device Fire Understanding
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising alternative to conventional fire detection systems by reasoning about the semantic context of a scene and thus reducing false alarms, yet their large model size makes deployment on embedded fire sensors impractical. In this paper, we study how domain-specialized VLMs can be compressed for fully on-device deployment without losing the safety-critical behavior required for fire detection. We develop a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework in which large VLMs fine-tuned for fire understanding can be distilled into lightweight students. Experiments across multiple VLM families and model scales show that compact students preserve most of their teachers' fire-understanding capability. We further deploy the distilled models on our commercial Detectium fire detection sensor and jointly evaluate reasoning accuracy, latency, and memory usage. The results show that compression and deployment affect not only accuracy but also model failure modes, with Qwen2.5-0.5B providing the strongest overall deployment trade-off. Our findings provide broader guidance for deploying domain-specialized VLMs in resource-constrained, safety-critical settings.

AI.tldr: Domain-specialized vision-language models can be compressed for on-device fire detection using knowledge distillation, achieving practical deployment on embedded sensors while maintaining safety-critical performance.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models show promise for fire detection by reducing false alarms through semantic reasoning, but their large size makes deployment on embedded sensors impractical. There's a need for compressed models that maintain safety-critical behavior for real-world deployment.
AI.method: Developed a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework where large VLMs fine-tuned for fire understanding are distilled into lightweight student models. Multiple VLM families and model scales were tested, with evaluation including reasoning accuracy, latency, and memory usage on commercial fire detection hardware.
AI.result: Compact student models preserved most of their teachers' fire-understanding capability. Qwen2.5-0.5B provided the strongest overall deployment trade-off when considering accuracy, latency, and memory usage. The study also found that compression and deployment affect not only accuracy but also model failure modes.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specialized VLMs can be successfully compressed for resource-constrained, safety-critical deployments using knowledge distillation. The findings provide broader guidance for deploying such models in embedded settings where size, latency, and reliability are critical factors.

title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Efficiency Methods for Multi-Agent Systems
comment: The 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
summary: Efficiency is increasingly important for Large Language Model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS), as larger models and more agents introduce substantial execution costs. Recent methods aim to make MAS cheaper by pruning agents, removing communication edges, or searching for compact structures. However, we argue that existing evaluations may overestimate their true ability to improve MAS efficiency. Reported gains are often measured under method-specific prompts and starting topologies, making them difficult to attribute to the proposed structural changes. Moreover, many reported successes appear in non-MAS-demanding settings, where a single agent or a randomly pruned system can already preserve strong performance. To study these issues, we introduce a controlled and MAS-demanding diagnostic benchmark for representative MAS efficiency methods. We evaluate methods under a shared backbone model, agent registry, and runtime, across controlled variations in topology, scale, depth, and tool use. Our analysis shows that many reported gains are setup-dependent and may arise from structural collapse, disabled tool pathways, or starting systems where random pruning already preserves accuracy, rather than robust improvements in MAS efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques existing LLM-based multi-agent system efficiency methods for having flawed evaluations and introduces a controlled diagnostic benchmark that reveals many reported gains are actually setup-dependent rather than robust efficiency improvements.
AI.motivation: Efficiency is crucial for LLM-based multi-agent systems due to high execution costs from larger models and more agents.
