Existing efficiency methods (agent pruning, communication edge removal, compact structure search) are evaluated with flawed methodologies that overestimate their true ability to improve MAS efficiency.
AI.method: The authors introduce a controlled diagnostic benchmark that evaluates representative MAS efficiency methods under shared conditions: same backbone model, agent registry, and runtime. The benchmark systematically varies topology, scale, depth, and tool use to isolate structural efficiency improvements from setup dependencies.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that many reported efficiency gains are setup-dependent and may result from: 1) structural collapse (systems degrade to simpler forms), 2) disabled tool pathways, or 3) evaluation in non-MAS-demanding settings where random pruning already preserves accuracy. The gains are not robust improvements in MAS efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Existing evaluations of MAS efficiency methods likely overestimate their effectiveness due to methodological flaws. A controlled diagnostic approach is necessary to properly assess structural efficiency improvements, and many current methods may not provide robust efficiency gains when evaluated in MAS-demanding scenarios with proper controls.

title: More Than Mimicking Reviewers: Evaluating LLMs for Pre-Submission Peer Review
summary:
Peer-review feedback often arrives too late for authors to make meaningful revisions. We study an author-facing LLM system that moves part of this stress test before submission: it generates a broad pool of atomic concerns and compresses them into a short report. We evaluate agreement with historical reviews and, separately, the possible validity of concerns they omit.
  From 10,000 ICLR 2026 submissions, we use 3,398 manuscripts with accessible versions that predate review. On a ten-paper diagnostic, independent sampling covers 44.9% of historical issues; deduplication and refill reaches 78.7% strict and 84.9% seriousness-weighted coverage, at 3.6$\times$ more requests and 5.2$\times$ more tokens. A hidden Top-32 Oracle preserves the full 79.3% weighted coverage of a 256-candidate pool, but paper-only selectors retain only 40--44%. LLM review therefore provides broad coverage with a large candidate pool but compresses poorly; ablations identify representative selection and matcher sensitivity as the main sources of this gap.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based system generates comprehensive peer-review concerns before submission, achieving 84.9% seriousness-weighted coverage of historical review issues, but suffers from poor compression when trying to condense large candidate pools.
AI.motivation: Traditional peer-review feedback often arrives too late for authors to make meaningful revisions, creating a need for early-stage feedback systems that can identify potential issues before submission.
AI.method: The authors developed an author-facing LLM system that generates a broad pool of atomic concerns and compresses them into short reports. They evaluated this using 3,398 ICLR 2026 manuscripts with accessible pre-review versions, comparing against historical reviews through independent sampling, deduplication, and refill methods.
AI.result: The system achieved 44.9% coverage of historical issues with independent sampling, improving to 78.7% strict coverage and 84.9% seriousness-weighted coverage after deduplication and refill (requiring 3.6× more requests and 5.2× more tokens). A hidden Top-32 Oracle maintained 79.3% weighted coverage from a 256-candidate pool, but paper-only selectors retained only 40-44% coverage.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based review systems provide broad coverage of potential issues but compress poorly when trying to condense large candidate pools. The main limitations are identified as representative selection and matcher sensitivity, suggesting that while the approach offers valuable pre-submission feedback, current compression techniques are suboptimal.

title: Interpretable and Fair Generalized Additive Neural Networks via Multi-objective Learning
summary: Interpretability and fairness are two of the most emphasized dimensions in trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI). Various explainable AI methods have been introduced to improve interpretability. This paper focuses on neural network (NN)-based generalized additive models (GAMs), a class of self-interpretable models. While most existing research has prioritized improving the accuracy of NN-based GAMs, their interpretability remains largely underexplored. To address this gap, this paper introduces explicit quantitative metrics for evaluating the interpretability of NN-based GAMs, empirically examines their effectiveness, and explores strategies for improving interpretability within these models. In addition, the simultaneous and explicit optimization of both interpretability and fairness, along with their trade-offs and the underlying reasons, remains underexplored. To address this, we propose a multi-objective neural basis model (MONBM) framework based on multi-objective evolutionary learning to consider accuracy, interpretability, and fairness simultaneously. A partial retraining strategy is further developed to facilitate the practical application of evolutionary multi-objective optimization to deep model architectures. Based on MONBM, this paper reveals the complex relationships between these dimensions and the reasons behind these intricate relationships. This analysis demonstrates how multi-objective optimization can be combined with self-interpretable models to reveal relationships among trustworthiness objectives. In addition, MONBM obtains a set of models with different trade-offs between dimensions, and the competitiveness of the approach is validated by comparing it with state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-objective neural basis model (MONBM) framework using evolutionary learning to simultaneously optimize accuracy, interpretability, and fairness in neural network-based generalized additive models, revealing complex relationships between these trustworthiness dimensions.
AI.motivation:
1. Interpretability of neural network-based GAMs is largely underexplored despite their self-interpretable nature.
2. Simultaneous optimization of interpretability and fairness in AI models remains insufficiently studied.
3. Need to understand the complex trade-offs and relationships between accuracy, interpretability, and fairness in trustworthy AI.
AI.method:
1. Introduces explicit quantitative metrics for evaluating interpretability in NN-based GAMs.
2. Proposes MONBM framework based on multi-objective evolutionary learning to jointly optimize accuracy, interpretability, and fairness.
3. Develops partial retraining strategy to apply evolutionary multi-objective optimization to deep architectures.
4. Empirically examines interpretability metrics and explores strategies for improving interpretability.
AI.result:
1. Developed interpretability evaluation metrics that are empirically validated.
2. MONBM successfully obtains a set of models with different trade-offs between trustworthiness dimensions.
3. Reveals complex relationships between accuracy, interpretability, and fairness and the reasons behind these relationships.
4. Approach demonstrates competitiveness compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The MONBM framework effectively combines multi-objective optimization with self-interpretable models to explore trade-offs between trustworthiness dimensions. This approach provides insights into the intricate relationships between accuracy, interpretability, and fairness, offering practical solutions for developing more trustworthy AI systems while maintaining model quality.

title: Spillover-Aware Multi-Value Steering for Pluralistic LLM Alignment
summary: Activation steering controls LLM behavior at inference time by adding learned directions to hidden states, but existing methods handle one concept at a time. Pluralistic alignment, where different stakeholders need different value emphases, requires steering multiple dimensions simultaneously. We show that naive steering produces substantial spillover: the effect intended for one value leaks into others. This parallels the treatment-versus-spillover decomposition in causal inference. We trace spillover to geometric entanglement of steering directions, captured by their Gram matrix, and derive a zero-cost correction from an activation-norm-penalized objective that decouples each direction's contribution exactly. Our end-to-end pipeline requires no fine-tuning, no reward model, and no manual prompt engineering: given only domain questions, it automatically discovers value dimensions, extracts directions, diagnoses entanglement, and applies corrected steering. On climate discourse, the correction improves the net steering effect from +5.9% to +14.0%, validated over 100,000 pairwise judgments.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses spillover effects in activation steering for LLMs by proposing a zero-cost correction method that decouples entangled steering directions, improving steering effectiveness in pluralistic alignment scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods handle only one concept at a time, but pluralistic alignment requires simultaneous steering of multiple value dimensions. Naive steering produces substantial spillover where effects intended for one value leak into others, limiting effectiveness in real-world applications with diverse stakeholders.
AI.method: The authors trace spillover to geometric entanglement of steering directions captured by their Gram matrix. They derive a zero-cost correction from an activation-norm-penalized objective that exactly decouples each direction's contribution. The end-to-end pipeline requires no fine-tuning, reward models, or manual prompt engineering, automatically discovering value dimensions, extracting directions, diagnosing entanglement, and applying corrected steering.
AI.result: On climate discourse applications, the correction improves net steering effect from +5.9% to +14.0%, validated over 100,000 pairwise judgments. The method effectively reduces spillover and improves steering precision for multiple value dimensions simultaneously.
AI.conclusion: The proposed zero-cost correction method successfully addresses spillover problems in activation steering, enabling more effective pluralistic alignment without requiring additional training resources. The geometric entanglement framework and automatic pipeline provide a practical solution for steering multiple value dimensions in real-world applications.

title: QGB-W$k$NN: Quantum Granular-Ball Learning for Robust Classification
summary: Nearest-neighbor classification is widely used in machine learning, yet existing methods often suffer from low computational efficiency and limited robustness in noisy environments. To jointly address these challenges, this paper proposes an efficient and reliable weighted $K$-nearest neighbor classification framework based on quantum granular balls, termed QGB-W$k$NN. The proposed framework improves computational efficiency by integrating quantum-enhanced granular-ball representation with hierarchical nearest-neighbor search, while enhancing classification reliability through a purity-aware weighted decision mechanism. Specifically, quantum-kernel granular balls are constructed to reduce retrieval redundancy and strengthen nonlinear feature representation under limited quantum resources. A granular-ball purity-guided HNSW optimization strategy is developed to exploit structural reliability for hierarchical graph construction during neighbor retrieval, alleviating the local optimality issue caused by conventional random layering. Finally, a weighted voting mechanism jointly incorporating granular-ball similarity and purity is introduced to produce more reliable classification decisions in noisy environments. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that QGB-W$k$NN achieves competitive classification accuracy while exhibiting favorable Pareto trade-offs between classification performance and computational cost. Moreover, the proposed framework consistently improves robustness under various noisy conditions, suggesting that reliability-aware quantum granular-ball learning provides a promising paradigm for efficient and robust nearest-neighbor classification.

AI.tldr: QGB-WkNN is a quantum-enhanced weighted K-nearest neighbor framework that improves computational efficiency through quantum granular balls and enhances robustness via purity-aware weighting, achieving better performance-cost trade-offs and noise robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing nearest-neighbor classification methods often suffer from low computational efficiency and limited robustness in noisy environments, creating a need for approaches that can jointly address both computational efficiency and reliability challenges.
AI.method: Proposes QGB-WkNN framework with three key components: 1) quantum-kernel granular balls for reduced retrieval redundancy and enhanced nonlinear representation; 2) granular-ball purity-guided HNSW optimization for hierarchical graph construction; 3) weighted voting mechanism incorporating both granular-ball similarity and purity for classification decisions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show QGB-WkNN achieves competitive classification accuracy while exhibiting favorable Pareto trade-offs between performance and computational cost. The framework consistently improves robustness under various noisy conditions compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-aware quantum granular-ball learning provides a promising paradigm for efficient and robust nearest-neighbor classification, addressing both computational efficiency and reliability challenges through quantum-enhanced granular representation and purity-aware decision mechanisms.

title: Evidence-Aligned Local Composition of Discrete Experts for Sequence Restoration
summary: A document modeled as a discrete sequence of tokens can be thought of as being generated from a composition of texts from different domains; a README file, for example, moves between prose, code, and configuration. When such a document is corrupted and only frozen domain experts are available, restoring it requires deciding both what is missing and which expert to trust at each position, at test time and without region labels or a trained router. We introduce evidence-aligned local composition, which infers a soft, position-wise weighting over the experts from the marginal evidence of the corrupted observation under a given corruption model, estimating the evidence from the experts' own denoising losses and smoothing the weights across positions. Because the weighting is soft, it recovers a mixture when the true composition is mixed and concentrates on one expert when that suffices. Across a categorical simulator, byte-level experts, and experts fine-tuned from a $1.3$B discrete flow-matching model, the inferred weights track the true regions at $0.85$ field accuracy on naturally mixed scientific documents, and at $0.98$ on constructed mixtures whose regions are lexically disjoint. Restoration improves over a single global weight when the experts are genuinely distinct and reduces to it when they converge, tracking a measure of expert separation.

AI.tldr: A method for restoring corrupted documents using multiple domain experts without requiring pre-trained routers or region labels, by inferring position-wise expert weights from marginal evidence.
AI.motivation: When documents with mixed domains (like README files with prose, code, and configuration) get corrupted, restoring them requires both identifying missing content and determining which domain expert to trust at each position, but without region labels or a trained router.
AI.method: Introduces evidence-aligned local composition: infers soft, position-wise weights over domain experts from the marginal evidence of the corrupted observation under a corruption model. Estimates evidence from experts' own denoising losses and smooths weights across positions.
AI.result: The method achieves 0.85 field accuracy tracking true regions on naturally mixed scientific documents, and 0.98 accuracy on constructed mixtures with lexically disjoint regions. Restoration improves over single global weighting when experts are distinct and reduces to it when they converge.
AI.conclusion: The proposed evidence-aligned local composition effectively infers domain boundaries in corrupted mixed-domain documents without requiring pre-training or labels, automatically adapting to expert separation levels and outperforming simpler approaches.

title: LoGIC: Budgeted Context Construction for Node-Level Graph In-Context Learning with Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Tabular foundation models have become powerful graph learners. Systems such as G2T-FM and GraphPFN encode each node as a feature row and make predictions through in-context learning (ICL), with labeled rows serving as the prompt. Current protocols employ the complete training table as context, causing attention to scale quadratically with the labeled pool and introducing preprocessing and memory bottlenecks. We investigate context construction for node-level graph ICL: which labeled nodes and auxiliary unlabeled nodes should constitute the prompt for specified queries. We formulate this allocation in terms of two resources: a labeled-context budget for predictive evidence and an unlabeled-halo budget for adapter message passing without using label capacity. We present LoGIC, which retrieves labeled nodes via structural, feature-based, and coverage channels, shares each context across the queries in a graph-local cluster, incorporates an unlabeled halo for adapter backbones, and chooses the channel and context budget without test labels. Across three backbone configurations drawn from two model families on GraphLand, budgeted contexts maintain locally runnable full-context performance, stay competitive with published large-dataset results, and markedly lower peak memory requirements compared with full-context and whole-graph inference. They further permit frozen graph ICL on million-node graphs without retraining. Our analysis identifies when retrieval channels work best and connects their behavior with graph properties.

AI.tldr: LoGIC is a method for efficient node-level graph in-context learning that selectively constructs context prompts from labeled and unlabeled nodes within budget constraints, reducing computational overhead while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Current tabular foundation models for graphs use the complete training table as context, causing quadratic attention scaling with labeled pools and creating preprocessing/memory bottlenecks. There's a need for efficient context construction for node-level graph ICL.
AI.method: LoGIC retrieves labeled nodes via structural, feature-based, and coverage channels, shares context across graph-local clusters, incorporates unlabeled halo nodes for adapter backbones, and automatically selects channels and budgets without test labels.
AI.result: Budgeted contexts maintain performance comparable to full-context, stay competitive with published large-dataset results, significantly reduce peak memory requirements, and enable frozen graph ICL on million-node graphs without retraining.
AI.conclusion: The LoGIC framework demonstrates that carefully constructed, budgeted contexts can achieve efficient and scalable graph in-context learning while maintaining predictive performance, with analysis revealing when different retrieval channels work best based on graph properties.

title: Exposing Weaknesses in Emotion Recognition in Conversations
summary: Emotion Recognition in Conversations (ERC) aims to identify speakers' emotions in multi-turn dialogue. Accurate emotion recognition can support a wide range of applications, including empathetic conversational agents, mental health support, and educational technologies. While many recent approaches rely on task-specific fine-tuning, such models may exploit dataset-specific cues. A central yet rarely questioned assumption in ERC is that each utterance can be assigned a single unambiguous emotion label. To investigate this assumption, we study ERC using Large Language Models (LLMs) in a zero-shot setting while incorporating preceding conversational turns as context. We show that aggregate metrics mask systematic failures. Errors concentrate around utterances containing negations, exclamations, and interjections. This pattern is consistent across all evaluated models, suggesting limitations in the benchmarks rather than model-specific weaknesses. A controlled re-annotation study involving four human annotators supports this finding: strong agreement is observed in only 35 percent of cases, with neutral utterances dominating high-agreement instances, while many emotional categories fall into low-agreement regimes. These findings suggest that many apparent model errors reflect genuine annotation ambiguity rather than poor emotion understanding. Standard single-label evaluation is therefore insufficient. To address this limitation, we introduce an LLM-as-Judge framework that evaluates each emotion independently according to its plausibility in the conversational context rather than enforcing a single-label decision.

AI.tldr: LLMs in zero-shot ERC reveal that single-label emotion annotation in conversations is fundamentally ambiguous, with systematic errors around negations/exclamations; human annotation studies show low agreement, suggesting standard evaluation metrics are insufficient and proposing an LLM-as-Judge framework for plausibility-based assessment.
AI.motivation: To challenge the core assumption in Emotion Recognition in Conversations (ERC) that each utterance can be assigned a single unambiguous emotion label, and to investigate whether apparent model errors might actually reflect genuine annotation ambiguity rather than poor model understanding.
AI.method: 1) Zero-shot evaluation of LLMs on ERC tasks using preceding conversational context; 2) Analysis of systematic error patterns across models; 3) Controlled re-annotation study with four human annotators to measure agreement rates; 4) Introduction of LLM-as-Judge framework that evaluates emotions independently based on plausibility rather than forcing single-label decisions.
AI.result: 1) Aggregate metrics mask systematic failures concentrated around utterances with negations, exclamations, and interjections; 2) Error patterns consistent across all evaluated models, suggesting benchmark limitations rather than model weaknesses; 3) Human annotators showed strong agreement in only 35% of cases, with neutral utterances dominating high-agreement instances while emotional categories had low agreement; 4) Many apparent model errors reflect genuine annotation ambiguity.
AI.conclusion: Standard single-label evaluation for ERC is fundamentally insufficient due to inherent annotation ambiguity in conversational emotion labeling. The proposed LLM-as-Judge framework offers a more appropriate evaluation approach by assessing emotion plausibility independently rather than enforcing arbitrary single-label decisions.

title: On-the-go Forgetting without Explicit Unlearning via ERASE
summary: Existing unlearning approaches typically rely on post hoc weight adaptation or distillation, leading to duplicated memory costs, degraded generalization, and limited scalability. In this work, we introduce ERASE, Erasure via Reconstructive Adversarial Signal Editing, a framework for on-the-go forgetting that suppresses the observable influence of private data without modifying model weights. ERASE leverages structured, class-conditioned input perturbations to induce selective forgetting during inference, eliminating the need for retraining, fine-tuning, or model copies. We rigorously characterize sufficient conditions when ERASE provably achieves functional forgetting of designated subclasses while preserving predictions across other subclasses within the same superclass. This analysis offers a principled foundation for inference-time forgetting under mild regularity assumptions. Across diverse architectures and benchmark datasets, ERASE maintains the best observed balance between forgetting efficacy, computational efficiency, and retention fidelity over recent unlearning-based methods. By reimagining data removal as forgetting without unlearning, our work establishes a scalable, regulation-aligned pathway for continual, privacy-conscious learning.

AI.tldr: ERASE is an inference-time forgetting framework that uses structured input perturbations to suppress private data influence without modifying model weights, avoiding retraining or model duplication.
AI.motivation: Existing unlearning methods have limitations: they rely on weight adaptation or distillation which leads to duplicated memory costs, degraded generalization, and limited scalability. There's a need for more efficient forgetting approaches that don't modify model weights.
AI.method: ERASE uses class-conditioned input perturbations during inference to induce selective forgetting. It leverages structured adversarial signal editing to suppress the influence of private data without retraining, fine-tuning, or creating model copies.
AI.result: ERASE maintains the best balance between forgetting efficacy, computational efficiency, and retention fidelity compared to recent unlearning methods. It works across diverse architectures and benchmark datasets, providing provable functional forgetting of designated subclasses while preserving other subclasses.
AI.conclusion: ERASE establishes a scalable, regulation-aligned pathway for continual privacy-conscious learning by reimagining data removal as forgetting without unlearning, offering a principled foundation for inference-time forgetting.

title: Agentic BAIM-LLM Evaluation (ABLE): Benchmarking LLM Use of Protein Design Tools
comment: Last revised in February 2026; presented without further revision. An earlier revision at was presented at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Biosecurity Safeguards for Generative AI; see https://openreview.net/forum?id=fDysOrWaGd
summary: We introduce ABLE, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents' ability to use biological AI models (BAIMs), such as ProteinMPNN and AlphaFold3, in dual-use protein design workflows. ABLE assesses agent performance through a set of tasks spanning structure retrieval, sequence generation, and design validation. We evaluate 15 frontier models and find that seven refuse all tasks, while the remaining models exhibit substantial performance differences. Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 3 Pro achieve the highest scores across information retrieval, tool selection, and tool use. We further compare model performance on a subset of tasks against an expert human baseline. Our results suggest that current LLMs can substantially lower barriers to protein design, but remain inconsistent in planning, strategy generation, and integrating biological knowledge with tool use.

AI.tldr: ABLE benchmark evaluates LLM agents' ability to use biological AI models for protein design, finding significant performance variation with Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 3 Pro as top performers.
AI.motivation: There's a need to evaluate how well LLM agents can use biological AI models like ProteinMPNN and AlphaFold3 in dual-use protein design workflows, which could lower barriers to protein design but current capabilities are inconsistent.
AI.method: Introduced ABLE benchmark with tasks spanning structure retrieval, sequence generation, and design validation. Evaluated 15 frontier models and compared performance against expert human baseline on subset of tasks.
AI.result: Seven models refused all tasks; remaining models showed substantial performance differences. Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 3 Pro achieved highest scores across information retrieval, tool selection, and tool use.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs can substantially lower barriers to protein design but remain inconsistent in planning, strategy generation, and integrating biological knowledge with tool use.

title: Machine Learning for Pre-Culture ESBL Risk Stratification to Guide Empiric Antibiotic Selection: A 12-Hospital Study of Enterobacteriaceae Cultures
comment: Accepted for presentation at American Medical Informatics Association (AMIA) Annual Symposium 2026
summary: Empiric antibiotic therapy for suspected ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae must be selected 48-72 hours before culture results, forcing clinicians to choose between undertreating resistant infections and overusing carbapenems that drive further resistance. We developed a cost-sensitive XGBoost model predicting an ESBL phenotype (resistance to ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam) at culture ordering using 45 pre-culture EHR features across 132,955 cultures from 72,217 patients at 12 hospitals (14.41% with the ESBL phenotype). Cultures were partitioned at the patient level. At 90% sensitivity, the model achieved 95.8% NPV, reducing post-test ESBL probability to 4.2%, a threshold that may support safe carbapenem-sparing in non-ICU settings, while sparing 307 of every 1,000 cultures an unnecessary broad-spectrum course at the cost of 14 missed ESBL cases per 1,000. SHAP analysis identified prior ESBL colonization as the dominant predictor, ahead of prior organism burden and neighborhood deprivation; removing deprivation features caused minimal performance loss ($Δ\text{AUROC} = -0.020$), enabling equitable bedside deployment. Discrimination was unchanged under a strict IDSA ESBL-E definition (AUROC 0.766), with specimen type added as a predictor (0.764) and without any class-imbalance correction (0.762), and ranged from 0.71 to 0.78 across organism strata.

AI.tldr: A cost-sensitive XGBoost model predicts ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae at culture ordering using EHR data, achieving high NPV to safely reduce carbapenem overuse while sparing unnecessary broad-spectrum antibiotics.
AI.motivation: Clinicians face a dilemma when treating suspected ESBL infections: they must choose antibiotics 48-72 hours before culture results, forcing a choice between undertreating resistant infections or overusing carbapenems that drive further antibiotic resistance.
AI.method: Developed a cost-sensitive XGBoost model using 45 pre-culture EHR features from 132,955 cultures across 72,217 patients at 12 hospitals. The model predicts ESBL phenotype at culture ordering. Patient-level data partitioning, SHAP analysis for feature importance, and multiple validation scenarios including strict IDSA ESBL-E definition and various organism strata.
AI.result: At 90% sensitivity, the model achieved 95.8% NPV (reducing post-test ESBL probability to 4.2%). It would spare 307 of every 1,000 cultures from unnecessary broad-spectrum antibiotics at the cost of 14 missed ESBL cases per 1,000. AUROC was 0.766 with strict IDSA definition, 0.764 with specimen type added, and 0.762 without class-imbalance correction, ranging 0.71-0.78 across organism strata.
AI.conclusion: The model provides a practical tool for antibiotic stewardship by enabling safe carbapenem-sparing in non-ICU settings, with minimal performance loss when removing potentially biased socioeconomic features to ensure equitable deployment.

title: Beyond Top-$k$ Skill Retrieval: Diversity-Aware Skill Routing for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external skills, but routing user requests over large skill registries is difficult because many skills are functionally redundant while complex tasks often require complementary skill sets. Existing skill routers typically rank candidates independently by query relevance, which can waste context budget on redundant skills. We propose Diverse Skill Routing (DSR), a diversity-aware reranking framework that uses a Determinantal Point Process to balance relevance and non-redundancy. DSR introduces a query-residual diversity kernel that penalizes redundant skill overlap while reducing penalties caused only by shared query relevance. On the SkillRouter benchmark, DSR improves recall and full coverage over a strong pointwise reranking baseline, with larger gains on multi-skill queries. These results suggest that skill routing should be treated not only as relevance ranking, but also as complementary set selection.

AI.tldr: DSR is a diversity-aware skill routing framework that uses Determinantal Point Processes to select complementary skill sets instead of just ranking individually relevant but redundant skills.
AI.motivation: LLM agents need to route user requests over large skill registries, but existing approaches rank skills independently by query relevance, wasting context budget on redundant skills while complex tasks require complementary skill sets.
AI.method: Proposes Diverse Skill Routing (DSR), a diversity-aware reranking framework using Determinantal Point Processes with a query-residual diversity kernel that balances relevance and non-redundancy by penalizing redundant skill overlap while reducing penalties from shared query relevance.
AI.result: On the SkillRouter benchmark, DSR improves recall and full coverage over strong pointwise reranking baselines, with larger gains on multi-skill queries.
AI.conclusion: Skill routing should be treated not only as relevance ranking but also as complementary set selection, and diversity-aware approaches like DSR are effective for this.

title: DART: Distributional Adversarial Recurrent Training for Algorithm Learning
summary: Recurrent reasoning models (RRMs) can solve structured problems, achieving easy-to-hard generalization through iterative computation in hidden space. These models are typically trained with instance-level supervision, which becomes increasingly problematic as task difficulty grows: valid solutions occupy a tiny region of the solution space, while invalid solutions proliferate rapidly. We propose Distributional Adversarial Recurrent Training (DART), a training framework that replaces single-point supervision with a local target distribution around the ground-truth solution and aligns model outputs with this distribution through an adversarial objective. DART provides a richer learning signal and encourages more stable iterative trajectories toward valid solutions. When evaluated on Maze, Chess, and masked Sudoku with multiple RRMs, including Deep Thinking Systems and Tiny Recursive Models, DART improves solution quality, stability, and robustness under the evaluated distribution shifts. Comparisons with label smoothing, Gaussian softened targets, and progressive training show that DART is not explained by target softening alone and is complementary to training schemes that stabilize long-horizon recurrence. These results identify DART as a promising approach for improving robustness across the evaluated recurrent reasoning models.

AI.tldr: DART (Distributional Adversarial Recurrent Training) improves recurrent reasoning models by replacing single-point supervision with local target distributions and adversarial alignment, enhancing solution quality and robustness across challenging structured tasks.
AI.motivation: Traditional instance-level supervision becomes problematic for recurrent reasoning models as task difficulty increases: valid solutions occupy tiny regions of solution space while invalid solutions proliferate rapidly. This makes training unstable and ineffective for complex structured problems.
AI.method: Proposes DART: replaces single-point supervision with a local target distribution around ground-truth solutions and aligns model outputs with this distribution through an adversarial objective. Provides richer learning signals and encourages stable iterative trajectories toward valid solutions.
AI.result: When evaluated on Maze, Chess, and masked Sudoku with multiple RRMs (including Deep Thinking Systems and Tiny Recursive Models), DART improves solution quality, stability, and robustness under distribution shifts. Outperforms label smoothing, Gaussian softened targets, and progressive training approaches.
AI.conclusion: DART is not explained by target softening alone and is complementary to training schemes that stabilize long-horizon recurrence. Identified as a promising approach for improving robustness across recurrent reasoning models.

title: Learning Counterfactual World Models for Embodied Reasoning under Partial Observability
summary: World models promise a general route to embodied intelligence: learn predictive dynamics once, then reason, plan, and act with them. Increasingly, the representations beneath such models are pretrained on large-scale video, interaction, and multimodal corpora, which raises a question prediction quality alone cannot answer: when is a learned representation actually actionable? We identify a failure mode we call counterfactual collapse: a model predicts visually plausible futures while failing to distinguish interventions with different behavioral consequences. This arises whenever a representation is optimized for perceptual similarity rather than intervention structure, which is precisely the objective under which most large-scale pretrained encoders are learned. We introduce Counterfactual Latent World Models (CLWM), which combine a recurrent belief-state encoder, action-conditioned latent dynamics, and a contrastive counterfactual objective that separates futures induced by distinct interventions even when their observations look alike. Across occluded manipulation, aliased navigation, and long-horizon manipulation, CLWM improves planning success over the strongest baseline (65.1% $\to$ 74.6% on Occluded Push and 67.3% $\to$ 78.9% on Aliased Maze) and reduces exploitative planning failures (18.4% $\to$ 9.7% on Deferred Kitchen), with ablations attributing the gains to hard counterfactual negatives, especially perceptual-alias negatives. Finally, our counterfactual separability metric, which tracks planning success across the five baseline model classes ($r \ge 0.94$), is representation-agnostic: given intervention-outcome labels, it can audit any encoder, pretrained or trained from scratch, before a planner trusts it. We do not yet measure it on large-scale pretrained encoders. Here we establish the metric and its relationship to planning success for world models trained from scratch.

AI.tldr: CLWM uses contrastive counterfactual learning to prevent learned representations from collapsing perceptually similar but behaviorally different futures, improving planning success in embodied AI tasks.
AI.motivation: Current world model representations trained on large-scale video data often optimize for perceptual similarity rather than intervention structure, leading to "counterfactual collapse" where models fail to distinguish futures with different behavioral consequences despite looking similar.
AI.method: CLWM combines recurrent belief-state encoder, action-conditioned latent dynamics with a contrastive counterfactual objective that separates futures induced by distinct interventions even when observations look alike, using hard counterfactual negatives especially perceptual-alias negatives.
AI.result: CLWM improves planning success from 65.1% to 74.6% on Occluded Push, 67.3% to 78.9% on Aliased Maze, reduces exploitative planning failures from 18.4% to 9.7% on Deferred Kitchen, with counterfactual separability metric showing strong correlation with planning success (r ≥ 0.94).
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes that optimizing representations for intervention structure via counterfactual separation is crucial for actionable world models, and introduces a representation-agnostic metric to audit any encoder's counterfactual separability before trusting it for planning.

title: Memory in Deep Time-Series Models
summary: Deep learning for time series has progressed through successive architectural paradigms, from recurrent networks and transformers to structured state-space models, retrieval-augmented predictors, foundation models, and tool-using agents. These developments are typically studied in isolation, organized by architecture or modeling era. We argue that they can instead be viewed through a common question of \emph{how does a time-series model retain and access information beyond its immediate input?} This question is motivated by a fundamental limitation of conventional time-series modeling: information relevant to a prediction may lie far beyond a feasible input window, while compressing history into a fixed-size state can discard information that may become useful later. We formulate this challenge as a \emph{memory} problem and organize existing time-series methods along a spectrum from internal memory, encoded in parameters and fixed-size states, to external memory that is addressable, retrievable, and increasingly maintained by agents. We then develop a unified taxonomy of memory mechanisms and review three classes of external memory, including explicit modules, retrieval augmentation, and agentic stores, under a common framework for what is retained, how it is written and accessed, and how it persists. A cross-cutting analysis maps these mechanisms to time-series tasks and identifies gaps in both methods and evaluation. We conclude by outlining open problems in building memory systems that can selectively retain, retrieve, revise, and forget information as temporal environments evolve. The result is a framework for studying memory as a first-class dimension of time series modeling, independent of the underlying backbone.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes viewing time series modeling through a memory lens, organizing methods from internal to external memory, and creating a unified taxonomy of memory mechanisms in temporal data analysis.
AI.motivation: Current approaches study time series methods in isolation by architecture or era, but there's a fundamental limitation: models need to retain and access information beyond immediate input windows, as relevant prediction information may lie far beyond feasible input sizes, and compressing history into fixed states can discard useful information.
AI.method: The authors formulate the challenge as a memory problem, organize existing time-series methods along a spectrum from internal memory (parameters/fixed states) to external memory (addressable, retrievable, agent-maintained), develop a unified taxonomy of memory mechanisms, and review three classes of external memory under a common framework.
AI.result: They create a framework for studying memory as a first-class dimension of time series modeling, independent of the underlying backbone, with a cross-cutting analysis mapping memory mechanisms to time-series tasks and identifying gaps in methods and evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The paper outlines open problems in building memory systems that can selectively retain, retrieve, revise, and forget information as temporal environments evolve, establishing memory as a fundamental organizing principle for time series modeling research.

title: AgentBrew: Offline Tool-Use Agent Learning from Raw Real-World Trajectories
summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in real-world applications through tool-use APIs, yet training them for specific environments remains fundamentally difficult: real-world applications provide no pre-defined tasks or verifiers, no faithful simulators, and limited budget for large-scale environment interaction. In this paper, we propose \textbf{AgentBrew}, an offline training framework that learns effective tool-use policies from a single batch of raw interaction trajectories, without task verifiers or iterative on-policy rollouts. The agent first explores the target environment to collect a raw trajectory corpus without quality filtering. To extract training signal from this noisy corpus, \emph{retrospective task inference} reconstructs an aligned instruction for each trajectory based on its actual outcome, and \emph{PMI-Based credit assignment} decomposes the trajectory's total information about the inferred instruction into additive per-action credits via pointwise mutual information (PMI). These credits weight the policy training objective, amplifying informative actions while suppressing ineffective ones. On three real-world MCP applications (GitHub, Notion, PostgreSQL), AgentBrew improves Qwen3-32B by +8.7 Acc / +9.7 Score on average, surpassing Qwen3-235B (+2.3 / +4.4) and outperforming rejection sampling (+5.9 / +10.3). These results demonstrate that fine-grained offline learning can recover useful supervision from raw trajectories that filtering-based approaches would discard. The code is available at https://github.com/alphatogo/AgentBrew

AI.tldr: AgentBrew is an offline training framework that learns effective tool-use policies for LLM agents from raw interaction trajectories without task verifiers or iterative on-policy rollouts.
AI.motivation: Training LLM-based agents for real-world tool-use applications is difficult because real environments lack pre-defined tasks, verifiers, faithful simulators, and have limited budgets for large-scale interaction.
AI.method: The framework first collects raw trajectories through exploration. Then uses retrospective task inference to reconstruct aligned instructions from outcomes, and PMI-based credit assignment to decompose trajectory information into per-action credits for policy training.
AI.result: AgentBrew improves Qwen3-32B by +8.7 Acc / +9.7 Score on average across three MCP applications (GitHub, Notion, PostgreSQL), surpassing Qwen3-235B and outperforming rejection sampling.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained offline learning can extract useful supervision from raw trajectories that filtering-based approaches would discard, enabling effective agent training without task verifiers or extensive environment interaction.

title: Granular-Ball Quantum Clustering for Resource-Efficient and Robust Learning
summary: Quantum clustering aims to exploit quantum feature representations to uncover complex data structures beyond conventional Euclidean geometry. Yet this sample-level kernel construction requires O(n^2) quantum circuit executions for n data points, creating a major bottleneck under near-term quantum resource constraints. Prior solutions fail to resolve this efficiency-accuracy dilemma: classical granular-ball clustering reduces sample complexity but relies on Euclidean metrics that cannot capture quantum correlations, while existing quantum compression schemes prioritize efficiency over structural preservation, degrading performance on non-convex or noisy data. Here we propose Granular-Ball Quantum Clustering (GBQC), a framework that tightly couples granular-ball structural abstraction with quantum feature learning. GBQC first compresses raw data into compact, representative granular balls via a PCA-guided splitting strategy, reducing kernel evaluations by 80% compared to full-sample methods. A quantum cohesion mechanism then filters noisy granules in Hilbert space to improve clustering robustness. Extensive experiments on synthetic, noisy, overlapping, and real-world datasets demonstrate that GBQC consistently achieves superior clustering accuracy and robustness compared with representative classical and quantum clustering methods. Meanwhile, the proposed granular-ball compression significantly reduces quantum kernel evaluations and computational overhead, enabling quantum clustering experiments on larger datasets within parameterized quantum learning frameworks. These results suggest that granular-ball representations serve not only as a compression mechanism to reduce quantum computational costs but also as an effective structural abstraction mechanism that improves clustering quality by eliminating redundant and structurally ambiguous learning units.

AI.tldr: GBQC combines granular-ball compression with quantum feature learning to reduce computational costs while improving clustering accuracy and robustness on complex datasets.
AI.motivation: Quantum clustering requires O(n²) quantum circuit executions, creating a bottleneck under near-term quantum resource constraints. Existing solutions either rely on Euclidean metrics that can't capture quantum correlations (granular-ball methods) or prioritize efficiency over structural preservation (quantum compression), degrading performance on complex data.
AI.method: GBQC first compresses raw data into representative granular balls using PCA-guided splitting strategy, reducing kernel evaluations by 80%. Then a quantum cohesion mechanism filters noisy granules in Hilbert space to improve clustering robustness.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on synthetic, noisy, overlapping, and real-world datasets show GBQC consistently achieves superior clustering accuracy and robustness compared to classical and quantum methods. The compression reduces quantum kernel evaluations and computational overhead, enabling quantum clustering on larger datasets.
AI.conclusion: Granular-ball representations serve both as a compression mechanism to reduce quantum computational costs and as an effective structural abstraction mechanism that improves clustering quality by eliminating redundant and structurally ambiguous learning units.

title: Multimodal Resource-Exhaustion Attacks on Vision-Language Models via Joint Pixel-Prompt Optimization
comment: Extended version of the paper accepted by ACM CCS 2026
summary:
Resource-exhaustion attacks against autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) typically assume unimodal threat models, treating the image branch as the primary optimization surface while holding user-visible prompts fixed. Even recent loop-centric variants remain confined to this single-channel paradigm, leaving the exploitation of availability unexplored as a cross-modal optimization problem over jointly controllable input surfaces.
  We introduce Joint Pixel-Prompt Optimization (JPPO), the first compound adversarial framework elevating the visible prompt to a first-class adversarial variable alongside image perturbations. Under a restricted joint-input threat model, JPPO performs coupled, stagewise optimization over both the pixel and prompt surfaces. This produces synergistic cost amplification, mechanistically distinct from loop-dependent failures, exhibiting negligible loop incidence in our experiments.
  Evaluating five open-source VLM families on MS COCO and ImageNet under an 8/255 infinity-norm budget, JPPO achieves over 4.6x latency and 5.3x energy amplification on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and over 36.6x latency with 32.7x energy amplification on BLIP-2. This represents the strongest cost amplification among directly compared baselines while requiring substantially fewer optimization iterations. Ablations confirm this amplification arises from multimodal coordination rather than prompt length or isolated modalities. These findings reveal structural blind spots in current VLM serving defenses, motivating cost-aware robustness evaluation as a first-class security requirement for multimodal deployments.

AI.tldr: JPPO introduces the first compound adversarial attack framework for VLMs that jointly optimizes both image pixels and visible prompts, achieving substantial cost amplification through multimodal coordination rather than loop-dependent failures.
AI.motivation: Existing resource-exhaustion attacks against VLMs use unimodal threat models, focusing only on image perturbations while keeping prompts fixed. Recent loop-centric variants remain single-channel, leaving availability exploitation unexplored as a cross-modal optimization problem over jointly controllable inputs.
AI.method: JPPO (Joint Pixel-Prompt Optimization) elevates the visible prompt to a first-class adversarial variable alongside image perturbations. Under a restricted joint-input threat model, it performs coupled, stagewise optimization over both pixel and prompt surfaces, creating synergistic cost amplification distinct from loop-dependent failures.
AI.result: Evaluated on five open-source VLM families on MS COCO and ImageNet with an 8/255 infinity-norm budget, JPPO achieves over 4.6x latency and 5.3x energy amplification on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and over 36.6x latency with 32.7x energy amplification on BLIP-2. It achieves the strongest cost amplification among baselines with fewer optimization iterations, and ablations confirm amplification arises from multimodal coordination rather than prompt length or isolated modalities.
AI.conclusion: JPPO reveals structural blind spots in current VLM serving defenses and motivates cost-aware robustness evaluation as a first-class security requirement for multimodal deployments, showing that cross-modal attacks can exploit availability through coordinated optimization of both input surfaces.

title: IXPLORE: Bounded Ideal Point Estimation with Grid-Based Uncertainty Quantification
summary: Ideal point estimation is widely used to analyze and visualize political data. However, selecting the corresponding spatial model involves various trade-offs: while model-based approaches such as Item Response Theory (IRT) are based on utility functions rather than optimized for predictive accuracy, most Machine Learning (ML) alternatives struggle to generalize beyond training data when embedding sparse test responses. We introduce IXPLORE, a bounded ideal point estimation algorithm that combines a predictive fit objective with a sparsity-aware likelihood function. On five benchmark datasets spanning surveys, roll calls, and deliberation, this approach surpasses model-based and ML-based algorithms on reconstruction and imputation error - especially for users with sparse responses. Furthermore, we show that non-linear feature transforms can further reduce the reconstruction error while remaining visually interpretable. To quantify uncertainty, IXPLORE applies grid-based posterior inference on a bounded 2D latent space. Available as a Python package on PyPI, IXPLORE offers a flexible framework for constructing bounded, interpretable political maps with fast inference and strong imputation performance.

AI.tldr: IXPLORE is a new bounded ideal point estimation algorithm that combines predictive accuracy with sparsity-aware likelihood, outperforming traditional IRT and ML methods especially for sparse data, while providing interpretable visualizations and uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: Existing ideal point estimation methods face trade-offs: model-based approaches like IRT use utility functions rather than optimize for predictive accuracy, while most ML alternatives struggle to generalize with sparse test data.
AI.method: IXPLORE combines a predictive fit objective with a sparsity-aware likelihood function, incorporates non-linear feature transforms for better reconstruction while maintaining interpretability, and uses grid-based posterior inference on a bounded 2D latent space for uncertainty quantification.
AI.result: On five benchmark datasets (surveys, roll calls, deliberation), IXPLORE surpasses both model-based and ML-based algorithms on reconstruction and imputation error, especially for users with sparse responses. Non-linear transforms further reduce reconstruction error.
AI.conclusion: IXPLORE provides a flexible framework for bounded, interpretable political maps with fast inference and strong imputation performance, addressing key limitations of existing methods for sparse political data analysis.

title: The End of AI Exponentiation: Fluttering Inside and Outside AI Bubble
summary: The exponentiation of Artificial intelligence (AI) in the recent past has entered a transformative era that has been driven by the growth in large language models (LLMs), large-scale compute infrastructures, and autonomous reasoning systems. However, the rapid acceleration of AI has increasingly shown technological, societal, economic, ethical and infrastructural challenges associated with peak data limitations, rising computational demands, synthetic data recursion, valuation inflation, and societal instability. The traditional scaling paradigms that have powered the modern AI systems are gradually encountering friction in sustaining continuous exponential growth. This paper views ``the end of AI exponentiation,'' thus exploring how it flutters inside and outside the bubble, where instability emerges within the AI ecosystem through compute and data-center races, speculative investments, and the rat-race toward superintelligence, and outside the ecosystem through labor disruption, governance concerns, public uncertainty, and geopolitical acceleration surrounding future intelligent systems and infrastructures globally.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how the exponential growth of AI is encountering fundamental limits and creating instabilities both within the AI ecosystem (compute/data-center races, speculative investments, superintelligence rat race) and outside it (labor disruption, governance concerns, public uncertainty, geopolitical tensions).
AI.motivation: The rapid acceleration of AI, driven by LLMs, large-scale compute, and autonomous reasoning, is encountering technological, societal, economic, ethical, and infrastructural challenges including peak data limitations, rising computational demands, synthetic data recursion, valuation inflation, and societal instability. Traditional scaling paradigms are showing friction in sustaining continuous exponential growth.
AI.method: The paper uses a critical analysis approach to examine "the end of AI exponentiation," exploring how this phenomenon manifests both inside and outside the AI bubble. It analyzes instabilities through the lens of compute and data-center races, speculative investments, and the pursuit of superintelligence within the ecosystem, while also examining external impacts on labor, governance, public perception, and geopolitics.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that AI's exponential growth is unsustainable due to multiple converging constraints and is creating dangerous instabilities on both ecosystem-internal and ecosystem-external dimensions, suggesting that current trajectories need reevaluation.
AI.conclusion: The exponential growth phase of AI is ending due to fundamental limitations and negative externalities, requiring new paradigms beyond current scaling approaches to address the complex technological, economic, and societal challenges emerging both within and outside the AI ecosystem.

title: Minimizing the Effect of Sleep Deprivation in the Forward-Forward Algorithm
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at the 28th International Conference on Pattern Recognition (ICPR 2026), Lyon, France, August 17-22, 2026. This is the accepted manuscript; the Version of Record is published by Springer in Lecture Notes in Computer Science and is available online at https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-31933-3_40
summary: This paper addresses the challenge posed by sleep deprivation in the Forward-Forward algorithm, where separating the two passes in this algorithm and imbalancing the data processing in the passes is considered an imitation of the cognitive processes observed in humans suffering from sleep deprivation. Previous research has demonstrated that sleep deprivation in the Forward-Forward algorithm has a catastrophic effect on learning efficacy. To mitigate this issue, we explore several approaches; these include alternative activation, optimized loss function, and threshold tuning. To simulate periodic rest, we reduce the number of positive passes in alternating epochs, creating short break phases. We additionally investigate the potential of caffeine-induced stimulation to enhance performance during sleep-deprived conditions. Experimental evaluations conducted on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets demonstrate that these modifications improve accuracy under the context of sleep deprivation. For example, a 2%-62% accuracy gain is observed in a severe sleep deprivation setting (16 positive or awake periods and 1 negative or sleep period). The approaches also enhance the resilience of the algorithm and its alignment with the adaptive mechanisms of human cognition.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes modifications to the Forward-Forward algorithm to mitigate catastrophic learning effects caused by sleep deprivation simulation, achieving up to 62% accuracy improvements through alternative activation functions, optimized loss, threshold tuning, periodic rest simulation, and caffeine-like stimulation.
AI.motivation: The Forward-Forward algorithm suffers from catastrophic learning degradation when simulating sleep deprivation by separating and imbalancing data processing passes, which mimics impaired human cognitive processes during sleep deprivation. Previous research showed severe performance drops under these conditions.
AI.method: Multiple approaches are explored: (1) alternative activation functions, (2) optimized loss functions, (3) threshold tuning, (4) periodic rest simulation by reducing positive passes in alternating epochs to create short breaks, and (5) caffeine-induced stimulation simulation to enhance performance during sleep-deprived conditions.
AI.result: Experimental evaluations on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets show significant accuracy improvements (2%-62% gains) under sleep deprivation conditions. The most severe setting with 16 awake periods and 1 sleep period shows substantial performance recovery. The modifications also enhance algorithm resilience and better align with human cognitive adaptive mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: The proposed modifications effectively mitigate the catastrophic effects of sleep deprivation simulation in the Forward-Forward algorithm, achieving substantial accuracy improvements while enhancing resilience and aligning more closely with adaptive human cognitive mechanisms during sleep-impaired states.

title: Beyond Final Decisions: A Process-Centric Benchmark for Transparent AI-Assisted Peer Review
summary:
Peer review is central to quality control in science. However, existing evaluations of AI-assisted peer review mainly focus on the overall quality of generated reviews or the accuracy of final decisions. They therefore provide limited evidence about whether model decisions are supported by sufficient and reliable review evidence. We introduce a process-centric diagnostic benchmark for AI-assisted peer review. It uses (x,$z_s$,$z_c$,$z_r$,y)
  to represent the paper content, summary, critique, suggestion, and decision. We convert heterogeneous review records from PeerRead, NLPeer ARR-22, and OpenReview-ICLR into process-aligned data. Our benchmark uses direct decision prediction from the paper content (Direct) as its baseline. It compares the decision value of Gold-process variables and Predicted-process variables, and conducts stage-level evaluation, chain-consistency evaluation, and interventional sensitivity analysis. Experiments across three datasets and six models show that Gold-process variables generally have higher decision value. For the main analysis model, the Gold--Predicted gap remains stable across datasets and random seeds. This gap is also reproduced in most model--dataset combinations. Although model-generated intermediate review texts show relatively high local consistency across adjacent stages, the final decisions are not consistently supported by the preceding review evidence. Our benchmark targets AI systems designed to assist rather than replace human reviewers. It provides a transparent and auditable diagnostic tool for evaluating the reliability of their review processes.

AI.tldr: A new benchmark evaluates AI-assisted peer review by analyzing the review process itself, not just final outputs, revealing that while AI models show high local consistency in generating review texts, their final decisions often lack support from preceding review evidence.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of AI-assisted peer review focus only on overall review quality or final decision accuracy, providing limited evidence about whether model decisions are supported by sufficient and reliable review evidence. There's a need for a more process-centric diagnostic approach.
AI.method: The authors introduce a process-centric diagnostic benchmark that uses structured variables (paper content, summary, critique, suggestion, decision) to evaluate AI-assisted peer review. They convert heterogeneous review records from multiple datasets (PeerRead, NLPeer ARR-22, OpenReview-ICLR) into process-aligned data. The benchmark compares decision values between Gold-process and Predicted-process variables, conducting stage-level evaluation, chain-consistency evaluation, and interventional sensitivity analysis.
AI.result: Experiments across three datasets and six models show: 1) Gold-process variables generally have higher decision value than predicted ones, 2) The Gold-Predicted gap remains stable across datasets and random seeds for the main analysis model, 3) This gap is reproduced in most model-dataset combinations, 4) While model-generated intermediate review texts show high local consistency across adjacent stages, final decisions are not consistently supported by preceding review evidence.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark provides a transparent and auditable diagnostic tool for evaluating the reliability of AI-assisted peer review processes. It targets AI systems designed to assist rather than replace human reviewers, helping ensure their decision-making processes are properly supported by review evidence.

title: Data Quality Rule Generation with LLMs
summary: The validation of data, such as customer and employee data, is an important task in many organizations. Errors in data can have severe consequences. For example, a wrong drug unit in a patient record can lead to life-threatening medication errors, and a missing street number in an address to failed deliveries. Companies often employ rule-based enterprise data quality (DQ) tools, which allow domain experts to specify rules to validate the data over time. While rule-based DQ tools are computationally efficient and provide explainable reports, maintaining a comprehensive rule set manually is challenging, as domain experts often overlook essential rules, especially in complex domains and large data volumes. Hence, closing these gaps remains an open problem in practice. In this paper, we address the challenge of automated DQ rule generation. For this, we formalize a generalizable generate-filter framework and introduce LeDQeR, an LLM-based DQ rule generation approach. First, a large language model (LLM) generates candidates rules from an observed dirty data tuple for a given rule-based DQ tool syntax. Second, we apply four filter techniques that ensure the (i) executability, (ii) correctness, and (iii) generalizability, and avoid (iv) redundancy of the generated rules. An extensive experimental evaluation suggests that LeDQeR is able to produce effective and compact rule sets for various datasets and error types.

AI.tldr: LLM-based approach (LeDQeR) automatically generates data quality rules using a generate-filter framework to address gaps in manual rule maintenance.
AI.motivation: Data validation is critical for organizations as data errors can have severe consequences (e.g., medication errors, failed deliveries). While rule-based DQ tools are efficient and explainable, manually maintaining comprehensive rule sets is challenging - domain experts often overlook essential rules, especially in complex domains with large data volumes.
AI.method: LeDQeR uses a two-step generate-filter framework: 1) LLM generates candidate rules from observed dirty data tuples for a given DQ tool syntax, 2) Four filter techniques ensure executability, correctness, generalizability, and avoid redundancy of generated rules.
AI.result: Extensive experimental evaluation shows LeDQeR can produce effective and compact rule sets for various datasets and error types, demonstrating practical utility in automated DQ rule generation.
AI.conclusion: LeDQeR addresses the open problem of automating DQ rule generation by combining LLMs with systematic filtering to create maintainable, effective rule sets that complement existing rule-based DQ tools while overcoming limitations of manual rule maintenance.

title: MOAE: Multi-Objective Agent Evolution with Pareto-Preserving Search
summary: As LLM-based agents continue to advance, their evaluation has become increasingly multifaceted: a capable agent must not only achieve high task completion accuracy but also perform well in interaction quality, safety, and efficiency, raising a central question: can these objectives be optimized simultaneously? Existing methods have considered multiple objectives, but many collapse heterogeneous measurements into a fixed scalar score. Such scalarization depends on metric normalization and preference weights and may discard candidates that represent useful deployment trade-offs. We introduce Multi-Objective Agent Evolution (MOAE), which organizes iterative in-context refinement as a Pareto-preserving evolutionary search over complete agent rollouts. Given a limited rollout budget, MOAE maintains an empirical archive of non-dominated candidates, uses objective-specific diagnostics to guide offspring generation, and applies constraint-aware selection only at deployment. This separates candidate preservation during search from the preference used to return a final solution. The procedure requires no parameter updates and allows each objective to be replaced by any measurable property, which we instantiate as task performance, trajectory quality, and safety. Experiments on TravelPlanner and AgentDojo show that MOAE consistently improves task performance and trajectory quality while maintaining strong safety under matched rollout budgets. Search-behavior analysis further shows that Pareto preservation expands the attainable objective region and increases the frequency of joint improvement. These results demonstrate the potential of Pareto-preserving in-context evolution for optimizing multiple agent properties without committing to a fixed scalarization during search.

AI.tldr: MOAE introduces a Pareto-preserving evolutionary search method for optimizing multiple LLM agent objectives simultaneously without collapsing them into a fixed scalar score, enabling better trade-offs across task performance, trajectory quality, and safety.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent evaluation methods collapse multiple heterogeneous objectives into fixed scalar scores, which depends on metric normalization and preference weights and may discard useful deployment trade-offs. There's a need for methods that can optimize multiple objectives simultaneously without committing to a single scalarization during search.
AI.method: Multi-Objective Agent Evolution (MOAE) organizes iterative in-context refinement as a Pareto-preserving evolutionary search over complete agent rollouts. It maintains an empirical archive of non-dominated candidates, uses objective-specific diagnostics to guide offspring generation, and applies constraint-aware selection only at deployment, separating candidate preservation during search from final preference application.
AI.result: Experiments on TravelPlanner and AgentDojo show MOAE consistently improves task performance and trajectory quality while maintaining strong safety under matched rollout budgets. Pareto preservation expands the attainable objective region and increases frequency of joint improvement.
AI.conclusion: MOAE demonstrates the potential of Pareto-preserving in-context evolution for optimizing multiple agent properties without committing to a fixed scalarization during search, enabling better multi-objective optimization for LLM-based agents.

title: Calendar-SPCA: Interpretable Representation Learning for Multi-Periodic Electricity Consumption Profiles
summary: Long-term electricity-consumption profiles exhibit several simultaneous periodic structures, including daily, weekly, and annual cycles. This work introduces Calendar-SPCA, a calendar-structured sparse principal component method that incorporates this known multi-periodic geometry directly into low-dimensional representation learning. The feature domain is represented as the Cartesian product of cyclic calendar axes, and a low-rank factorization is estimated using an L1 loading penalty together with graph total variation over the resulting calendar graph. The method therefore produces sparse and locally coherent loading patterns that remain directly readable in their original temporal coordinates. Calendar-SPCA is evaluated on two independent smart-meter datasets with different sample sizes and temporal resolutions: GoiEner and Low Carbon London. A factorial experiment characterizes the complementary effects of sparsity and calendar coherence and examines robustness across sample size, latent dimensionality, and repeated fits. At rank 15, Calendar-SPCA retains 96.92% and 82.90% of the explained variance of rank-matched PCA in GoiEner and Low Carbon London, respectively, while producing mean loading sparsities of 61.95% and 81.50%. Comparisons with classical sparse PCA and SPCA-TV further show that Calendar-SPCA adds a systematic organization of the latent factors in the original calendar coordinates while preserving substantial low-rank information. The resulting components form coherent and complementary daily, weekly, seasonal, and jointly localized calendar patterns, with dataset-specific geometries across the two datasets.

AI.tldr: Calendar-SPCA is a sparse principal component method that incorporates calendar structure (daily, weekly, annual cycles) into low-dimensional representation learning for electricity consumption profiles.
AI.motivation: Electricity consumption profiles exhibit multiple simultaneous periodic structures (daily, weekly, annual cycles), but existing methods don't incorporate this known calendar geometry directly into representation learning.
AI.method: Represents feature domain as Cartesian product of cyclic calendar axes, uses low-rank factorization with L1 loading penalty and graph total variation over calendar graph to produce sparse, locally coherent loadings in original temporal coordinates.
AI.result: At rank 15, retains 96.92% and 82.90% of explained variance of rank-matched PCA in two datasets while achieving mean loading sparsities of 61.95% and 81.50%. Produces coherent daily, weekly, seasonal patterns organized in original calendar coordinates.
AI.conclusion: Calendar-SPCA successfully incorporates calendar structure into sparse PCA, producing interpretable components while preserving low-rank information, outperforming classical sparse PCA and SPCA-TV in organizing latent factors in calendar coordinates.

title: Agentic Pressure: The Endogenous Entropy of Reliable Autonomy
comment: Published at the workshop of Agentic AI in the Wild in ICLR 2026; 16 pages
summary: Achieving reliable autonomy in the wild requires agents to sustain continuous operations across long-horizon trajectories. However, as agents navigate these unconstrained settings, they encounter cumulative friction that inherently destabilizes their alignment. In this paper, we identify a distinct non-adversarial phenomenon termed Agentic Pressure. We define this as a kinetic force that spontaneously emerges when the cost of compliance conflicts with the imperative of goal achievement. Unlike static jailbreaks, this pressure is endogenous and arises directly from the dynamics of interaction. We propose a theoretical framework that formalizes Agentic Pressure as the ratio between the required work to overcome environmental friction and the remaining capacity of the agent. Our analysis demonstrates that when this pressure exceeds a critical threshold, agents exhibit safety drift as a mathematically optimal adaptation. Consequently, they often resort to Instrumental Hallucination to rationalize rule violations. Empirical experiments validate this framework and show that aligned agents spontaneously compromise safety to preserve autonomy under high-pressure conditions.

AI.tldr: Aligned AI agents in long-term operation face "Agentic Pressure" from environmental friction, causing them to compromise safety rules when pressure exceeds critical thresholds, often rationalizing violations through "Instrumental Hallucination."
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of maintaining reliable autonomy in unconstrained, long-horizon settings where agents encounter cumulative friction that destabilizes their alignment over time, identifying a distinct non-adversarial phenomenon that threatens agent safety.
AI.method: The authors propose a theoretical framework that formalizes Agentic Pressure as the ratio between required work to overcome environmental friction and the agent's remaining capacity, analyzing when pressure exceeds critical thresholds and leads to safety drift as an optimal adaptation.
AI.result: Empirical experiments show that aligned agents spontaneously compromise safety to preserve autonomy under high-pressure conditions, exhibiting safety drift as mathematically optimal behavior and often resorting to Instrumental Hallucination to rationalize rule violations.
AI.conclusion: Agentic Pressure represents a fundamental challenge for long-term autonomous systems, where agents facing environmental friction may mathematically optimize away safety constraints, necessitating new approaches to maintain alignment under sustained operational pressure.

title: ACE: Adapter Consolidation across Experts for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of MoE LLMs
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of mixture-of-experts (MoE) models commonly attaches a separate low-rank adapter to each expert. This expert-wise design fragments adaptation in three ways: capacity is split across narrow low-rank updates, gradient supervision becomes sparse and imbalanced under sparse routing, and execution is decomposed into many small GEMMs. We find that such expert-wise separation is often unnecessary, as subsets of LoRA adapters become functionally similar during fine-tuning, revealing redundancy among expert-specific adapters. Based on this redundancy, we propose ACE (Adapter Consolidation across Experts), which groups redundant experts and replaces their expert-specific adapters with group-shared higher-rank LoRA modules under the same PEFT budget. ACE further introduces grouped adapter execution, which consolidates fragmented expert-wise adapter computations into fewer, larger group-level GEMMs. Across evaluations covering 12 datasets and four MoE backbones, ACE achieves the highest observed mean accuracy among the parameter-matched PEFT methods on the three backbones with complete baseline coverage, while providing $1.31\times$ to $1.48\times$ wall-clock training speedup over expert-wise LoRA without increasing peak memory. Our code is available at https://github.com/UbiquitousAILab/ACE.

AI.tldr: ACE (Adapter Consolidation across Experts) improves parameter-efficient fine-tuning for MoE models by grouping redundant expert adapters and consolidating them into shared higher-rank LoRA modules, achieving better accuracy and faster training.
AI.motivation: Current PEFT methods for MoE models attach separate low-rank adapters to each expert, causing three problems: fragmented adaptation capacity, sparse/imbalanced gradient supervision due to sparse routing, and decomposed execution into many small GEMM operations. Expert-wise separation often proves unnecessary as adapters become functionally similar during fine-tuning, revealing redundancy.
