AI.method: ACE groups redundant experts and replaces their expert-specific adapters with group-shared higher-rank LoRA modules under the same PEFT budget. It introduces grouped adapter execution that consolidates fragmented expert-wise adapter computations into fewer, larger group-level GEMM operations.
AI.result: Across 12 datasets and four MoE backbones, ACE achieves the highest mean accuracy among parameter-matched PEFT methods on three backbones with complete baseline coverage. It provides 1.31× to 1.48× wall-clock training speedup over expert-wise LoRA without increasing peak memory consumption.
AI.conclusion: ACE effectively addresses the fragmentation issues in expert-wise PEFT for MoE models by leveraging observed redundancy in expert adapters, demonstrating that consolidating adapters across functionally similar experts improves both accuracy and training efficiency while maintaining the same parameter budget.

title: Generator-Independent Runtime Assurance under Partial Observation
summary: Proposal-based controllers---learned policies, language-model planners, and other black-box \emph{generators}---are increasingly deployed behind runtime verification gates. We ask when the closed-loop safety guarantee decouples from the generator. The prevailing per-candidate certification pattern does not compose: under retry or best-of-$k$ selection a per-candidate false-admission level $α$ can inflate to $1-(1-α)^{k}$. Our main theorem shows that \emph{simultaneous setwise soundness}---certifying a set of admissible proposals containing no nonviable action---is necessary and sufficient for generator-independent \emph{admission soundness}, the worst case over all generators of executing a nonviable proposal equalling the probability of setwise failure; together with a design-time certificate and a no-bypass rule it is sufficient for \emph{contract safety}, with violation bound $Γ+\sum_t\varepsilon_t+η$ invariant under arbitrary, even adversarial, replacement of the generator. A second theorem bounds every admission mechanism under partial observation: for a fixed probing and admission policy, if two state hypotheses whose information laws lie within total-variation distance $δ$ require different safe decisions, then $\abar+β+δ\ge1$. A sequential risk ledger makes the guarantee implementable with time-uniform confidence tubes, and shows that deterministic admission computations concentrate all statistical risk in state estimation. Simplex-style runtime assurance and control-barrier-function filtering are recovered as degenerate cases.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a theoretical framework for generator-independent safety guarantees in runtime verification systems, showing that simultaneous setwise soundness is necessary and sufficient for admission soundness, with applications to various runtime assurance approaches.
AI.motivation: With the increasing deployment of proposal-based controllers (learned policies, language-model planners, etc.) behind runtime verification gates, there's a need to understand when closed-loop safety guarantees can be decoupled from the specific generator being used, as current per-candidate certification approaches don't compose well under retry or best-of-k selection.
AI.method: The paper uses theoretical analysis with two main theorems: 1) establishing that simultaneous setwise soundness is necessary and sufficient for generator-independent admission soundness, and 2) bounding admission mechanisms under partial observation. The framework includes sequential risk ledgers and time-uniform confidence tubes to make guarantees implementable.
AI.result: The main result shows that contract safety can be achieved with violation bound Γ+∑ε_t+η that remains invariant under arbitrary (even adversarial) generator replacement. The second theorem provides bounds on admission mechanisms under partial observation, showing deterministic admission computations concentrate statistical risk in state estimation.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a foundational theory for runtime safety verification that generalizes existing approaches like Simplex-style runtime assurance and control-barrier-function filtering, providing composable safety guarantees independent of the specific proposal generator being used.

title: FedSubMuon: Communication-Efficient Federated LLM Fine-Tuning via Structured Subspace Muon
summary: Federated fine-tuning adapts large language models (LLMs) to decentralized client data, but its scalability in cross-device training is often limited by the high communication cost. Muon is an optimizer that improves optimization performance by orthogonalizing momentum for matrix-valued parameters. Existing federated Muon methods demonstrate the benefit of matrix-aware optimization in federated learning, but still require transmitting full layer-size updates and optimizer state. A natural way to reduce communication is to directly apply Muon to LoRA factors, but this changes the optimized object and weakens Muon's matrix-aware update geometry. We propose FedSubMuon, a communication-efficient federated Muon fine-tuning method that optimizes compact coefficient matrices within shared structured subspaces. This design keeps Muon on a single matrix-valued trainable object, while reducing the client upload to compact coefficient matrices. We further introduce FedSubMuon-GT, an accuracy-oriented extension that uses projected gradients to adapt tracked subspace bases toward task-relevant gradient directions. Experiments on instruction tuning and mathematical reasoning show that FedSubMuon-GT achieves the best overall accuracy on four of five dataset-model pairs, while FedSubMuon performs best under all matched communication budgets. On Dolly-15K, the closest communication baseline requires 5.5 times and 1.4 times more total communication on Llama-1B and Qwen-4B, respectively.

AI.tldr: FedSubMuon and FedSubMuon-GT are communication-efficient federated fine-tuning methods that optimize compact coefficient matrices within shared structured subspaces, significantly reducing communication costs while maintaining or improving accuracy compared to existing approaches.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the high communication cost limitation in federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) for cross-device training. Existing federated Muon methods require transmitting full layer-size updates and optimizer states, which is inefficient. While applying Muon to LoRA factors reduces communication, it changes the optimized object and weakens Muon's matrix-aware update geometry.
AI.method: The authors propose two methods: 1) FedSubMuon - optimizes compact coefficient matrices within shared structured subspaces, keeping Muon on a single matrix-valued trainable object while reducing client upload to compact coefficient matrices. 2) FedSubMuon-GT - an accuracy-oriented extension that uses projected gradients to adapt tracked subspace bases toward task-relevant gradient directions.
AI.result: Experiments on instruction tuning and mathematical reasoning show that FedSubMuon-GT achieves the best overall accuracy on four of five dataset-model pairs, while FedSubMuon performs best under all matched communication budgets. On Dolly-15K, the closest communication baseline requires 5.5 times more total communication on Llama-1B and 1.4 times more on Qwen-4B compared to FedSubMuon.
AI.conclusion: FedSubMuon methods successfully address the communication efficiency problem in federated fine-tuning by optimizing compact coefficient matrices within structured subspaces, maintaining Muon's matrix-aware optimization benefits while dramatically reducing communication overhead, making federated fine-tuning more scalable for cross-device training.

title: DAREBench: Deployment-Aware and Reliable Evaluation of Models as Agents
summary: As large language models evolve from question-answering systems into general-purpose agents, evaluation must move beyond static answer correctness to assess multimodal perception, multi-step execution, tool use, and artifact delivery. However, existing benchmarks are often tied to specific task types, execution environments, or scoring protocols, limiting their comparability, interpretability, and reliability for deployment decisions. We introduce DAREBench (Deployment-Aware and Reliable Evaluation of Models as Agents), a benchmark designed to capture workload variation and support reliable agent evaluation. Built on a shared OpenClaw execution environment, DAREBench organizes 233 tasks selected and adapted from 22 source benchmarks into a $2\times3$ workload matrix defined by input modality and execution form, and evaluates them under a unified contract-based protocol with evidence-based score auditing. We evaluate 23 commercial API models and 12 locally deployed open-weight models over 7,587 model--task runs, reporting accuracy and token consumption alongside reference costs for API models. Results show that no single model dominates all workload groups, text and multimodal tasks exhibit distinct accuracy--cost trade-offs, and local open-weight models are competitive in several groups but still trail frontier commercial models overall. These findings suggest that agent deployment and model selection should consider workload profiles, deployment mode, and accuracy--cost trade-offs rather than rely on a single aggregate score.

AI.tldr: DAREBench is a new benchmark for evaluating general-purpose AI agents across diverse workloads with multimodal inputs and multi-step execution, featuring standardized evaluation and cost analysis to inform deployment decisions.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks for evaluating AI agents are limited by being tied to specific task types, execution environments, or scoring protocols, making them non-comparable, less interpretable, and unreliable for real-world deployment decisions. As LLMs evolve into general-purpose agents, evaluation needs to assess more complex capabilities like multimodal perception, multi-step execution, tool use, and artifact delivery.
AI.method: The authors built DAREBench on a shared OpenClaw execution environment, organizing 233 tasks from 22 source benchmarks into a 2×3 workload matrix defined by input modality (text vs. multimodal) and execution form. They use a unified contract-based protocol with evidence-based score auditing, evaluating 23 commercial API models and 12 open-weight models over 7,587 model-task runs, measuring both accuracy and token consumption with reference costs for API models.
AI.result: No single model dominates all workload groups; text and multimodal tasks show distinct accuracy-cost trade-offs; local open-weight models are competitive in several groups but still trail frontier commercial models overall. Performance patterns vary significantly across different workload types rather than showing consistent superiority of any single model.
AI.conclusion: Agent deployment and model selection should consider workload profiles, deployment mode, and accuracy-cost trade-offs rather than relying on a single aggregate score. The benchmark reveals that different models excel in different contexts, emphasizing the need for workload-aware evaluation for practical deployment decisions.

title: Beyond Retraining-Free MoE Compression: A Cost-Normalized Study of Post-Compression Adjustment
summary: Retraining-free MoE compression reduces deployment memory by pruning or merging experts, but often treats the compressed checkpoint as the final artifact. We argue that this view is incomplete: compressed MoE checkpoints are better understood as compressed initializations that benefit from a tiny post-compression adjustment stage. Across two MoE LLM backbones, four pruning/merging methods, three expert-retention ratios, and 28 benchmarks, we compare LM fine-tuning and teacher-based KD under matched small-data budgets and measured GPU costs. Using only 3,000 C4 examples and a single epoch of adjustment, Full FT recovers 37.3% of the original-to-compressed performance gap on average. Moreover, LM fine-tuning is more cost-effective than standard token-level KD, and full-parameter adjustment gives the strongest cost--recovery trade-off among the tested scopes. These results suggest that retraining-free compression should be paired with small post-compression adjustment to recover a substantial portion of the performance lost during compression.

AI.tldr: Compressed MoE checkpoints should be treated as compressed initializations that benefit from small post-compression adjustment, not final artifacts, with full fine-tuning recovering substantial performance gaps cost-effectively.
AI.motivation: Current retraining-free MoE compression methods treat compressed checkpoints as final artifacts, but this view is incomplete. The authors argue compressed MoE checkpoints should instead be seen as compressed initializations that can benefit from small post-compression adjustment to recover performance lost during compression.
AI.method: The study compares LM fine-tuning and teacher-based knowledge distillation under matched small-data budgets and GPU costs. Experiments span two MoE LLM backbones, four pruning/merging methods, three expert-retention ratios, and 28 benchmarks. Post-compression adjustment uses only 3,000 C4 examples with a single epoch.
AI.result: Full fine-tuning recovers 37.3% of the original-to-compressed performance gap on average. LM fine-tuning is more cost-effective than standard token-level KD, and full-parameter adjustment provides the strongest cost-recovery trade-off among tested scopes.
AI.conclusion: Retraining-free compression should be paired with small post-compression adjustment to recover a substantial portion of performance lost during compression, with compressed checkpoints better understood as compressed initializations rather than final artifacts.

title: Explaining AI Agents Through Execution Traces
summary: AI Agents are increasingly deployed in real-world settings, where they interact with external tools and make sequential decisions with limited human oversight. This creates a pressing need for reliable and auditable explanations of what an agent did and why. However, traditional Explainable AI (XAI) methods fall short of providing the process-level transparency required for such interactive, multi-step systems, motivating a paradigm shift toward approaches specifically designed for AI Agents. To address this gap, we present a post-hoc XAI framework that transforms a lengthy agent's execution trace into a structured report and a faithful natural-language explanation explicitly grounded in its observable behavior. Because it relies solely on execution traces, the framework applies across different agent architectures, environments, and tasks. Human and automated evaluations across multiple benchmarks and architectures show that our framework produces high-quality, trace-faithful explanations while reliably identifying unsupported claims, unjustified actions, and evidence gaps, outperforming naive LLM-generated explanations.

AI.tldr: Proposes a post-hoc XAI framework for AI agents that transforms execution traces into structured reports and faithful natural-language explanations, enabling cross-architecture transparency and identifying unsupported claims.
AI.motivation: Traditional XAI methods are inadequate for AI agents operating in real-world settings with sequential decisions and tool interactions, creating a need for process-level transparency and auditable explanations.
AI.method: A post-hoc framework that takes lengthy agent execution traces and converts them into structured reports with natural-language explanations explicitly grounded in observable behavior, working across different architectures and environments.
AI.result: Human and automated evaluations across multiple benchmarks and architectures show the framework produces high-quality, trace-faithful explanations and reliably identifies unsupported claims, unjustified actions, and evidence gaps, outperforming naive LLM-generated explanations.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an effective solution for agent transparency that is architecture-agnostic and can handle complex multi-step interactions, addressing critical needs for audibility and reliability in real-world agent deployments.

title: PhenoBench: Mapping What a Deeply Phenotyped Human Cohort Can Tell Us
comment: 33 pages; 5 main figures and 5 supplementary figures. Project website: https://galsapir.github.io/phenobench-benchmark/ . Code and benchmark materials: https://github.com/galsapir/phenobench-benchmark
summary: Deeply phenotyped cohorts combine clinical, imaging, molecular, and wearable observations across timescales from seconds to years. This breadth can reveal which measurements inform which health-related questions, but heterogeneous analyses are not directly comparable. We present PhenoBench, an executable benchmark built around the Human Phenotype Project, in which more than 13,000 participants have completed the initial visit. Each question fixes the target, eligible population, timing, and allowed information; its evaluation contract specifies the split, metric, baseline, and claim boundary. The benchmark defines 90 clinically grounded tasks across 15 domains and 26 input modalities. Measurements showed question- and representation-dependent predictive value, including positive, near-zero, and negative changes in held-out performance relative to matched baselines. We used PhenoBench to evaluate emerging tabular foundation models across 160 matched regression comparisons spanning 52 tasks. These models ranked above standard task-specific models in aggregate but, averaged across the three pretrained models within each cell, improved on ridge by a median of only 0.004 $R^2$ (95% CI, 0.002--0.006). We then used the same cohort data and evaluation contracts to evaluate 14 language models, collectively covering 40 tasks spanning phenotype recovery, classification, follow-up forecasting, and participant ordering. Without cohort-specific fitting, language models made informative predictions on some tasks, but showed task-specific capability gaps, shared failures of scale, and rarely surpassed models fitted on the same fields. PhenoBench turns a multimodal longitudinal cohort into a versioned, auditable evaluation system where new questions, measurements, and models can be added without redefining existing comparisons.

AI.tldr: PhenoBench is a benchmark framework that turns multimodal longitudinal cohort data into an auditable evaluation system for clinically-grounded tasks, enabling systematic comparison of models across different input modalities and time scales.
AI.motivation: Deeply phenotyped cohorts combine diverse clinical, imaging, molecular, and wearable data across multiple timescales, but heterogeneous analyses are not directly comparable. There's a need for a standardized way to evaluate which measurements inform which health-related questions.
AI.method: PhenoBench is an executable benchmark built around the Human Phenotype Project with over 13,000 participants. It defines questions with fixed targets, eligible populations, timing, and allowed information, with evaluation contracts specifying splits, metrics, baselines, and claim boundaries. The benchmark includes 90 clinically-grounded tasks across 15 domains and 26 input modalities.
AI.result: The benchmark revealed question- and representation-dependent predictive value. For tabular foundation models across 160 regression comparisons (52 tasks), they ranked above standard task-specific models but only improved on ridge regression by median 0.004 R². For 14 language models across 40 tasks, they made informative predictions without cohort-specific fitting but showed task-specific capability gaps and rarely surpassed models fitted on the same fields.
AI.conclusion: PhenoBench provides a versioned, auditable evaluation system where new questions, measurements, and models can be added without redefining existing comparisons, enabling systematic assessment of predictive value across multimodal health data.

title: Generating Instance Generators in PDDL Planning
summary: PDDL, the de-facto standard language in the AI Planning community, is designed to specify planning domains: sets of instances that share the same predicates and action schemas. Yet it does not provide any means to specify the actual instance set, i.e., legality constraints on initial states and goal conditions, as well as possibly domain subset constraints specifying an instance subset we are interested in. One consequence of this is that instance generation has always been ad-hoc, with manually written domain- and subset-specific instance generators. Recent work has started to address this, through reasoning and learning methods that however suffer from scalability limitations. Here we introduce an alternative approach, leveraging LLMs to generate instance-generation programs, with built-in soundness guarantees through prescribed checks. We show that these automatically generated instance generators return large numbers of sound and diverse instances efficiently.

AI.tldr: LLMs are used to automatically generate instance-generation programs for PDDL domains with built-in soundness checks, addressing the lack of instance specification in standard PDDL.
AI.motivation: PDDL lacks means to specify instance sets (legality constraints on initial states/goal conditions and domain subset constraints), leading to ad-hoc, manually-written instance generators. Recent methods face scalability limitations.
AI.method: Leverage LLMs to generate instance-generation programs with built-in soundness guarantees through prescribed checks, ensuring the generated instances are valid for the domain.
AI.result: Automatically generated instance generators return large numbers of sound and diverse instances efficiently, solving the scalability issues of previous approaches.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based approach successfully addresses the PDDL instance generation problem by creating scalable, automated instance generators with soundness guarantees, overcoming limitations of manual and recent reasoning/learning methods.

title: Learning to Price and Stock Under Contextual and Censored Demand
summary: To make optimal joint pricing and inventory control decisions is a critical challenge for modern retailers. In practice, retailers face changing market conditions where demands are influenced by various contextual factors, while simultaneously dealing with the difficulty of lost sales that obscure true demand information. However, existing approaches often fail to account for both contextual information and censored demand observations. We address this gap by presenting a framework where we model demand as a linear combination of basis functions with unknown coefficients, allowing for adaptive pricing and inventory decisions that respond to changing contexts. We propose an efficient algorithm to achieve regret bound $\mathcal{O}(K\sqrt{T}\log T)$ under concave revenue conditions and $\mathcal{O}(K^{2/3}T^{2/3}(\log T)^{1/2})$ for the general case, with matching lower bounds confirming optimality. Extensive numerical experiments across diverse scenarios demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness.

AI.tldr: A framework for joint pricing and inventory control that handles contextual factors and censored demand observations with optimal regret bounds.
AI.motivation: Retailers face changing market conditions where demands are influenced by contextual factors while dealing with lost sales that obscure true demand information. Existing approaches often fail to account for both contextual information and censored demand observations.
AI.method: Model demand as a linear combination of basis functions with unknown coefficients, allowing for adaptive pricing and inventory decisions that respond to changing contexts. Propose an efficient algorithm to achieve optimal regret bounds.
AI.result: Achieve regret bound $\mathcal{O}(K\sqrt{T}\log T)$ under concave revenue conditions and $\mathcal{O}(K^{2/3}T^{2/3}(\log T)^{1/2})$ for the general case, with matching lower bounds confirming optimality. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate effectiveness across diverse scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses the gap in joint pricing and inventory control by incorporating both contextual information and censored demand observations with provably optimal performance.

title: LayerRoute: Action-Conditioned Mixture-of-Layers Routing for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies leverage pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to guide action generation for robot control. VLMs provide hierarchical visual-semantic representations that evolve across layers, from local visual geometry to abstract, language-aligned semantics; different manipulation tasks may therefore require different mixtures of layer representations. Meanwhile, the action module maintains intermediate representations that evolve throughout action computation and may provide useful information for subsequent decisions. However, existing VLA interfaces offer limited flexibility in representation access: VLM information is exposed through fixed layer assignments for each action layer, while intermediate action states are only propagated implicitly through residual streams without explicit reuse. We introduce LayerRoute, an action-conditioned representation routing interface that enables adaptive access to VLM layers and action representations. The Layer Mixture Router dynamically forms mixtures of cached VLM representations, while Action-State Reread reuses earlier action representations. Across diverse simulation and real-world benchmarks, LayerRoute consistently improves StarVLA-$π$ and $π_{0.5}$, achieving up to 7.2 gains on LIBERO Long with only 0.31% / 3.87% additional parameters. Ablation studies validate the benefit of action-conditioned layer routing, while routing analyses reveal structured allocation patterns across action layers and task settings.

AI.tldr: LayerRoute introduces an action-conditioned representation routing interface that enables adaptive access to vision-language model layers and action representations, improving VLA policies for robot control.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA interfaces have limited flexibility: VLM information uses fixed layer assignments for each action layer, and intermediate action states are only propagated implicitly without explicit reuse. Different manipulation tasks may require different mixtures of VLM layer representations (from local visual geometry to abstract semantics), while action module representations contain useful information for subsequent decisions.
AI.method: LayerRoute includes two components: 1) Layer Mixture Router that dynamically forms mixtures of cached VLM representations, and 2) Action-State Reread that reuses earlier action representations. The system enables action-conditioned adaptive routing to access VLM layers and action representations flexibly.
AI.result: LayerRoute consistently improves StarVLA-π and π₀.₅ across diverse simulation and real-world benchmarks, achieving up to 7.2 gains on LIBERO Long with only 0.31%/3.87% additional parameters. Ablation studies validate action-conditioned layer routing benefits, and routing analyses reveal structured allocation patterns across action layers and task settings.
AI.conclusion: LayerRoute's adaptive representation routing interface successfully addresses limitations of existing VLA policies by enabling flexible access to VLM layer mixtures and action representations, leading to improved performance with minimal parameter overhead across diverse manipulation tasks.

title: Connectome-to-Function: Conditional Generative Latent Representations for Reservoir Computing
summary: Connectomes, graph-level maps of neurons and their synaptic connections, provide a structural basis for understanding how brain circuits support function and computation. However, mapping connectome structure to computation remains difficult because these graphs are high-dimensional, sparse, and sensitive to local structural variation. Existing approaches often depend on hand-crafted structural descriptors or task-specific predictors, which limits their ability to represent connectomes in a form that is both generative and functionally meaningful. We propose a conditional generative latent framework that encodes connectome graphs into a compact structural space while using available node-level conditions to guide reconstruction and generation. From this space, the model can reconstruct observed connectivity with a mean edge-reconstruction AUC up to 0.910 and generate new candidate connectomes, enabling a unified analysis of graph structure and computational behavior. Using connectome-derived graphs as recurrent computational substrates, we found that the learned latent space captures functional variation across reservoir-computing experiments, with cross-validated $R^2$ values up to approximately 0.87. Interpretability analysis further revealed task-specific structural mechanisms: in our examples, memory performance is associated with reciprocal recurrent connectivity, whereas prediction and classification are more strongly associated with spectral properties of the recurrent network. These findings suggest an AI-for-science approach to linking neural connectivity to computation and provide a generative and interpretable basis for studying how distinct structural mechanisms shape computational capacity.

AI.tldr: A conditional generative latent framework that encodes connectomes into a compact structural space for unified analysis of graph structure and computational behavior, enabling reconstruction, generation, and interpretable linking of connectivity to computation.
AI.motivation: Mapping connectome structure to computation is difficult due to high-dimensionality, sparsity, and sensitivity to local structural variation. Existing approaches using hand-crafted structural descriptors or task-specific predictors are limited in their ability to represent connectomes in a form that is both generative and functionally meaningful.
AI.method: A conditional generative latent framework that encodes connectome graphs into a compact structural space while using available node-level conditions to guide reconstruction and generation. The model uses connectome-derived graphs as recurrent computational substrates.
AI.result: The model can reconstruct observed connectivity with mean edge-reconstruction AUC up to 0.910 and generate new candidate connectomes. The learned latent space captures functional variation across reservoir-computing experiments with cross-validated R² values up to ~0.87. Interpretability analysis revealed task-specific structural mechanisms: memory performance is associated with reciprocal recurrent connectivity, while prediction and classification are more strongly associated with spectral properties.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an AI-for-science approach to linking neural connectivity to computation, offering a generative and interpretable basis for studying how distinct structural mechanisms shape computational capacity in neural circuits.

title: SAP: State-Guided Data Synthesis with Argument Provenance for Multi-Turn Tool Use
summary: High-quality multi-turn tool-use data is essential for training agentic models, yet existing data synthesis methods often underrepresent the argument-level dependencies that are critical to long-horizon tool use. As a result, even when a model selects the correct tool, task execution may still fail because the model fills tool arguments with fabricated, stale, or weakly grounded values. To address this problem, we propose \textbf{State-Guided Data Synthesis with Argument Provenance (SAP)}. SAP combines state guidance, tool-argument provenance constraints, and turn-level validation to efficiently construct tool-use trajectories with long-range dependencies and high accuracy. Using data generated by SAP, we build SAP-4B, which is highly competitive even when compared with much larger models across multiple benchmarks. Source code, synthesized data, and trained weights are available at https://github.com/Zichen1024/SAP.

AI.tldr: SAP is a data synthesis method that creates high-quality multi-turn tool-use data with proper argument-level dependencies, enabling training of competitive agentic models like SAP-4B.
AI.motivation: Existing data synthesis methods often lack proper argument-level dependencies for long-horizon tool use, leading to task failures even when correct tools are selected due to fabricated, stale, or weakly grounded argument values.
AI.method: Proposed State-Guided Data Synthesis with Argument Provenance (SAP), combining state guidance, tool-argument provenance constraints, and turn-level validation to construct tool-use trajectories with long-range dependencies and high accuracy.
AI.result: Built SAP-4B using SAP-generated data, which shows high competitiveness compared to much larger models across multiple benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: SAP effectively addresses the argument dependency problem in tool-use data synthesis, enabling the creation of high-quality training data that leads to competitive agentic models, with open-sourced code, data, and weights.

title: VERPO: Verified Evidence Regularized Policy Optimization
summary: Verifiable outcome rewards guide language-model post-training, but sequence-level advantages do not identify which token-level decisions should be preserved or revised. Evidence-conditioned Teachers provide denser supervision by replaying sampled trajectories with privileged feedback. Yet indiscriminate imitation risks transferring formatting or reasoning-style shifts that do not support task success. We introduce VERPO, a Verified Evidence Regularized Policy Optimization framework that treats evidence as a proposal for policy correction while retaining the outcome objective. It separates evidence-free reference restoration from signed token-level evidence corrections. Fisher Evidence Contrast attenuates corrections along an estimated evidence-presence direction. A stopped token-wise ZPD controller scales acceptance according to local reward alignment and Fisher movement cost, while the reference channel remains independent of acceptance. Across five scientific-reasoning and tool-use tasks, the best variant on each backbone exceeds the strongest compared baseline in average score. The averages rise from 0.6826 to 0.6857 on Qwen3-4B, from 0.6895 to 0.7058 on Qwen3-8B, and from 0.4751 to 0.5657 on Llama-3.2-1B.

AI.tldr: VERPO is a new RL framework that separates token-level evidence corrections from reference restoration, using Fisher Evidence Contrast and a token-wise ZPD controller to improve policy optimization while avoiding transfer of irrelevant formatting or reasoning-style changes.
AI.motivation: Current verifiable outcome rewards in language model post-training only provide sequence-level advantages but fail to identify which specific token-level decisions should be preserved or revised. While Evidence-conditioned Teachers offer denser supervision, they risk transferring irrelevant formatting or reasoning-style shifts that don't contribute to task success.
AI.method: VERPO treats evidence as a proposal for policy correction while maintaining the outcome objective. It separates evidence-free reference restoration from signed token-level evidence corrections. The method uses Fisher Evidence Contrast to attenuate corrections along an estimated evidence-presence direction and a stopped token-wise ZPD controller that scales acceptance based on local reward alignment and Fisher movement cost, while keeping the reference channel independent of acceptance.
AI.result: Across five scientific-reasoning and tool-use tasks, the best VERPO variant on each backbone model outperformed the strongest baseline. Performance improved from 0.6826 to 0.6857 on Qwen3-4B, from 0.6895 to 0.7058 on Qwen3-8B, and from 0.4751 to 0.5657 on Llama-3.2-1B, demonstrating consistent gains across different model sizes.
AI.conclusion: VERPO provides an effective framework for verifiable evidence regularized policy optimization that better utilizes token-level evidence while avoiding the transfer of irrelevant stylistic changes, leading to improved performance across various reasoning and tool-use tasks with different model architectures.

title: CWF: A Collaborative Writing Framework for Personalized and Reliable Popular Science Writing
summary: We introduce Personalized and Reliable Popular Science Writing, a novel task that requires adapting scientific explanations to audiences with different cognitive levels while preserving factual accuracy. However, improving personalization often introduces simplifications that increase the risk of hallucination and factual distortion. To address these challenges, we first construct a dataset of 39,134 entries and a reader-centric Personalized Science Communication Benchmark (PSCB) that jointly evaluates audience adaptation and factual accuracy. To reduce data and computational requirements while improving generalization across domains and audiences, we introduce DA-MoE, which explicitly decouples audience adaptation from domain knowledge through separate modeling. To enable robust verification and revision in evidence-scarce scenarios, a multi-agent fact-checking mechanism that augments limited evidence with role-specific agent debate and propagates confidence over a graph is proposed. Experiments on PSCB show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/DPInnovationWorks/CWF.

AI.tldr: DA-MoE framework for personalized science writing decouples audience adaptation from domain knowledge, uses multi-agent fact-checking with confidence propagation, and achieves SOTA on new benchmark dataset.
AI.motivation: Personalizing scientific explanations for different cognitive levels risks factual distortion and hallucination. Existing methods struggle to balance personalization with accuracy, especially when adapting across diverse audiences and domains with limited evidence.
AI.method: 1) Created PSCB dataset with 39,134 entries and joint evaluation benchmark; 2) Proposed DA-MoE framework that explicitly decouples audience adaptation from domain knowledge; 3) Multi-agent fact-checking mechanism with role-specific agent debate and confidence propagation over graph structure.
AI.result: DA-MoE achieves state-of-the-art performance on the PSCB benchmark, demonstrating effective personalization while preserving factual accuracy across different cognitive levels and domains.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully addresses the trade-off between personalization and factual accuracy in science communication, with potential applications for making complex scientific knowledge accessible to diverse audiences while maintaining reliability.

title: FANS: Federated Adaptive Network Search Learning for Heterogeneous Devices
summary: Heterogeneous Federated Learning (HFL) aims to train models across devices with diverse resource budgets while preserving data privacy. Existing HFL methods typically bind training to a small predefined menu of model configurations, which limits architectural coverage. To address this bottleneck, we introduce Federated Adaptive Network Search (FANS), a hypernetwork-based framework that learns a shared architecture space rather than a fixed set of client models. To optimize this shared space efficiently, we propose the Federated Parallel Scaling (FPS) algorithm, which jointly trains multiple sampled subnetworks in parallel with self-distillation so that larger sampled subnetworks can supervise smaller ones during local updates. We evaluate FANS on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNLI using ResNet-18, DenseNet-121, and BERT-base, respectively. Across all benchmarks, FANS expands the feasible subnetwork pool by orders of magnitude (e.g., 4,680 candidates for ResNet-18 vs. 4 in existing methods) and improves the average accuracy-efficiency trade-off relative to representative HFL baselines. Device heterogeneity is emulated through resource tiers, and evaluation covers accuracy, parameter count, and MACs.

AI.tldr: FANS introduces a hypernetwork-based federated learning framework that learns a shared architecture space instead of fixed models, enabling thousands of subnet configurations for heterogeneous devices.
AI.motivation: Existing heterogeneous federated learning methods are limited by small predefined model menus that restrict architectural coverage and flexibility for diverse device resource budgets.
AI.method: FANS uses a hypernetwork-based framework to learn a shared architecture space. It employs Federated Parallel Scaling (FPS) algorithm that jointly trains multiple sampled subnetworks in parallel with self-distillation, where larger subnetworks supervise smaller ones during local updates.
AI.result: FANS expands the feasible subnetwork pool by orders of magnitude (e.g., 4,680 candidates for ResNet-18 vs. 4 in existing methods) and improves average accuracy-efficiency trade-off across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNLI benchmarks using ResNet-18, DenseNet-121, and BERT-base.
AI.conclusion: FANS provides a more flexible and scalable approach to heterogeneous federated learning by enabling thousands of model configurations rather than limited fixed sets, while maintaining privacy and improving accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.

title: Substrate-Portable Execution for Production LLM Workflows
summary: Production LLM agents execute tool-calling loops, retrieval chains, and compositional workflows in multiple modes, yet execution semantics are often coupled to one runtime. We encountered this portability problem in Rufus, a conversational AI assistant with a large tool catalog that serves millions of Amazon customers. Rufus supports real-time serving, asynchronous background tasks, and high-volume batch workloads such as evaluation and content pregeneration. Each mode has distinct service-level objectives and typically uses a separate runtime. Reusing streaming orchestration makes asynchronous and batch workloads blocking and prevents use of batch inference APIs, which offer a 50 percent discount at published prices. We present a binding-adaptive agent execution platform that separates workflow definition from execution substrate. Developers define a workflow once as a typed dataflow graph. The platform compiles the graph to in-process streaming for real-time serving, durable AWS SWF orchestration for asynchronous execution, or distributed Apache Flink stream processing for batch inference. No workflow code changes are required. LLM inference is represented as a suspendable graph node whose behavior depends on the substrate: streaming delivery online, durable retry asynchronously, and batched submission offline. We validated dozens of production agent configurations across five orchestration patterns: single-inference RAG, iterative ReAct, compositional PreAct, conditional routing, and multi-agent deep research. Across all three bindings, we found no detectable difference in output quality. Batch execution reduced per-query inference cost in line with published batch API pricing while operating alongside the streaming path at production scale.

AI.tldr: A binding-adaptive agent execution platform separates workflow definition from execution substrate, allowing LLM agent workflows to run across streaming, asynchronous, and batch runtimes without code changes, reducing inference costs by 50% for batch workloads.
AI.motivation: Production LLM agents face portability problems when their execution semantics are coupled to specific runtimes. Different operational modes (real-time serving, asynchronous tasks, batch workloads) have distinct service-level objectives and typically require separate runtimes, making reuse of streaming orchestration inefficient and preventing cost savings from batch inference APIs.
AI.method: Developers define workflows once as typed dataflow graphs. The platform compiles these graphs to different execution substrates: in-process streaming for real-time serving, durable AWS SWF orchestration for asynchronous execution, or distributed Apache Flink stream processing for batch inference. LLM inference is represented as a suspendable graph node whose behavior adapts to the substrate.
AI.result: Validated dozens of production agent configurations across five orchestration patterns with no detectable difference in output quality across all three bindings. Batch execution reduced per-query inference cost by approximately 50% in line with published batch API pricing while operating at production scale alongside streaming paths.
AI.conclusion: The binding-adaptive approach successfully decouples workflow definition from execution substrate, enabling portable LLM agent execution across multiple runtime modes without compromising output quality, while achieving significant cost reductions through batch inference optimization.

title: DataFlex-RL: An Evaluation Platform for RLVR Data Policies
summary: Data policies for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) determine which rollouts are used, how strongly they are weighted, and which domains contribute to subsequent training batches. We introduce DataFlex-RL, an evaluation platform for comparing these choices under a common GRPO recipe. Our primary experiment evaluates 13 configurations across 12 matched seeds using Qwen2.5-7B-Base and 12 mathematics, logic, and science benchmarks. Uniform GRPO improves the domain-balanced average accuracy by 7.76 percentage points over the untrained checkpoint. None of the eight rollout-selection or reweighting methods achieves a paired 95% confidence interval that excludes zero relative to uniform sampling, and none of the three adaptive mixtures outperforms a fixed equal mixture at the same level of precision. A corrected 12-seed extension on Llama-3.1-8B-Base places the additional methods on the same score scale as the original controls, but does not reveal a consistent winner in terms of observed mean performance. We also quantify evaluation sensitivity by rescoring nine Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct runs using a math-heavy six-benchmark summary, consisting of five mathematics benchmarks and GPQA-Diamond but no logic benchmark, and comparing it with the domain-balanced 12-benchmark summary. The resulting rankings are negatively correlated, with a correlation coefficient of -0.33, whereas summaries that retain all 12 benchmarks largely agree. Across the controlled settings studied here, changing the data policy measurably changes the training process but does not produce a reproducible improvement over uniform training.

AI.tldr: DataFlex-RL evaluation shows no RLVR data policy consistently beats uniform sampling for LLM fine-tuning across math/logic/science benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate different data policies for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) in LLM fine-tuning, comparing rollout selection, reweighting, and adaptive mixture methods against uniform sampling.
AI.method: Developed DataFlex-RL evaluation platform using GRPO recipe; tested 13 configurations across 12 matched seeds on Qwen2.5-7B-Base and Llama-3.1-8B-Base across 12 mathematics, logic, and science benchmarks; analyzed sensitivity with different benchmark subsets.
AI.result: Uniform GRPO improved accuracy by 7.76 percentage points over baseline, but no alternative data policy (8 rollout-selection/reweighting methods, 3 adaptive mixtures) outperformed uniform sampling at 95% confidence; evaluation sensitivity analysis showed negative correlation (-0.33) between math-heavy vs domain-balanced benchmark rankings.
AI.conclusion: Data policies change training process but don't produce reproducible improvements over uniform training in controlled settings; benchmark composition significantly affects performance rankings.

title: IIns-VAE+: A Robust Transfer Learning Framework for Environmental Identification in Wireless Sensing
summary: Environmental identification in wireless sensing is essential for 6G integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems to achieve reliable situational awareness. However, deep learning (DL) models for this task often fail to generalize under domain shift across diverse environments. While the Inter-Instance Variational Auto-encoder (IIns-VAE) learns features of rich representation, its neural classifier remains vulnerable to these distribution changes. In this paper, we propose IIns-VAE+, a hybrid model that combines the IIns-VAE framework with Minimax Risk Classifiers (MRC) to improve adaptability in transfer learning scenarios. We use real-world datasets to evaluate our framework across three transfer learning scenarios, including general to specific room environments, high to low label resolutions, and mixed to specific environments. The experimental results indicate that IIns-VAE+ significantly outperforms baselines, demonstrating its critical value in building adaptable and robust perceptive networks in future 6G systems.

AI.tldr: IIns-VAE+ combines Inter-Instance VAE framework with Minimax Risk Classifiers to improve generalization under domain shift for 6G wireless sensing environmental identification, achieving better performance across transfer learning scenarios.
AI.motivation: DL models for environmental identification in 6G ISAC systems often fail to generalize under domain shift across diverse environments. While IIns-VAE learns rich representations, its neural classifier remains vulnerable to distribution changes.
AI.method: Propose IIns-VAE+, a hybrid model combining IIns-VAE framework with Minimax Risk Classifiers (MRC) to improve adaptability in transfer learning scenarios.
AI.result: Evaluated on real-world datasets across three transfer learning scenarios: general to specific room environments, high to low label resolutions, and mixed to specific environments. IIns-VAE+ significantly outperforms baselines.
AI.conclusion: IIns-VAE+ demonstrates critical value in building adaptable and robust perceptive networks for future 6G systems by addressing domain shift challenges in wireless sensing environmental identification.

title: Sparse Incident-Cluster Learning for 12-hour Port Flood Pre-warning in Digital-Twin Analytics
summary: Port flood digital twins require analytics that warn operators before disruption, but official warning incidents are often few and adjacent observations are temporally dependent. Row-level classification can therefore overstate performance by placing windows from the same event in both model-development and evaluation data. We formulate 12-hour port flood pre-warning as an incident-cluster learning problem and evaluate a digital-twin analytics module using eight-point water-level histories, prediction-time contextual covariates, and interpretable short-window dynamics. The protocol combines fold-specific sparse feature selection, warning-cluster grouping, negative-label controls, 100-repeat random top-k controls, and alert-episode evaluation. Liverpool is the primary four-cluster case study, with harmonised Humber/Hull-proxy and Wessex South data used for protocol-transfer checks. Across the Liverpool folds, the top-10 ElasticNet model achieves mean F2 = 0.696, compared with 0.633 without top-k truncation and 0.681 for full-feature weighted XGBoost. It is the strongest ElasticNet variant, remains competitive with the nonlinear reference using only ten predictors, and exceeds the repeat-level 95th percentile of broad and same-family random subsets. Contextual covariates provide a strong prediction-time anchor, complemented by physically interpretable local dynamics. Historical replay converts risk scores into alert episodes and measures alert duration and false-episode burden. The result is an offline-evaluated analytics and validation module designed for integration into a port digital twin.

AI.tldr: A port flood warning system using incident-cluster learning with interpretable features achieves strong performance in digital twin applications, outperforming alternatives while using fewer predictors.
AI.motivation: Current port flood digital twin analytics face issues with few official warning incidents and temporal dependence between observations, causing row-level classification to overstate performance by mixing windows from the same event in both training and evaluation data.
AI.method: Formulates 12-hour port flood pre-warning as incident-cluster learning problem using eight-point water-level histories, prediction-time contextual covariates, and interpretable short-window dynamics. Employs fold-specific sparse feature selection, warning-cluster grouping, negative-label controls, 100-repeat random top-k controls, and alert-episode evaluation.
AI.result: Top-10 ElasticNet model achieves mean F2 = 0.696 in Liverpool case study, outperforming non-truncated models (0.633) and remaining competitive with full-feature XGBoost (0.681) using only ten predictors. Exceeds 95th percentile of random subsets. Contextual covariates provide strong prediction anchor with physically interpretable local dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The system provides an offline-evaluated analytics and validation module with interpretable features designed for integration into port digital twins, effectively addressing temporal dependency issues through incident-cluster learning approach.

title: MVFA: A Multi-View Text-Guided Multimodal Fusion LLM Adapter for Sentiment Analysis and Emotion Recognition
summary: Multimodal sentiment analysis and emotion recognition in conversations demand effective modeling of heterogeneous interactions across textual, acoustic, and visual modalities. Although large language models (LLMs) offer powerful language understanding, adapting them to multimodal affective computing remains challenging: full-model fine-tuning is computationally prohibitive, while many existing lightweight adapters fail to preserve rich textual cues during cross-modal fusion. To address these limitations, we propose the multi-view text-guided multimodal fusion adapter (MVFA), a parameter-efficient framework that augments frozen LLMs with strong multimodal reasoning capability. MVFA first constructs complementary text views via max pooling, mean pooling, and attention pooling; these views then guide cross-modal interactions with audio and visual features. The fused multimodal representations are subsequently compressed into a compact set of learnable pseudo-tokens through an Enhanced Q-Former Fusion Module. Using ChatGLM3-6B-base as the primary backbone, we further validate MVFA on LLaMA2-7B and Qwen3-8B to examine its portability across multiple frozen LLM backbones. MVFA is evaluated on three challenging datasets: CH-SIMS V2.0, MELD, and CHERMA. Experimental results demonstrate that MVFA achieves state-of-the-art performance on key metrics while updating only a small fraction of parameters. Specifically, it attains 84.62\% Acc2 and 84.59\% F1 on CH-SIMS V2.0, 67.36\% Acc and 66.03\% WF1 on MELD, and 74.66\% Acc on CHERMA. These findings establish multi-view text-guided fusion as an effective and scalable paradigm for parameter-efficient multimodal LLM adaptation in affective computing. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Overwhelm1208/MVFA.

AI.tldr: MVFA is a parameter-efficient multimodal fusion adapter that enhances frozen LLMs for sentiment analysis and emotion recognition by constructing complementary text views and using pseudo-tokens for cross-modal fusion.
AI.motivation: Multimodal affective computing needs effective modeling of heterogeneous interactions across text, audio, and visual modalities. While LLMs offer strong language understanding, full-model fine-tuning is computationally prohibitive, and existing lightweight adapters often fail to preserve rich textual cues during cross-modal fusion.
AI.method: MVFA constructs complementary text views via max pooling, mean pooling, and attention pooling to guide cross-modal interactions with audio and visual features. These fused representations are compressed into learnable pseudo-tokens through an Enhanced Q-Former Fusion Module. The approach is tested with ChatGLM3-6B-base, LLaMA2-7B, and Qwen3-8B backbones.
AI.result: MVFA achieves state-of-the-art performance on CH-SIMS V2.0 (84.62% Acc2, 84.59% F1), MELD (67.36% Acc, 66.03% WF1), and CHERMA (74.66% Acc) while updating only a small fraction of parameters.
AI.conclusion: Multi-view text-guided fusion provides an effective and scalable paradigm for parameter-efficient multimodal LLM adaptation in affective computing, establishing MVFA as a powerful framework for multimodal sentiment analysis and emotion recognition.

title: Compressed Recurrent Feedback in Tsetlin Machines: A Reproducible Boolean-FSM Study
summary: Sequential inference on small devices requires a model to retain useful history without repeatedly processing a long input record. A Recurrent Tsetlin Machine (RTM) provides this memory by returning Boolean clause outputs from one time step as inputs to the next. Direct feedback, however, grows with the clause bank and can make the recurrent input unnecessarily wide. This paper investigates a fixed-width alternative. We combine clause activations by exclusive-OR (XOR) folding, retain the folded bits at two time scales, and threshold them back to a binary state. The resulting design reduces 480 clause activations to 96 recurrent bits. We evaluate the method on a reproducible Boolean finite-state-machine benchmark with explicit transition rules, data splits, and random seeds. Across 144 runs, the compressed model obtains $61.47 \pm 6.74\%$ and $62.94 \pm 9.92\%$ accuracy on the two task families. Raw clause feedback changes these means by less than one percentage point, while increasing the recurrent width tenfold and measured host execution time by $4.38\times$ and $3.71\times$. Gated neural models remain more accurate, and a no-feedback control retaining only short input history achieves comparable or slightly higher accuracy. On this benchmark, folding matches raw feedback within small empirical margins at a much narrower interface; these findings also underscore the critical necessity of no-feedback recurrence controls when benchmarking sequence models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an XOR folding technique to compress recurrent feedback in Recurrent Tsetlin Machines, reducing 480 clause activations to 96 bits while maintaining similar accuracy as raw feedback, but with much lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Sequential inference on small devices requires efficient memory retention without repeatedly processing long inputs. While Recurrent Tsetlin Machines (RTMs) provide memory through Boolean clause feedback, direct feedback grows with clause bank size and creates unnecessarily wide recurrent inputs.
AI.method: The authors propose an XOR folding technique that combines clause activations via exclusive-OR operations, retains folded bits at two time scales, and thresholds them back to binary states. This compresses 480 clause activations down to 96 recurrent bits while preserving memory capabilities.
AI.result: The compressed model achieved 61.47 ± 6.74% and 62.94 ± 9.92% accuracy on two Boolean finite-state-machine benchmark task families. Raw clause feedback performed similarly (±1% difference) but required 10x wider interface and 4.38×/3.71× higher execution time. No-feedback controls achieved comparable or slightly better accuracy.
AI.conclusion: XOR folding matches raw feedback accuracy with much narrower interface and lower computational cost on the benchmark. The results highlight the critical importance of including no-feedback recurrence controls when benchmarking sequence models to properly assess memory benefits.

title: Customer Relationship Intelligence: Integrating CRM and MDM for Enhanced Customer Engagement
comment: Preprint submitted to 16th IEEE ICCCNT 2025. 8 pages, 12 tables
summary: This study examines how Customer Relationship Management (CRM), Master Data Management (MDM), and Customer Knowledge Management (CKM) jointly constitute a Customer Relationship Intelligence (CRI) framework for enhanced Customer Engagement (CE). A cross-sectional survey of 100 participants across retail, healthcare, IT, and telecommunications sectors was analysed using Spearman rho correlation and ordinal logistic regression (IBM SPSS). Bivariate correlations were weak and non-significant (r<0.19, p>0.06). Regression identified CRM (beta=0.717, p=0.002) and CKM (beta=0.581, p=0.009) as significant positive predictors of CE; MDM showed a positive but non-significant direct effect (beta=0.346, p=0.071). The model explained 20.5% of CE variance (Nagelkerke R^2=0.205). Parallel mediation analysis (Hayes PROCESS Model 4, 5,000 bootstrap samples) found no significant indirect effects of MDM on CE via CRM (IE=0.021, 95% BC CI [-0.072, 0.121]) or CKM (IE=0.032, 95% BC CI [-0.061, 0.126]); Hypothesis H4 was not supported. CRM and CKM emerge as the principal drivers of CE within the CRI framework, while MDM functions as a foundational data quality enabler whose strategic value is realised through its enabling effect on CRM execution and knowledge management. Findings should be treated as exploratory given the sample size and cross-sectional design. Future research should replicate with larger sector-specific samples and longitudinal designs, particularly in regulated BFSI contexts where MDM architecture is shaped by data governance mandates.

AI.tldr: CRM and CKM significantly predict customer engagement, while MDM has no significant direct or indirect effects; CRM and CKM are key drivers within Customer Relationship Intelligence framework.
AI.motivation: To examine how CRM, MDM, and CKM jointly constitute a Customer Relationship Intelligence framework for enhanced Customer Engagement across multiple industries.
AI.method: Cross-sectional survey of 100 participants across retail, healthcare, IT, and telecommunications sectors analyzed using Spearman rho correlation, ordinal logistic regression (SPSS), and parallel mediation analysis (Hayes PROCESS Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap samples).
AI.result: CRM (beta=0.717, p=0.002) and CKM (beta=0.581, p=0.009) significantly predict CE; MDM showed positive but non-significant effect (beta=0.346, p=0.071). Model explained 20.5% of CE variance. No significant indirect effects of MDM on CE via CRM or CKM. Bivariate correlations were weak and non-significant.
AI.conclusion: CRM and CKM are principal drivers of CE within CRI framework, while MDM functions as foundational data quality enabler. Findings are exploratory due to sample limitations; future research needs larger sector-specific samples and longitudinal designs, especially in regulated BFSI contexts.

title: Rethinking One-Shot Federated Graph Learning: Training-Free Statistical Estimation
summary: One-shot federated graph learning generally aims to train Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) across clients with disconnected subgraphs in a single communication round. Existing methods predominantly design advanced optimization strategies under the premise that local GNN training is indispensable. However, empirical observations reveal that under extreme non-IID conditions, local GNN training suffers from severe cross-client representation misalignment, becoming a major source of error rather than a remedy. Motivated by this, we reformulate one-shot FGL as a statistical estimation problem. We propose SPEAR (Statistical Prototype Estimation with Adaptive Reliability), a completely training-free framework that directly computes topology-smoothed class prototypes from local graphs in the original feature space. The server then aggregates these prototypes using a sample-size-adaptive shrinkage estimator that down-weights unreliable local estimates, producing robust global class prototypes. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate that SPEAR consistently achieves state-of-the-art accuracy under extreme heterogeneity. Moreover, SPEAR delivers at least an order-of-magnitude speedup over all baselines, reaching several orders of magnitude against generative and distillation-based methods. Our findings suggest that training-free statistical estimation, rather than local GNN optimization, provides the key to robust and efficient one-shot federated graph learning. The code is available at https://github.com/Yodeesy/SPEAR .

AI.tldr: SPEAR is a training-free framework for one-shot federated graph learning that computes class prototypes directly from local graph features using topological smoothing, then aggregates them with adaptive shrinkage for robustness, achieving SOTA accuracy with massive speedups.
AI.motivation: Existing one-shot federated graph learning methods rely on local GNN training, but under extreme non-IID conditions, this causes severe cross-client representation misalignment that becomes a major source of error rather than a solution.
AI.method: Reformulates one-shot FGL as statistical estimation problem. Uses topology-smoothed class prototypes computed from local graphs in original feature space (no training). Server aggregates prototypes using sample-size-adaptive shrinkage estimator that down-weights unreliable local estimates.
AI.result: Consistently achieves state-of-the-art accuracy under extreme heterogeneity across seven benchmarks. Delivers at least order-of-magnitude speedup over all baselines, reaching several orders of magnitude against generative and distillation-based methods.
AI.conclusion: Training-free statistical estimation, rather than local GNN optimization, provides the key to robust and efficient one-shot federated graph learning.

title: SCIRIGOR:Evaluating Open-Ended Scientific Analysis Beyond Final Scores
summary:
Scientific coding agents produce interdependent code, results, figures, and claims, yet evaluating final
  outputs alone does not establish whether their conclusions are scientifically supported. We formulate
  evidence-grounded multimodal scientific analysis, requiring agents to produce executable analyses and claims
  supported by results and visualizations from the same run. We introduce SciRIGOR, an evaluation framework and
  benchmark comprising 100 cases from scientific articles across six domains and 17 subfields. The framework
  reconstructs typed evidence graphs, separates artifact fidelity from relational validity, and scores complete
  claim-support paths while localizing the earliest unsupported relation. Source-grounded alternative paths
  accommodate scientifically equivalent analyses and visualizations. We evaluate 11 agent/model configurations.
  On full-benchmark runs, claims agree with faithful and unfaithful results at nearly identical rates (91.8%
  versus 91.0%). Yet no system exceeds 62.6% on the soft evidence-chain score or 18.0% strict whole-chain
  success. These findings show that internal coherence does not establish scientific correctness: evaluation
  must verify support along the complete data-to-claim path.

AI.tldr: SciRIGOR: A framework for evaluating scientific coding agents by verifying evidence chains from data to claims, showing current agents produce internally consistent but scientifically unsupported outputs.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of scientific coding agents only looks at final outputs without verifying whether conclusions are scientifically supported by evidence from the same execution run.
AI.method: Created SciRIGOR evaluation framework with 100 cases across 6 domains/17 subfields. Uses typed evidence graphs to separate artifact fidelity from relational validity, scores complete claim-support paths, and identifies earliest unsupported relation while accommodating scientifically equivalent analyses.
AI.result: Evaluated 11 agent/model configurations. Claims agreed with results at similar rates (91.8% faithful vs 91.0% unfaithful), but no system exceeded 62.6% on soft evidence-chain score or 18.0% strict whole-chain success, revealing internal coherence ≠ scientific correctness.
AI.conclusion: Scientific coding agents produce internally consistent outputs but often lack proper evidence chains. Evaluation must verify complete data-to-claim support paths to establish scientific correctness, not just final outputs.

title: All for 1-Bit: Towards Genuine 1-Bit Post-Training Quantization for LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress, yet their massive storage and memory-bandwidth demands still hinder efficient deployment. Weight binarization is a promising solution, but existing binarization-based post-training quantization (PTQ) methods usually far exceed the nominal 1-bit storage target due to hidden overhead. To address this gap, we propose All for 1-Bit (AF1), a genuine 1-bit PTQ framework for LLMs. AF1 comprises two complementary components: (1) Null-space-Aware Binary Factorization (NABF) for improving binary reconstruction through Hessian-aware surrogate reparameterization, null-space-aware binary factorization, and scale-only global reconstruction; and (2) Hierarchical Shapley Allocation (HiSA) for assigning structural capacity using hierarchical Shapley sensitivity. Together, they preserve model accuracy under a strict 1.0-BPW budget in the PTQ setting. Experiments on LLaMA, Qwen, and Gemma families show that AF1 consistently outperforms existing binarization-based PTQ methods in perplexity and zero-shot accuracy. Compared with BF16, AF1 achieves an average 2.5 times inference speedup and over 90% memory reduction across evaluated models, providing a practical path toward deployable genuine 1-bit compression for LLMs. The code for reproducibility is available at https://github.com/Kishon-zzx/AF1.

AI.tldr: AF1 is a genuine 1-bit post-training quantization framework for LLMs that achieves true 1-bit storage with minimal hidden overhead while maintaining accuracy through novel binary factorization and capacity allocation techniques.
AI.motivation: While LLMs have shown remarkable progress, their massive storage and memory-bandwidth demands hinder efficient deployment. Existing binarization-based PTQ methods often exceed the nominal 1-bit storage target due to hidden overhead, creating a gap between theoretical and practical 1-bit compression.
AI.method: AF1 consists of two complementary components: 1) Null-space-Aware Binary Factorization (NABF) for improving binary reconstruction using Hessian-aware surrogate reparameterization, null-space-aware binary factorization, and scale-only global reconstruction; and 2) Hierarchical Shapley Allocation (HiSA) for assigning structural capacity using hierarchical Shapley sensitivity analysis.
AI.result: Experiments on LLaMA, Qwen, and Gemma families show AF1 consistently outperforms existing binarization-based PTQ methods in perplexity and zero-shot accuracy. Compared to BF16, AF1 achieves average 2.5x inference speedup and over 90% memory reduction while maintaining strict 1.0-BPW budget.
AI.conclusion: AF1 provides a practical path toward deployable genuine 1-bit compression for LLMs, demonstrating that true 1-bit quantization is achievable without sacrificing accuracy, offering significant improvements in memory efficiency and inference speed for real-world deployment.

title: Predicting Wind Turbine Power Using Machine Learning and Weather Forecasts
summary: Offshore wind turbines are widely used to generate renewable energy, but their maintenance can result in decreased efficiency due to forced shutdowns. Accurate wind turbine power predictions can identify periods of low power that would be ideal for scheduling maintenance. However, the effects of data volume, feature selection, and data preprocessing on the performance of such power prediction models have not been thoroughly studied. Besides, current models have limited transferability between different wind turbines. Therefore, this study developed a baseline Linear Regression for performance comparison with a more complex Artificial Neural Network model to predict the power output of a wind turbine, using weather conditions only to enhance applicability. A range of data preprocessing techniques were studied, and models were trained on one month and one year of data to determine the effects of data preprocessing and volume on model performance. Feature selection was explored using a Random Forest Regressor. The best results from the different models showed that the Artificial Neural Network models provided the highest accuracy, with an R2 score of 0.98 and a low Mean Absolute Error of 194, when compared with the baseline model (R2 score of 0.94 and Mean Absolute Error of 441). The model performance is comparable to the range of results in past studies, with the advantage that the proposed method leverages a separate weather dataset from a nearby weather station, enabling future applications for similar wind turbines in different locations. The Artificial Neural Network model was then used to identify 4-h periods of low power predictions over 2 months (simulating application for future periods), providing power output savings of approximately 2000 kW for each maintenance event.

AI.tldr: Study develops wind turbine power prediction models using Linear Regression and Artificial Neural Networks with weather data, achieving 0.98 R2 score, enabling maintenance scheduling during low-power periods.
AI.motivation: Offshore wind turbine maintenance causes forced shutdowns reducing efficiency. Need accurate power prediction to identify low-power periods for maintenance scheduling. Existing studies lack comprehensive analysis of data volume, feature selection, and preprocessing effects, and current models have limited transferability between turbines.
AI.method: Developed baseline Linear Regression and more complex Artificial Neural Network models using weather conditions only for enhanced applicability. Tested range of data preprocessing techniques, trained on one month and one year of data to study data volume effects. Used Random Forest Regressor for feature selection. Applied models to identify 4-hour low-power periods.
AI.result: ANN models outperformed baseline with R2 score of 0.98 and MAE of 194 vs Linear Regression's R2 of 0.94 and MAE of 441. Models comparable to past studies but advantage of using separate weather dataset enabling transferability. ANN identified 4-hour low-power periods over 2 months, providing ~2000 kW power savings per maintenance event.
AI.conclusion: ANN models with weather data provide accurate wind turbine power predictions for maintenance scheduling, with better performance than linear regression. The approach using separate weather datasets enhances transferability to different locations. Practical application can yield significant power savings during maintenance events.

title: Decision-Aware Suffix Prediction and Reasoning of Business Processes
summary: Suffix prediction forecasts the remaining sequence of events of a running case until completion. Most approaches rely on neural networks trained on event logs, which, on average, perform well but struggle with short prefixes or targets belonging to a rare process variant. In such scenarios, the correct path may cross multiple branching decisions, determined primarily by case- and event-level attributes, a signal that NN-based suffix prediction models tend to underweight because they may heavily weight (dense) event labels. Decision mining extracts rules for such decisions from the event log, but has so far been applied only to post-hoc and what-if analysis, not suffix prediction. We therefore extend suffix prediction with decision mining, introducing a decision-aware suffix prediction framework, a neuro-symbolic approach that enables reasoning about predicted events via mined decision rules. Experiments on three of four event logs and three suffix predictors show that the framework can improve suffix prediction, especially for short prefixes but also for rare process variants, and adds intrinsic interpretability.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic framework that combines neural suffix prediction with decision mining rules to improve performance on short prefixes and rare process variants while adding interpretability.
AI.motivation: Neural network-based suffix prediction models struggle with short prefixes and rare process variants, as they underweight important case- and event-level attributes while heavily weighting dense event labels. Decision mining can capture branching rules but hasn't been applied to suffix prediction.
AI.method: Extends suffix prediction with decision mining, creating a decision-aware neuro-symbolic framework. The approach mines decision rules from event logs and integrates them with neural suffix predictors to enable reasoning about predicted events via symbolic rules.
AI.result: Experiments on three out of four event logs show the framework improves suffix prediction, particularly for short prefixes and rare process variants, while adding intrinsic interpretability to the predictions.
AI.conclusion: Combining neural suffix prediction with decision mining creates a neuro-symbolic framework that addresses limitations of pure NN approaches, improving performance on challenging cases and enhancing model interpretability through rule-based reasoning.

title: AutoKD: Autonomous Knowledge Discovery
summary: Scientific discovery in data-rich domains is currently constrained by human bandwidth: the growth in the volume and complexity of real-world data far outpaces the rate at which researchers can read, reason, and synthesize. Recent LLM-based multi-agent systems have begun to automate portions of the research cycle, but they target hypothesis generation in settings where validation cannot itself be automated, and each run is one-shot, with no mechanism for findings to accumulate or steer subsequent inquiry. This paper introduces AutoKD, a multi-agent framework for autonomous knowledge discovery that is both computational and cumulative, allowing validated findings to persist and inform subsequent inquiry. Six coordinated LLM agents collaborate in an open-ended discovery loop, where accepted findings are stored in a persistent insight graph that serves as both long-term memory and an exploration-steering mechanism. We evaluate AutoKD on three diverse datasets from two perspectives: Open-ended Quality against published findings, and Conditioned Quality via literature-derived queries. Across both evaluation perspectives, AutoKD covers known findings and surfaces substantive discoveries that complement human-driven research. Our code is available at https://github.com/GeQinwen/AutoKD.

AI.tldr: AutoKD is a multi-agent LLM framework that enables computational and cumulative autonomous knowledge discovery, using six coordinated agents and a persistent insight graph to accumulate validated findings and steer ongoing research.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery is limited by human bandwidth as data volume/complexity grows faster than researchers can process. Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems have limitations: they only handle hypothesis generation without automated validation, operate as one-shot systems without accumulation of findings, and lack mechanisms for findings to steer subsequent inquiry.
AI.method: AutoKD uses six coordinated LLM agents in an open-ended discovery loop. It features a persistent insight graph that stores accepted findings, serving as both long-term memory and an exploration-steering mechanism.
