Absent such features, reaching sufficient accuracy requires increasing the number and complexity of individual rules, which diminishes the interpretability of the model. Here, we extend classical rule ensembles by introducing logical propositions with learnable sparse linear transformations of input variables, i.e., propositions of the form $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{w} \geq t$, where $\mathbf{w}$ is a learnable sparse weight vector, enabling decision regions as general polyhedrons with oblique faces. We propose a learning method using gradient boosting based on a weighted logistic regression. Empirical results across 14 regression and classification tasks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves lower model complexity than competitive baselines while maintaining similar or better predictive accuracy. Hence, the approach provides a favorable trade-off between interpretability and accuracy and reduces the reliance on manual feature engineering.

AI.tldr: Rule ensembles extended with learnable sparse linear transformations achieve better accuracy-interpretability trade-off than traditional axis-parallel rule ensembles.
AI.motivation: Traditional rule ensembles use axis-parallel decision regions (x ≥ t) which require expressive curated features to achieve good accuracy with small models. Without such features, models become too complex for interpretability.
AI.method: Extend rule ensembles with propositions of form x^Tw ≥ t, where w is a learnable sparse weight vector, enabling oblique decision boundaries. Propose gradient boosting method using weighted logistic regression.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across 14 regression/classification tasks shows proposed method achieves lower model complexity than competitive baselines while maintaining similar or better predictive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides favorable trade-off between interpretability and accuracy, reducing reliance on manual feature engineering while preserving rule ensemble interpretability.

title: Improving Proficiency and Efficiency of Android GUI Agents via Self-Generating Tool Actions
summary: Android agents using a hybrid action space that combines GUI actions and tool actions (e.g., accessing application data via APIs) remain largely underexplored, mainly due to the excessive effort required to create tools. To address this gap, we introduce DroidTool, a framework for augmenting the agents with self-generated tools, which are realized as Python functions operating on application states (e.g., a database). To create tools with minimal human labor, DroidTool employs an agentic workflow featuring stages: proposal, implementation, test generation and execution, and repair. Notably, when testing the created tools for verification, it constructs relational tests across relevant tools for natural preparation of appropriate test preconditions and improved test coverage, rather than testing each tool separately. The GUI agents augmented with the generated tools achieved approximately 4.47%p higher performance with approximately 20.05% fewer interactions than the GUI-only agents, averaged across representative benchmarks: AndroidWorld, B-MoCA, and MobileSafetyBench.

AI.tldr: DroidTool is a framework that enables Android agents to autonomously generate their own tools (Python functions) for accessing app data via APIs, creating a hybrid action space that combines GUI actions with programmatic tool actions to improve efficiency and performance.
AI.motivation: Android agents using hybrid action spaces (GUI + tool actions) are underexplored due to the excessive effort required to manually create tools for accessing application data via APIs. There's a need for automated tool generation to enable more capable agents.
AI.method: DroidTool employs an agentic workflow with four stages: 1) tool proposal, 2) implementation (as Python functions), 3) test generation and execution, and 4) repair. Notably, it uses relational tests across relevant tools for natural precondition preparation and improved test coverage, rather than testing each tool in isolation.
AI.result: GUI agents augmented with DroidTool-generated tools achieved approximately 4.47% higher performance (percentage points) with about 20.05% fewer interactions compared to GUI-only agents. Results were averaged across three benchmarks: AndroidWorld, B-MoCA, and MobileSafetyBench.
AI.conclusion: DroidTool successfully addresses the tool creation bottleneck in Android agents by enabling autonomous tool generation through an agentic workflow. The framework demonstrates that hybrid action spaces (GUI + generated tools) significantly improve both performance and efficiency of Android agents across multiple benchmarks.

title: Stability and Generalization of Straight-Through Estimators for Training Two-Layer Quantized Neural Networks
summary: We study the identity straight-through estimator (STE) for training a two-layer binary-activation network with hinge loss from the perspective of Statistical Learning Theory (SLT). Our central question is whether algorithmic stability can explain the statistical generalization of the estimator produced by the discontinuous STE training rule. In the saturated-output regime, the zero-initialized samplewise STE recursion is exactly the stochastic subgradient descent on the convex latent loss $(-yu^\top x)_+$. This representation makes a stability analysis possible. We derive an exact distance identity for two coupled updates and prove approximate non-expansiveness of the common-example map, with a quadratic defect only when the two latent margins straddle zero. We then obtain explicit $\ell_2$ on-average model-stability and generalization bounds, transferring stability isometrically from the latent vector to the full first-layer matrix. Combining stability with a standard optimization bound yields an explicit excess induced-risk guarantee and the rate $O(n^{-1/2})$ when $T=n^2$. Under margin separability, a complementary argument gives the optimal-order $O(R^2/(γ^2n))$ expected excess misclassification error for a randomized one-pass STE iterate and a corresponding majority-vote bound.

AI.tldr: The paper provides statistical learning theory analysis showing that algorithmic stability can explain generalization in identity straight-through estimators for binary neural networks, yielding optimal-order generalization bounds under margin conditions.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand whether algorithmic stability can explain the statistical generalization of discontinuous straight-through estimators (STEs) used to train binary neural networks, which are non-convex and discontinuous optimization problems.
AI.method: The authors analyze the identity STE for two-layer binary networks with hinge loss. They show that in the saturated-output regime, zero-initialized STE is equivalent to stochastic subgradient descent on a convex latent loss. They prove distance identities for coupled updates, establish approximate non-expansiveness, and derive explicit model-stability bounds.
AI.result: The authors obtain explicit ℓ₂ on-average model-stability and generalization bounds, showing stability transfers from latent vectors to full weight matrices. They achieve O(n^{-1/2}) excess risk rate when T=n². Under margin separability, they get optimal-order O(R²/(γ²n)) expected excess misclassification error for randomized one-pass STE and majority-vote bounds.
AI.conclusion: Algorithmic stability successfully explains generalization in discontinuous STE training, providing theoretical justification for practical STE methods and establishing optimal-order generalization guarantees under margin conditions.

title: Unsound Search with Policy and Value Networks in Legends of Code and Magic
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Also available as a Zenodo preprint, doi:10.5281/zenodo.22547763
summary: Decision-time search in perfect and imperfect information games with enumerable belief states are effective methods for game AI. Collectible card games are imperfect information games with large belief states. Legends of Code and Magic is a collectible card game competition where the belief states are $2^{101}$. The Legends of Code and Magic (LoCM) champion, ByteRL, plays with no search. Other works claim sound enumeration-based search is unusable in the genre due to the number of belief states. We measured three previously defined properties that predict where theoretically unsound perfect information Monte Carlo's defects are cheap and found LoCM sits in the favorable region. Starting with imitation learning of the runner-up policy, NeteaseOPD, we created a policy and value feed-forward network. Our agent searches over worlds sampled from a prior over the opponent's deck built from the runner-up's drafts. Using our strictest configuration in the battle phase we beat ByteRL with a win percentage of 51.35% 95% CI [50.37, 52.33], over 10,000 pre-registered games using the LoCM official referee and time limit. Search is not a minor factor on the matchup between our agent and ByteRL. Without search this agent scores 26.8% and adding search adds +24.6 points. Unsound search in imperfect information games could be exploitable. We replicate a published best-response attack against ByteRL. We then apply the same attack protocol to two search configurations of our agent, and each one resists it better than ByteRL at every iteration. In LoCM unsound search gives us a stronger and more resilient agent.

AI.tldr: Sound enumeration-based search was previously considered unusable for collectible card games due to massive belief states, but this paper shows unsound search can work effectively in Legends of Code and Magic, beating the champion agent with 51.35% win rate while being more resilient to attacks.
AI.motivation: Collectible card games like Legends of Code and Magic have enormous belief states (2^101), making sound enumeration-based search theoretically infeasible. Previous work claimed such search was unusable, but the authors suspected that perfect information Monte Carlo search's defects might be affordable in practice for this game.
AI.method: Used imitation learning on runner-up policy (NeteaseOPD) to create policy and value networks, then performed search over worlds sampled from a prior over opponent's deck built from the runner-up's drafts. Applied unsound perfect information Monte Carlo search despite theoretical limitations.
AI.result: Beat the champion agent ByteRL with 51.35% win rate (95% CI [50.37, 52.33]) over 10,000 games. Search contributed +24.6 percentage points (from 26.8% without search to 51.35% with). The search-based agent also showed better resilience against best-response attacks than ByteRL.
AI.conclusion: Unsound search can be effective in imperfect information games with large belief states like Legends of Code and Magic, producing stronger and more resilient agents than search-free approaches, challenging previous assumptions about search feasibility in such games.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Masked Pretraining (MPT)
summary: Recently, Masked Pretraining (MPT) based on reconstruction pretraining tasks has risen to a promising self-supervised learning paradigm across various domains and achieves remarkable performance in multiple downstream tasks. However, the theoretical understanding of the working mechanism behind MPT is still limited. In this paper, we introduce a new theoretical framework to analyze MPT and understand the crucial role of masking in extracting meaningful representations. We establish theoretical connections between MPT and another popular self-supervised paradigm: contrastive learning. We prove that the masking technique implicitly creates positive pairs that are semantically similar and the reconstruction loss pulls them together in the feature space. Besides, as a result of the implicit alignment, we point out the dimensional collapse issue of MPT and propose a Uniformity-enhanced MPT (U-MPT) loss that can effectively address this issue and bring significant improvements in downstream tasks including linear evaluation, cross-dataset fine-tuning and out-of-distribution generalization on real-world data sets. Furthermore, we establish downstream guarantees of U-MPT and theoretically analyze the influence of masking strategies. Based on the theoretical analysis, we propose a new masking strategy which enhances the downstream performance of MPT and explains current improvements of masking strategies with our theoretical perspective.

AI.tldr: The paper provides theoretical analysis of Masked Pretraining (MPT), connects it to contrastive learning, identifies dimensional collapse issues, proposes a Uniformity-enhanced MPT loss and new masking strategies to improve downstream performance.
AI.motivation: Despite the remarkable success of Masked Pretraining (MPT) across various domains, there is limited theoretical understanding of its working mechanism and the crucial role of masking in extracting meaningful representations.
AI.method: The authors introduce a new theoretical framework to analyze MPT, establish connections to contrastive learning, prove that masking implicitly creates semantically similar positive pairs, identify dimensional collapse issues, and propose a Uniformity-enhanced MPT (U-MPT) loss and new masking strategies.
AI.result: The proposed U-MPT loss effectively addresses dimensional collapse and brings significant improvements in downstream tasks including linear evaluation, cross-dataset fine-tuning, and out-of-distribution generalization on real-world datasets. New masking strategies based on theoretical analysis enhance downstream performance.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive theoretical understanding of MPT, bridges the gap between MPT and contrastive learning, offers practical solutions to dimensional collapse, and provides theoretical guidance for developing better masking strategies in self-supervised learning.

title: Formation of structural attractors in neuromorphic systems
summary: This paper examines the theory of Invariant Structural Learning (ISL), which proposes a non-optimization approach to concept formation. Learning is interpreted as convergence to structural attractors in a hypergraph space, rather than as the minimization of a global loss function. The paper presents the ISL model, including its mathematical formalization, computational verification, and a hypothetical neurobiological interpretation. The mathematical section introduces the formal apparatus of the structural reduction process and proves its finite convergence, the existence and uniqueness of class structural attractors, and the self-organization of attractor maps. The computational section demonstrates the feasibility of the proposed approach on classical image recognition tasks, utilizing the proposed learning mechanism without backpropagation and with extremely small training datasets. Finally, the neurobiological section formulates hypotheses regarding the possible implementation of structural attractors in dendritic trees, neural coding as a projection of internal attractor dynamics, and the development of neural architectures supporting the proposed learning concept. These hypotheses are discussed in the context of modern experimental data in the fields of dendritic computations, synaptic plasticity, and the structural organization of neural circuits. The proposed neurobiological mechanisms are presented as testable hypotheses rather than established biological facts. The results demonstrate the mathematical consistency and computational feasibility of the proposed model, while the neurobiological hypotheses outline potential directions for its experimental verification.

AI.tldr: Invariant Structural Learning (ISL) proposes a non-optimization approach where learning converges to structural attractors in hypergraph space, mathematically consistent and computationally feasible without backpropagation using small datasets.
AI.motivation: To develop an alternative learning theory that doesn't rely on optimization/minimization of global loss functions, potentially offering a more biologically plausible approach to concept formation.
AI.method: ISL model formalized mathematically with proofs of finite convergence and attractor existence; computational verification on image recognition tasks without backpropagation using small datasets; neurobiological interpretation through hypotheses about dendritic trees and neural coding.
AI.result: Mathematical consistency demonstrated with proofs of finite convergence, existence/uniqueness of class structural attractors, and self-organization of attractor maps. Computational feasibility shown on classical image recognition tasks with small training datasets without backpropagation.
AI.conclusion: ISL provides a mathematically consistent and computationally feasible alternative to optimization-based learning, with neurobiological hypotheses offering testable directions for experimental verification of the model's biological plausibility.

title: Local and Global Stability in Performative Reinforcement Learning
summary: In performative reinforcement learning the deployed policy shapes the environment that generates the learner's future data, and the natural solution concept is a performatively stable policy that is optimal in the environment it induces. Existing convergence guarantees rely on Lipschitz sensitivity assumptions on the environment map $π\mapsto (P_π, r_π)$, which are hard to verify and fail in settings such as multi-agent best-response dynamics. We instead study stability for mixtures of policies, and show that the resulting picture is fundamentally different from performative prediction, where randomization removes the need for any sensitivity assumption. We distinguish local mixed stability, an occupancy-weighted first-order relaxation that we show is equivalent to stationarity, from global mixed stability, which certifies against arbitrary deviating policies. Our first result is that a weighted per-state Hedge dynamic drives the local stability gap to zero at an $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rate for an arbitrary, possibly discontinuous, environment map, both with exact and with trajectory feedback. The two notions genuinely differ: we exhibit an instance where local stability is achieved exactly but every mixture has global stability gap bounded away from zero. For global stability we introduce a bounded transition range assumption, strictly weaker than Lipschitz sensitivity, under which unweighted per-state Hedge converges up to a floor of $O(γε_P/(1-γ)^3)$, and we prove a matching-in-$ε_P$ lower bound of $Ω(γε_P/(1-γ))$ under trajectory feedback, so this floor is unavoidable. Finally, we extend both notions to $n$-player performative Markov games, obtaining local stability with no assumption on the joint environment map or game structure, and global stability for performative Markov potential games.

AI.tldr: Randomization enables stability in performative RL without Lipschitz assumptions; per-state Hedge achieves local stability but global stability requires stronger assumptions with unavoidable error floor.
AI.motivation: Existing performative RL convergence guarantees rely on Lipschitz sensitivity assumptions that are hard to verify and fail in multi-agent settings like best-response dynamics. The authors want to overcome this limitation by studying stability for policy mixtures rather than deterministic policies.
AI.method: Introduce two stability notions for policy mixtures: local mixed stability (occupancy-weighted first-order relaxation) and global mixed stability (against arbitrary deviations). Use weighted per-state Hedge dynamics for local stability and unweighted per-state Hedge for global stability under bounded transition range assumption.
AI.result: Weighted per-state Hedge achieves local stability at O(1/√T) rate even with discontinuous environment maps. Local and global stability genuinely differ - instances exist where local is perfect but global has bounded gap. For global stability, convergence up to O(γε_P/(1-γ)³) error floor, with matching lower bound showing this floor is unavoidable.
AI.conclusion: Randomization through policy mixtures removes need for Lipschitz assumptions in performative RL, enabling local stability guarantees in discontinuous settings. The tradeoff between local and global stability reveals fundamental limitations, with unavoidable error floor for global stability even under weaker assumptions than Lipschitz.

title: NormViz: A Benchmark and Framework for Grounding Multimodal Reasoning in Global Cultures
comment: Accepted to Conference on Language Modeling (COLM) 2026. 37 pages, 23 figures
summary: AI systems are used worldwide, but they struggle to serve the needs of culturally diverse populations. Prior work on cultural understanding evaluates AI systems on text-only settings or on visual artifact recognition (e.g. foods, clothing). The ability to reason about visually observable behaviors through local social norms, which we call visual norm understanding, remains unexamined. We introduce NormViz-Bench, a high quality, human-validated benchmark of 3,268 contrastive image pairs (6,536 images) spanning 16 countries. Each pair varies only in the culturally relevant behavior (e.g., objects, attributes, spatial relations, and actions) that alters how each image is interpreted. Each image is labeled as conforming to, violating, or irrelevant to local social norms, and pair-level evaluation requires both images to be correctly classified, thereby preventing reliance on superficial visual shortcuts. Even the strongest VLMs, Gemini 3.0 Flash and Qwen2.5 VL 7B, succeed on only 26.6% and 21.6% of pairs, struggling most with identifying violating and culturally benign visual behaviors. Towards bridging this, we introduce NormViz-Train, a training dataset of 64k images paired with explanations. Though absolute performance remains low (<30%), finetuning on NormViz-Train improves pair accuracy relatively by up to 125% and 36% Qwen3-VL 4B and 8B respectively, showing a path forward to teach models to connect visual perception to cultural significance. Together, NormViz-Bench and NormViz-Train establish visual norm understanding as a challenging and consequential frontier for multimodal AI.

AI.tldr: A new benchmark (NormViz-Bench) and training dataset (NormViz-Train) for evaluating and improving visual norm understanding in AI systems, revealing current models' significant limitations in recognizing culturally appropriate behaviors from images.
AI.motivation: Current AI systems fail to serve culturally diverse populations, with prior work limited to text-only cultural understanding or simple visual artifact recognition. There's a gap in evaluating AI's ability to reason about visually observable behaviors through local social norms (visual norm understanding).
AI.method: Created NormViz-Bench: a human-validated benchmark with 3,268 contrastive image pairs (6,536 images) from 16 countries. Each pair varies only in culturally relevant behaviors (objects, attributes, spatial relations, actions), requiring classification of images as conforming to, violating, or irrelevant to local norms. Also developed NormViz-Train: a 64k-image training dataset with explanations.
AI.result: State-of-the-art vision-language models performed poorly: Gemini 3.0 Flash (26.6% accuracy) and Qwen2.5 VL 7B (21.6%). Models struggled most with identifying violating and culturally benign behaviors. Finetuning on NormViz-Train improved performance significantly: Qwen3-VL 4B improved by 125% and 8B by 36% relatively, though absolute performance remains below 30%.
AI.conclusion: Visual norm understanding is a challenging but critical frontier for multimodal AI. The work establishes foundational datasets for measuring and improving AI's ability to connect visual perception with cultural significance, demonstrating both the difficulty of the task and a promising path forward through targeted training.

title: Sector-Mean: Deterministic Initialization of K-Means Centroids via Angular Sector Partitioning
summary: K-Means is one of the most widely used clustering algorithms, but its susceptibility to initial centroid selection remains a primary bottleneck for its convergence speed and clustering accuracy. This paper proposes Sector-Mean Initialization, a deterministic initialization strategy with O(N) time complexity that partitions the two-dimensional data space into angular sectors around the global centroid and initializes centroids using sector-wise means. We evaluate the method on established two-dimensional benchmarks (SIPU, Birch) and multiple real-world datasets, comparing against random, K-Means++, and Max-Min initialization under identical Lloyd iterations. The statistical analysis of Friedman's test (p<0.05) and Nemenyi post-hoc comparison indicates that, while delivering equivalent clustering quality as K-Means++ and Max-Min, Sector-Mean offers significant computational efficiency. Experimental results show that Sector-Mean reduces the initialization time by 74.9% and 59.8% in comparison to K-Means++ and max-min, respectively. And, it yields the lowest average number of iterations, achieving approximately 5% fewer iterations than K-Means++ and 16% fewer than max-min. These results highlight that Sector-Mean initialization offers a deterministic and computationally efficient initialization strategy while preserving cluster quality.

AI.tldr: Sector-Mean is a deterministic K-Means initialization method that partitions 2D data into angular sectors around the global centroid, offering significant computational efficiency while maintaining clustering quality comparable to K-Means++ and Max-Min.
AI.motivation: K-Means clustering's susceptibility to initial centroid selection remains a bottleneck for convergence speed and accuracy. Random initialization can lead to suboptimal results, and existing methods like K-Means++ have computational overhead. There's a need for deterministic, computationally efficient initialization strategies.
AI.method: Proposes Sector-Mean Initialization with O(N) time complexity. Partitions two-dimensional data space into angular sectors around the global centroid, then initializes centroids using sector-wise means of the data points within each sector. This provides a deterministic initialization strategy.
AI.result: Sector-Mean reduces initialization time by 74.9% vs K-Means++ and 59.8% vs Max-Min. Achieves approximately 5% fewer iterations than K-Means++ and 16% fewer than Max-Min. Statistical analysis (Friedman's test p<0.05) shows equivalent clustering quality to K-Means++ and Max-Min while offering significantly better computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Sector-Mean initialization offers a deterministic and computationally efficient initialization strategy for K-Means in 2D spaces that preserves clustering quality while dramatically reducing initialization time and iteration count compared to existing methods.

title: Learning transferable human physiology from two million hours of sleep with SleepFM-2
summary: Sleep provides a nightly window into health by capturing coordinated activity across the brain, heart, muscles and respiratory system. We introduce SleepFM-2, a sleep foundation model developed and evaluated on 282,511 polysomnography recordings from 26 cohorts, including 235,865 used for pretraining. These data span more than two million hours of multimodal physiology. Compared with SleepFM, SleepFM-2 improves disease prediction and sleep scoring, supports arousal, limb movement and respiratory event detection, and transfers to wearable sensing and subjective sleep phenotypes. A model combining its PSG representation with age, sex and BMI met a prespecified discrimination and significance criterion for 215 subsequently recorded EHR phenotypes in two held-out cohorts, including one health system unseen during pretraining. For 155 phenotypes, the PSG representation added reproducible information beyond demographics. SleepFM-2 also outperformed a 480-feature baseline derived from the same recordings. Its disease scores revealed a reproducible principal component associated with reduced sigma-band spatial coupling and increased hypnodensity entropy. The frozen encoder performed within the observed range of expert scorers for sleep events and transferred to wakeful EEG, headband and in-ear EEG, wrist PPG and wrist accelerometry. It improved sleep staging across six accelerometry cohorts and achieved disease-prediction performance in UK Biobank similar to models pretrained directly on accelerometry. Finally, SleepFM-2 captured aspects of subjective sleep not recovered by conventional PSG summaries, particularly reports of the recorded night. These results show that multimodal sleep physiology can provide a transferable representation of human health across diseases, clinical tasks, sensors and subjective experience.

AI.tldr: SleepFM-2 is a large-scale sleep foundation model trained on 282K+ polysomnography recordings that improves disease prediction, sleep scoring, and transfers across sensors and subjective sleep experiences.
AI.motivation: Sleep captures coordinated activity across multiple physiological systems (brain, heart, muscles, respiratory), making it a valuable window into overall health, but existing models have limited scope and generalizability.
AI.method: Developed and evaluated on 282,511 polysomnography recordings from 26 cohorts (235,865 for pretraining), spanning over 2 million hours of multimodal physiology data. Used a frozen encoder approach.
AI.result: The model met prespecified criteria for 215 EHR phenotypes, added reproducible information beyond demographics for 155 phenotypes, outperformed 480-feature baseline, performed within expert scorer range for sleep events, transferred to various wearable sensors, improved sleep staging across accelerometry cohorts, and captured subjective sleep aspects.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal sleep physiology can provide a transferable representation of human health across diseases, clinical tasks, sensors, and subjective experience, demonstrating the value of sleep as a comprehensive health biomarker.

title: One Step, One Lead: Mitigating Higher-Order Interference in Multi-Domain Reinforcement Learning via Cross-Step Control
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) across multiple domains can broaden the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet joint training often degrades individual-domain performance and can destabilize optimization. Existing work typically diagnoses such interference from a single-step view using first-order gradient alignment or curvature-based proxies. We show that this view can miss a critical form of sequential interference: same-point domain gradients may remain nearly orthogonal even when consecutive realized updates partially reverse one another in output space. We further show that consecutive token log-probability footprints recover this interaction directly from adjacent checkpoints as a local second-order interaction in output space, without explicitly reconstructing same-step curvature. Building on this insight, we propose OSOL, which designates a focus domain at each iteration, uses the preceding checkpoint footprint to rank token-level rebound risk, and applies a drift-ranked, adaptively scaled correction within the standard GRPO update. Our analysis shows that this correction suppresses the targeted cross-step output backtracking component. Controlled studies further show that cross-step backtracking is more strongly associated with subsequent task damage than same-point gradient diagnostics, while the preceding footprint ranks future rebound risk more accurately than Hessian-based proxies. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, OSOL reaches a domain-macro average of 0.4822, improving by 5.7% over the strongest compared baseline, without explicit higher-order differentiation.

AI.tldr: OSOL is a new RL training method for LLMs that detects and corrects sequential interference across domains by using token log-probability footprints from consecutive checkpoints, improving multi-domain performance without higher-order differentiation.
AI.motivation: Multi-domain RL training for LLMs often suffers from performance degradation and instability due to interference between domains. Existing methods focus on single-step gradient analysis, which may miss sequential interference where consecutive updates partially reverse each other in output space.
AI.method: OSOL uses token log-probability footprints from adjacent checkpoints to detect sequential interference as local second-order interactions. It designates a focus domain each iteration, ranks token-level rebound risk using preceding checkpoint footprints, and applies drift-ranked, adaptively scaled corrections within standard GRPO updates.
AI.result: On Qwen3-30B-A3B, OSOL achieved a domain-macro average of 0.4822, improving by 5.7% over the strongest baseline. Cross-step backtracking was more predictive of task damage than same-point gradient diagnostics, and preceding footprints ranked future rebound risk better than Hessian-based proxies.
AI.conclusion: OSOL successfully addresses sequential interference in multi-domain RL by using checkpoint footprints to detect and correct cross-step backtracking, achieving better performance without explicit higher-order differentiation, showing that sequential interference is critical to multi-domain optimization.

title: A visual large language foundational model for medical image recognition using clinician-oriented social media
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across diverse domains, showing considerable potential in medicine. However, their application in medical settings remains limited by the scarcity of visual question answering (VQA) datasets that capture clinical reasoning and explicit image-text alignment. Here, we leverage de-identified medical images and expert commentaries shared on clinician-oriented social media. By combining an advanced LLM with clinician-in-the-loop verification, we established a rigorous pipeline to construct ThoughtMed-1M, a long-form medical VQA dataset containing over one million VQA pairs and designed to capture structured clinical logic and medical image-text alignment. To demonstrate its utility, we developed a FOundational LLM Trained on ThoughtMed-1M (FOLTMed). FOLTMed achieved state-of-the-art performance across 42 medical VQA benchmark datasets, with a macro accuracy of 85.4%, and generated more clinically coherent responses on the ThoughtMed-1M test set. It outperformed state-of-the-art models by 3--5% across factuality and similarity metrics, highlighting a scalable paradigm for advancing research on clinically grounded multimodal LLMs.

AI.tldr: Researchers created ThoughtMed-1M, a large medical VQA dataset with over 1 million Q&A pairs using clinician social media data and LLM+expert pipeline, then trained FOLTMed model which achieved SOTA performance on 42 medical VQA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLMs show strong potential in medicine but their application is limited by the scarcity of medical VQA datasets that capture clinical reasoning and explicit image-text alignment, necessitating high-quality multimodal medical datasets.
AI.method: Used de-identified medical images and expert commentaries from clinician social media, combined advanced LLM with clinician-in-the-loop verification to create ThoughtMed-1M dataset, then trained foundational LLM (FOLTMed) on this data.
AI.result: FOLTMed achieved state-of-the-art performance across 42 medical VQA benchmarks with 85.4% macro accuracy, outperformed SOTA models by 3-5% on factuality and similarity metrics, and generated more clinically coherent responses.
AI.conclusion: The study presents a scalable paradigm for advancing clinically grounded multimodal LLMs by creating a large, high-quality medical VQA dataset and demonstrating its utility through a foundational model that significantly outperforms existing approaches.

title: Steering Under Compression: Dose-Response, Capability Cost, and Failure Asymmetry in Quantized LLMs
summary: Inference-time activation steering enables behavioral control of large language models without parameter modification, while post-training quantization reduces memory and compute costs for deployment. Despite their growing convergence in practice, the interaction between these two techniques remains uncharacterized. We systematically study activation steering under weight-only quantization (INT8 and NF4) across four open-weight 7-9B models and two behavioral targets: judged sentiment and judge-free reasoning length. Using an iso-effect framework that compares capability costs at matched behavioral effect, we find that sentiment steering survives quantization intact. After correcting a GSM8K parser artifact with a uniform v2.3.1 rescore, the pooled INT8 contrast is -0.010 (90% CI [-0.026, +0.007]), descriptively Equivalent under the preregistered three-label rule, while NF4 remains Inconclusive at -0.017 ([-0.067, +0.033]). In contrast, reasoning length exhibits a surprising asymmetric dose-response: lengthening is graded but terminates in cap-runaway and collapse, while shortening is a step function with only 12-30% shortening (model-dependent) before discontinuous failure. We expose a methodological pitfall: the naive iso-effect ladder anchors on the collapse floor for floor-bounded targets, and we introduce a censored construction that restores interpretable crossings. We also quantify a substantial baseline capability shift for Mistral-NF4 (0.545 to 0.365 GSM8K at alpha=0), demonstrating that compression can dominate the steering intervention. Despite this, steering vectors remain highly collinear with their FP16 siblings (cosine similarity 0.989-0.998 for INT8, 0.945-0.990 for NF4), confirming that the behavioral direction survives quantization even when the cost structure does not. All code and data are released.

AI.tldr: Activation steering largely survives weight-only quantization (INT8/NF4) for sentiment control but shows asymmetric effects for reasoning length control, with methodology issues requiring correction.
AI.motivation: Activation steering enables behavioral control of LLMs without parameter modification, while quantization reduces deployment costs, but their interaction remains uncharacterized despite growing convergence in practice.
AI.method: Systematically studied activation steering under weight-only quantization (INT8 and NF4) across four 7-9B models using iso-effect framework to compare capability costs at matched behavioral effect. Used sentiment and reasoning length as behavioral targets, with methodology improvements for censored construction.
AI.result: Sentiment steering survives quantization intact (INT8: -0.010, descriptively Equivalent; NF4: -0.017, Inconclusive). Reasoning length shows asymmetric dose-response: lengthening graded but collapses, shortening step function with 12-30% shortening before failure. Steering vectors remain highly collinear with FP16 versions (0.989-0.998 INT8, 0.945-0.990 NF4).
AI.conclusion: Behavioral direction of activation steering survives quantization even when cost structure changes, but methodological pitfalls exist for floor-bounded targets requiring censored construction. Compression can dominate steering intervention in capability shifts.

title: When and Why LLM Causal Priors Help: Closed-Loop Prior Selection for Amortized Causal Inference
summary: Causal effect estimation asks how an outcome would change under an intervention, and medicine, economics, and public policy all treat it as a foundational task. Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) amortize the task: a model trained on large numbers of programmatically generated synthetic causal tasks reads a new problem's observational data into context and returns an interventional-effect estimate in a single forward pass. The capability of such models is largely determined by the synthetic training prior, which is currently designed by hand, a bottleneck acknowledged by both Do-PFN and CausalPFN. Large language models (LLMs) can now ``draw'' plausible causal graphs for a given domain, suggesting that LLM-distilled graphs could serve as prior material. Whether injecting such graphs helps at all, where any gain comes from, and when injection helps. Practice has so far relied on manual trial and error. We propose a \emph{closed-loop prior selection framework} that casts prior injection as a budget-constrained optimization over a candidate prior pool. Candidates undergo cheap post-training and are scored by a composite metric dominated by real-domain generalization; the winner then receives full training and paired statistical validation. On a 7.34M-parameter Do-PFN, the framework's winner attains a formally significant $2.75\times$ gain on the primary evaluation domain, and its error falls below that of the uninjected official base. Generalization on an adjacent monitoring domain improves significantly, and no monitored capability degrades. Mechanism experiments show that the gain depends on the semantic content of the distilled graph rather than its structural diversity alone does not produce it (directional evidence). With this framework and this regularity in hand, the use of LLM causal priors stops being manual trial and error and becomes an empirically verifiable selection problem.

AI.tldr: LLM-distilled causal graphs as training priors improve causal effect estimation when selected via optimization framework, achieving 2.75× gain without manual trial-and-error.
AI.motivation: Current PFNs rely on manually designed synthetic training priors, creating a bottleneck. LLMs can generate plausible causal graphs for domains, but it's unclear if injecting these helps, how much gain comes from semantic content vs. structural diversity, and optimal selection requires trial-and-error.
AI.method: Proposed closed-loop prior selection framework: treat prior injection as budget-constrained optimization over candidate prior pool. Candidates undergo cheap post-training, scored by composite metric dominated by real-domain generalization. Winner receives full training and statistical validation.
AI.result: On 7.34M-parameter Do-PFN, framework winner attains 2.75× gain on primary evaluation domain, error falls below uninjected official base. Adjacent domain generalization improves significantly, no monitored capability degrades. Gain depends on semantic content of distilled graphs, not just structural diversity.
AI.conclusion: LLM causal priors can improve causal effect estimation when selected via systematic framework rather than manual trial-and-error. Framework transforms prior selection into empirically verifiable optimization problem with verifiable regularities about semantic content importance.

title: Learning Kernels by Alignment for Multiclass Bayes Classification
summary: Kernel methods separate data representation from decision-making, but typically require the kernel to be chosen in advance. We show that this kernel can instead be learned by alignment, and develop the resulting framework through the recently introduced Collaborative Learning and Inference (CLaI). We show that Collaborative Learning can be viewed as a kernel alignment process, in which an embedding is trained so that its induced similarity matches a label-derived target kernel. We also prove that Collaborative Inference is equivalent to kernel Bayes classification with Parzen-window density estimation. Motivated by these perspectives, we generalise CLaI by replacing cosine similarity with a learned Mahalanobis distance and extend it to multiclass classification. On CIFAR-10, PathMNIST, and SleepEDF, the Mahalanobis formulation improves accuracy, converges faster, and yields lower calibration error than the cosine-based variant. Auxiliary experiments further support these connections, showing that CLaI produces latent signals of the same form as a Gaussian process, while achieving competitive calibration on sepsis prediction. Together, these results establish a principled learned-kernel framework that unifies representation learning, kernel alignment, and Bayesian classification, and extends naturally to the multiclass setting.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that Collaborative Learning and Inference (CLaI) can be viewed as kernel alignment, connects it to kernel Bayes classification, generalizes it with Mahalanobis distances, and demonstrates improved performance on multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Kernel methods require pre-specified kernels, limiting flexibility. The paper aims to develop a framework where kernels can be learned through alignment rather than chosen in advance.
AI.method: Frame Collaborative Learning as kernel alignment where embeddings are trained to match label-derived target kernels. Show Collaborative Inference equals kernel Bayes classification with Parzen windows. Generalize CLaI by replacing cosine similarity with learned Mahalanobis distance and extend to multiclass classification.
AI.result: Mahalanobis formulation improves accuracy, converges faster, and yields lower calibration error than cosine-based variant on CIFAR-10, PathMNIST, and SleepEDF. CLaI produces latent signals similar to Gaussian processes and achieves competitive calibration on sepsis prediction.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a principled learned-kernel framework unifying representation learning, kernel alignment, and Bayesian classification that extends naturally to multiclass settings.

title: iBrain: A Unified Foundation Model Reading the Brain from Surface to Spikes
summary: Invasive neural recordings provide high-fidelity measurements of brain activity, with signals such as intracranial EEG (iEEG) and intracortical spiking activity capturing neural dynamics at different spatial and temporal scales. Yet existing neural foundation models have largely been developed independently for different invasive recording paradigms, leaving joint pretraining across heterogeneous invasive signals underexplored. In this work, we introduce iBrain, a unified foundation model that jointly learns from iEEG and spiking activity. iBrain employs signal-specific encoders to accommodate their distinct signal characteristics and a shared spatiotemporal Transformer backbone to model dependencies across recording channels and time. We pretrain iBrain on over 7,000 hours of heterogeneous neural recordings using masked signal reconstruction and channel-view alignment, promoting contextual modeling of neural dynamics and robustness across different channels. iBrain consistently outperforms single-signal pretraining baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. Further experiments demonstrate that iBrain exhibits transferability and data efficiency across diverse recording settings. These results highlight the potential of joint pretraining on heterogeneous invasive neural recordings to support scalable neural modeling and transferable representations across recording settings and downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: iBrain is a unified foundation model that jointly learns from both iEEG and spiking activity neural recordings through signal-specific encoders and a shared Transformer backbone, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing neural foundation models are developed independently for different invasive recording paradigms (iEEG and spiking activity), leaving joint pretraining across heterogeneous invasive signals underexplored despite their complementary nature.
AI.method: iBrain uses signal-specific encoders to handle distinct characteristics of iEEG and spiking signals, with a shared spatiotemporal Transformer backbone to model dependencies across channels and time. It's pretrained on over 7,000 hours of neural recordings using masked signal reconstruction and channel-view alignment.
AI.result: iBrain consistently outperforms single-signal pretraining baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. It demonstrates transferability and data efficiency across diverse recording settings.
AI.conclusion: Joint pretraining on heterogeneous invasive neural recordings supports scalable neural modeling and transferable representations across recording settings and downstream tasks, highlighting the potential of unified foundation models for brain activity analysis.

title: How Does Parameter Pruning Reshape DNN Representations? An Interaction-Driven Exploration
summary: This study focuses on the scientific problem of understanding internal factors that govern the diverse performance degradation of deep neural networks (DNNs) when different parameters are pruned. In order to explain why pruning certain parameters leads to significant performance degradation but pruning other parameters does not, we examine how the pruning operation affects the interaction patterns encoded by the DNN. We find that when we progressively increase the pruning ratio, the interaction patterns encoded by DNNs exhibit a distinct three-phase dynamics, \emph{i.e.}, model performance is not largely affected until the pruning operation begins to remove low-order interactions, and low-order interactions exhibit strong generalizability. Moreover, we find that the high sensitivity of DNN performance to the pruning of certain modules is attributed to whether the pruning operation removes generalizable low-order interaction patterns.

AI.tldr: Pruning certain DNN parameters causes significant performance degradation due to removal of generalizable low-order interactions, while pruning others doesn't because they contain less important high-order interactions.
AI.motivation: To understand why pruning different parameters in deep neural networks leads to diverse performance degradation levels, and to explain what internal factors govern this sensitivity to pruning.
AI.method: Examine how pruning affects interaction patterns encoded by DNNs, analyze the dynamics of interaction patterns as pruning ratio increases progressively, and identify three-phase dynamics in interaction patterns.
AI.result: Found that DNNs exhibit three-phase dynamics in interaction patterns when pruning increases: performance remains stable until pruning begins to remove low-order interactions. Low-order interactions show strong generalizability, and performance sensitivity depends on whether pruning removes these generalizable low-order patterns.
AI.conclusion: The key factor determining DNN performance degradation during pruning is whether the pruning operation removes generalizable low-order interaction patterns, explaining why some parameters are more critical than others for maintaining model performance.

title: SSP-DMGTimeNet: Physics-Constrained Learning for Spatiotemporal Trajectory Prediction of Vehicle Platoons
summary: Existing car-following prediction methods mainly optimize trajectory accuracy, while rarely considering whether predicted disturbances propagate realistically along a vehicle platoon. This limitation may lead to accurate but string-unstable predictions. We propose SSP-DMGTimeNet, a physics-constrained learning framework for spatiotemporal trajectory prediction of vehicle platoons. The model combines multi-scale temporal representations with cross-vehicle interaction features to capture complex and time-varying platoon dynamics. A propagation-delay-aware causal attention mechanism explicitly models upstream-to-downstream disturbance propagation by learning response delays between adjacent vehicles and accumulating them along the platoon. In addition, time- and frequency-domain string-stability losses relieve disturbance amplification across both adjacent vehicles and arbitrary sub-platoons during training. Experiments on HighD show that SSP-DMGTimeNet achieves an unstable-window rate of 0.65\% for five-vehicle platoons and a maximum head-to-tail amplification of 0.898 on the ground-truth excitation subset, while maintaining competitive trajectory prediction performance. In zero-shot evaluation on NGSIM US-101 and I-80, the model achieves velocity MAEs of 1.316~m/s and 1.252~m/s, with unstable-window rates of 3.90\% and 4.10\%, respectively. These results demonstrate that incorporating platoon-level physical constraints can effectively balance trajectory prediction accuracy and disturbance propagation stability.

AI.tldr: SSP-DMGTimeNet is a physics-constrained learning framework that predicts vehicle platoon trajectories while ensuring string stability, achieving both accurate predictions and realistic disturbance propagation.
AI.motivation: Existing car-following prediction methods focus only on trajectory accuracy but ignore whether predicted disturbances propagate realistically through vehicle platoons, potentially leading to string-unstable predictions that don't reflect real-world physics.
AI.method: The model combines multi-scale temporal representations with cross-vehicle interaction features. It uses a propagation-delay-aware causal attention mechanism to explicitly model upstream-to-downstream disturbance propagation by learning response delays between vehicles. Time- and frequency-domain string-stability losses prevent disturbance amplification across both adjacent vehicles and arbitrary sub-platoons during training.
AI.result: On HighD dataset: achieved 0.65% unstable-window rate for 5-vehicle platoons and maximum head-to-tail amplification of 0.898. On NGSIM datasets (zero-shot evaluation): velocity MAEs of 1.316~m/s and 1.252~m/s with unstable-window rates of 3.90% and 4.10% respectively, while maintaining competitive trajectory prediction performance.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating platoon-level physical constraints (particularly string stability) can effectively balance trajectory prediction accuracy with realistic disturbance propagation, addressing a key limitation of existing methods that optimize only for accuracy without considering physical plausibility.

title: Second-Order Smooth Planning with Optimal-Transport Bellman Smoothing
comment: Published at the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Planning with a generative model aims to estimate the value of a state using as few simulator calls as possible. SmoothCruiser achieves problem-independent complexity $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-4})$ by exploiting the smoothness of the entropy-regularized Bellman backup, but its estimator is only first-order. We show that the sample-complexity exponent of SmoothCruiser-type planners is governed by the order $β$ of the local Taylor remainder, giving oracle complexity $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-(2+2/(β-1))})$: the first-order case $β=2$ recovers SmoothCruiser, while a second-order/cubic remainder $β=3$ yields $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})$. We reach this regime with an optimal-transport-smoothed Bellman backup over action distributions, which has a closed form, a policy gradient, and a Lipschitz Hessian, and whose quadratic correction admits an unbiased cross-product estimator. The resulting SecondOrderSmoothCruiser achieves $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ oracle complexity for fixed OT parameters, and we relate the OT, entropy-regularized, and unregularized objectives through explicit regularization-bias bounds.

AI.tldr: SecondOrderSmoothCruiser improves planning complexity from Õ(ε⁻⁴) to Õ(ε⁻³) by using second-order approximations and optimal transport smoothing.
AI.motivation: Existing planners like SmoothCruiser achieve Õ(ε⁻⁴) complexity but are limited to first-order approximations. There's a need for better sample efficiency in planning with generative models.
AI.method: Develops an optimal-transport-smoothed Bellman backup over action distributions with closed form, policy gradient, and Lipschitz Hessian. Uses second-order/cubic remainder (β=3) with unbiased cross-product estimator for quadratic correction.
AI.result: Achieves Õ(ε⁻³) oracle complexity for fixed OT parameters, improving over the Õ(ε⁻⁴) of first-order SmoothCruiser. Provides explicit regularization-bias bounds relating OT, entropy-regularized, and unregularized objectives.
AI.conclusion: Higher-order approximations (β>2) can significantly improve planning complexity. The SecondOrderSmoothCruiser framework demonstrates practical second-order planning with formal guarantees and connections to various regularization schemes.

title: RedKnot-MLA: Multi-Head Offline-Online Reuse for DeepSeek-V4 Long-Context Serving
summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) exposes many logical query heads through one packed latent KV stream. This representation is memory efficient, but it removes the physical per-head cache boundary assumed by conventional head-wise reuse. We present our system, a DeepSeek-V4 realization of RedKnot's head-aware reuse principle. Each immutable document is processed offline at canonical position zero; certified Local-head contributions are retained as MLA-Off. At serving time, query-side RoPE relocation restores the document's request position, a small Global-head set and protected Local token rows are recomputed as MLA-Online, and the two paths are merged before a single shared output projection. The packed MLA latent is never split. DeepSeek-V4-Flash uses 37 reusable layers and a 56/8 Local/Global partition, giving a 75.29% analytic logical head-row ceiling; the Pro-0813 profile uses 55 layers and 112/16 heads, giving 78.89%. Frozen Flash operating points show hot-artifact TTFT speedups of 2.02-3.84x. At 256K, the archived three-dataset study reports an aggregate F1 change of +3.24 percentage points, an EM change of +4.16 points, and a 78.7-79.5% analytic major-operator arithmetic saving, while one dataset decreases by 2.81 F1 points. A separate author-reported 256K hot-artifact QPS measurement is approximately 2.0x; because its raw concurrency trace is not included in this bundle, we mark it as preliminary rather than archived evidence. We describe the factorization, position repair, token-row closure, sparse-MoE support, TP8 integration, and the measurement boundaries needed to interpret these results.

AI.tldr: DeepSeek-V4 introduces a system for efficient multi-head latent attention that separates offline document processing from online serving, achieving significant performance improvements while maintaining memory efficiency.
AI.motivation: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) is memory efficient but removes the physical per-head cache boundary assumed by conventional head-wise reuse, requiring a new approach to maintain efficiency while preserving attention mechanisms.
AI.method: The system processes immutable documents offline at position zero (MLA-Off), then at serving time relocates query positions with RoPE, recomputes a small Global-head set and protected Local token rows online (MLA-Online), merging both paths before output projection while keeping the packed MLA latent intact.
AI.result: DeepSeek-V4-Flash achieves 75.29% analytic logical head-row ceiling, while Pro-0813 reaches 78.89%. The system provides 2.02-3.84x TTFT speedups for hot artifacts, +3.24% aggregate F1, +4.16% EM improvement, and 78.7-79.5% arithmetic savings on major operators at 256K context length.
AI.conclusion: The proposed head-aware reuse system effectively addresses MLA's limitations, achieving significant performance gains while maintaining memory efficiency, though careful interpretation of results is needed due to measurement boundaries.

title: Power Mean Estimation in Stochastic Continuous Monte Carlo Tree Search
comment: Published at the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025)
summary: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) has demonstrated success in online planning for deterministic environments, yet significant challenges remain in adapting it to stochastic Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), particularly in continuous state-action spaces. Existing methods, such as HOOT, which combines MCTS with the Hierarchical Optimistic Optimization (HOO) bandit strategy, address continuous spaces but rely on a logarithmic exploration bonus that lacks theoretical guarantees in non-stationary, stochastic settings. Recent advancements, such as POLY-HOOT, introduced a polynomial bonus term to achieve convergence in deterministic MDPs, though a similar theory for stochastic MDPs remains undeveloped. In this paper, we propose a novel MCTS algorithm, \Algname, designed for continuous, stochastic MDPs. \Algname integrates a power mean as a value backup operator, alongside a polynomial exploration bonus to address the non-stationarity inherent in continuous action spaces. Our theoretical analysis establishes that \Algname converges at a polynomial rate of $\mathcal{O}(n^{-ζ})$, $ζ\in (0,1/2)$, where \( n \) is the number of visited trajectories, thereby extending the non-asymptotic convergence guarantees of POLY-HOOT to stochastic environments. Experimental results on stochastic tasks validate our theoretical findings, demonstrating the effectiveness of \Algname in continuous, stochastic domains.

AI.tldr: A novel MCTS algorithm with polynomial convergence guarantees for continuous, stochastic MDPs, using power mean backup and polynomial exploration bonus.
AI.motivation: MCTS has worked well for deterministic environments but faces challenges in stochastic MDPs with continuous state-action spaces. Existing methods like HOOT address continuous spaces but lack theoretical guarantees in stochastic settings, and recent advances like POLY-HOOT only work for deterministic MDPs.
AI.method: Proposed algorithm \Algname integrates a power mean as a value backup operator and uses a polynomial exploration bonus to handle non-stationarity in continuous action spaces. This extends POLY-HOOT concepts to stochastic environments.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows \Algname converges at polynomial rate O(n^{-ζ}) where ζ∈(0,1/2) and n is number of visited trajectories. Experimental results on stochastic tasks validate these theoretical findings.
AI.conclusion: \Algname effectively extends MCTS convergence guarantees to continuous, stochastic MDPs, providing both theoretical guarantees and empirical validation for the first time in this challenging domain.

title: Beyond One-Shot Expansion: Contrastive Evidence Exploration for Multi-Hop Retrieval
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) critically depends on retrieving the evidence necessary for effective reasoning. However, this remains particularly challenging in multi-hop question answering (QA), where supporting passages are often linked through intermediate entities and relations that must be progressively uncovered. Existing retrieval approaches typically rely on a single retrieval intent or one-shot query expansion, limiting their ability to adapt to newly retrieved evidence and potentially introducing noisy or redundant retrieval signals. To address these limitations, we propose a training-free multi-hop retrieval framework that integrates evidence-conditioned exploration, passage-specific contrastive refinement, and coverage-aware final ranking. During offline indexing, the framework constructs passage-specific contrastive facets that characterize each passage relative to its semantically similar neighbors, providing fine-grained signals to distinguish closely related candidates. At inference time, the framework iteratively retrieves evidence, generates probes targeting unresolved information needs, refines candidate relevance using the contrastive facets, and selects a complementary set of passages that collectively cover diverse evidence-seeking intents. Experiments on MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA demonstrate consistent improvements in retrieval quality and downstream QA performance over baselines.

AI.tldr: A training-free multi-hop retrieval framework that improves evidence retrieval for complex QA by combining evidence-conditioned exploration, passage-specific contrastive refinement, and coverage-aware ranking.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG systems struggle with multi-hop QA where supporting passages are connected through intermediate entities/relations. Current retrieval approaches use single retrieval intent or one-shot query expansion, which can't adapt to new evidence and may introduce noise/redundancy.
AI.method: Training-free framework with: 1) Offline indexing creating passage-specific contrastive facets to distinguish similar passages, 2) Inference-time iterative process with evidence retrieval → probe generation → contrastive refinement → coverage-aware ranking, selecting complementary passages covering diverse intents.
AI.result: Consistent improvements in retrieval quality and downstream QA performance on MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA datasets compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training-free framework effectively addresses multi-hop retrieval challenges by adaptively exploring evidence space, refining relevance through contrastive signals, and ensuring comprehensive evidence coverage through iterative, intent-aware retrieval.

title: Structural Entropy-Driven Graph Diffusion Generation for One-Shot Federated Graph Learning
summary: One-shot federated graph learning (FGL) requires the server to estimate client contributions from highly compressed information, yet conventional volume-based weighting captures the amount of client data while overlooking how its connectivity is organized. In this paper, we propose SPIRE, a Structural Entropy-Driven Graph Diffusion Generation method that introduces topology-aware client differentiation into one-shot FGL. Specifically, we employ first-order degree-distribution structural entropy as a compact descriptor of degree-mass dispersion and use it to derive structural client weights, providing an inductive bias that accounts for differences in graph topology beyond data volume. On the generation side, a graph diffusion model on the server synthesizes pseudographs conditioned on the weighted client prototypes, capturing both semantic and structural information without requiring additional client-side training. The generated pseudographs are then assembled via disjoint union fusion to train a global graph neural network. Extensive experiments on seven real-world graph datasets demonstrate that SPIRE consistently outperforms conventional and one-shot FGL methods, with particularly strong gains under highly heterogeneous (non-IID) and graph-perturbed settings.

AI.tldr: SPIRE introduces structural entropy-based weighting for one-shot federated graph learning, using graph diffusion to generate pseudographs from weighted client prototypes, achieving superior performance especially in non-IID and graph-perturbed scenarios.
AI.motivation: Current one-shot federated graph learning methods estimate client contributions based primarily on data volume, ignoring the structural organization and connectivity patterns of graph data, which limits performance particularly in heterogeneous settings.
AI.method: Proposes SPIRE with: 1) first-order degree-distribution structural entropy as compact topology descriptor for client differentiation, 2) structural client weights derived from entropy, 3) graph diffusion model on server to synthesize pseudographs conditioned on weighted client prototypes, 4) disjoint union fusion to assemble generated pseudographs for training global GNN.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 7 real-world graph datasets show SPIRE consistently outperforms conventional and one-shot FGL methods, with particularly strong gains under highly heterogeneous (non-IID) and graph-perturbed settings.
AI.conclusion: SPIRE successfully introduces topology-aware client differentiation into one-shot FGL, demonstrating that accounting for graph structural organization beyond mere data volume leads to improved federated learning performance, especially in challenging heterogeneous and perturbed scenarios.

title: VST: Verifiable Structured Transport for Auditable Agent-to-Agent Alpha Discovery
summary: Agent-to-agent (A2A) alpha discovery is slowed by repeated feedback cycles between mining and evaluation agents, whose hand-offs, in contemporary LLM multi-agent systems, are free-form natural-language messages that carry no stable contract and cannot be replayed. We first restructure this communication as a structured agent-to-agent protocol of \emph{typed, causally addressable, unicast records}, so that the committed stream forms a causal trajectory. On that trajectory a single predictor with four typed heads forecasts the accumulated guidance the two miners would receive several cycles ahead; a transactional verify--leap controller then commits a multi-cycle speculative outcome only when it passes a four-level gate, and otherwise rolls back to the exact prior state. Structure is the enabling contribution, and its value is not accuracy. A controlled ablation shows an equal-information free-text channel reaches the same predictor hit rate. What typing provides is a state that can be schema-checked, replayed deterministically, and prevented by construction from leaking a forecast to an evaluator: auditability by construction, not an empirically stress-tested guarantee. On a CSI~1000 out-of-sample holdout, our single run is the only one among eight methods (seven baselines and ours) to hold a positive median annualized return and Sharpe at the factor level, though the median return \emph{in excess} of the benchmark stays negative for every method including ours; its development-selected top-20 portfolios reach a $0.71$ median holdout Sharpe, selected on a split inside the optimization horizon. We report these single-run results descriptively, gross of costs, and are explicit about their limits throughout; in particular we do not isolate the effect of the leap machinery from the inherited search substrate, which we leave to future work.

AI.tldr: A2A alpha discovery is accelerated by replacing free-form natural language messages with structured typed records and using a predictor with transactional verify-leap control to commit speculative multi-cycle outcomes only when they pass strict validation gates.
AI.motivation: Current LLM multi-agent systems use free-form natural language messages for agent-to-agent communication, which lack stable contracts, cannot be replayed deterministically, and slow down alpha discovery through repeated feedback cycles between mining and evaluation agents.
AI.method: Restructure communication as typed, causally addressable, unicast records forming a causal trajectory. Use a single predictor with four typed heads to forecast accumulated guidance several cycles ahead, then apply a transactional verify-leap controller that commits multi-cycle speculative outcomes only when passing a four-level gate, otherwise rolling back to exact prior state.
AI.result: The single run was the only method among eight (seven baselines and theirs) to hold a positive median annualized return and Sharpe at factor level on CSI 1000 out-of-sample holdout. Development-selected top-20 portfolios reached 0.71 median holdout Sharpe, though median returns in excess of benchmark stayed negative for all methods.
AI.conclusion: Structure (not accuracy) enables auditable by-construction systems that can be schema-checked, replayed deterministically, and prevented from leaking forecasts to evaluators. The leap machinery's effect isn't isolated from the search substrate, requiring future work.

title: Bi-HYCO: Bi-Objective Cooperative Learning for PDE Parameter Identification under Fragmented Observations
summary: Physical and synthetic models may describe complementary aspects of the same PDE-governed system while receiving different, possibly fragmented, observations. We propose Bi-Objective HYCO (Bi-HYCO), a cooperative framework that retains both representations and their local observational objectives while coupling their predicted states at unlabeled interaction points. These points contain no measurements and do not augment the data; they provide a communication mechanism in the common state space. The two criteria form a vector-valued objective, and weighted scalarizations provide computational realizations. For the deterministic shared-observation algorithm with fixed interaction points, we prove sufficient decrease and finite length of the whole alternating sequence, which converges to a mixed critical point under the stated Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz-type assumptions. Elliptic transmission and two-dimensional Navier-Stokes experiments assess parameter and state reconstruction, noise and scalarization effects, and PINN/XPINN references. Ablations show that removing state interaction while retaining aggregation deteriorates parameter recovery in the tested configurations, particularly for Navier-Stokes.

AI.tldr: Bi-HYCO is a cooperative framework that integrates physical and synthetic models for PDE systems by coupling their predictions at unlabeled interaction points while maintaining separate observational objectives.
AI.motivation: Physical and synthetic models can describe complementary aspects of the same PDE-governed system but often receive different, fragmented observations. There's a need to integrate both representations while respecting their distinct observational contexts.
AI.method: Bi-HYCO retains both physical and synthetic models with their local observational objectives while coupling their predicted states at unlabeled interaction points (which serve as communication mechanisms without adding data). The framework uses a vector-valued objective approach with weighted scalarizations for computation, and employs an alternating optimization scheme.
AI.result: Theoretical results include proof of sufficient decrease and finite length of alternating sequences, with convergence to mixed critical points under Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz-type assumptions. Experimental validation on elliptic transmission and 2D Navier-Stokes problems shows effective parameter and state reconstruction, with assessments of noise and scalarization effects compared to PINN/XPINN references.
AI.conclusion: The Bi-HYCO framework successfully integrates complementary model representations for PDE systems, with ablation studies showing that removing state interaction while keeping aggregation deteriorates parameter recovery, especially for complex systems like Navier-Stokes.

title: A Hierarchical Consistency Framework for Auditing Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is commonly evaluated by whether the final answer is correct. That test is insufficient: an answer can match its reference while the context that produced it contains a direct contradiction, leaving the contested evidence invisible to answer-only review and retrieval relevance scores. This paper presents the Hierarchical Consistency Framework (HCF), a post-hoc, model-agnostic audit of three distinct levels of a RAG process: the knowledge corpus, the final retrieved context, and the generated answer. HCF represents corpus conflicts as source-linked atomic facts, thereby identifying the documents responsible, and returns each Answer Consistency Score (ACS) with an explanation of supporting and contradictory contextual statements. We evaluate HCF on several controlled corpora spanning five domains and 100 query-corpus instances. A human evaluator compares every generated response with its supplied ground-truth response. The results show that the three diagnostic levels can dissociate: the corpus with the highest mean retrieval similarity has the lowest mean ACS, while a structurally degraded corpus performs worse at corpus level but better at answer level. Most importantly, HCF identifies contradictory retrieved evidence in several cases where the answer still matches the ground truth. HCF does not certify factual truth; it makes the evidence supporting and challenging an answer inspectable and attributable.

AI.tldr: HCF is a framework for auditing RAG systems by evaluating consistency at three levels (corpus, retrieved context, and generated answer) to identify contradictions that answer-only evaluation misses.
AI.motivation: Current RAG evaluation only checks if final answers are correct, which is insufficient because answers can match references even when the retrieved context contains contradictions, making flawed evidence invisible to traditional evaluation methods.
AI.method: Hierarchical Consistency Framework (HCF): A post-hoc, model-agnostic audit that evaluates three RAG levels - knowledge corpus, retrieved context, and generated answer. It represents corpus conflicts as source-linked atomic facts to identify responsible documents and provides Answer Consistency Scores with explanations.
AI.result: Evaluation on controlled corpora across five domains shows three diagnostic levels can dissociate: highest retrieval similarity doesn't guarantee answer consistency, and degraded corpora can perform worse at corpus level but better at answer level. HCF successfully identifies contradictory retrieved evidence even when answers match ground truth.
AI.conclusion: HCF doesn't certify factual truth but makes supporting and contradictory evidence inspectable and attributable, providing more transparent evaluation of RAG systems beyond just answer correctness.

title: Model-Adaptive and Risk-Constrained Frequency Hopping Against Predictive Jammers
summary: Adaptive frequency hopping against predictive jamming must address both model uncertainty and policy exposure: the context-loss relationship may vary across operating regimes, while persistent hopping patterns may expose high-probability channels to attack. We propose D-PACT-AFH, a model-adaptive and risk-constrained adversarial contextual-bandit framework in which a Tsallis-FTRL master combines a global linear learner with a partitioned local learner and selects the model class online. D-PACT-Hit incorporates channel-wise marginal hit risk into model selection, while D-PACT-Safe applies a minimum-Kullback-Leibler projection to enforce a per-slot risk budget. We establish estimator validity under non-anticipating attacks, an oracle decomposition relative to the better fixed base, and an exact conditional-risk guarantee for the Safe projection. Experiments across diverse channel regimes and jammer types demonstrate effective model adaptation and a controllable goodput-risk tradeoff: D-PACT-AFH recovers 95.5% of the local learner's gain under observable switching while avoiding 77.7% of its degradation in a negative-control regime.

AI.tldr: D-PACT-AFH: A model-adaptive, risk-constrained adversarial contextual bandit framework for adaptive frequency hopping that combines global and local learners with risk-aware model selection to handle predictive jamming.
AI.motivation: Adaptive frequency hopping needs to address both model uncertainty (context-loss relationships vary across operating regimes) and policy exposure (persistent hopping patterns may expose high-probability channels to predictive jamming attacks).
AI.method: Proposes D-PACT-AFH framework using Tsallis-FTRL master that combines global linear learner with partitioned local learner, selecting model class online. Includes D-PACT-Hit for incorporating channel-wise marginal hit risk into model selection, and D-PACT-Safe using minimum-KL projection to enforce per-slot risk budget.
AI.result: Establishes estimator validity under non-anticipating attacks, oracle decomposition relative to better fixed base, exact conditional-risk guarantee for Safe projection.
