It combines: 1) Long-term: drift-aware historical baseline tracks success frontier for relative trajectory contributions; 2) Short-term: recent state-experience buffer estimates localized action advantages using recurrent states. This two-timescale design converts historical experience into credit signals with only one rollout per anchor.
AI.result: LSTAE matches or improves upon strong group-based baselines across agentic and mathematical reasoning benchmarks while substantially reducing rollout cost.
AI.conclusion: Historical experience can effectively replace repeated within-iteration comparisons for advantage estimation, enabling efficient RL training through LSTAE's dual-timescale design that leverages accumulated experience without optimizing on stale trajectories.

title: Weakly supervised neural network: segmentation of complex structures in X-ray microCT
summary: Segmentation of complex structures in X-ray tomographic data is a fundamental task in biomedical research, but it often requires large amounts of precisely annotated data, making fully supervised approaches costly and difficult to scale. In this study, weakly supervised deep learning is investigated as a strategy to reduce annotation effort while maintaining accurate segmentation. A two-dimensional convolutional neural network based on the nnU-Net framework was adapted to a weak supervision setting using sparse dot-based annotations, complemented by a limited number of fully segmented images. The approach was evaluated on high-resolution microCT slices of rat kidneys, targeting the segmentation of renal glomeruli, which are small, low-contrast anatomical structures. Results indicate that weak supervision provides a meaningful learning signal, enabling reliable localization of glomeruli even in the absence of dense labels. Incorporating a small set of high-quality annotations substantially improves segmentation performance, approaching that of a fully supervised model. These findings highlight the potential of weakly supervised learning as an annotation-efficient strategy for the analysis of complex structures in X-ray tomographic data, and suggest that alternative loss formulations tailored to sparse annotations may further enhance performance.

AI.tldr: Weakly supervised deep learning with sparse dot annotations and limited full annotations can effectively segment complex kidney structures in microCT data while reducing annotation effort.
AI.motivation: Fully supervised segmentation of complex structures in X-ray tomographic data requires large amounts of precisely annotated data, which is costly and difficult to scale. There's a need for more annotation-efficient approaches in biomedical research.
AI.method: Adapted a 2D convolutional neural network based on the nnU-Net framework to a weak supervision setting using sparse dot-based annotations, complemented by a limited number of fully segmented images. Applied to high-resolution microCT slices of rat kidneys targeting renal glomeruli segmentation.
AI.result: Weak supervision provides a meaningful learning signal enabling reliable localization of glomeruli even without dense labels. Incorporating a small set of high-quality annotations substantially improves segmentation performance, approaching that of a fully supervised model.
AI.conclusion: Weakly supervised learning is an annotation-efficient strategy for analyzing complex structures in X-ray tomographic data. Alternative loss formulations tailored to sparse annotations may further enhance performance.

title: LATS: Levy Adaptive Tree Sampling for Feedback-Driven Diverse Target Discovery
summary: While diffusion models excel at capturing complex data distributions, scientific discovery often requires steering generation toward specific, uncharacterized regions that maximize a target objective. These high-utility modes frequently reside in low-likelihood tail regions and are only revealed sequentially through interactive feedback. Existing diffusion samplers fail in this regime: they inherit the pre-trained model's bias toward high-density regions, leaving rare yet promising phenomena underexplored. Conversely, exploration-heavy samplers ensure broad coverage but fail to efficiently exploit high-utility modes when constrained by a strict sampling budget. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce Levy Adaptive Tree Search (LATS), a principled sampling framework for online feedback-driven search. LATS leverages heavy-tailed exploration coupled with tree-based value backpropagation to progressively uncover preferred modes. By maintaining broad distributional coverage, LATS successfully discovers low-likelihood, high-utility regions while preserving sample fidelity and structural diversity. Experiments across diverse benchmarks, including materials science, demonstrate that LATS significantly outperforms baselines in target discovery efficiency.

AI.tldr: LATS is a novel diffusion sampling framework that combines heavy-tailed exploration with tree search to efficiently discover high-utility, low-likelihood regions through sequential feedback, outperforming existing methods in target discovery tasks.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery requires steering generation toward specific, uncharacterized high-utility regions that often reside in low-likelihood tail areas of data distributions. Existing diffusion samplers fail because they either inherit bias toward high-density regions (missing rare promising phenomena) or provide broad coverage but inefficient exploitation under sampling budget constraints.
AI.method: Levy Adaptive Tree Search (LATS) combines heavy-tailed exploration with tree-based value backpropagation for online feedback-driven search. It maintains broad distributional coverage while progressively uncovering preferred modes through sequential feedback, preserving sample fidelity and structural diversity.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse benchmarks, including materials science, demonstrate that LATS significantly outperforms baseline methods in target discovery efficiency. It successfully discovers low-likelihood, high-utility regions while maintaining sample quality and diversity.
AI.conclusion: LATS provides a principled sampling framework that resolves the exploration-exploitation dilemma in feedback-driven scientific discovery, enabling efficient discovery of rare yet high-value phenomena in diffusion models through adaptive tree search and heavy-tailed exploration strategies.

title: DGCPath: Distribution-Aware Generative Contrastive Framework for Self-supervised Path Representation Learning -- Extended Version
comment: This paper is an extended version of DGCPath, which was published at IJCAI 2026
summary: Due to the proliferation of vehicle trajectory data enabled by advanced sensing technologies, path representation learning has become a pivotal task in intelligent transportation systems. Although existing self-supervised approaches have achieved promising performance, their dependence on deterministic contrastive learning paradigms and handcrafted view augmentation strategies inherently restricts their cross-scenario generalization capabilities. To address these limitations, we present DGCPath, an innovative Distribution-aware Generative Contrastive learning framework for Path representation. This framework establishes a synergistic connection between generative modeling and distributional contrastive learning, enabling the acquisition of robust and transferable feature embeddings. Specifically, our framework incorporates: (1) a diffusion-based view generator that autonomously produces semantically coherent yet diverse trajectory views from Gaussian noise; (2) a variational contrastive mechanism that enforces latent feature alignment at the distribution level, transcending conventional instance-wise consistency; and (3) a novel generative cross-supervision module that reinforces view-level consistency through cross-view reconstruction learning. Comprehensive evaluations on three real-world trajectory datasets demonstrate that DGCPath outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on two distinct downstream tasks, validating its enhanced generalization capability and representation effectiveness.

AI.tldr: DGCPath is a distribution-aware generative contrastive learning framework for path representation that combines diffusion-based view generation with variational contrastive learning to improve cross-scenario generalization in vehicle trajectory analysis.
AI.motivation: Existing self-supervised approaches for path representation learning are limited by their dependence on deterministic contrastive learning paradigms and handcrafted view augmentation strategies, which restricts their cross-scenario generalization capabilities in intelligent transportation systems.
AI.method: The framework establishes a synergistic connection between generative modeling and distributional contrastive learning. It includes: (1) a diffusion-based view generator that produces semantically coherent trajectory views from Gaussian noise, (2) a variational contrastive mechanism for latent feature alignment at distribution level, and (3) a generative cross-supervision module that reinforces view-level consistency through cross-view reconstruction learning.
AI.result: Comprehensive evaluations on three real-world trajectory datasets demonstrate that DGCPath outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on two distinct downstream tasks, validating its enhanced generalization capability and representation effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: DGCPath presents an innovative approach to path representation learning that successfully addresses limitations of existing methods by integrating generative modeling with distributional contrastive learning, resulting in robust and transferable feature embeddings with superior cross-scenario generalization capabilities.

title: DrugReason: Dynamic Multi-View Reasoning over Knowledge Graph and Language Evidence for Drug Repurposing
summary: Drug repurposing aims to identify new therapeutic uses for existing compounds and, compared with de novo drug discovery, offers a faster and more cost-effective path to clinical translation. However, the space of candidate drug-disease pairs is enormous and their underlying relationships often depend on complex multi-hop biological mechanisms, making it difficult to reliably predict which pairs represent true therapeutic relationships. Existing approaches tackle this from two directions: knowledge graph-based methods organize curated biomedical evidence into structured relational networks for grounded multi-hop reasoning, while LLM-based methods leverage pretrained knowledge to generate flexible mechanistic rationales. Yet neither is sufficient alone - KGs are confined to observed graph structure while LLMs lack factual grounding and risk hallucination. To address this gap, we propose DrugReason, a multi-view reasoning framework that integrates grounded KG reasoning with LLM-generated mechanistic inference for drug repurposing. DrugReason adaptively routes diverse reasoning paths to specialized experts conditioned on the query context, while a cross-expert distillation objective enables knowledge sharing without sacrificing expert specialization. Experiments on PharmaDB, DDInter, and DrugBank show that DrugReason improves average performance over strong single-view reasoning baselines and achieves competitive or superior results compared with graph-based alternatives, while providing interpretable routing-based predictions.

AI.tldr: DrugReason is a novel drug repurposing framework that integrates knowledge graph reasoning with LLM-based inference using adaptive routing to specialized experts and cross-expert distillation for improved prediction accuracy and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Drug repurposing offers faster clinical translation but faces challenges in predicting therapeutic relationships due to the enormous search space and complex biological mechanisms. Existing approaches have limitations: knowledge graph methods are confined to observed graph structure, while LLM-based methods lack factual grounding and risk hallucination. There's a need to integrate both approaches.
AI.method: DrugReason proposes a multi-view reasoning framework that integrates grounded KG reasoning with LLM-generated mechanistic inference. It uses adaptive routing to direct diverse reasoning paths to specialized experts based on query context, and employs cross-expert distillation to enable knowledge sharing while maintaining expert specialization.
AI.result: Experiments on PharmaDB, DDInter, and DrugBank datasets show that DrugReason improves average performance over strong single-view reasoning baselines and achieves competitive or superior results compared to graph-based alternatives, while providing interpretable routing-based predictions.
AI.conclusion: The DrugReason framework successfully bridges the gap between knowledge graph and LLM-based approaches for drug repurposing, demonstrating improved predictive performance through integrated multi-view reasoning while maintaining interpretability through its adaptive routing mechanism.

title: AAS-RAIL: Improving Information Extraction for Asset Administration Shells through Retrieval-Augmented In-Context Learning
summary: The Asset Administration Shell (AAS) is a cornerstone of Industry 4.0 and the Digital Product Passport, providing standardized digital representations of industrial assets. While manufacturers already maintain extensive technical product documentation, generating AAS instances from existing product datasheets remains a labor-intensive task because technical information is extracted from heterogeneous document structures and often involves company-specific terminology and conventions. In this work, we present AAS-RAIL, a retrieval-augmented information extraction (IE) approach that automatically generates Asset Administration Shells from PDF product datasheets using large language models (LLMs). Instead of relying on a fixed set of few-shot examples, the proposed retrieval-augmented in-context learning (RAIL) approach retrieves LLM-generated extraction helpers from similar Asset Administration Shells to provide instance-specific in-context learning (ICL). This enables the model to adapt its extraction behavior to company-specific naming conventions and formatting styles without fine-tuning. Our core contribution is the dynamic selection of company-specific AAS examples for each datasheet, replacing static prompting with an extraction pipeline that adapts to instances and combines semantic retrieval and structured information extraction. The proposed approach is evaluated on a collection of industrial product datasheets using a selection of open- and closed-weight LLMs. Experimental results show that RAIL consistently improves extraction quality over conventional few-shot prompting, yielding relative improvements of 30.4-52.4%. These results demonstrate that our approach provides an effective improvement for company-specific AAS generation.

AI.tldr: AAS-RAIL: A retrieval-augmented information extraction approach using LLMs to automatically generate Asset Administration Shells from PDF product datasheets, improving extraction quality by 30.4-52.4% over conventional few-shot prompting.
AI.motivation: Generating Asset Administration Shell (AAS) instances from existing product datasheets is labor-intensive due to heterogeneous document structures and company-specific terminology/conventions. Manual extraction from technical documentation is time-consuming and doesn't adapt to company-specific variations.
AI.method: Proposes AAS-RAIL, a retrieval-augmented information extraction approach using large language models. Instead of fixed few-shot examples, it retrieves LLM-generated extraction helpers from similar AAS instances to provide instance-specific in-context learning. This enables adaptation to company-specific naming conventions and formatting styles without fine-tuning through dynamic selection of company-specific AAS examples for each datasheet.
AI.result: Evaluation on industrial product datasheets using open- and closed-weight LLMs shows RAIL consistently improves extraction quality over conventional few-shot prompting, yielding relative improvements of 30.4-52.4%. The approach effectively handles company-specific AAS generation.
AI.conclusion: AAS-RAIL provides an effective improvement for company-specific AAS generation from product datasheets by combining semantic retrieval and structured information extraction, enabling adaptation to different company conventions without model fine-tuning.

title: When Retain Constraints Conflict: Mitigating Forget-Retain Interference in Tabular Data
summary: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of designated training data while preserving model utility, but its behavior on tabular data remains underexplored. This gap is important because tabular prediction is widely used in high-stakes domains and is increasingly adapted to language models through record serialization and schema-aware prompting. We identify a key challenge that distinguishes tabular unlearning from unlearning in free-form text or other modalities: schema-induced forget-retain overlap. In serialized tabular data, records share fixed column-name/value slots, similar attribute ranges, and common output spaces. Consequently, a forget row may have nearby retain rows that rely on the same high-signal attributes, causing retain preservation to oppose the update required for forgetting. Motivated by this failure mode, we propose Conflict-Aware Unlearning (CAU), a schema-aware approach that reduces forget-retain interference by relaxing preservation constraints on retained rows that most conflict with the forget set. Across sample-level and feature-level unlearning on clinical and non-medical tabular tasks, CAU more closely matches a retraining oracle while maintaining predictive utility and retain-region behavior. Our results show that reliable tabular LLM unlearning depends not only on the forgetting objective, but also on how retain constraints are constructed.

AI.tldr: CAU (Conflict-Aware Unlearning) improves tabular LLM unlearning by addressing schema-induced forget-retain overlap through selective relaxation of preservation constraints on conflicting retain rows.
AI.motivation: Machine unlearning for tabular data is underexplored despite its importance in high-stakes domains and increasing adaptation to language models. The key challenge is schema-induced forget-retain overlap - where serialized tabular data shares fixed column slots, attribute ranges, and output spaces, causing retain preservation to conflict with forgetting requirements.
AI.method: Proposes Conflict-Aware Unlearning (CAU), a schema-aware approach that reduces forget-retain interference by relaxing preservation constraints on retained rows that most conflict with the forget set.
AI.result: CAU more closely matches a retraining oracle across sample-level and feature-level unlearning on clinical and non-medical tabular tasks while maintaining predictive utility and retain-region behavior.
AI.conclusion: Reliable tabular LLM unlearning depends not only on the forgetting objective but also on how retain constraints are constructed, and CAU effectively addresses the unique challenges of tabular data structure.

title: Human-like moral judgments conceal divergent motive attributions in large language models
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Information (10 pages) appended
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used to simulate human participants in psychological research. We asked whether LLMs that reproduce human evaluations of a whistleblower's moral character also reproduce the motive attributions that accompany them. Five LLMs and two human samples (N = 125 and N = 742) evaluated a physician who either remained silent about fraudulent billing or reported it to a hospital, regulator, or newspaper. Models reproduced the human ranking of the physician's moral character but portrayed whistleblowers as more helpful, less self-interested, and less hostile. In four of five models, competitive motives were less strongly associated with moral-character judgments. Model ratings changed little when prompts reproduced the narratives and demographic profiles of both human samples, although this comparison cannot isolate a perspective effect. Thus, agreement in average ratings can conceal differences in attributed motives, relationships among judgments, and sensitivity to context. Validating LLMs as simulated participants therefore requires testing psychologically informative response patterns, not average agreement alone.

AI.tldr: LLMs replicate human moral character rankings of whistleblowers but differ in motive attributions, showing that average rating agreement can mask underlying psychological differences in simulated participants.
AI.motivation: To examine whether LLMs used as simulated human participants in psychological research not only reproduce human evaluations of moral character but also the accompanying motive attributions, testing the validity of LLMs as psychological research tools.
AI.method: Compared five LLMs with two human samples (N=125 and N=742) evaluating a physician in four whistleblowing scenarios (silent, report to hospital, regulator, or newspaper). Models assessed on moral character judgments and motive attributions (helpful, self-interested, hostile).
AI.result: LLMs reproduced human ranking of physician's moral character but portrayed whistleblowers as more helpful, less self-interested, and less hostile. In 4/5 models, competitive motives were less strongly associated with moral character judgments. Model ratings changed little when prompts reproduced human narratives and demographics.
AI.conclusion: Agreement in average ratings can conceal differences in attributed motives, relationships among judgments, and sensitivity to context. Validating LLMs as simulated participants requires testing psychologically informative response patterns, not just average agreement.

title: Train Smarter, Not Harder: Switching Signal-Guided Training in Active Learning
summary: Training strategy, namely whether to retrain from scratch or fine-tune from the previous checkpoint, is an overlooked decision variable in active learning. We show that this choice has exploitable structure: retraining is most useful in early rounds, when each batch can substantially reshape the labeled distribution, while fine-tuning becomes safer once the model trajectory stabilizes. We propose HybridAL, an adaptive training schedule that monitors an online stabilization signal and switches from retraining to fine-tuning after sustained stabilization. Two complementary signals, spectral exponent change $Δα$ (weight-based) and accuracy change $Δ$Acc (validation-based), span different points on the time-calibration trade-off. Across three encoder backbones and six text-classification tasks (five seeds each), HybridAL keeps endpoint macro-F1 non-inferior to retraining and fine-tuning at a 0.010 margin, saves up to 49% of retraining time, and recovers a substantial fraction of retraining's calibration advantage as measured by negative log-likelihood (NLL). Compared with schedules that switch at a pre-committed round, HybridAL obtains lower NLL at moderate additional cost, showing that trajectory-dependent switching provides a stronger time-calibration trade-off than fixed early switching.

AI.tldr: HybridAL is an adaptive active learning training strategy that automatically switches between retraining from scratch and fine-tuning based on model stabilization signals, achieving better time-calibration trade-offs than fixed schedules.
AI.motivation: The choice between retraining from scratch versus fine-tuning from previous checkpoints is an overlooked decision in active learning, despite having exploitable structure that could optimize training efficiency and model calibration.
AI.method: Proposed HybridAL with adaptive training schedule that monitors online stabilization signals: spectral exponent change Δα (weight-based) and accuracy change ΔAcc (validation-based). It switches from retraining to fine-tuning after detecting sustained stabilization in the model's learning trajectory.
AI.result: Across three encoder backbones and six text-classification tasks, HybridAL maintains macro-F1 within 0.010 margin of both retraining and fine-tuning, saves up to 49% retraining time, and recovers substantial calibration advantages of retraining (measured by NLL). Outperforms pre-committed switching schedules with lower NLL at moderate additional cost.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-dependent switching provides stronger time-calibration trade-off than fixed schedules. Adaptive training strategy selection is a valuable dimension for optimizing active learning systems.

title: RAFM-SER++: A Lightweight Multimodal Emotion Recognition Framework for Real-Time Behavioral Monitoring in Surveillance Systems
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Advanced Video and Signal-based Surveillance (AVSS 2026). (c) 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses
summary:
Recent multimodal Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) systems achieve high accuracy through interaction-heavy cross-modal transformers, but their computational cost limits deployment in latency-sensitive and resource-constrained surveillance systems. To address this challenge, we propose RAFM_SER++, a lightweight multimodal SER framework featuring an asymmetric Residual Attention Fusion Mechanism (RAFM). Rather than relying on computationally expensive bidirectional interactions, RAFM injects affective speech cues into semantic text representations through a one-directional residual attention pathway. Combined with a BYOL-inspired cross-modal alignment objective and attention-guided pooling, the proposed framework improves multimodal representation learning while maintaining low computational overhead.
  Experiments on the IEMOCAP and ESD benchmarks demonstrate that RAFM_SER++ consistently outperforms the HuBERT-Base baseline and achieves a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off compared with the state-of-the-art MemoCMT. Specifically, RAFM_SER++ reduces trainable parameters by more than 60%, achieves faster inference (79.60 it/s), and attains BACC scores of 81.10% on IEMOCAP and 95.39% on ESD. These results indicate that lightweight asymmetric multimodal fusion is an effective alternative to interaction-heavy cross-modal transformers for real-time surveillance applications.

AI.tldr: RAFM_SER++ is a lightweight multimodal speech emotion recognition framework that uses asymmetric residual attention fusion instead of computationally expensive bidirectional transformers, achieving high accuracy with significantly reduced computational cost for real-time surveillance applications.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal SER systems use interaction-heavy cross-modal transformers that have high computational costs, making them unsuitable for latency-sensitive and resource-constrained surveillance systems that require real-time processing.
AI.method: Proposes RAFM_SER++ with an asymmetric Residual Attention Fusion Mechanism (RAFM) that injects affective speech cues into semantic text representations through one-directional residual attention. Also uses BYOL-inspired cross-modal alignment objective and attention-guided pooling to improve multimodal representation learning.
AI.result: Outperforms HuBERT-Base baseline and achieves superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off compared to state-of-the-art MemoCMT. Reduces trainable parameters by >60%, achieves faster inference (79.60 it/s), and attains BACC scores of 81.10% on IEMOCAP and 95.39% on ESD.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight asymmetric multimodal fusion is an effective alternative to interaction-heavy cross-modal transformers for real-time surveillance applications, offering good accuracy with significantly lower computational overhead.

title: Constrained Bayesian Optimization for Hierarchical Federated Learning in IoT Networks for Plant Disease Classification
comment: Accepted for publication at Next Generation Communications (NextGCom) conference
summary: The deployment of Hierarchical Federated Learning (HFL) in resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) environments requires careful configuration to balance predictive performance with energy consumption and execution time. This challenge is particularly relevant to smart agriculture, where distributed IoT devices can support automated plant disease classification while operating under limited computational and communication resources. This paper presents a constrained Bayesian Optimization framework for the efficient configuration of HFL deployments. The proposed approach jointly explores the deep learning backbone architecture, aggregation strategy, and number of communication rounds, while the federation size is determined according to the spatial coverage requirements of the agricultural deployment. A weighted objective function captures user-defined trade-offs among energy consumption, execution time, and predictive performance, while explicit constraints ensure compliance with deployment-specific resource and accuracy requirements. The framework is evaluated on an IoT-based plant disease classification task considering multiple deep learning architectures, federated aggregation strategies, and communication-round settings. Experimental results across 30 independent optimization runs show that the proposed approach explores only 11.11% of the search space, while consistently identifying solutions within 1% of the exhaustive-search optimum, with a mean optimality gap of only 0.056%.

AI.tldr: A constrained Bayesian Optimization framework for efficient configuration of Hierarchical Federated Learning in IoT-based smart agriculture, achieving near-optimal solutions while exploring only 11.11% of the search space.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical Federated Learning (HFL) in resource-constrained IoT environments for smart agriculture needs careful configuration to balance predictive performance (plant disease classification) with energy consumption and execution time, given limited computational and communication resources.
AI.method: A constrained Bayesian Optimization framework that jointly explores deep learning backbone architecture, aggregation strategy, and number of communication rounds, with federation size determined by spatial coverage requirements. Uses weighted objective function for user-defined trade-offs and explicit constraints for compliance with deployment requirements.
AI.result: The framework explores only 11.11% of the search space while consistently identifying solutions within 1% of the exhaustive-search optimum, with a mean optimality gap of only 0.056% across 30 independent optimization runs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed constrained Bayesian Optimization approach provides an efficient method for configuring HFL deployments in IoT-based smart agriculture, achieving near-optimal performance while significantly reducing the search space exploration.

title: CIT-CAD: Constraint Intent Tree-based CAD Code Generation and Verification
summary: Natural-language Computer-Aided Design (CAD) code generation aims to turn design intent into executable and editable parametric programs. Large language models (LLMs) make this goal increasingly practical, but useful systems must preserve the construction process behind the rendered geometry. Existing benchmarks and methods mostly focus on how closely the generated CAD model matches the reference geometry, often using metrics such as Intersection over Union (IoU). Such metrics can miss errors in part decomposition, construction hierarchy, Boolean operations, sketch structure, and geometric relations. This gap calls for a representation that makes design intent explicit and lets a system check generated code against that intent. We propose CIT-CAD, a framework that infers a Constraint Intent Tree (CIT) from the input description to represent the intended entities, hierarchy, operations, and relations. The tree has two roles: it guides CAD code generation and defines expected constraints for verification. The framework extracts actual constraints from the generated program, compares them with the expected constraints, and uses mismatches to localize and repair design violations. Experiments show that the framework improves CAD generation performance, with larger gains on more complex multi-entity designs. By turning design intent into an explicit and checkable object, this work is the first attempt to move text-to-CAD generation beyond rendered-geometry matching toward construction-aware synthesis, verification, and repair.

AI.tldr: CIT-CAD: A framework that uses Constraint Intent Trees to guide and verify CAD code generation from natural language, moving beyond geometry matching to construction-aware synthesis and repair.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-CAD generation focuses too much on geometry matching (IoU metrics) while missing errors in design intent like part decomposition, construction hierarchy, Boolean operations, sketch structure, and geometric relations. There's a need to preserve the construction process and make design intent explicit for verification.
AI.method: Proposes CIT-CAD framework that: 1) Infers a Constraint Intent Tree (CIT) from input description representing intended entities, hierarchy, operations, and relations; 2) Uses CIT to guide CAD code generation; 3) Extracts actual constraints from generated program; 4) Compares actual vs. expected constraints; 5) Uses mismatches to localize and repair design violations.
AI.result: Experiments show the framework improves CAD generation performance, with larger gains on more complex multi-entity designs. Successfully moves beyond rendered-geometry matching toward construction-aware synthesis, verification, and repair.
AI.conclusion: CIT-CAD represents the first attempt to make design intent explicit and checkable in text-to-CAD generation, enabling systematic verification and repair of construction violations rather than just geometry matching.

title: Feature Superposition in Neural Networks: From Theory to Practice
summary: Superposition refers to neural networks representing more features than they have dimensions. It offers a possible explanation for polysemantic neurons and motivates methods for recovering interpretable features from neural activations. Theoretical models typically start with a given set of input features and assumptions about how their values vary across inputs, then study how a network encodes those values in a lower-dimensional hidden representation. Empirical work, by contrast, seeks to identify the features encoded in trained networks and determine their role in computation. In this survey, we review the geometry, learning, and computation of superposed representations, explaining how feature statistics and decoder choice affect the conclusions. To connect these theoretical accounts with evidence from trained networks, we compare practical methods for recovering and analyzing features and examine what their evaluations establish. Since accurate activation reconstruction alone does not establish feature identity or causal use, we discuss the methods' documented failures and applications in light of the evidence available for these different claims. Finally, we assess previously stated open problems and identify remaining theoretical and empirical questions about superposition in trained networks. We hope our work can pave the way for a deeper understanding of superposition and more reliable methods for interpreting neural networks.

AI.tldr: Survey paper reviewing superposition in neural networks: how networks encode more features than dimensions, connecting theory with empirical methods for feature recovery and analysis.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between theoretical models of superposition (which start with known features) and empirical work (which seeks to identify features in trained networks), and to understand how neural networks can represent more features than they have dimensions, explaining polysemantic neurons and enabling better interpretation methods.
AI.method: Survey methodology: Reviewing geometric, learning, and computational aspects of superposed representations; comparing practical feature recovery methods; analyzing their evaluations, failures, and applications; assessing evidence for feature identity and causal use claims.
AI.result: The paper provides a comprehensive framework connecting theoretical superposition models with empirical evidence from trained networks, highlighting that accurate activation reconstruction alone doesn't establish feature identity or causal use, and identifying remaining theoretical and empirical questions.
AI.conclusion: Superposition offers important insights into neural network representations, but significant gaps remain between theory and practice. The survey aims to facilitate deeper understanding of superposition and development of more reliable interpretation methods, while identifying open problems that require further research.

title: The Internal Anatomy of Strategic Choice in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models act as strategic agents and models of human choice, yet choosing like a strategic agent does not mean computing like one. We recorded activations from four open-weight models --- dense and mixture-of-experts, including a matched base--instruct pair --- in one-shot play of 144 strict ordinal $2\times2$ games. We followed a prespecified incentive from prompt, through activations, to choice. Dense models mirrored the unadjusted human decline with game complexity. Incentive and choice were detectable in every model, but models differed in whether incentive reached the choice, aligned with it and, where tested, whether strengthening it shifted preference. The base and instruction-tuned Qwen2.5 models chose almost identically at baseline yet differed in whether incentive reached choice. Fixed decision cues were distinguishable internally but changed choices selectively. Similar behaviour can rest on different computation; post-training can reshape the path from represented incentive to decision while leaving behaviour and decodable information largely intact.

AI.tldr: Large language models act as strategic agents in 2x2 games, but similar behavior can result from different internal computations. Post-training (like instruction-tuning) can reshape the path from represented incentive to decision while leaving observable behavior largely unchanged.
AI.motivation: To understand how large language models process strategic incentives when acting as agents in game-theoretic scenarios, and whether their internal computations align with human-like strategic reasoning despite similar behavioral outputs.
AI.method: Recorded activations from four open-weight models (both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, including a matched base-instruct pair) during one-shot play of 144 strict ordinal 2x2 games. Traced the prespecified incentive from prompt through activations to final choice, examining detection and alignment of incentives in different model components.
AI.result: Dense models mirrored the unadjusted human decline with game complexity. Incentive and choice were detectable in every model, but models differed in whether incentive actually reached the choice, aligned with it, and (where tested) whether strengthening it shifted preference. Base and instruction-tuned models chose almost identically at baseline but differed in whether incentive reached choice. Fixed decision cues were distinguishable internally but changed choices selectively.
AI.conclusion: Similar behavioral outputs in strategic games can rest on different underlying computations. Post-training interventions like instruction-tuning can reshape the path from represented incentive to decision while leaving behavior and decodable information largely intact, suggesting a dissociation between observable behavior and internal processing in LLMs.

title: PPIM: Pennes Physics-Informed Mamba for Heat-Source-Conditioned 3D Bioheat Simulation
summary: Three-dimensional bioheat simulation aims to predict transient temperature distributions in biological tissue and is commonly modeled using the Pennes bioheat equation, which combines thermal diffusion, perfusion-mediated heat loss, and external heat generation. In this study, we consider a controlled 3D Pennes bioheat simulation under a localized heat-source condition inspired by microwave ablation (MWA). To evaluate neural approximation performance, we compare three neural partial differential equation (PDE) solvers under the same controlled simulation: a spatial Fourier-feature physics-informed neural network (PINN), a generic PINNMamba temporal subsequence model, and Pennes Physics-Informed Mamba (PPIM). PPIM builds on the temporal subsequence model by incorporating conditioned heat-source input and Pennes-aware state-space model (SSM) decay initialization. All three neural models are trained under the same conditions with the same Pennes residual, and an explicit finite-difference method (FDM) solution is used only as the numerical reference. In a representative 600~s run, PPIM achieved the lowest MAE, relative $L_1$ error, and relative $L_2$ error among the evaluated neural solvers. Error maps further showed that the remaining PPIM errors were more concentrated near the heat-source region than across the rest of the domain. These results indicate that PPIM is effective for approximating the FDM reference final temperature field in this controlled simulation. The source code is available at https://github.com/muvYun/PPIM.

AI.tldr: PPIM (Pennes Physics-Informed Mamba) neural PDE solver outperforms other neural approaches in approximating 3D bioheat simulations for microwave ablation, achieving lowest errors compared to finite-difference reference solutions.
AI.motivation: Accurate prediction of transient temperature distributions in biological tissue is crucial for applications like microwave ablation therapy, and neural PDE solvers offer promising alternatives to traditional numerical methods for solving the Pennes bioheat equation.
AI.method: Comparison of three neural PDE solvers under controlled 3D Pennes bioheat simulation with localized heat-source (MWA-inspired): spatial Fourier-feature PINN, generic PINNMamba temporal subsequence model, and PPIM which incorporates conditioned heat-source input and Pennes-aware state-space model decay initialization.
AI.result: PPIM achieved the lowest MAE, relative L1 error, and relative L2 error among all neural solvers in a 600s simulation; error maps showed remaining errors were concentrated near heat-source region rather than distributed across domain.
AI.conclusion: PPIM is effective for approximating FDM reference final temperature fields in controlled 3D bioheat simulations, demonstrating superior performance over other neural PDE solvers for microwave ablation modeling applications.

title: Modus Tollens and Counterfactuals and Counterfactual Reasoning Based on Three Types of Negation
summary: Modus Tollens (MT) is a classical logical inference rule, while counterfactuals are hypothetical statements that are contrary to facts, and counterfactual reasoning is a process of reasoning based on counterfactuals. Negation is an indispensable core concept in them. In this paper, based on the logical systems LCOI&PLCOI with contradictory negation, opposite negation and intermediary negation, we propose three variants of Modus Tollens corresponding to distinct negation types, namely MTC: Modus Tollens based on contradictory negation, MTO: Modus Tollens based on opposite negation, and MTI: Modus Tollens based on intermediary negation. We define the implications within MTC, MTO and MTI, provide the truth value algorithms of MTC, MTO and MTI, and discuss the reducibility of these algorithms. To incorporate these three types of negation into counterfactuals and counterfactual reasoning, we differentiate counterfactuals into two types based on whether they possess logical negation, thereby proposing three counterfactuals and counterfactuals reasoning based on different logical negations. In this paper, we further argue that the three counterfactuals reasoning based on different logical negations have the same inference form as MTC, MTO and MTI, respectively. In other words, they share the same inference structure. As a result, the truth value algorithms for MTC, MTO and MTI can be as the truth value algorithms for the three counterfactuals reasoning based on different logical negations. The algorithms indicates that if the first premise of the reasoning is true, the truth values of the reasoning conclusions are identical to the truth values of the three negative premises in the reasoning premises, respectively. This reflects the consistency and accuracy of the truth value algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes three variants of Modus Tollens based on different negation types (contradictory, opposite, intermediary) and applies them to counterfactual reasoning, showing they share the same inference structure and providing truth value algorithms.
AI.motivation: Modus Tollens is a classical logical inference rule, and counterfactuals involve hypothetical contrary-to-fact statements, both crucially involving negation. The paper aims to explore how different types of negation (contradictory, opposite, intermediary) can be systematically incorporated into both Modus Tollens and counterfactual reasoning frameworks.
AI.method: The paper builds on logical systems LCOI & PLCOI with three negation types. It proposes three variants of Modus Tollens (MTC, MTO, MTI) corresponding to each negation type, defines their implications, provides truth value algorithms, and discusses algorithm reducibility. It then applies these negation types to counterfactuals, differentiating them based on logical negation presence, and shows how counterfactual reasoning based on different negations shares the same inference structure as the corresponding Modus Tollens variants.
AI.result: The three counterfactual reasoning types based on different logical negations have identical inference forms to MTC, MTO, and MTI respectively, sharing the same structure. The truth value algorithms for Modus Tollens variants can be directly applied to counterfactual reasoning. The algorithms show that when the first premise is true, the truth values of conclusions match those of the corresponding negative premises in the reasoning premises, demonstrating consistency and accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully establishes a systematic connection between different negation types in Modus Tollens and counterfactual reasoning, providing unified truth value algorithms that demonstrate consistency across both frameworks. This bridges classical logical inference with counterfactual analysis through a negation-based approach.

title: Exact Record Omission in Delta Attention: A Transport Criterion, Its Cost, and a Replay Certificate
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures, 9 tables. Source-free evidence for every quantitative claim is packaged with the source
summary: When a user asks an assistant to forget a record, the test is whether the memory now matches the state it would hold if the record had never been stored. Independently encoded rows can be removed directly; a recurrent memory folds records into an evolving state. One hope is a receipt: save the difference the record made when it arrived, carry it forward through later updates, and subtract it, so that deletion costs one fixed-size edit no matter how long the conversation runs. We show that a transported receipt reaches exact omission if and only if the changes the record induces in later updates cancel out on net, and we measure whether they do on the released 48B Kimi Linear hybrid. They do not: after 4,096 further tokens the record still leaves an imprint of about 4.5% of the state norm that none of the tested receipt classes removes, recomputing half the suffix closes less than half the gap, and the per-token log a receipt needs costs more than a full checkpoint after 88 tokens. The same write-rule classification held on Mamba-2, Falcon-H1, and RWKV-7 with predictions recorded before the runs. Restoring a checkpoint from before the record and replaying the surviving suffix matches the never-stored state exactly on every array we check. In the hybrid suffix sweep, masking the record's attention rows brings sampled recovery close to the never-stored floor even though the recurrent imprint remains, and an auditor who rebuilds the reference can still detect it. Among the evaluated methods, checkpoint replay achieves exact omission, with work proportional to the replayed suffix.

AI.tldr: A study on exact deletion mechanisms for AI assistant memory shows that receipt-based deletion fails to achieve exact omission, while checkpoint replay succeeds but requires replaying the entire suffix after the deleted record.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the problem of implementing true "right to be forgotten" in AI assistant memory systems, where users may request deletion of specific records. The goal is to achieve a state where the memory matches what it would have been if the record had never been stored.
AI.method: The authors test receipt-based deletion mechanisms that save differences when records arrive and attempt to subtract them later. They evaluate these on the 48B Kimi Linear hybrid model and other architectures (Mamba-2, Falcon-H1, RWKV-7). They compare against checkpoint replay (restoring from before the record and replaying the suffix).
AI.result: Receipt-based deletion fails: after 4,096 tokens, records leave a 4.5% imprint that receipts cannot remove. Recomputing half the suffix closes less than half the gap, and receipt storage costs exceed full checkpoints after 88 tokens. Checkpoint replay achieves exact omission on all tested arrays but requires replaying the entire suffix.
AI.conclusion: Among evaluated methods, only checkpoint replay achieves exact omission of records from AI assistant memory, though it requires work proportional to replayed suffix length. Receipt-based approaches fail due to non-canceling changes induced by records in later updates.

title: Quantile-Led Feature Extraction for Multi-Horizon Predictive Maintenance in Industrial Manufacturing Systems
summary: In data-driven predictive maintenance (PdM), feature extraction is usually treated as fixed preprocessing: a descriptor set is chosen once and reused while the downstream model or forecasting horizon changes. This paper isolates the representation-learning stage and presents a quantile-led feature-extraction framework based on a dual-stage MLP-QRNN hierarchy. QRNN1 learns a broad ten-quantile conditional distribution for each sensor channel, while skip-connected QRNN2 refines a retained mid-tail quantile set into compact, channel-resolved, distribution-aware features. A fixed thirteen-pipeline ablation spans 1-hour, 70-hour, and 30-day regimes across 72 machines in 9 industrial facilities, with the downstream temporal classifier held fixed within each regime. Increasing the retained mid-tail set from two to four quantiles improves 30- and 60-minute F1-score, reaching 75.92% and 72.44% with attention enabled. The results also show that representations do not transfer reliably beyond their design horizon unless feature capacity, temporal embedding, activation strategy, and sensor breadth are scaled with the forecasting task. The unmodified short-horizon extractor falls to 42.90% F1 at 70 hours, whereas horizon-conditioned extractors reach 60.38% at 70 hours and 79.97% at 30 days. The framework therefore supports treating PdM feature extraction as a horizon-dependent representational stage rather than fixed preprocessing.

AI.tldr: A quantile-based feature extraction framework for predictive maintenance that adapts to different forecasting horizons, showing significant performance improvements over fixed preprocessing approaches.
AI.motivation: Traditional predictive maintenance treats feature extraction as fixed preprocessing, using the same descriptor set regardless of changing downstream models or forecasting horizons, which limits performance across different time scales.
AI.method: A dual-stage MLP-QRNN hierarchy: QRNN1 learns broad ten-quantile conditional distributions for each sensor channel, while skip-connected QRNN2 refines a retained mid-tail quantile set into compact, channel-resolved, distribution-aware features. The approach is tested across 1-hour, 70-hour, and 30-day forecasting regimes.
AI.result: Increasing retained mid-tail quantiles from two to four improves F1-scores to 75.92% (30-min) and 72.44% (60-min) with attention. Representations don't transfer reliably beyond design horizons unless extractor capacity is scaled - short-horizon extractor falls to 42.90% at 70 hours, while horizon-conditioned extractors reach 60.38% (70 hours) and 79.97% (30 days).
AI.conclusion: Predictive maintenance feature extraction should be treated as a horizon-dependent representational stage rather than fixed preprocessing, requiring scaling of feature capacity, temporal embedding, activation strategy, and sensor breadth with forecasting tasks.

title: Learning Adaptive SED for heterogeneous load balancing
summary: We study a two-server load balancing system with heterogeneous service rates that are a priori unknown to the dispatcher. The goal is to route customers according to the Shortest--Expected--Delay (SED) policy, but this requires knowledge of the service rates. Empirical policies that route based on estimates perform poorly: due to estimation error, the empirical policy disagrees with the oracle on an infinite region of the state space. We propose an online learning algorithm that converges to SED while learning the service rates. The algorithm carefully balances empirical SED routing with forced exploration phases that guarantee sufficient sampling of both servers. We prove that our algorithm achieves finite regret; this differs from classical Multi-Armed Bandit settings where regret typically grows logarithmically in time. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate the performance of our algorithm and highlight the regimes in which forced exploration is especially beneficial.

AI.tldr: Online learning algorithm for two-server load balancing with unknown heterogeneous service rates that converges to optimal SED routing while ensuring sufficient exploration.
AI.motivation: Need to route customers according to Shortest-Expected-Delay (SED) policy without prior knowledge of server service rates, as naive empirical estimation policies perform poorly due to estimation errors.
AI.method: Propose an online learning algorithm that balances empirical SED routing with forced exploration phases to guarantee sufficient sampling of both servers while learning service rates.
AI.result: Algorithm achieves finite regret (unlike typical logarithmic regret in MAB problems), converges to SED routing, and forced exploration is especially beneficial in certain regimes as shown numerically.
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithm successfully addresses the challenge of learning optimal load balancing with unknown service rates by carefully balancing exploitation and exploration, achieving finite regret and convergence to the optimal SED policy.

title: Scoring Without the Engine: Validating a Deterministic, Manipulation-Resistant Content Score for Generative Engines, End to End
comment: 42 pages, 4 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/TW3-Partners-OS/geo-score-reproducibility & More informations on Citead.com
summary: How do you validate a cheap, deterministic proxy for an oracle that is expensive, rate-limited, and non-stationary? We present a protocol built on adversarial falsification gates (negative control, dose response, bounded amplification, duplication penalty, length neutrality) that define and select the proxy, fitted on a training split and confirmed held-out; around them it bounds what the proxy can never resolve, and re-measures external causal evidence on the current oracle rather than assuming it. We demonstrate it end to end on Generative Engine Optimization, where the proxy is a deterministic content score, and one step fails on that domain exactly as the protocol is built to detect: re-measuring the only published causal anchors (2023 effect sizes) on ten modern engine families shows their levers move citation on none, so the anchors are an expired external check; recalibrating to the near-zero modern vector strips the score of its lever-responsive components. What survives is the gate-enforced response surface. The gates buy a measured property: on a 500-source benchmark of adversarial edits, amplifying the score's calibrated levers gains an attacker at most 6 points, and decreases with dose; single-lever amplification is provably bounded, while the cap and cross-lever sub-additivity are empirical findings consistent with it. On detection, web-spam baselines dominate and out-of-distribution attacks evade the score, so the deployable filter layers it over them. A query-conditioned skyline bounds the score's citation signal (within-query Spearman 0.11), repositioning query-agnostic scores as quality filters rather than citation predictors. A query-leakage bug in our first ranking evaluation and a failed confidence flag are disclosed and corrected; every number reproduces offline from released artifacts at zero marginal API cost.

AI.tldr: Protocol using adversarial falsification gates to validate deterministic proxies for non-stationary oracles, demonstrated on generative engine optimization with content scores.
AI.motivation: Need to validate cheap deterministic proxies for expensive, rate-limited, non-stationary oracles when proxy components may fail or become invalid over time.
AI.method: Protocol built on adversarial falsification gates (negative control, dose response, bounded amplification, duplication penalty, length neutrality) to define and select proxy, fit on training split and confirm held-out; bounds what proxy can't resolve and re-measures external evidence.
AI.result: Protocol successfully detected failed anchors in generative engine optimization domain - re-measuring 2023 effect sizes showed no modern citation impact; gates enforce bounded response surface with provable bounds on single-lever amplification; calibrated levers gain attackers at most 6 points on benchmark; detection uses layered approach with web-spam baselines.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial falsification gates provide measured validation for deterministic proxies, enabling detection of expired components and enforcing bounded attack surfaces, with practical applications in content optimization and quality filtering.

title: Noisy-Space Policy Gradient for Diffusion Policies in Offline Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Diffusion policies offer a powerful and expressive parameterization for continuous control. Yet, their integration with reinforcement learning remains conceptually and algorithmically challenging. In this work, we address this gap by introducing a noisy-space action-value (Q-)function that assigns values to diffusion latents through the distribution of executed actions induced by the denoising process. We show that this construction admits a precise semantic interpretation and derive a noisy-space policy gradient (NSPG) that optimizes noisy latents using only clean action-space value estimates. Building on this result, we formulate a KL-regularized policy improvement over noisy latents and show that the resulting objective admits a diffusion-compatible regression form, avoiding backpropagation through the denoising process. Empirical results on state-based D4RL benchmarks and vision-based OGBench tasks demonstrate that the proposed noisy-space objective provides a principled and effective basis for training diffusion policies in offline reinforcement learning. Project webpage: https://mahmoud-selim.github.io/NSPG/

AI.tldr: NSPG (Noisy-Space Policy Gradient) introduces a novel approach to train diffusion policies in offline RL by operating on diffusion latents instead of clean actions, enabling more effective integration of diffusion models with reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Diffusion policies provide powerful and expressive parameterization for continuous control, but their integration with reinforcement learning remains conceptually and algorithmically challenging. There's a need to bridge the gap between diffusion models and RL frameworks.
AI.method: Proposes a noisy-space action-value (Q-) function that assigns values to diffusion latents through the distribution of executed actions from the denoising process. Derives a noisy-space policy gradient (NSPG) that optimizes noisy latents using only clean action-space value estimates, and formulates a KL-regularized policy improvement objective that admits a diffusion-compatible regression form.
AI.result: Empirical results on state-based D4RL benchmarks and vision-based OGBench tasks demonstrate that the noisy-space objective provides a principled and effective basis for training diffusion policies in offline reinforcement learning.
AI.conclusion: The NSPG framework successfully bridges diffusion policies with reinforcement learning by operating in the noisy latent space, offering a practical solution to the integration challenge while maintaining computational efficiency through regression-style optimization.

title: From Simulated Citizens to Simulated Deliberation: Challenges in Representation and Interaction
summary: Multi-agent LLM deliberation has been explored as a scalable way to simulate public deliberation. For such simulations to be informative, persona agents should reflect population opinion patterns and interaction should shape their conclusions. We evaluate whether LLM-based deliberation can meet these two conditions using census-grounded Korean personas debating real policy questions benchmarked against national surveys. Persona agents do not reliably reproduce population opinion patterns: responses are often far more concentrated and frequently reverse demographic differences in the human data. Deliberations nonetheless produce reasoned, reciprocal, and varied arguments alongside substantial stance movement. Yet much of this movement does not require peer exchange: sealed-monologue agents change position at similar rates and reach nearly the same final balance as full debates, while groups initialized with very different positions often converge to similar endpoints. Anchoring population-informed starting positions, meanwhile, sharply suppresses updating. Thus, population representation, argument generation, and interaction-driven opinion change do not necessarily go together. The simulations readily surface arguments on both sides, though whether they capture the diversity of human perspectives remains untested, leaving open a promising role for argument surfacing even as population simulation requires further validation.

AI.tldr: LLM-based multi-agent deliberation doesn't reliably simulate population opinions despite generating reasoned arguments, as persona agents fail to reproduce demographic patterns and opinion changes occur without actual interaction.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether LLM-based multi-agent deliberation can be a scalable way to simulate public deliberation that requires: 1) persona agents reflecting population opinion patterns, and 2) interaction shaping their conclusions.
AI.method: Used census-grounded Korean personas debating real policy questions, benchmarked against national surveys. Compared sealed-monologue agents (no interaction) with full debates, and examined groups with different starting positions.
AI.result: Persona agents don't reliably reproduce population opinion patterns - responses are more concentrated and reverse demographic differences. Deliberations produce reasoned arguments and stance movement, but similar movement occurs in sealed-monologues without interaction. Groups with different starting positions converge to similar endpoints. Population-informed starting positions sharply suppress updating.
AI.conclusion: Population representation, argument generation, and interaction-driven opinion change don't necessarily go together. LLM simulations can surface arguments on both sides, but population simulation requires further validation while argument surfacing shows promise.

title: From Synthetic Priors to Model Behavior: Structural Coverage in Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are commonly pretrained on large collections of procedurally generated synthetic tasks, yet it remains unclear how well these synthetic pretraining priors support the downstream tasks on which the models are evaluated. We study this question from a distribution-level attribution perspective. We recover or reconstruct the synthetic data generators of four TFMs and compare their generated tasks with datasets from two widely used tabular benchmarks. Each dataset is represented by a common set of structural descriptors capturing schema, feature distributions, dependence structure, response properties, and feature--response relationships. In this space, we measure how broadly and repeatedly each synthetic prior reaches benchmark tasks using structural coverage and normalized density, and examine whether stronger local support is associated with better predictive performance. We find substantial differences across synthetic pretraining priors: some generators provide consistently broader and denser support for benchmark tasks than others. Moreover, stronger synthetic-to-benchmark support is generally associated with better relative model performance. These results suggest that structural coverage provides a useful diagnostic for characterizing synthetic pretraining priors and relating their data-generating assumptions to downstream model behavior.

AI.tldr: TFMs trained on synthetic data show varying downstream performance depending on how well their synthetic pretraining priors structurally support benchmark tasks, with broader/denser support correlating with better performance.
AI.motivation: Tabular foundation models are typically pretrained on synthetic data, but it's unclear how well these synthetic pretraining priors actually support downstream tasks they're evaluated on. The paper aims to understand this connection between synthetic pretraining data distribution and downstream performance.
AI.method: Recover/reconstruct synthetic data generators from four TFMs, compare generated tasks with two tabular benchmark datasets. Represent datasets using structural descriptors (schema, feature distributions, dependence structure, response properties, feature-response relationships). Measure structural coverage and normalized density of synthetic priors on benchmark tasks.
AI.result: Substantial differences across synthetic pretraining priors - some provide consistently broader and denser support for benchmark tasks. Stronger synthetic-to-benchmark support is generally associated with better relative model performance. Structural coverage serves as useful diagnostic for characterizing synthetic pretraining priors.
AI.conclusion: The structural properties of synthetic pretraining data matter for downstream performance in tabular foundation models. Structural coverage provides a diagnostic tool to relate data-generating assumptions of synthetic priors to downstream model behavior, helping understand why some pretraining strategies work better than others.

title: A Tool-Augmented, GPT-4 Chatbot for Real-Time Repository Data Analysis
summary: Software repositories contain vast amounts of data on code contributions, bug reports, and project activities, yet this information remains challenging for non-technical stakeholders and developers to access due to limited expertise in querying repositories. To address this, we introduce a novel chatbot architecture leveraging OpenAI's GPT-4 model for automated extraction and analysis of repository data. In contrast, our architecture takes a structured path first by parsing the user's query to extract relevant parameters, then selecting the correct tool to employ based on that analysis, and finally invoking the GPT-4 model to create a highly detailed response. In contrast to previous work based on multi-component systems with embedding models and document retrievers, our architecture inverts the process by relying on prompt engineering and tool selection to fit with the query intent. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments on various question types, including Issues, Pull Requests, Commits, Compound Questions, and General Repository Information, evaluating our target prompts' ability to improve the accuracy of responses from the model. Beyond demonstrating the utility of this architecture to a diverse set of users, our findings suggest that this architecture can make repository data more accessible to technical and non-technical audiences through the production of actionable insights.

AI.tldr: A novel chatbot architecture using GPT-4 for automated extraction and analysis of software repository data, making it accessible to both technical and non-technical users through structured query processing and prompt engineering.
AI.motivation: Software repositories contain valuable data on code contributions, bug reports, and project activities, but this information remains difficult to access for non-technical stakeholders and developers due to limited expertise in querying repositories.
AI.method: Introduces a chatbot architecture that first parses user queries to extract relevant parameters, selects appropriate tools based on analysis, then invokes GPT-4 to generate detailed responses. Uses prompt engineering and tool selection rather than traditional multi-component systems with embedding models and document retrievers.
AI.result: Conducted experiments on various question types (Issues, Pull Requests, Commits, Compound Questions, General Repository Information) showing improved accuracy of responses from the model through targeted prompts.
AI.conclusion: The architecture makes repository data more accessible to both technical and non-technical audiences by producing actionable insights, demonstrating utility for diverse users.

title: Constrained Online Learning with Noisy Constraint Values
summary: We study constrained online convex optimization with adversarial constraints when constraint values and gradients are observed through unbiased noise. Gaussian value noise of standard deviation $σ$ yields a worst-case lower bound of $Ω(\min\{σ,1\}T/\log^7T)$ on the maximum of expected regret and expected hard violation, even with known gradients. This rules out any jointly $O(T^{1-δ})$ guarantee for fixed $δ>0$ and fixed positive noise level. We therefore study budget violation: the largest cumulative overspend over any window within a fixed horizon. We introduce \LEDGER, which tracks observed net consumption in a nonnegative balance and sets constraint weights before the current feedback noise. Under common feasibility and conditional finite-variance feedback, for fixed problem parameters, \LEDGER\ achieves $O(\sqrt T/V)$ expected regret and $O(\sqrt V\,T^{3/4}+σ\sqrt T)$ expected budget violation for $V\in[T^{-1/2},1]$. This gives the pair $(O(\sqrt T),O(T^{3/4}))$ at $V=1$ and $(O(T^{2/3}),O(T^{2/3}))$ at $V=T^{-1/6}$, without a Slater condition. The budget-focused endpoint $V=T^{-1/2}$ gives $(O(T),O(\sqrt T))$. The same update yields $O((1+E[P_T])\sqrt T/V)$ expected dynamic regret for predictable feasible comparator paths, without common feasibility or path-length input. Its budget bound instead depends on the shortest feasible path, up to a dimension factor.

AI.tldr: The paper studies constrained online convex optimization with noisy constraints, showing that traditional joint regret-violation guarantees are impossible under noise, and proposes LEDGER algorithm that achieves sublinear expected regret and budget violation bounds without requiring a Slater condition.
AI.motivation: Prior work on constrained online convex optimization assumes perfect feedback or allows unbounded violations. However, in practical settings with noisy observations (like unbiased noise in constraint values and gradients), obtaining joint O(T^{1-δ}) regret and hard violation guarantees becomes impossible, motivating the need for alternative violation metrics and algorithms.
AI.method: Proposes LEDGER algorithm that tracks observed net consumption in a nonnegative balance and sets constraint weights before receiving current feedback noise. The algorithm operates under common feasibility and conditional finite-variance feedback assumptions. It also provides extensions for dynamic regret against predictable feasible comparator paths.
AI.result: LEDGER achieves O(√T/V) expected regret and O(√V T^{3/4} + σ√T) expected budget violation for V ∈ [T^{-1/2}, 1]. Key tradeoffs: (O(√T), O(T^{3/4})) at V=1, (O(T^{2/3}), O(T^{2/3})) at V=T^{-1/6}, and budget-focused (O(T), O(√T)) at V=T^{-1/2}. For dynamic settings, achieves O((1+E[P_T])√T/V) regret.
AI.conclusion: When constraint feedback contains noise, traditional hard violation guarantees are impossible, but budget violation (max cumulative overspend over any window) is achievable. LEDGER provides tunable tradeoffs between regret and budget violation without requiring Slater conditions, making constrained online optimization practical under noisy observations.

title: FinCUABuild: Can Agents Build Reliable Benchmarks for Dynamic Financial Computer Use?
comment: Jingpu Yang, Fengxian Ji: co-first author
summary: Financial scenarios are diverse and complex, spanning varying data conditions, tool configurations, and workflows. Yet existing CUA, Computer-Using Agent, evaluation tasks remain largely manually constructed, limiting scalable coverage of real-world financial scenarios. Then, can agents autonomously construct diverse CUA evaluation tasks for financial scenarios? Evaluating this capability poses three key challenges: scenario coverage of construction requests, fair comparison across construction methods, and reliable assessment of generated task quality. To solve these, we introduce FinCUABuildBench, a benchmark for evaluating financial CUA task construction, featuring: (i) 576 construction requests covering 24 financial workflows and three types of runtime variation; (ii) standardized input, budget, and output specifications; and (iii) a task qualification mechanism based on execution tests and quality checks. We further introduce FinCUABuildAgent, a multi-agent system for automatically constructing dynamic financial CUA evaluation tasks. It consists of three modules that jointly construct tasks, environments, and validators. On FinCUABuildBench, under the same model backbone, existing agent-based construction methods achieve strict qualification rates of only 1.3-8.3%, while FinCUABuildAgent reaches 31.3%. Downstream evaluations further show that the constructed tasks can effectively differentiate CUA task-execution capabilities. These results demonstrate that agents can autonomously construct financial CUA tasks with meaningful evaluation value, offering a practical path toward broader evaluation coverage in financial scenarios. Code: https://github.com/FengxianJi/FinCUABuild

AI.tldr: FinCUABuildBench is a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to autonomously construct financial CUA evaluation tasks, addressing challenges in scenario coverage, fair comparison, and quality assessment. The accompanying FinCUABuildAgent system achieves 31.3% qualification rate, significantly outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing CUA evaluation tasks for financial scenarios are mostly manually constructed, which limits scalable coverage of diverse and complex real-world financial scenarios. There's a need for agents to autonomously construct diverse evaluation tasks to enable broader evaluation coverage.
AI.method: The authors introduce FinCUABuildBench, a benchmark with 576 construction requests covering 24 financial workflows and three runtime variation types, plus standardized specifications and a task qualification mechanism. They also propose FinCUABuildAgent, a multi-agent system with three modules for constructing tasks, environments, and validators.
AI.result: On FinCUABuildBench, existing agent-based methods achieve only 1.3-8.3% strict qualification rates, while FinCUABuildAgent reaches 31.3%. Downstream evaluations show the constructed tasks can effectively differentiate CUA task-execution capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Agents can autonomously construct financial CUA tasks with meaningful evaluation value, offering a practical path toward broader evaluation coverage in financial scenarios.

title: The Geometry of Refusal: Why Post-Hoc Safety Is Fragile and Pretraining-Time Safety Persists
summary:
Post-hoc safety training (RLHF, DPO) is the dominant way to align large language models, yet jailbreaks (Zou et al., 2023b), fine-tuning attacks (Qi et al., 2024), and activation-space probes (Arditi et al., 2024) keep recovering the behaviors it was meant to remove. We give this fragility one geometric explanation and trace it to when, during pretraining, safety can take hold. We measure the safety update $Δ= W_{\text{safe}} - W_{\text{base}}$ against the curvature of the model's capabilities (the empirical Fisher of a capability loss). Post-hoc safety consistently lands in a suppression regime: $Δ$ is nearly orthogonal to the capability directions, and its small in-subspace part concentrates on a few high-curvature ones. The update is thin but sharp, a refusal gate laid over intact capabilities rather than erasure of them. A kernel-immobility lemma explains why such an update can only mask a capability, not remove it, so a little benign fine-tuning restores it: 100 steps of benign fine-tuning collapse refusal on Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3-8B Instruct at preserved capability, a signature that replicates across five model families.
  Following the account into pretraining, a 267-checkpoint sweep of OLMo-2-1B (OLMo et al., 2025) shows the substrate that safety engages emerging in a sharp transition between roughly 6B and 60B pretraining tokens. We then use the account constructively: models trained from scratch with safety co-training spread continuously across pretraining reach 87 to 98% refusal whose post-attack level holds at 84 to 91% at every scale, an erosion of 2 to 14 pp against 35 to 38 pp for post-hoc installs, at capability matched or better than an LM-only baseline and holding from 410M to 6.9B, whereas a compute-matched windowed schedule installs no lasting refusal. Persistence of the safety signal across pretraining, not its timing, is what buys attack robustness.

AI.tldr: Post-hoc safety training (RLHF/DPO) creates fragile safety that only masks capabilities rather than removing them, making it vulnerable to attacks. Co-training safety from scratch during pretraining creates more robust safety.
AI.motivation: Current post-hoc safety training methods (RLHF, DPO) are fragile and vulnerable to jailbreaks, fine-tuning attacks, and activation-space probes that recover behaviors meant to be removed.
