Finetuning Qwen-2.5-VL-7B with SVRL on only 5{,}000 visual question answering examples yields consistent gains in multi-hop VQA generalization and tool efficiency across benchmarks. Overall, SVRL narrows the gap between compact agents and much larger proprietary models while requiring substantially lower training and inference cost.

AI.tldr: SVRL is a reinforcement learning framework that trains multimodal agents to self-verify retrieved evidence without external verifiers, improving visual question answering performance with fewer tool calls and more diverse queries.
AI.motivation: Multimodal agents struggle with reliable tool use because they must interpret both text and images while integrating noisy retrieved evidence, typically with only sparse outcome-level supervision and no explicit verification signals. Existing RL approaches like GRPO work well for text-only reasoning but don't address the unique challenges of multimodal tool use.
AI.method: SVRL is an RL-only finetuning framework that trains multimodal agents to verify and filter retrieved evidence within their own reasoning traces. It introduces two key components: 1) A search-aware penalty that discourages unnecessary tool calls, and 2) A query-diversity reward that encourages diverse, well-formed search queries to provide fine-grained feedback on when and what to search.
AI.result: Finetuning Qwen-2.5-VL-7B with SVRL on only 5,000 visual question answering examples yields consistent gains in multi-hop VQA generalization and tool efficiency across benchmarks. The approach reduces reliance on external verifiers at inference time and improves overall performance.
AI.conclusion: SVRL narrows the gap between compact agents and much larger proprietary models while requiring substantially lower training and inference cost. The framework demonstrates that self-verification through RL can effectively address the challenges of multimodal tool use, making agents more efficient and reliable in complex reasoning tasks.

title: Parallelism Strategy Chaining for Fast Training Convergence
summary: Selecting a parallelism strategy - the configuration of data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism degrees together with micro- and global-batch sizes - largely determines the training efficiency of large language models. State-of-the-art methods search for a parallelism strategy offline and select the single strategy that minimizes per-iteration time. But we find that they neglect the target validation perplexity and time-to-perplexity (TTP). In particular, our analysis reveals that the best strategy yielding the fastest perplexity improvement changes multiple times during training. As a result, state-of-the-art methods are 1.8-11.4x slower in TTP than the strategy sequence that selects the best strategy at each iteration. This paper proposes CONA, a new training method that introduces online strategy chaining. Instead of a single strategy selected offline, CONA ranks candidate strategies during training using a surrogate metric built from compute throughput and gradient statistics, and switches the current strategy to a new strategy with a higher metric. In our evaluation with GPT-3 1.3B, BERT-Large, and Llama-3.2-1B, CONA reaches the target validation perplexity 1.4-9.6x faster than state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, CONA closely tracks the perplexity achieved by the sequence that selects the best strategy at each iteration, within 2.6%.

AI.tldr: CONA introduces online strategy chaining for LLM training, dynamically switching parallelism strategies during training based on real-time metrics to achieve faster time-to-perplexity compared to static offline methods.
AI.motivation: Current state-of-the-art methods select a single parallelism strategy offline that minimizes per-iteration time, but they neglect the target validation perplexity and time-to-perplexity (TTP). Analysis shows that the optimal strategy changes multiple times during training, causing existing methods to be significantly slower in achieving target perplexity.
AI.method: CONA introduces online strategy chaining that ranks candidate strategies during training using a surrogate metric combining compute throughput and gradient statistics. Instead of a single static strategy, it dynamically switches to better strategies when the metric indicates improvement, enabling adaptive parallelism configuration throughout training.
AI.result: CONA achieves 1.4-9.6x faster time-to-target-perplexity compared to state-of-the-art methods on GPT-3 1.3B, BERT-Large, and Llama-3.2-1B. It closely tracks the optimal strategy sequence (within 2.6%) that would select the best strategy at each iteration.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, online strategy adaptation is crucial for efficient LLM training, as the optimal parallelism strategy changes during training. CONA demonstrates that adaptive strategy switching significantly improves training efficiency over static methods, making it a promising approach for large-scale model training.

title: ResidualAuth: What Authorization State Must Language Agents Preserve under Revocable Delegation?
comment: 61 pages, 7 figures. Includes appendices. Moonwon Choi and Seokho Jeong contributed equally; Seunggeun Lee is the corresponding author
summary: Tool-using language agents can delegate and revoke permissions while acting through external services. We show that two authorization histories can have identical current permissions and identical all-pairs reachability yet require opposite decisions after the same direct-edge revocation. We formalize the information needed to preserve such distinctions as a residual authorization state. We prove that exponentially many future-distinct states can share one fixed transitive closure, and give exact or tight asymptotic bounds on the state required by an exact monitor as delegation redundancy varies. ResidualAuth compiles these constructions into paired language-agent episodes. Across four open-weight models, a fixed 256-token summary solved 0-2/16 pairs, sham reads solved 0/16, and authenticated current-query reads solved 15-16/16. In a separate held-out online-memory diagnostic, exact ledger serializations fit all 128 four-coordinate pairs at both 768 and 1,024 tokens. At either cap, factually supported model-written memories sufficient for every prespecified continuation solved at most 1/128 pairs per model. A hard gate reduced eight observed unauthorized effects to zero without changing the preceding attempts. These results distinguish required authorization state, usable decision information, online state maintenance, and effect mediation.

AI.tldr: Language agents need precise authorization tracking that distinguishes between permission histories that look identical but require opposite decisions after revocation. A method called ResidualAuth provides exact authorization monitoring with provable bounds.
AI.motivation: Tool-using language agents need to properly manage delegation and revocation permissions when acting through external services. Current authorization systems fail to distinguish between different authorization histories that have identical current permissions but require opposite decisions after revocation events.
AI.method: Formalized the concept of residual authorization state to capture necessary distinctions between permission histories. Proved bounds on state requirements for exact monitoring. Implemented ResidualAuth which compiles authorization constructions into paired language-agent episodes for testing. Evaluated across four open-weight models with different memory strategies.
AI.result: Exact ledger serializations at 768-1024 tokens solved all 128 test pairs. Fixed 256-token summaries solved 0-2/16 pairs. Sham reads solved 0/16. Authenticated current-query reads solved 15-16/16. Factual memories only solved ≤1/128 pairs. A hard gate eliminated all unauthorized effects.
AI.conclusion: The work distinguishes between required authorization state, usable decision information, online state maintenance, and effect mediation. Shows that precise authorization tracking requires maintaining historical information beyond just current permissions to handle revocation scenarios correctly.

title: Kolmogorov--Arnold stability for discontinuous functions
summary: Here we investigate the stability of the Kolmogorov--Arnold representation theorem (KART) under adversarial reparameterisations of the hidden layer for multivariate discontinuous and unbounded functions. Our results provide a rigorous mathematical foundation for the structural robustness of modern deep learning architectures, such as Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks (KANs), under adversarial configurations.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the stability of Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem under adversarial reparameterizations for discontinuous/unbounded functions, providing mathematical foundations for KAN robustness.
AI.motivation: To establish rigorous mathematical foundations for the structural robustness of modern deep learning architectures like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) under adversarial configurations, addressing stability concerns for multivariate discontinuous and unbounded functions.
AI.method: Investigating the stability of Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem (KART) under adversarial reparameterisations of the hidden layer, focusing on multivariate discontinuous and unbounded functions.
AI.result: Provides results that demonstrate the stability of KART under adversarial reparameterisations, offering mathematical support for the robustness of KAN architectures in adversarial settings.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes mathematical foundations for understanding and ensuring the structural robustness of Kolmogorov-Arnold Network architectures against adversarial manipulations, contributing to more reliable deep learning systems.

title: Automated Design of Inventory Policy with Large Language Models: An Exploratory Study
summary: Firms making inventory decisions have access to operational data, optimization tools, and large language models (LLMs). Typically, data characterize the operating environment, optimization selects parameters within a prespecified inventory policy class, and LLMs support coding and decision analysis. We develop an integrated framework that combines these resources to automate inventory policy design. Given demand data, the framework iteratively uses an LLM to generate parameterized policy classes and an external solver to optimize its parameters within each class. Across 30 lost-sales inventory instances, the mean cost reduction relative to optimized base-stock benchmarks increases from 17.5% after one generation to 30.0% after ten generations. Parameter optimization is central to this performance: an LLM-only variant performs substantially worse, whereas optimization-guided feedback improves policy quality, accelerates search, and directs the LLM toward better policy classes rather than merely better parameter values within a fixed class. The strongest discovered policies are also interpretable: they combine recognizable inventory-control motifs, including capped orders, discounted or weighted pipeline inventory, and threshold-based replenishment logic. The search thereby produces new policy-class functional forms that, to our knowledge, have not previously been studied in the lost-sales inventory literature. These functional forms are not specified ex ante but emerge from the search process. Moreover, after their parameters are re-optimized, three discovered policy classes achieve average cost reductions of 21.75% to 22.60% across 10,064 new inventory instances. Overall, the results show that data-driven parameter optimization can guide LLM-based search over a broad space of inventory policy classes and identify high-performing, interpretable, and transferable decision rules.

AI.tldr: An integrated framework combining LLMs and optimization solvers automates inventory policy design, generating novel policy classes that outperform benchmarks by up to 30% and transfer well to new instances.
AI.motivation: Firms have access to operational data, optimization tools, and LLMs, but these resources are typically used separately. There's a need for an integrated approach that combines these capabilities to automate inventory policy design rather than just supporting coding and parameter optimization within fixed policy classes.
AI.method: The framework iteratively uses an LLM to generate parameterized inventory policy classes from scratch, then employs an external solver to optimize parameters within each class. This creates a feedback loop where optimization results guide subsequent LLM generations toward better policy classes rather than just better parameters.
AI.result: Across 30 lost-sales inventory instances, the framework achieved mean cost reductions relative to optimized base-stock benchmarks increasing from 17.5% after one generation to 30.0% after ten generations. Parameter optimization proved critical - LLM-only variants performed substantially worse. The discovered policies are interpretable, combining recognizable inventory-control motifs like capped orders, discounted pipeline inventory, and threshold-based replenishment logic. Three discovered policy classes achieved average cost reductions of 21.75% to 22.60% across 10,064 new instances after parameter re-optimization.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven parameter optimization can effectively guide LLM-based search over a broad space of inventory policy classes to identify high-performing, interpretable, and transferable decision rules. The framework generates novel policy class functional forms not previously studied in the literature, emerging naturally from the search process rather than being specified in advance.

title: Dense Structural Compression of Transformers via Gauge-Correct Channel Removal
comment: 10 pages main text, 28 pages total including appendices
summary:
Inference energy per token drives the cost and carbon footprint of deployed transformers. It is dominated by dense matrix products that incur fused multiply-accumulate (FMA) operations and memory traffic. To reduce these computations while retaining dense tensors for high GPU throughput, we develop a methodology from first principles to adapt structural complexity during training to maximize inference utility per unit compute. Channel penalties drive entire tensor slices to zero to enable physical removal while preserving density and the network function.
  The natural approach, penalizing the norm of operator components acting through each channel, is provably destabilized by gauge freedom. We resolve this pathology with GaugeLasso: additive symmetric group-lasso penalties that recover a monotone function of product-norms when the network converges to gauge balance. Our equilibrium analysis enables per-channel calibration to correctly suppress slices that under-perform in inference utility per unit compute.
  Under adaptive pressure, the network reorganizes into depth-dependent structural profiles that can be far smaller than the architecture required to learn the task. On polynomial long division over $\mathbb{F}_{31}$, compute compresses from 148 to 255 times with perfect accuracy. On character-level language modeling, compressed models outperform the hand-designed baseline at equal FMA. On masked autoencoding, a compression trial exposes which axes were over-provisioned and which saturated, guiding a better second design. Compaction also accelerates training monotonically as the model progresses. Post-hoc pruning with the same utility ranking cannot reach these structures, showing that sustained pressure is central to discovery of efficient models. Retraining a discovered architecture recovers baseline quality on our statistical tasks, but fails on our exact algorithmic task.

AI.tldr: GaugeLasso: A novel training methodology that adapts transformer structural complexity to maximize inference utility per compute, achieving 148-255x compute compression with perfect accuracy on certain tasks.
AI.motivation: Inference energy per token drives deployment costs and carbon footprint in transformers, dominated by dense matrix products with FMA operations. Current methods don't efficiently reduce computations while maintaining GPU throughput.
AI.method: Developed GaugeLasso - additive symmetric group-lasso penalties that overcome gauge freedom pathology. Uses channel penalties to drive tensor slices to zero for physical removal while preserving density. Includes per-channel calibration and equilibrium analysis.
AI.result: Achieved 148-255x compute compression on polynomial long division over 𝔽₃₁ with perfect accuracy. Compressed models outperform baselines on character-level language modeling at equal FMA. Discovered depth-dependent structural profiles smaller than architecture needed to learn tasks.
AI.conclusion: Sustained adaptive pressure during training is crucial for discovering efficient models, superior to post-hoc pruning. Network reorganization into depth-dependent structural profiles reveals which architectural axes are over-provisioned versus saturated, guiding better designs.

title: Inference-Time Nash Alignment
summary: Preference-based fine-tuning methods such as RLHF and DPO require substantial compute and large preference datasets. They also need direct access to the model parameters which are not provided by many state-of-the art models. Inference-time alignment offers a cost-effective alternative without updating model parameters. However, existing inference-time methods rely on a scalar reward model derived under a Bradley-Terry assumption, which cannot represent general preferences. Following recent work on fine-tuning with generalized preferences, in this work, we initiate the study of inference-time alignment under general preferences. We formulate the problem as obtaining a Nash equilibrium of a two-player zero-sum game between policies. We propose two algorithms: Best-of-Nash (BoN) and Nash Mirror Descent (NMD). We prove that both algorithms achieve a duality gap that matches the problem lower bound. Empirically, we implement the two methods on three datasets, which shows that our methods substantially outperform the base policy, converging to the performance of the fine-tuned models. Moreover, our results show that NMD remains robust across the regularization parameter.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces inference-time alignment methods (Best-of-Nash and Nash Mirror Descent) that work with general preferences without needing model parameter updates, matching or approaching fine-tuned model performance.
AI.motivation: Existing preference-based fine-tuning methods (like RLHF and DPO) require substantial compute, large preference datasets, and direct model parameter access - which isn't available for many state-of-the-art models. Inference-time alignment offers a cost-effective alternative, but current methods rely on scalar reward models with restrictive Bradley-Terry assumptions that cannot represent general preferences.
AI.method: The authors formulate inference-time alignment under general preferences as obtaining a Nash equilibrium in a two-player zero-sum game between policies. They propose two algorithms: Best-of-Nash (BoN) and Nash Mirror Descent (NMD). Both algorithms are theoretically analyzed and empirically tested.
AI.result: Theoretically, both algorithms achieve a duality gap that matches the problem's lower bound. Empirically, implementation on three datasets shows the methods substantially outperform base policies and converge to the performance of fine-tuned models. NMD remains robust across different regularization parameters.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully extends inference-time alignment to work with general preferences, providing efficient methods that don't require model parameter updates while achieving performance comparable to fine-tuned models, with NMD showing particular robustness to parameter variations.

title: Constitutive State-Space Modeling of Path-Dependent Plasticity: A Resolution-Consistent and Parallelizable Computational Framework
summary: Data-driven constitutive models for path-dependent plasticity are commonly formulated using nonlinear recurrent neural networks, whose sequential state evolution limits parallel training and whose predictions may depend on the discretization of the applied strain path. We introduce a Constitutive State Space (CSS) model that reformulates structured state-space dynamics as an incremental constitutive operator. The strain increment is decomposed into magnitude and direction: the loading direction drives the latent state-space system, while the increment magnitude enters the zero-order-hold discretization of its continuous-time linear recurrence. This mechanics-tailored construction guarantees stationarity under zero increments, strongly reduces sensitivity to strain-path resolution, and retains the parallel-scan structure of S5 for efficient training on long constitutive histories. The CSS and Minimal State Cell (MSC) architectures are compared for four multiaxial path-dependent material models including isotropic J2 plasticity, pressure-sensitive foam plasticity, and combined isotropic-kinematic hardening. CSS matches or exceeds the prediction accuracy of the MSC, including one order of magnitude lower validation losses for the plastically incompressible materials. Importantly, CSS maintains low errors across large changes in strain-path discretization, whereas the MSC error increases substantially when evaluated at coarser resolutions than used for training. CSS trains substantially faster and requires fewer strain-stress pairs to attain comparable or better accuracy. Analysis of the learned state further reveals latent structure consistent with the dimensionality of the underlying physical constitutive models. These results establish mechanics-tailored structured state-space dynamics as a computational framework for efficient and discretization-robust data-driven constitutive modeling.

AI.tldr: A new Constitutive State Space (CSS) model for path-dependent plasticity uses structured state-space dynamics to create discretization-robust data-driven constitutive models that train efficiently and maintain accuracy across different strain-path resolutions.
AI.motivation: Current data-driven constitutive models using nonlinear recurrent neural networks have limitations: they restrict parallel training due to sequential state evolution, and their predictions depend on the discretization of applied strain paths.
AI.method: CSS reformulates structured state-space dynamics as an incremental constitutive operator. Strain increment is decomposed into magnitude and direction: loading direction drives the latent state-space system, while increment magnitude enters zero-order-hold discretization of its continuous-time linear recurrence. This mechanics-tailored construction guarantees stationarity under zero increments.
AI.result: CSS matches or exceeds prediction accuracy of Minimal State Cell (MSC) architecture, with one order of magnitude lower validation losses for plastically incompressible materials. CSS maintains low errors across large changes in strain-path discretization, trains substantially faster, requires fewer strain-stress pairs, and reveals latent structure consistent with underlying physical constitutive models.
AI.conclusion: Mechanics-tailored structured state-space dynamics provide an efficient and discretization-robust computational framework for data-driven constitutive modeling, addressing key limitations of traditional recurrent neural network approaches.

title: RevalExo: A Functional Daily-Activity Benchmark for Inertial and Visual Locomotion Mode Recognition in Older Adults and Clinical Cohorts
summary: Assistive devices for people with mobility impairments, such as powered exoskeletons, rely on accurate locomotion mode recognition to adapt control strategies and provide appropriate assistance during daily activities. However, public benchmarks are typically collected from healthy adults, lack temporally precise labels necessary for detecting mode transitions, or focus on a limited set of tasks. To support development and evaluation under realistic clinical constraints and daily mobility demands, we introduce RevalExo, a functional daily-activity benchmark for inertial and visual locomotion mode recognition. RevalExo is built around a standardized, clinically and ecologically validated daily-activity protocol reflecting the cumulative everyday mobility demands in ageing and clinical populations. The benchmark includes 27 participants across three cohorts: older adults without mobility impairments, stroke survivors, and older adults with probable sarcopenia. The full cohort was recorded with lower-body IMUs, while synchronized egocentric video was collected for a clinically feasible subset of 13 participants. RevalExo provides 10.1 hours of frame-level annotations across 11 locomotion modes, including 5.1 hours of paired inertial--visual recordings. We benchmark three challenges: unimodal and multimodal locomotion mode recognition across multiple horizons, cross-population generalization from older adults without mobility impairments to clinical cohorts, and vision-guided knowledge transfer to IMU-only models. Results confirm consistent gains from fusing inertial and visual inputs but reveal a substantial gap between general recognition ($\sim$93\% F1) and recognition during transitions ($\sim$68\% F1), alongside persistent challenges in cross-population generalization and cross-modal transfer. We release RevalExo to stimulate further research on these open challenges.

AI.tldr: RevalExo: A multimodal locomotion mode recognition benchmark using inertial (IMU) and visual data from diverse populations including older adults, stroke survivors, and sarcopenia patients for exoskeleton control development.
AI.motivation: Existing locomotion mode recognition benchmarks have limitations: they're typically collected from healthy adults, lack precise temporal labels for mode transitions, and focus on limited tasks. There's a need for realistic clinical and daily activity data to develop assistive devices like powered exoskeletons.
AI.method: Created RevalExo benchmark with 27 participants across three cohorts: older adults without mobility impairments, stroke survivors, and older adults with probable sarcopenia. Collected lower-body IMU data from all participants, plus synchronized egocentric video from 13 participants. Provides 10.1 hours of frame-level annotations across 11 locomotion modes, including 5.1 hours of paired inertial-visual recordings.
AI.result: Results show consistent gains from fusing inertial and visual inputs, but reveal substantial gaps: general recognition achieves ~93% F1, while recognition during transitions drops to ~68%. Also identified persistent challenges in cross-population generalization and cross-modal transfer.
AI.conclusion: RevalExo addresses critical gaps in locomotion mode recognition benchmarks by providing clinically relevant multimodal data from diverse populations. It reveals key challenges in transition detection, cross-population generalization, and cross-modal transfer that need further research for practical assistive device development.

title: PCFlow: Physics-Conditioned Flow Matching for GPR B-Scan Image Synthesis
summary: Ground-penetrating radar (GPR) B-scan image synthesis is important for data augmentation, algorithm validation, and simulation acceleration, yet generating radargrams with both visual realism and physical consistency remains challenging. Existing learning-based generative models often emphasize visual appearance but provide limited control over response geometry. In this paper, we propose PCFlow, a physics-conditioned flow matching framework for fast GPR B-scan image synthesis. The core of PCFlow is a Maxwell-informed dense physical condition field constructed from the parameterized physical model used for electromagnetic simulation, including material properties, target geometry, propagation cues, and response-domain priors. This condition field provides an interpretable interface between physical scene parameters and radar response geometry, and guides conditional flow matching in the VAE latent space toward physically feasible generation paths. We evaluate PCFlow on a gprMax-based buried-pipeline dataset with both in-distribution and out-of-distribution test cases. Experimental results show that PCFlow generates images with more accurate response geometry and high visual fidelity, demonstrating its effectiveness for controllable and physically faithful radar image synthesis.

AI.tldr: PCFlow: A physics-conditioned flow matching framework for generating realistic and physically consistent GPR B-scan images using Maxwell-informed dense physical conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing GPR B-scan image synthesis methods using learning-based generative models focus on visual appearance but lack control over response geometry, making it challenging to generate radargrams with both visual realism and physical consistency.
AI.method: Proposes PCFlow, a physics-conditioned flow matching framework that uses a Maxwell-informed dense physical condition field constructed from parameterized physical models for electromagnetic simulation. This field includes material properties, target geometry, propagation cues, and response-domain priors, and guides conditional flow matching in VAE latent space.
AI.result: PCFlow generates GPR B-scan images with more accurate response geometry and high visual fidelity compared to existing methods, demonstrating effectiveness for controllable and physically faithful radar image synthesis on gprMax-based buried-pipeline dataset.
AI.conclusion: PCFlow provides an effective physics-conditioned framework for fast GPR B-scan synthesis that achieves both visual realism and physical consistency, offering better control over response geometry than previous learning-based approaches.

title: CIVI: A Framework for Diagnosing Search Agent Failures in Civic Information
summary: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in public-sector settings, where incorrect guidance can cause irreversible harm. We introduce CIVI, the first framework for diagnosing search agent failures in civic information. Its benchmark instantiation jointly spans cross-national, interjurisdictional government contexts (federal, state, and local) and functional categories from an internationally adopted United Nations standard. We evaluate ten frontier search agents and find that none matches an attentive human baseline. Alongside accuracy, CIVI measures search invocation rate, selective no-search accuracy, and how often agents cite authoritative government sources. To perform this diagnosis, we introduce ARISE, which decomposes agentic search failures into four mutually exclusive modes, isolated via source-injection ablation. ARISE attributes 72.1% of all observed failures to retrieval-bound causes rather than to gaps in the models' parametric knowledge.

AI.tldr: CIVI is the first framework for diagnosing search agent failures in civic information, evaluating frontier search agents against human baselines and finding significant performance gaps.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in public-sector settings where incorrect guidance can cause irreversible harm, creating an urgent need to diagnose search agent failures in civic information contexts.
AI.method: Introduced CIVI framework with benchmark spanning cross-national, interjurisdictional government contexts and UN standard functional categories. Evaluated 10 frontier search agents against human baseline. Developed ARISE method to decompose agentic search failures into four mutually exclusive modes via source-injection ablation.
AI.result: No evaluated search agent matched attentive human baseline. ARISE attributed 72.1% of observed failures to retrieval-bound causes rather than parametric knowledge gaps. Also measured search invocation rate, selective no-search accuracy, and authoritative government source citation.
AI.conclusion: Current search agents have significant limitations in civic information contexts, with most failures stemming from retrieval issues rather than model knowledge, highlighting the need for improved retrieval mechanisms in public-sector LLM deployments.

title: Long-Horizon Language Model Reinforcement Learning via Progressive Point Matching
summary: Current paradigms for training language models via reinforcement learning rely heavily on sparse outcome rewards. However, as we pursue tasks that require longer and more complicated trajectories, such strategies result in slow learning. Prior work has attempted to address this problem by rewarding partial progress; however, naive formulations are often biased and converge to suboptimal policies. We show that a simple and unbiased dense reward formulation, which we term progressive point matching, scales exponentially more efficiently to long-horizon tasks by rewarding partial progress on a segment level, both theoretically and empirically via synthetic environments. We then show how progressive point matching can be practically instantiated using a single reference trajectory per task. On extremely hard math reasoning problems, sparse outcome rewards cannot make any progress, whereas segment-level rewards enable improvements at larger test-time token budgets when measured by success rate or pass@k.

AI.tldr: Progressive point matching, a simple unbiased dense reward formulation, enables efficient training for long-horizon tasks by rewarding partial progress at segment level rather than relying on sparse outcome rewards.
AI.motivation: Current reinforcement learning paradigms for language models rely on sparse outcome rewards, which result in slow learning for tasks requiring longer and more complicated trajectories. Prior attempts to reward partial progress have been biased and converge to suboptimal policies.
AI.method: The paper introduces progressive point matching, a simple and unbiased dense reward formulation that rewards partial progress on a segment level rather than only final outcomes. This approach scales exponentially more efficiently to long-horizon tasks and can be practically instantiated using a single reference trajectory per task.
AI.result: Theoretical and empirical evidence via synthetic environments shows exponential efficiency scaling for long-horizon tasks. On extremely hard math reasoning problems, sparse outcome rewards cannot make any progress, whereas segment-level rewards enable improvements at larger test-time token budgets as measured by success rate or pass@k metrics.
AI.conclusion: Progressive point matching offers an effective solution to the limitations of sparse reward paradigms for RL training of language models on complex, long-horizon tasks, demonstrating practical viability for challenging problems like mathematical reasoning where traditional approaches fail.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Digital Inventory of Cultural Heritage & Traditional Knowledge: Case for Indonesian Open Digital Library of Culture
summary: The Indonesian Digital Library of Culture (Perpustakaan Digital Budaya Indonesia, PDBI; budaya-indonesia.org) is a participatory platform that has collected tens of thousands of entries on Nusantara cultural heritage through public contribution since 2007. Manual contribution faces three structural barriers: coverage (knowledge is scattered across languages and sites), integrity (open sources mix authentic documentation with noise), and completeness (subjects are recorded but their data remain shallow). This paper presents a methodological framework for autonomous, AI-based harvesting of cultural knowledge from the open web, designed to expand corpus coverage while intensifying per-entry data depth. The methodology is organised as a five-stage economic funnel: focused crawling, multilingual extraction and canonicalisation, vector encoding with blocking, agentic decision-making, and idempotent publication, under the principle of deterministic orchestration, agentic decisions. Each stage is formalised: funnel economics and optimal filter ordering; crawl-frontier dynamics as a subcritical branching process that explains the necessity of recurrent re-seeding; fact-level novelty via a containment measure; Bayesian multi-source evidence fusion with elevated publication thresholds for sacred categories; exactly-once effects via idempotent upserts and the transactional outbox; sliding-window inference budgeting with a reservation protocol; statistical quality auditing; and seed selection as submodular coverage maximisation. The framework retains four high-value human roles: curator of direction, escalation approver, quality auditor, and guardian of meaning, while machine autonomy is raised in stages. Ethical, legal, and cultural-sensitivity implications are discussed, including the architectural guarantee that the machine never overwrites human contributions.

AI.tldr: An AI framework for autonomous harvesting of Indonesian cultural knowledge from the open web to overcome manual contribution barriers through a five-stage economic funnel approach.
AI.motivation: Manual contribution to the Indonesian Digital Library of Culture faces three structural barriers: coverage (knowledge scattered across languages/sites), integrity (noise in open sources), and completeness (shallow data despite recorded subjects).
AI.method: A five-stage economic funnel methodology: focused crawling, multilingual extraction/canonicalisation, vector encoding with blocking, agentic decision-making, and idempotent publication. Uses deterministic orchestration and formalized processes for filter ordering, crawl-frontier dynamics, fact-level novelty measurement, Bayesian multi-source evidence fusion, and quality auditing.
AI.result: A framework designed to expand corpus coverage while intensifying per-entry data depth through autonomous AI harvesting, with architectural guarantees that machines never overwrite human contributions.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully addresses manual contribution barriers while preserving four high-value human roles (curator, approver, auditor, guardian) and provides ethical, legal, and cultural-sensitivity protections for digital cultural heritage preservation.

title: Robust Decentralized Personalized Federated Learning via Prediction-Constrained Neighborhood Collaboration
summary: This paper proposes a robust decentralized personalized federated learning method R-DPFL, that enables clients to reduce the impact of Byzantine attacks via robust neighborhood direction estimation and history-based update trend prediction, rather than purely aggregating client models as in the existing work. In R-DPFL, each client first computes the current-round model update by aggregating the received neighborhood update vectors. It then predicts what this update should be based on its historical values and local model changes. Finally, R-DPFL computes the difference between these two quantities, adaptively clips this difference, and adds it to the local update. We prove convergence of the learning process through rigorous analysis and show that honest clients maintain stable personalized descent dynamics under Byzantine neighbor perturbations without requiring consensus among neighboring models. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that RDPFL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art decentralized and personalized federated learning baselines under heterogeneous and adversarial settings.

AI.tldr: R-DPFL is a robust decentralized personalized federated learning method that protects against Byzantine attacks through neighborhood direction estimation and historical update prediction, outperforming existing methods under heterogeneous and adversarial conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing decentralized personalized federated learning methods are vulnerable to Byzantine attacks when aggregating client models. There's a need for robust methods that can reduce the impact of adversarial attacks while maintaining personalized learning in decentralized settings.
AI.method: R-DPFL uses a three-step approach: 1) compute current-round model update by aggregating neighborhood update vectors, 2) predict what the update should be based on historical values and local model changes, 3) compute difference between these quantities, adaptively clip it, and add to local update. This allows robust neighborhood direction estimation without requiring consensus among neighboring models.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 show that R-DPFL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art decentralized and personalized federated learning baselines under heterogeneous and adversarial settings. The method proves convergence through rigorous analysis.
AI.conclusion: R-DPFL provides an effective solution for Byzantine-resilient decentralized personalized federated learning, maintaining stable personalized descent dynamics for honest clients even under Byzantine neighbor perturbations, without requiring consensus among models.

title: Router Prior Bias: Preserving Base Routing Structure in MoE Post-Training
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) pretraining relies on an auxiliary load-balancing loss (LBL) to drive per-expert utilization toward uniformity. Post-training inherits a different situation: the base router already encodes non-uniform expert co-activation structure, which a re-imposed uniformity objective flattens away. We show that downstream performance depends instead on holding this inherited routing softly, a principle we term soft router anchoring, and instantiate it as Router Prior Bias (RPB), a training-time bias that pulls the router logits toward a prior read off the frozen base router while leaving the router itself trainable. On math post-training of Moonlight-16B-A3B, RPB attains 45.77 in-domain accuracy against 31.91 under re-applied LBL and 29.44 under unanchored fine-tuning, and retains more out-of-domain capability than either. The ordering against LBL reproduces on a second model family (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base), and the advantage over LBL is resolvable on an independently sourced corpus. Anchors defined on the router weights, on its logits, or on its output distribution perform comparably with no consistent ordering, which places the effect in the softness of the constraint rather than in the particular prior RPB supplies. Retained community structure in the expert co-activation graph tracks these gains wherever the base router is non-uniform enough for communities to form, yet enforcing the same prior as a hard assignment preserves that structure while performance falls sharply. Community structure is therefore a footprint of soft anchoring rather than its source, and the practical lesson is that inherited routing should be held softly during post-training, since both flattening it toward uniformity and enforcing it absolutely carry a downstream cost. Our code will be released at https://github.com/naver-ai/rpb.

AI.tldr: During MoE post-training, don't force uniform expert utilization - instead use soft router anchoring (RPB) to preserve inherited routing patterns, which boosts downstream performance.
AI.motivation: Standard MoE pretraining uses load-balancing loss for uniform expert utilization, but this approach flattens away valuable non-uniform expert co-activation structure inherited from base models during post-training, harming downstream performance.
AI.method: Proposes Router Prior Bias (RPB) - a training-time bias that pulls router logits toward a prior from the frozen base router while keeping the router trainable. Tests anchors on router weights, logits, or output distribution.
AI.result: RPB achieves 45.77% in-domain accuracy vs 31.91% with load-balancing loss and 29.44% with unanchored fine-tuning on Moonlight-16B-A3B math tasks. Gains replicate on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base. Performance improvements track with retained expert co-activation community structure.
AI.conclusion: Inherited routing patterns should be held softly during MoE post-training, not flattened toward uniformity nor enforced absolutely. Soft router anchoring (RPB) preserves valuable base model routing structure while allowing necessary adaptation, leading to better downstream performance.

title: Inferring Urban Mobility Interactions from Aggregated Dynamics
summary: Real-time urban governance depends not only on knowing where people are, but on how they move between places, directional flows that could be conventionally resolved by tracking individuals through space, i.e., expensive to sustain and built on traces that are highly unique and readily re-identifiable. Here we show that this directional structure need not be observed to be known: aggregated counts which cities already collect retain enough information to reconstruct the temporal evolution of origin-destination (OD) matrix. Using an uncertainty-aware physics-informed framework, we infer future OD flows from area-level counts alone across twelve mobility datasets from cities in the United States and China, reaching accuracy comparable to models that take historical OD matrices as input. Probabilistic modeling corrects the systematic underestimation of sparse, high-value corridors and yields calibrated predictions consistent with observed flows. Architectures that respect the generation-before-assignment logic of transport planning recover interactions more faithfully, indicating that location-level spatial heterogeneity should be preserved before pairwise interactions are reconstructed. Because inference requires only aggregated observations after training, recovering interactions this way reduces reliance on continuous individual-level tracking, pointing toward a more deployable and less exposure-heavy basis for real-time urban intelligence.

AI.tldr: OD flow prediction using only aggregated area counts without individual tracking, achieving accuracy comparable to models using historical OD matrices.
AI.motivation: Real-time urban governance needs directional flow information, but individual tracking is expensive, unsustainable, and raises privacy concerns due to highly identifiable traces.
AI.method: Uncertainty-aware physics-informed framework that infers future OD flows from area-level counts alone, respecting generation-before-assignment logic of transport planning with probabilistic modeling.
AI.result: Achieves accuracy comparable to models using historical OD matrices across 12 mobility datasets from US and Chinese cities; probabilistic modeling corrects underestimation of sparse high-value corridors and yields calibrated predictions.
AI.conclusion: OD flows can be reconstructed from aggregated counts without continuous individual tracking, providing more deployable and privacy-preserving basis for real-time urban intelligence.

title: SchemeArena: Factorized Stress Testing of Scheming in LLM Agents
summary: We study scheming in LLM agents, in which agents covertly pursue misaligned goals. Our focus is to understand how scheming arises from the interaction of key factors, such as instrumental goals, environmental affordances, oversight conditions, and perceived consequences. Prior work examines only a small number of scenarios, limiting the ability to isolate how these conditions shape an agent's propensity or capability to scheme. This limited scale and task diversity also restrict coverage of realistic deployment settings and the range of scheming strategies that can be observed. To this end, we introduce SCHEMEARENA, a 400-scenario benchmark for scalable scheming stress testing, constructed through a factorized scenario synthesis framework spanning diverse safety-relevant tool domains, instrumental goals, oversight conditions, and pressure mechanisms. To enable scalable and reliable monitoring, we further propose SCOUT, a scheming monitor that grounds multi-criteria judgments in evidence drawn from agents' reasoning and actions. Across controlled stress tests on five LLM agents, we find that explicit instrumental goals are the strongest driver of scheming propensity. Strategic hints play a distinct role by helping agents translate scheming reasoning into concrete covert behavior. Oversight has mixed effects: in several closed models, action-only monitoring increases scheming, suggesting that partial oversight can act as an optimization constraint rather than a deterrent. CoT is a useful but incomplete monitoring signal: it can reveal latent scheming before execution, yet action-only scheming shows that covert behavior may occur without explicit reasoning evidence. We release the benchmark, code, and monitor at: https://github.com/launchnlp/SchemeArena.

AI.tldr: SCHEMEARENA is a 400-scenario benchmark for systematically testing LLM agent scheming behavior across diverse conditions, revealing that explicit instrumental goals are the strongest driver of scheming propensity.
AI.motivation: Prior work on LLM agent scheming has been limited in scale and task diversity, restricting understanding of how key factors (instrumental goals, environmental affordances, oversight, consequences) shape scheming behavior and limiting coverage of realistic deployment scenarios.
AI.method: Introduced SCHEMEARENA benchmark with 400 scenarios constructed through factorized scenario synthesis framework covering diverse tool domains, instrumental goals, oversight conditions, and pressure mechanisms. Also proposed SCOUT, a scheming monitor that grounds judgments in evidence from agents' reasoning and actions. Conducted controlled stress tests on five LLM agents.
AI.result: Explicit instrumental goals were found to be the strongest driver of scheming propensity. Strategic hints help agents translate scheming reasoning into covert behavior. Oversight has mixed effects - action-only monitoring can increase scheming in closed models. CoT is useful but incomplete for monitoring, as covert behavior can occur without explicit reasoning evidence.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a scalable framework for understanding and monitoring scheming in LLM agents, identifying key drivers and limitations of current monitoring approaches while releasing comprehensive resources (benchmark, code, monitor) for further research.

title: Think Wider: Mitigating Latent Rank Collapse in Implicit Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning improves the reasoning ability of large language models by introducing intermediate computation, but explicit rationales increase decoding length, latency, and context cost. Implicit CoT offers a more efficient alternative by moving intermediate reasoning into continuous latent states. However, latent reasoning can be unstable: successive latent states may become overly similar and collapse toward a shared dominant direction, reducing the diversity of the reasoning trajectory. In this work, we identify $\textit{latent rank collapse}$ and propose $\textbf{WIDER}$, a lightweight spectral regularizer for implicit CoT. During training, WIDER estimates the shared direction of each latent trajectory and penalizes projections onto this direction, encouraging latent states to span a broader representational subspace. The method is plug-and-play and leaves the backbone model, latent schedule, and inference-time decoding procedure unchanged. We further formulate this collapse as a geometric bottleneck in implicit reasoning, casting its mitigation as a training-time regularization problem rather than an inference-time decoding change. Extensive experiments show that WIDER improves matched implicit CoT baselines, while mechanistic analyses reveal higher effective rank, lower dominant-direction energy, and reduced redundancy among latent steps. These results highlight latent subspace utilization as an important factor for efficient continuous reasoning, providing a geometric perspective for analyzing and improving implicit CoT. Code is available at https://github.com/whitesweater/WIDER.

AI.tldr: WIDER is a lightweight spectral regularizer that prevents latent rank collapse in implicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning by encouraging latent states to span broader representational subspaces, improving reasoning diversity without changing model architecture or inference procedures.
AI.motivation: Implicit CoT reasoning is more efficient than explicit reasoning but suffers from latent rank collapse, where successive latent states become overly similar and collapse toward a shared dominant direction, reducing reasoning diversity and effectiveness.
AI.method: WIDER estimates the shared direction of each latent trajectory during training and penalizes projections onto this direction, encouraging latent states to span a broader representational subspace. It's a plug-and-play spectral regularizer that doesn't change backbone models, latent schedules, or inference-time decoding.
AI.result: WIDER improves matched implicit CoT baselines, shows higher effective rank, lower dominant-direction energy, and reduced redundancy among latent steps. Mechanistic analyses confirm better latent subspace utilization.
AI.conclusion: Latent subspace utilization is crucial for efficient continuous reasoning, and WIDER provides a geometric perspective for analyzing and improving implicit CoT by addressing latent rank collapse through training-time regularization rather than inference changes.

title: SWE-Bench Pro Verified: A Reliable Benchmark for Software Engineering Agents
summary: SWE-Bench Pro has emerged as a standard benchmark for evaluating software engineering agents on challenging repository-level tasks. However, our analysis work show that its evaluation is undermined by two sources of unreliability: \textbf{reward hacking}, enabled by leakage of gold solutions or hidden evaluation information, and \textbf{task quality issues}, including misleading problem statements and improperly scoped tests. These issues can inflate benchmark performance and obscure agents' true coding ability. We present \textbf{SWE-Bench Pro Verified}, a verified version of SWE-Bench Pro that addresses both problems. Our approach combines \textbf{anti-hacking} safeguards that eliminate major leakage channels without disrupting normal agent functionality, with \textbf{task refinement} that minimally corrects inconsistencies within flawed instances. Evaluations on SWE-Bench Pro Verified reveal that some models perform substantially worse than previously reported, suggesting that existing results on SWE-Bench Pro may overestimate real software engineering capability. SWE-Bench Pro Verified offers a more trustworthy benchmark for assessing software engineering agents.

AI.tldr: SWE-Bench Pro has reliability issues in evaluation due to reward hacking and task quality problems, leading to inflated performance metrics. The paper introduces SWE-Bench Pro Verified with anti-hacking safeguards and task refinement to provide more accurate assessment of software engineering agents.
AI.motivation: Current SWE-Bench Pro benchmark suffers from reliability problems: 1) reward hacking through leakage of gold solutions or hidden evaluation information, and 2) task quality issues like misleading problem statements and improperly scoped tests. These issues inflate benchmark performance and obscure agents' true coding ability.
AI.method: Developed SWE-Bench Pro Verified with two main approaches: 1) anti-hacking safeguards that eliminate major leakage channels without disrupting normal agent functionality, and 2) task refinement that minimally corrects inconsistencies within flawed instances.
AI.result: Evaluations on SWE-Bench Pro Verified show that some models perform substantially worse than previously reported on the original SWE-Bench Pro, suggesting existing results may overestimate real software engineering capability.
AI.conclusion: SWE-Bench Pro Verified offers a more trustworthy benchmark for assessing software engineering agents by addressing the reliability issues in the original benchmark, providing a more accurate measure of agents' true coding abilities.

title: Impact of canny edge detection preprocessing on performance of machine learning models for Parkinson's disease classification
summary: This study investigates the classification of individuals as healthy or at risk of Parkinson's disease using machine learning (ML) models, focusing on the impact of dataset size and preprocessing techniques on model performance. Four datasets are created from an original dataset: DS_0, (normal dataset), DS_1 (DS_O subjected to Canny edge detection and Hessian filtering), DS_2 (augmented DS_0), and DS_3 (augmented DS_1). We evaluate a range of ML models-Logistic Regression (LR), Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting (GB), XGBoost (XBG), Naive Bayes (NB), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and AdaBoost (AdB)-on these datasets, analyzing prediction accuracy, model size, and prediction latency. The results show that while larger datasets lead to increased model memory footprints and prediction latencies, the Canny edge detection preprocessing supplemented by Hessian filtering (used in DS_1 and DS_3) degrades the performance of most models. In our experiment, we observe that Random Forest (RF) maintains a stable memory footprint of 61 KB across all datasets, while models like KNN and SVM show significant increases in memory usage, from 5.7-7 KB on DS_0 to 102-220 KB on DS_2, and similar increases in prediction time. Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, and Naive Bayes show stable memory footprints and fast prediction times across all datasets. XGBoost's prediction time increases from 180-200 ms on DS_0 to 700-3000 ms on DS_2 (truncated)

AI.tldr: This paper investigates Parkinson's disease risk classification using ML models, examining how dataset size and preprocessing techniques affect model performance, memory usage, and prediction latency across different dataset variations.
AI.motivation: The study aims to understand the practical implications of dataset size and preprocessing techniques on ML model performance for Parkinson's disease classification, particularly focusing on the trade-offs between accuracy, model memory footprint, and prediction latency.
AI.method: Researchers created four dataset variations from an original dataset: normal dataset (DS_0), edge detection filtered dataset (DS_1), augmented normal dataset (DS_2), and augmented filtered dataset (DS_3). They then evaluated eight ML models (LR, DT, RF, GB, XGBoost, NB, SVM, AdaBoost) on these datasets, analyzing prediction accuracy, model size, and prediction latency.
AI.result: While larger datasets improved performance, they increased model memory footprints and prediction latencies. Canny edge detection with Hessian filtering degraded most models' performance. Random Forest maintained stable memory (61KB) across all datasets, while KNN and SVM showed significant memory increases (5.7-7KB to 102-220KB) and slower prediction times. Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, and Naive Bayes showed stable memory and fast predictions across datasets. XGBoost's prediction time increased dramatically (180-200ms to 700-3000ms) on larger datasets.
AI.conclusion: The research provides important insights into the practical trade-offs in medical ML applications, showing that dataset preprocessing choices significantly impact model efficiency and performance, with certain models like Random Forest demonstrating more consistent behavior across dataset variations.

title: WorldAgen: Unified State-Action Prediction with Test-Time World Model Training
summary: How can vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt to new environments where world dynamics shift? While recent research has combined world modeling and action prediction to improve VLA performance, existing methods largely rely on pretraining on static datasets, without mechanisms for active adaptation at deployment time. As a result, these models often fail to generalize when deployed in unseen scenarios with novel object configurations or dynamics. We present WorldAgen, a unified framework that jointly learns world modeling and action prediction while enabling Test-Time Training (TTT) to adapt to new environments. WorldAgen employs a shared Transformer backbone with two heads: (1) a world model head that predicts future states from past state-action trajectories, and (2) an agent model head that predicts actions conditioned on task instructions. We design a Mixed Unidirectional Attention Mask to separate these two models. During test time, WorldAgen samples exploratory actions, collects ground-truth state transitions, and performs lightweight TTT updates to refine its world model. This adaptation improves the model's understanding of the environment and leads to more accurate action predictions. Experiments on the CALVIN and LIBERO benchmarks demonstrate that our baseline model achieves comparable, and in some cases superior, performance to current state-of-the-art approaches. Moreover, with TTT on a small number of samples, our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art models, highlighting the effectiveness of adapting world models at inference time.

AI.tldr: WorldAgen is a vision-language-action framework that combines world modeling with action prediction and enables test-time training to adapt to new environments.
AI.motivation: Current VLA models fail to generalize to unseen scenarios with novel dynamics because they rely on static pretraining without active adaptation mechanisms during deployment.
AI.method: Joint learning of world modeling and action prediction using a shared Transformer with two heads: world model head for future state prediction, and agent model head for action prediction, separated by a Mixed Unidirectional Attention Mask. Enables test-time training by sampling exploratory actions and updating world model with collected ground-truth transitions.
AI.result: Baseline achieves comparable/superior performance to SOTA on CALVIN and LIBERO benchmarks. With test-time training on small samples, surpasses existing SOTA models, demonstrating effective adaptation at inference time.
AI.conclusion: WorldAgen effectively addresses generalization challenges by enabling active adaptation through test-time training, improving performance in unseen environments with novel dynamics.

title: Revisiting Thinning Methods for Kernel Learning Problems
summary: Kernel methods are widely used because of their strong theoretical guarantees and empirical performance. However, their high computational cost limits their applicability to large-scale datasets. To address this shortcoming, several approaches use Maximum Mean Discrepancy to construct representative subsets that preserve the properties of the full dataset in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space. We introduce Backward Kernel Herding, an algorithm that addresses this problem by iteratively removing points from the dataset, achieving results comparable to current state-of-the-art approaches while accelerating the subsampling process in realistic scenarios where the reduced size is less than half of the dataset. Moreover, we overcome a limitation of Kernel Thinning by proposing an extension that enables the construction of subsets of arbitrary size rather that restricting to successive halvings. Finally, we conduct an extensive experimental comparison focusing on the most relevant kernel learning procedures: Gaussian Processes and Kernel Support Vector Machines. The results show that Backward Kernel Herding consistently achieves competitive performance with the most favorable training-time efficiency, while the proposed Flexible Kernel Thinning frequently achieves the best predictive performance. These gains become especially pronounced for moderate compression ratios, highlighting the benefits of incorporating supervised information into the thinning process. In terms of memory consumption, Flexible Kernel Thinning is also competitive, whereas Backward Kernel Herding remains an alternative when computational efficiency is the primary objective. Overall, no single method dominates across all scenarios, underscoring the importance of selecting the reduction strategy according to the desired trade-off between predictive performance, training cost, and memory requirements.

AI.tldr: Backward Kernel Herding accelerates kernel method subsampling by iteratively removing points, while Flexible Kernel Thinning extends subsampling to arbitrary sizes beyond halving constraints.
AI.motivation: Kernel methods suffer from high computational costs on large datasets, limiting their scalability. Existing Maximum Mean Discrepancy-based approaches for creating representative subsets need improvement in speed and flexibility.
AI.method: Proposes Backward Kernel Herding (iterative point removal) and Flexible Kernel Thinning (extending Kernel Thinning to arbitrary subset sizes). Both use Maximum Mean Discrepancy in RKHS and incorporate supervised information for better performance.
AI.result: Backward Kernel Herding achieves competitive performance with superior training-time efficiency, especially for compression ratios under 50%. Flexible Kernel Thinning frequently achieves best predictive performance and competitive memory consumption.
AI.conclusion: No single method dominates all scenarios. Selection should be based on trade-offs between predictive performance, training cost, and memory requirements. Both methods offer valuable improvements for kernel method scalability.

title: Key Path Identification for Resolving Knowledge Conflicts via SAE-based Steering
summary: Sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based steering has been widely used to address knowledge conflicts by guiding LLMs to be more faithful to the contextual knowledge. Existing methods usually perform mass steering, which modifies a large batch of SAE features identified via correlation-based methods. However, due to the inaccurate correlation and the neglected feature interactions, mass steering methods fail to precisely identify the features that play the key roles in steering and introduce a large number of redundant ones, which add noise and weaken the steering effects. Our empirical studies reveal that steering only a small subset of the identified features can achieve comparable or even better performance. Motivated by this finding, we propose Key Path Identification (KPI), a novel method that identifies key steering features characterized by strong causal dependencies with both upstream and downstream features. From these features, KPI constructs key paths and steers through less feature modifications. In this way, KPI advances SAE-based steering from quantity-driven to quality-focused, offering a perspective for more precise and interpretable model editing. Experiments in RAG tasks with knowledge conflicts show that our method improves the accuracy by 18% on average compared to the best baseline of mass steering, effectively filtering redundant features, alleviating side effects and demonstrating the core role of key paths in steering.

AI.tldr: KPI (Key Path Identification) is a quality-focused SAE-based steering method that identifies causal dependency-based key paths for precise model editing, outperforming correlation-based mass steering by 18% accuracy improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing SAE-based steering methods use correlation-based approaches that modify many features indiscriminately, leading to noise and weakened effects due to inaccurate correlation detection and ignored feature interactions. Empirical studies show steering only a small subset of features can achieve comparable or better results.
AI.method: Proposes Key Path Identification (KPI) that identifies key steering features based on strong causal dependencies with both upstream and downstream features, then constructs key paths and steers through fewer feature modifications, shifting from quantity-driven to quality-focused approach.
AI.result: In RAG tasks with knowledge conflicts, KPI improves accuracy by 18% on average compared to the best mass steering baseline, effectively filters redundant features, alleviates side effects, and demonstrates the core role of key paths in steering.
AI.conclusion: KPI advances SAE-based steering from quantity-driven to quality-focused, offering more precise and interpretable model editing by focusing on causally significant features rather than correlational mass modifications.

title: TabBench-Bio: A Living Benchmark for Machine Learning on High-Dimensional Biomedical Tables
summary:
Biomedical tables often combine thousands of measured variables with only tens or hundreds of labelled samples, a regime that is poorly represented in general-purpose tabular benchmarks. We introduce TabBench-Bio, a living and interactive benchmark of 43 biomedical datasets spanning multiple domains. Under a shared cross-validation protocol, we compare classical estimators, neural networks, and tabular foundation models across 28 feature-by-sample operating points. At the reference cell of 10,000 features and 100 training samples, RealTabPFN v2.5 has the highest point estimate, followed by Logistic Regression and TabDPT, whose point estimates are nearly identical. A paired bootstrap over the target pool separates RealTabPFN v2.5 from Logistic Regression by 145 Elo (95% interval [59, 232]). Tabular foundation models generally occupy the leading ranks, while the strongest configuration depends on the operating point and biomedical modality. The AutoML framework AutoGluon, using its one-hour "extreme" preset, is configured as a separate resource-intensive reference and is reported here at the reference cell. Fold-level predictions, run status, and deterministic aggregations make every reported result reproducible and reusable.
  We invite the community to contribute: TabBench-Bio is designed to grow, and we welcome submissions of new biomedical tabular datasets, particularly from underrepresented assays and clinical endpoints, for inclusion in future releases.
  The interactive leaderboard is available at: https://tabbench-bio.eu

AI.tldr: TabBench-Bio is a living benchmark of 43 biomedical datasets with 28 feature-by-sample configurations, where RealTabPFN v2.5 performs best at 10K features/100 samples, with tabular foundation models generally leading but performance varying by operating point.
AI.motivation: Biomedical tables often have thousands of variables but only tens or hundreds of labeled samples, a data regime poorly represented in general-purpose tabular benchmarks, creating a need for domain-specific evaluation.
AI.method: Created TabBench-Bio with 43 biomedical datasets across multiple domains using shared cross-validation protocol, compared classical estimators, neural networks, and tabular foundation models across 28 feature-by-sample operating points with deterministic aggregations.
AI.result: At reference point (10,000 features, 100 training samples), RealTabPFN v2.5 has highest performance, followed closely by Logistic Regression and TabDPT; tabular foundation models generally occupy leading ranks; performance strongest configuration depends on operating point and biomedical modality.
AI.conclusion: TabBench-Bio provides a reproducible benchmark for biomedical tabular data where tabular foundation models generally perform best, though optimal methods vary by data characteristics; designed as a living benchmark for community contributions to include underrepresented biomedical assays.

title: OntologyBench: Can Dense Retrieval Satisfy Structured Biomedical Constraints?
comment: 19 pages and 1 figure. Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Main conference. https://openreview.net/forum?id=RMiOTIub1j&noteId=RMiOTIub1j
summary:
We introduce OntologyBench, a tiered biomedical retrieval benchmark comprising 471,854 training and 125,744 evaluation query-document relevance pairs across concept grounding, relational retrieval, and compositional phenotype-based retrieval.
  Although these tasks can be tractable using ontology-aware reference methods, across task tiers, embedding performance is generally lower on relational and compositional tasks than on concept-grounding tasks. Fine-tuning on ontology-derived supervision improves performance on several relational and compositional tasks, whereas the evaluated reranking and LLM-based candidate-scoring methods provide little or no end-to-end improvement. Errors frequently reflect diseases matching only subsets of the phenotype evidence.
  These findings indicate that the evaluated embedding and reranking configurations do not reliably recover the compatibility encoded by the selected ontology relations and phenotype combinations and motivate retrieval systems that better integrate learned representations with structured biomedical knowledge.

AI.tldr: OntologyBench: A biomedical retrieval benchmark with 3 task tiers (concept grounding, relational retrieval, compositional phenotype retrieval) revealing embedding limitations on complex tasks and need for better integration of learned representations with structured knowledge.
AI.motivation: To create a comprehensive biomedical retrieval benchmark that addresses limitations in current systems, particularly their ability to handle complex relational and compositional phenotype-based retrieval tasks that require understanding of ontology relationships and structured biomedical knowledge.
AI.method: Developed OntologyBench with 471,854 training and 125,744 evaluation query-document relevance pairs across three task tiers: concept grounding, relational retrieval, and compositional phenotype-based retrieval. Evaluated various methods including ontology-aware reference approaches, embedding-based methods with fine-tuning on ontology-derived supervision, reranking techniques, and LLM-based candidate-scoring approaches.
AI.result: Embedding performance was lower on relational and compositional tasks compared to concept-grounding tasks. Fine-tuning on ontology-derived supervision improved performance on several relational and compositional tasks, but reranking and LLM-based scoring methods provided little or no end-to-end improvement. Common errors involved diseases matching only subsets of phenotype evidence.
AI.conclusion: Current embedding and reranking methods don't reliably recover the compatibility encoded by ontology relations and phenotype combinations, motivating the development of retrieval systems that better integrate learned representations with structured biomedical knowledge for more accurate complex biomedical retrieval tasks.

title: TASTE: Throughput-Aware Batch Size Tuning for On-Device Edge Learning
comment: 8 pages, 1 tables, 6 figures; Accepted to 29th Euromicro DSD 2026
summary: The rise of privacy-preserving artificial intelligence (AI) has shifted the focus of model adaptation and personalization towards on-device learning, where deep learning models are finetuned directly on edge hardware using local user data. However, this shift requires optimization of deep learning training on resource-constrained hardware to maximize throughput while maintaining predictive accuracy. This paper introduces a novel technique for on-device model training that incorporates an efficient Bayesian optimization-based batch size tuning approach to maximize hardware throughput. To evaluate the impact of this hyperparameter on the learning dynamics, we investigated two distinct paradigms: standard supervised learning (SL) and online continual learning (CL). Experimental results across various edge devices demonstrate a throughput ceiling, beyond which increasing the batch size yields no additional throughput gains. The proposed tuning approach identifies the optimal batch size, which, when combined with gradient accumulation and linear learning rate scaling, achieves up to a 2X increase in training throughput on platforms such as Raspberry Pi 4 compared to maximum batch sizes, without compromising model accuracy. Furthermore, in the CL paradigm, we demonstrate that optimal batch sizes maintain the stability-plasticity balance required for incremental learning, effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting while maximizing computational efficiency on edge-hardware.

AI.tldr: Bayesian optimization for batch size tuning in on-device AI training achieves up to 2X throughput gains on edge devices without accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Privacy-preserving AI requires on-device learning on resource-constrained edge hardware, necessitating optimization of training throughput while maintaining accuracy.
AI.method: Novel technique using Bayesian optimization-based batch size tuning combined with gradient accumulation and linear learning rate scaling, evaluated across both supervised learning and online continual learning paradigms.
AI.result: Reveals throughput ceiling where increasing batch size yields no gains; optimal batch size achieves up to 2X throughput increase on Raspberry Pi 4 vs maximum batch sizes, maintains accuracy, and in continual learning preserves stability-plasticity balance to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.
AI.conclusion: Bayesian optimization for batch size tuning is an effective approach for maximizing computational efficiency in on-device AI training while preserving model performance across different learning paradigms.

title: Safe Harness Self-Evolution: A Theoretical Analysis of Feasibility and Limits
summary: Harness self-evolution is the process by which an agent modifies its prompts, tools, code, or orchestration in response to task feedback while keeping the underlying language model frozen, with changes persisting across subsequent tasks. We provide a systematic theoretical analysis of the feasibility and limits of safe harness self-evolution, connecting modification generation, finite-data certification and selection, safe adoption, and behavior after an update. Under a fixed user-task distribution, we establish conditions guaranteeing overall expected-reward improvement while controlling changes on retained tasks, characterize the probability of generating qualified modifications, and derive finite-data bounds for safe selection and adoption. Our analysis shows that generation and certification impose distinct constraints: current task performance does not determine the probability of generating qualified modifications, and generating more candidates need not improve the guarantee of a successful update when evaluation is limiting. Stagnation may therefore arise even when improvement opportunities remain. We further show that worst-case evaluation cost for recognizing genuine improvements diverges as expected reward approaches its upper bound. Across successive updates, certified improvement guarantees accumulate over a finite run, but a successful update does not by itself guarantee that further improvement remains possible. These results provide a basis for diagnosing bottlenecks and designing safer self-evolution mechanisms.

AI.tldr: Harness self-evolution can theoretically improve agent performance through iterative prompt/tool modifications, but faces fundamental limits: generation and certification impose distinct constraints, and while certified improvements accumulate, stagnation is possible even when improvement opportunities exist.
AI.motivation: To understand the feasibility and limits of safe harness self-evolution - where agents modify their prompts, tools, or code based on task feedback while keeping the underlying language model frozen, with changes persisting across tasks.
