Across sixteen open-weight language models and four reasoning benchmarks, we show that traces with the same endpoint and similar entropy profiles can exhibit substantially different reasoning dynamics. We further find substantial variation in these dynamics both within and across models and tasks, with different objectives favoring different dynamical profiles. Additionally, we show that training and inference choices systematically reshape these profiles. Our results suggest that answer-distribution trajectories provide a rich framework for analysing and evaluating the dynamics of LLM reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces answer-distribution trajectories to track LLM reasoning dynamics, showing that models with similar endpoint accuracy and entropy can have fundamentally different reasoning processes.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of chain-of-thought reasoning focuses mainly on endpoint accuracy and entropy profiles, which ignore the full reasoning dynamics and don't reveal which competing hypotheses account for uncertainty during the reasoning process.
AI.method: Introduces answer-distribution trajectories, a stochastic-dynamics-inspired representation that tracks the full predictive distribution over answers as reasoning unfolds, enabling characterization of reasoning profiles spanning exploration, revision, motion, and commitment.
AI.result: Across 16 open-weight language models and 4 reasoning benchmarks, the study reveals that traces with same endpoints and similar entropy profiles exhibit substantially different reasoning dynamics, with substantial variation both within and across models/tasks, and different objectives favor different dynamical profiles. Training and inference choices systematically reshape these profiles.
AI.conclusion: Answer-distribution trajectories provide a rich framework for analyzing and evaluating LLM reasoning dynamics, offering insights beyond traditional endpoint accuracy and entropy-based evaluations.

title: Risk-Conditioned Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in settings where rare but severe harmful generations can have significant consequences. Existing Risk-Averse RLHF addresses this issue by optimizing Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR), but it trains policies for fixed risk levels and therefore cannot adjust the desired degree of risk aversion at inference time. In this paper, we propose risk-conditioned RLHF, a framework that trains a single policy that provides a continuous risk-control interface, enabling users to select different degrees of risk aversion without retraining or deploying multiple risk-specific models. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that a single risk-conditioned policy can adapt to different risk levels at inference time, enabling more flexible and risk-aware LLM deployment.

AI.tldr: Proposes risk-conditioned RLHF framework that trains a single LLM policy with adjustable risk aversion control, enabling dynamic risk management without retraining multiple models.
AI.motivation: Current Risk-Averse RLHF optimizes for fixed risk levels using CVaR, requiring separate models for different risk aversion levels, which is inflexible and resource-intensive for deployment where users need to adjust risk aversion dynamically.
AI.method: Risk-conditioned RLHF framework that trains a single policy conditioned on risk levels, providing a continuous interface to control risk aversion. This allows adjusting the degree of risk aversion at inference time without retraining.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that a single risk-conditioned policy can successfully adapt to different risk levels during inference, providing flexible risk-aware LLM deployment capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The proposed risk-conditioned RLHF enables more practical and flexible deployment of risk-aware LLMs by allowing dynamic adjustment of risk aversion levels with a single model, improving over fixed-risk approaches.

title: A Machine Learning Framework for Predicting Restaurant Food Waste to Support Sustainable Food Management
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures. Accepted and presented at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Signal Processing, Information, Communication and Systems (SPICSCON 2026). Accepted for publication in the conference proceedings
summary: Food waste in the restaurant sector poses a substantial challenge to environmental sustainability and economic efficiency. This paper presents an exploratory machine learning framework for estimating daily restaurant food waste quantities from operational and contextual features. A structured dataset was constructed by integrating restaurant demand records, meteorological data and temporal event indicators, yielding 77,980 records across 27 features. Because large-scale ground-truth food waste measurements are not publicly available, the target variable was derived from operationally justified assumptions, with the complete construction formula and controlled stochastic variability disclosed for full reproducibility. Four supervised regression models, namely Linear Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest and Gradient Boosting, were evaluated under a chronological 70-30 train-test split that respects the temporal ordering of restaurant operations, augmented by 5-fold time-series cross-validation. All reported metrics are explicitly scoped to performance against the constructed target and do not imply validation against measured food waste. Ensemble methods consistently outperformed linear baselines. Random Forest attained an MAE of 6.19 kg, RMSE of 8.36 kg and $R^2$ of 0.817 on the realistic feature subset following systematic exclusion of algebraically leakage-prone variables. Feature importance analysis identified menu diversity, operational area and temporal activity patterns as the primary predictive drivers. The full dataset, target construction formula, codebase and experimental configurations are publicly released to support reproducibility and future extension to empirically measured waste data.

AI.tldr: An ML framework for estimating restaurant food waste from operational data using four regression models, with Random Forest achieving best performance and the full methodology made publicly available for reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Food waste in restaurants presents significant environmental and economic challenges, but there's a lack of large-scale ground-truth waste measurements available publicly for direct modeling.
AI.method: Constructed a dataset of 77,980 records with 27 features from restaurant demand, weather, and temporal data. Used derived target variable since real waste measurements weren't available. Evaluated Linear Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting with chronological 70-30 train-test split and 5-fold time-series cross-validation.
AI.result: Random Forest performed best with MAE of 6.19 kg, RMSE of 8.36 kg, and R² of 0.817 after removing leakage-prone variables. Feature analysis identified menu diversity, operational area, and temporal patterns as key predictors.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates ML's potential for food waste estimation when real measurements are unavailable, with ensemble methods outperforming linear models. Full transparency in methodology supports reproducibility and future extension to real waste data.

title: Everything in Moderation: Per-Domain Coverage Optima and Alignment-Resistant Domain Gaps in Multi-Domain Mid-Training
summary: Mid-training, the stage between pre-training and alignment, is where a model's per-domain data composition is typically set by data availability rather than principled design. We ask what that decision buys, and whether a later alignment pass can undo it. In a controlled logical-reasoning setting (Qwen3-8B-Base, with a 4B replication; five semantically rule-disjoint KOR-Bench domains) we train 30 allocations spanning the five-domain simplex, 24 sweep configurations plus six withheld from the fit, at five seeds each. Three findings emerge. First, every domain has an interior coverage optimum: the moderate band ($10\%$-$40\%$) is best for all five domains, and a calibrated permutation test for quadratic interiority gives $P\approx0.010$; the fitted mid-training-only curves, with 8B peaks between $9.9\%$ and $35.1\%$, reproduce for curve shape but not peak location. Second, the gaps survive a fixed-budget alignment pass: compensatory SFT raises 116/120 cells (mean $+4.32\%$) yet bridges $0/240$ pairs at a $5\%$ threshold and $30/240$ at a $10\%$ ratio, an equal-budget uniform control behaves almost identically, and a permutation null would bridge $13.8\pm3.3$ and $77.9\pm8.5$ pairs ($P<0.001$). Third, zero coverage collapses mid-training-only accuracy, though a FineWeb-Edu-only control shows the collapse is commingled with generic drift. An exploratory $θ^*$ allocation attains the largest full-pipeline gain ($+4.36\%$ vs. $+0.80\%$/$+0.64\%$\,pp) but is marginal under Welch test.

AI.tldr: Mid-training data allocation between domains has persistent effects that survive alignment, with optimal performance achieved at moderate (10-40%) domain coverage rather than extremes, and these allocation differences cannot be fully compensated by later alignment.
AI.motivation: Current mid-training (between pre-training and alignment) uses data allocations based on availability rather than principled design. The authors investigate whether these allocation decisions matter and if later alignment can compensate for suboptimal mid-training allocations.
AI.method: Controlled experiments with Qwen3-8B-Base (plus 4B replication) on five rule-disjoint logical reasoning domains (KOR-Bench). Trained 30 different data allocations spanning the five-domain simplex, with 24 configurations for model fitting and 6 withheld, at five random seeds each. Tested both mid-training-only and post-alignment performance.
AI.result: 1) Every domain has an interior optimum: moderate coverage (10-40%) performs best (P≈0.010). 2) Performance gaps survive alignment: SFT improves overall (+4.32% mean) but bridges few performance gaps between allocations (0/240 at 5% threshold). 3) Zero coverage causes accuracy collapse, but this is partly due to generic drift rather than just allocation effects.
AI.conclusion: Mid-training data allocation decisions have lasting effects that alignment cannot fully compensate. Optimal allocations exist at moderate coverage levels, suggesting current allocation practices based on availability rather than design may be suboptimal and these choices persist through the training pipeline.

title: Proactive Context-Forecasted Safety Constraints for Nonstationary Reinforcement Learning
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures. Accepted at the 5th Conference on Lifelong Learning Agents (CoLLAs 2026)
summary:
Ensuring safety in reinforcement learning under nonstationarity requires anticipating changes in risk before they lead to unsafe behavior. Existing approaches typically rely on safety constraints defined at design time or updated reactively during execution, assuming that such constraints remain valid over time. However, in nonstationary environments with evolving contexts and changing driving layouts, these assumptions may fail.
  We propose a framework for proactive safety constraint generation based on context forecasting. The approach infers latent environmental context from observations, predicts its future evolution, and constructs safety constraints adapted to anticipated conditions. This enables the agent to proactively avoid unsafe regions instead of reacting only after safety violations occur.
  We evaluate the method in driving environments with structured context variation. The experiments include a sweep over nonstationarity intensities and additional held-out driving layouts, including highway, intersection, and racetrack scenarios. Results show that proactive constraint generation substantially reduces collisions under both seen and out-of-training nonstationarity intensities and generally remains effective across held-out driving layouts while maintaining usable task performance. These findings suggest that context-based constraint generation is a promising approach for safe reinforcement learning under nonstationarity.

AI.tldr: A proactive safety framework for RL in nonstationary environments that forecasts context changes to generate safety constraints ahead of time, reducing collisions while maintaining task performance.
AI.motivation: Existing safety approaches in reinforcement learning assume static or slowly-changing environments with predefined constraints, which fail in nonstationary environments where driving layouts and contexts evolve over time, requiring proactive rather than reactive safety measures.
AI.method: A framework that infers latent environmental context from observations, predicts its future evolution, and constructs safety constraints adapted to anticipated conditions, enabling proactive avoidance of unsafe regions before violations occur.
AI.result: Proactive constraint generation substantially reduces collisions under both seen and out-of-training nonstationarity intensities, remains effective across different held-out driving layouts (highway, intersection, racetrack), and maintains usable task performance.
AI.conclusion: Context-based constraint generation is a promising approach for safe reinforcement learning under nonstationarity, enabling agents to proactively adapt to evolving environments while maintaining safety and performance.

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Approximate Value Iteration in Self-Play
summary: Combining search with function approximation has driven major advances in game-playing programs, making self-play algorithms more competitive than ever. Still, the computational overhead of the most popular methods, based on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), can be substantial. In this work, we investigate whether simpler methods remain competitive in non-trivial, moderately sized games such as Connect Four, Hex(7x7) and synthetic games. We train a minimal self-play implementation of Approximate Value Iteration (AVI) and use ground-truth oracles for exact evaluation. Contrary to expectations, our results demonstrate the surprising effectiveness of AVI: it learns more accurate value functions than those learned by AlphaZero, while its one-step-lookahead greedy policies remain competitive with MCTS-based policies at substantially lower training and inference costs. Preliminary experiments on Othello and Go(9x9) show that AVI trains stably on larger games and learns effective value functions. These findings suggest that the success of MCTS-based methods may have eclipsed simpler approaches that have become increasingly practical with modern deep-learning tools.

AI.tldr: AVI (Approximate Value Iteration) surprisingly outperforms AlphaZero in learning accurate value functions and matches MCTS performance at much lower computational cost, suggesting simpler methods deserve reconsideration with modern deep learning.
AI.motivation: MCTS-based methods like AlphaZero have driven major advances but come with substantial computational overhead. The authors investigate whether simpler approaches remain competitive in moderately sized games, questioning if the success of complex MCTS methods has overshadowed potentially practical simpler alternatives.
AI.method: The researchers implemented minimal self-play Approximate Value Iteration (AVI) and used ground-truth oracles for exact evaluation. They tested on Connect Four, Hex(7x7), and synthetic games, with preliminary experiments on Othello and Go(9x9). They compared AVI's performance against AlphaZero's learned value functions and MCTS-based policies.
AI.result: AVI learned more accurate value functions than AlphaZero, and its one-step-lookahead greedy policies remained competitive with MCTS-based policies at substantially lower training and inference costs. Preliminary experiments on larger games (Othello and Go 9x9) showed AVI trains stably and learns effective value functions.
AI.conclusion: The success of MCTS-based methods may have eclipsed simpler approaches that are increasingly practical with modern deep-learning tools. AVI demonstrates surprising effectiveness, suggesting simpler methods deserve reconsideration for competitive game AI at lower computational cost.

title: Learning Metamaterial Eigenmodes with Wavelet-Encoded Fourier Neural Operators
summary: Machine learning surrogates based on neural operators have shown broad applicability in solving forward PDE problems. However, eigenvalue problems, in which an eigenparameter and one of several valid eigenmodes must be simultaneously solved, remain difficult because standard operator learning formulations assume a unique input-output map. This work demonstrates that Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs), combined with wavelet-based encodings of PDE inputs, can learn and predict multiple eigenmodes of the elastic wave equation, corresponding to deformation modes of acoustic waves propagating through arbitrary metamaterial geometries. We provide a mechanistic explanation and experimental evidence for why wavelet encodings are well matched to the dual spatial-spectral structure of the FNO, enabling deterministic mode selection on both continuous-valued and binary-valued geometries within a single model, and for why prediction accuracy varies with geometric discontinuities. For metamaterial design, the resulting surrogate accelerates the simulation stage of the design cycle by three orders of magnitude relative to finite element analysis on a consumer-grade CPU, while preserving high fidelity. These results also carry broader implications for designing input encodings in other multi-mode PDE solvers based on spectral neural operators.

AI.tldr: Fourier Neural Operators with wavelet-based encodings can accurately predict multiple eigenmodes of elastic wave equations in metamaterials, accelerating simulations by 1000x compared to finite element analysis.
AI.motivation: Eigenvalue problems in PDEs are challenging for neural operator surrogates because they require simultaneously solving for eigenparameters and eigenmodes, which conflicts with the standard assumption of unique input-output mappings in operator learning.
AI.method: Combines Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) with wavelet-based encodings of PDE inputs to learn and predict multiple eigenmodes of the elastic wave equation for arbitrary metamaterial geometries, enabling deterministic mode selection within a single model.
AI.result: The approach achieves deterministic mode selection on both continuous-valued and binary-valued geometries, with prediction accuracy varying with geometric discontinuities. The surrogate accelerates metamaterial design simulations by three orders of magnitude (1000x) relative to finite element analysis while maintaining high fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Wavelet encodings are well-matched to the dual spatial-spectral structure of FNOs for solving multi-mode eigenvalue problems, with broader implications for designing input encodings in other spectral neural operators for multi-mode PDE solvers.

title: SAEScientist-Bench: Can AI Agents Conduct Autonomous SAE Interpretability Research?
summary: While research on recursive self-improvement (RSI) has predominantly automated model training pipelines, reliable autonomous development demands a missing pillar: post-hoc monitoring and auditing to understand what models learn and ensure safe alignment. Mechanistic interpretability tools are essential to bridge this gap, among which Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) serve as a cornerstone by isolating interpretable features for model inspection and steering. In this paper, we introduce SAEScientist-Bench to evaluate whether AI agents can act as scientists utilizing SAE tools for autonomous mechanistic discovery. Given a target concept, an agent designs contrastive probes and navigates a Gemma Scope dictionary of 131K+ features in Gemma-2-9B-IT to discover the optimal feature, evaluated against curated expert reference features anchored on Neuronpedia across activation rank, concept selectivity on contrastive texts, and causal steering. Across 10 agent configurations and 20 tasks, frontier agents demonstrate genuine discovery capabilities and lead different evaluation dimensions, but remain well behind the expert baseline, approaching expert levels on separating target concepts from contrastive controls while lagging substantially in causal generation steering. Further analysis reveals that although agents can design contrasts to rule out spurious candidates, they frequently misinterpret experimental measurements. These results establish experimental model understanding as a measurable capability for closed-loop autonomous AI R&D. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trae1ounG/SAEScientist.

AI.tldr: SAEScientist-Bench is introduced to evaluate AI agents' ability to autonomously use Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for mechanistic interpretability discovery in language models, showing they can perform some discovery tasks but still lag behind human experts.
AI.motivation: Current recursive self-improvement (RSI) research focuses on automating training pipelines but lacks reliable post-hoc monitoring and auditing. Mechanistic interpretability tools like Sparse Autoencoders are essential for understanding what models learn and ensuring safe alignment, but autonomous AI agents need to be evaluated on their ability to use these tools effectively.
AI.method: Developed SAEScientist-Bench where AI agents act as scientists using SAE tools for autonomous mechanistic discovery. Given a target concept, agents design contrastive probes and navigate a Gemma Scope dictionary of 131K+ features in Gemma-2-9B-IT to discover optimal features. Evaluation compares against expert reference features from Neuronpedia across three dimensions: activation rank, concept selectivity on contrastive texts, and causal steering.
AI.result: Across 10 agent configurations and 20 tasks, frontier agents demonstrate genuine discovery capabilities and lead different evaluation dimensions, but remain well behind expert baselines. Agents approach expert levels on separating target concepts from contrastive controls but lag substantially in causal generation steering. Analysis reveals agents can design contrasts to rule out spurious candidates but frequently misinterpret experimental measurements.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes experimental model understanding as a measurable capability for closed-loop autonomous AI R&D, showing that while AI agents can use mechanistic interpretability tools for discovery tasks, significant gaps remain compared to human experts, particularly in causal understanding and measurement interpretation.

title: Nyström Attention Matches Full Attention for Cross-Sectional Stock Prediction
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures. A short version is under review at the TS-LIMITS workshop, NeurIPS 2026
summary: MASTER's inter-stock multi-head attention -- the module responsible for modeling cross-sectional stock relationships -- accounts for 42.5% of model parameters and 25% of predictive value. We systematically decompose this module and uncover a surprising structure: the learned attention is near-uniform (perplexity 278/300), yet forcing exact uniformity eliminates all cross-sectional discrimination. Spectral analysis resolves this paradox: the deviation from uniformity is low-rank (effective rank ~65, top-10 modes capture 96.5% of energy), explaining why sparse approximations consistently fail while Nystrom low-rank attention (m=32 landmarks) matches full O(N^2) attention at O(mN) cost -- certified equivalent via TOST at both N=300 (5 seeds, Rank IC p=0.003) and N=800 (10 seeds, Rank IC p=0.034). Additional findings include: (i) attention anti-correlates with return similarity (Spearman rho = -0.614; on the industry-labeled subset, -0.645 unconditionally and -0.627 after controlling for industry, beta, and volatility), suggesting complementarity-seeking rather than correlation mining; (ii) all graph-based alternatives degrade performance, with hard masking worse than complete module removal; and (iii) at N ~ 3,500 with adapted architectures, no cross-stock module (GCN, Nystrom, or MASTER-style pipeline) significantly outperforms a per-stock LSTM baseline (n=4 seeds), indicating that the benefits observed at smaller scales do not trivially transfer. These results establish that the inter-stock attention's value resides in a compressible, dynamic, near-global redistribution that rewards low-rank approximation but resists sparsification.

AI.tldr: The inter-stock attention module in MASTER model accounts for significant parameters/predictive value; analysis reveals it's near-uniform but low-rank deviating, enabling efficient Nystrom approximation while resisting sparsification.
AI.motivation: To understand the structure and value of the inter-stock multi-head attention module in MASTER stock prediction models, which accounts for 42.5% of parameters and 25% of predictive value, and to determine whether its complexity can be effectively approximated or simplified.
AI.method: Systematic decomposition and spectral analysis of the attention module, evaluation of uniform vs. learned attention, comparison of sparse vs. low-rank approximations (Nystrom with m=32 landmarks), statistical testing via TOST equivalence tests, correlation analysis with return similarity, and testing alternative graph-based architectures at different scales.
AI.result: Learned attention is near-uniform (perplexity 278/300) but not exactly uniform; low-rank structure (effective rank ~65) enables Nystrom approximation to match full attention at O(mN) cost; attention anti-correlates with return similarity (rho=-0.614); graph-based alternatives degrade performance; benefits don't transfer to very large scales (N~3,500).
AI.conclusion: The inter-stock attention's value comes from compressible, dynamic, near-global redistribution that rewards low-rank approximation (Nystrom) but resists sparsification, suggesting complementarity-seeking behavior rather than correlation mining in stock relationships.

title: MeClear: Cooperative Game-Theoretic Attribution and Risk-Aware Memory Clearance for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents rely on external memory systems to preserve user preferences and task knowledge across extended interactions. Conventional retrieval mechanisms optimize semantic compatibility rather than downstream utility, frequently introducing outdated, misleading, or conflicting evidence into the active context. We present MeClear, a task conditioned memory clearance framework that identifies memories featuring negative downstream utility through cooperative attribution and selectively suppresses them from agent execution. MeClear combines Leave One Out screening with sampled cooperative Shapley attribution to distribute utility across interacting evidence, effectively resolving redundant conflict masking where single removal evaluations fail. Utilizing attribution rankings, MeClear executes a query scoped minimal clearance strategy over a nested filtration, verifying task recovery on the cleared context without permanently altering the persistent memory bank. Comprehensive experimental evaluations across ten long dialogue memory pools demonstrate that MeClear achieves a target recall of 85.9% and an overall task recovery rate of 82.3%, representing a 25.5 percentage point improvement over Leave One Out (LOO) baselines.

AI.tldr: MeClear is a memory clearance framework for LLM agents that identifies and suppresses harmful memories with negative downstream utility using cooperative attribution methods, improving task recovery by 25.5 percentage points over baseline methods.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents using external memory systems often retrieve outdated, misleading, or conflicting evidence because conventional retrieval mechanisms optimize for semantic compatibility rather than downstream utility, introducing harmful information into active context.
AI.method: MeClear uses task-conditioned memory clearance with cooperative attribution (Leave One Out screening + sampled cooperative Shapley attribution) to identify memories with negative utility. It then executes query-scoped minimal clearance over nested filtration, verifying task recovery without permanently altering persistent memory.
AI.result: Experimental evaluations across ten long dialogue memory pools show MeClear achieves 85.9% target recall and 82.3% overall task recovery rate, representing a 25.5 percentage point improvement over Leave One Out baselines.
AI.conclusion: MeClear effectively resolves the problem of harmful memory retrieval in LLM agents by using cooperative attribution to identify and suppress negatively impactful memories, significantly improving downstream task performance compared to conventional methods.

title: Sparse Data Augmentation for Optimization with Provable Guarantees
comment: 32 pages, 1 figure. Published at IEEE CDC 2026
summary: In nonconvex optimization problems arising in geometric machine learning, data augmentation is commonly used to promote invariance by averaging empirical losses over transformations of the data. Computing the fully augmented objective, however, requires access to every element of the transformation group $G$, which may be prohibitively expensive when $G$ is large or accessible only through sampling. We study whether full augmentation can instead be approximated using a small, fixed sample of transformations acquired before optimization and reused thereafter. Under suitable regularity conditions, we show that, with probability at least $1-δ$, gradient descent (GD) on the resulting sparsely augmented objective returns an $\varepsilon$-stationary point of the fully augmented objective using $\mathcal{O}\bigl((\log |G|+\log(1/δ))/\varepsilon^2\bigr)$ group-transformation-oracle queries. By comparison, standard group stochastic gradient descent (group-SGD), which samples a fresh transformation at every iteration, uses $\mathcal{O}(1/\varepsilon^4)$ transformation queries. Therefore, gradient descent with fixed sparse augmentation requires fewer transformation queries than both GD applied to the fully augmented objective and group-SGD. Our proof techniques, which may be of independent interest, establish a uniform approximation of the full group-averaged gradient field by a random group average using spectral properties of group-induced operators and tools from representation theory.

AI.tldr: Gradient descent with fixed sparse augmentation (sampling transformations once before optimization) achieves ε-stationary points of fully augmented objectives with only O(log|G|/ε²) transformation queries, outperforming full augmentation and group-SGD.
AI.motivation: In geometric machine learning, data augmentation promotes invariance but computing fully augmented objectives requires access to all transformations in group G, which can be prohibitively expensive when G is large or accessible only through sampling. The authors want to know if full augmentation can be approximated using a small, fixed sample of transformations acquired before optimization.
AI.method: Instead of sampling fresh transformations at every iteration (group-SGD) or accessing all transformations (full augmentation), the authors propose using gradient descent on a sparsely augmented objective where transformations are sampled once before optimization and reused thereafter. They establish uniform approximation of the full group-averaged gradient field by random group averages using spectral properties of group-induced operators and representation theory tools.
AI.result: With probability at least 1-δ, gradient descent on the sparsely augmented objective returns an ε-stationary point of the fully augmented objective using O((log|G| + log(1/δ))/ε²) group-transformation-oracle queries. This compares favorably to standard group-SGD which uses O(1/ε⁴) transformation queries.
AI.conclusion: Gradient descent with fixed sparse augmentation is provably more efficient than both full augmentation and group-SGD in terms of transformation queries required, providing a practical solution for expensive group operations in nonconvex optimization problems with invariance requirements.

title: A Generalization of Amari's Bayesian Duality
summary: Amari's contributions to information geometry and machine learning are well known. Here, we revisit Amari's work on Bayesian duality which has not received as much attention. We connect Amari's Bayesian duality to a convex duality of Bayes' rule. Using this connection, we present a generalization of Amari's Bayesian duality and discuss its relevance for modern artificial intelligence.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits Amari's Bayesian duality, connects it to convex duality of Bayes' rule, generalizes it, and discusses its relevance for modern AI.
AI.motivation: Amari's contributions to information geometry and machine learning are well-known, but his work on Bayesian duality has not received as much attention. The authors aim to revisit and revitalize this important but overlooked aspect of Amari's work.
AI.method: The authors connect Amari's Bayesian duality to convex duality of Bayes' rule, then use this connection to present a generalization of Amari's Bayesian duality framework.
AI.result: Establishes a connection between Amari's Bayesian duality and convex duality of Bayes' rule, and develops a generalized version of Amari's Bayesian duality framework.
AI.conclusion: The generalized Bayesian duality has relevance for modern artificial intelligence, suggesting applications and insights for contemporary AI research that builds on this previously overlooked aspect of Amari's work.

title: KBBQ: A Predictive Noise Law and the Limits of Spectrum Flattening in FP4 Quantization
summary: We develop a second-order theory of quantization noise in matrix multiplication in which the quantization format is characterized by the variance it assigns to each element. The constant variance profile of integer quantization recovers existing integer-noise theory, while the multiplicative profile of floating-point rounding reduces the data dependence to a scalar, the participation factor $κ$, yielding a closed-form signal-to-noise-ratio law. The resulting functional also admits a closed-form upper bound $κ^{*}$ that no function-preserving linear transform can exceed and that is attained by a recent state-of-the-art method. Building on this analysis, we introduce KBBQ (\textbf{K}appa-\textbf{B}raked \textbf{B}lockwise \textbf{Q}uantization), which parameterizes the extent to which a transform approaches this ceiling. At W4A4, across four base models and two FP4 formats, KBBQ outperforms the prior state of the art without additional deployment-time computation.

AI.tldr: Paper develops second-order quantization noise theory for matrix multiplication, introduces KBBQ method that outperforms SOTA at W4A4 without extra deployment cost
AI.motivation: Need better understanding of quantization noise in matrix multiplication, especially for different quantization formats (integer vs floating-point), to develop more effective quantization methods
AI.method: Develops second-order theory of quantization noise characterized by variance profiles; introduces closed-form signal-to-noise-ratio law using participation factor κ; derives optimal bound κ*; creates KBBQ method parameterizing approach to this bound
AI.result: At W4A4 quantization across four base models and two FP4 formats, KBBQ outperforms prior state-of-the-art without additional deployment-time computation
AI.conclusion: The theoretical framework provides insights into quantization noise limits, and KBBQ demonstrates practical improvement by systematically approaching the theoretical optimal bound

title: ExecCritic: Learn to Test, Test to Improve for Coding Agents
summary: Execution feedback can guide coding agents toward correct repository repairs, but only when the tests capture the behavior requested by the issue. Agent-generated tests can encode incomplete or incorrect behavioral targets; when the same trajectory writes both the patch and the test, their errors can agree and create false confidence. We introduce ExecCritic, combining a test--verify--revise scaffold with a role-specific reinforcement learning recipe for training agents within it. The scaffold separates test construction from source-code repair: a Test agent independently generates repository-native tests, a fail-closed harness qualifies and freezes them, and a Repair agent revises source code from their execution feedback without changing the tests. Both roles use Qwen-3.5-35B-A3B as the backbone and are trained separately. In Learn to Test, the Test agent learns to produce behaviorally valid tests that distinguish correct from incorrect patches. In Test to Improve, the Repair agent learns both direct task resolution and feedback-guided revision. On SWE-bench Verified, test quality determines whether feedback helps: holding the base Repair agent fixed, tests from the base Test agent reduce resolved rate from a no-test baseline of 61.2% to 57.3%, whereas tests from GPT-5.6-sol raise it to 65.3%. Role-specific post-training raises the Qwen Test agent's Base-to-Gold success from 22.2% to 62.2%; composing the two post-trained Qwen agents reaches 72.6%, an 11.4-point gain over the original no-test baseline without stronger-model or Oracle feedback at evaluation time. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/execcritic.

AI.tldr: ExecCritic is a novel framework that separates test generation from code repair using specialized agents, preventing correlated errors between tests and patches while improving repository repair accuracy through reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Current coding agents can produce false confidence when the same agent generates both tests and patches, as their errors can be correlated (e.g., both test and patch may have the same misunderstandings). This creates unreliable execution feedback for repository repairs.
AI.method: ExecCritic uses a test-verify-revise scaffold with role-specific reinforcement learning. It separates test construction from source-code repair: a Test agent generates repository-native tests, a fail-closed harness qualifies/freezes them, and a Repair agent revises source code using test execution feedback without modifying tests. Both roles use Qwen-3.5-35B-A3B backbone and are trained separately with specialized RL objectives.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified: Base Test agent tests reduced resolved rate from 61.2% to 57.3%, while GPT-5.6-sol tests improved to 65.3%. Role-specific post-training boosted Qwen Test agent's Base-to-Gold success from 22.2% to 62.2%. Composed post-trained Qwen agents achieved 72.6% resolution, an 11.4-point gain over baseline without stronger-model or Oracle feedback at evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Separating test generation from code repair with specialized, RL-trained agents significantly improves repository repair accuracy by preventing correlated errors and ensuring higher-quality behavioral targets. Test quality is crucial for effective execution feedback in coding tasks.

title: GPU-Enabled Large-Scale Optimization Using Randomized Linear Algebra
summary: This paper introduces rlaopt, a PyTorch-based package for large-scale optimization and scientific computing using randomized numerical linear algebra (RandNLA). Despite substantial progress in RandNLA-based algorithms, few implementations combine GPU acceleration with a simple interface for specifying optimization problems. rlaopt addresses this gap by providing GPU-enabled solvers for positive-definite linear systems and convex empirical risk minimization with constraints and regularizers. These solvers use RandNLA to accelerate conjugate gradient (NystromPCG), operator splitting (NysADMM), and stochastic gradient methods (SAPPHIRE). Moreover, rlaopt includes a modeling language that lets users specify problems using natural mathematical syntax. rlaopt automatically checks compatibility with the selected solver and performs the required problem decomposition. The solvers also support differentiation through their iterations, enabling applications such as hyperparameter tuning. Experiments on ridge regression, bounded multinomial logistic regression, and bounded elastic net identify when randomized preconditioning improves performance and demonstrate substantial speedups from GPU execution. The package is open-source under an Apache license, with source code at https://github.com/udellgroup/rlaopt and version 0.1.0 available on PyPI.

AI.tldr: rlaopt is a PyTorch-based package for GPU-accelerated large-scale optimization using randomized numerical linear algebra, featuring solvers for linear systems and convex empirical risk minimization with constraints and regularizers, automatic problem decomposition, and differentiation support.
AI.motivation: Despite substantial progress in RandNLA-based algorithms, few implementations combine GPU acceleration with simple interfaces for specifying optimization problems. There's a gap in available tools that provide both computational efficiency and user-friendly problem specification.
AI.method: rlaopt provides GPU-enabled solvers using RandNLA techniques: NystromPCG for conjugate gradient, NysADMM for operator splitting, and SAPPHIRE for stochastic gradient methods. It includes a modeling language for natural mathematical syntax problem specification, automatic compatibility checking, and problem decomposition. The solvers support differentiation through iterations.
AI.result: Experiments on ridge regression, bounded multinomial logistic regression, and bounded elastic net show when randomized preconditioning improves performance and demonstrate substantial speedups from GPU execution. The package successfully addresses the identified gap with effective GPU acceleration and intuitive interface.
AI.conclusion: rlaopt fills an important gap by providing GPU-accelerated RandNLA optimization tools with a user-friendly interface, supporting differentiation for applications like hyperparameter tuning. The open-source package enables accessible large-scale scientific computing with randomized numerical methods.

title: Co-Evolving Harnesses and Models: On-Policy Correction Helps Weaker Models Catch Up Where Imitation Fails
summary: Agent harnesses (the system prompt, tool set, execution hooks, and context-management scaffolding around a model) are a critical determinant of agentic task success. Automated harness evolution can enable smaller models to perform well on domain-specific tasks at a fraction of frontier-model cost. Since both the harness and model weights shape behavior, we ask how harness evolution and lightweight fine-tuning should be combined. Across seven enterprise agent tasks, we first evolve a harness with the weaker model, then find that a stronger expert often uses it more effectively, suggesting expert supervision could close the remaining gap. However, training the weaker model on the expert's complete trajectories under the evolved harness backfires: performance regresses on all seven tasks by 4 to 30 points across Qwen3-Coder and Gemma 4, even though the same procedure helps under the unevolved harness. Our analysis shows that imitation transfers knowledge and increases scaffold usage, but disrupts model-harness fit: the weaker model adopts the expert's planning strategy without the competence to execute it and no longer matches the harness evolved around its native planning style. We therefore develop an on-policy expert-correction pipeline, automated by a meta-level MLE agent, that localizes the failing turn in the weaker model's own rollout and asks the expert to rewrite only that turn. This preserves the model's planning style and combines the gains of harness evolution and model adaptation. Our results identify and resolve a source of contention between harness and weight updates, yielding a compatibility-preserving recipe for economical co-evolution on domain-specific enterprise tasks.

AI.tldr: Harness evolution and lightweight fine-tuning can conflict when combined; on-policy expert-correction preserves model-harness compatibility for better domain-specific performance.
AI.motivation: Agent harnesses (system prompts, tools, execution hooks, context scaffolding) critically determine agentic task success, and automated harness evolution enables smaller models to perform domain-specific tasks at lower cost. Since both harness and model weights shape behavior, understanding how to combine harness evolution with lightweight fine-tuning is needed.
AI.method: 1) Evolve harness using weaker model, 2) Test stronger expert using evolved harness, 3) Analyze imitation training failures, 4) Develop on-policy expert-correction pipeline automated by meta-level MLE agent that localizes failing turns in weaker model's rollout and asks expert to rewrite only that turn.
AI.result: Training weaker model on expert's complete trajectories under evolved harness backfired: performance regressed 4-30 points across Qwen3-Coder and Gemma 4 on all seven enterprise tasks. Analysis showed imitation transfers knowledge but disrupts model-harness fit. The on-policy expert-correction pipeline preserved model's planning style and combined gains of harness evolution with model adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Identified and resolved contention between harness and weight updates, yielding compatibility-preserving recipe for economical co-evolution on domain-specific enterprise tasks. Harness evolution should be complemented by expert supervision that respects the model's native planning style.

title: Topology-induced Operators Reveal Complementary Graph Representations without Training
summary: Graph representation learning has largely focused on designing increasingly sophisticated models to transform graph topology into vector representations, or embeddings. However, the extent to which embedding quality depends on model learning, rather than on the underlying topological transformations, remains unclear. Here, we show that informative embeddings can be derived without complicated model design and gradient-based training. Propagating random features through implicit hierarchical structures induced by random walks and anonymous walks yields embeddings that capture node proximity and structural role, respectively. These two training-free embeddings preserve complementary aspects of graph organization and perform competitively with classic and recent methods across various node-, edge-, and graph-level tasks. They often require substantially less computation, resulting in a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. Combining the two types of embeddings further improves inference quality of some tasks compared with using either embedding type alone. Our results suggest that informative graph embeddings can arise from carefully chosen topological transformations before any learning operation is applied.

AI.tldr: Training-free graph embeddings using random feature propagation through random walks and anonymous walks capture node proximity and structural roles, achieving competitive performance with much lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether graph embedding quality depends primarily on sophisticated model learning or underlying topological transformations, and to explore if informative embeddings can be derived without complex model design and gradient-based training.
AI.method: Propagating random features through implicit hierarchical structures induced by random walks (for node proximity) and anonymous walks (for structural roles). Both approaches are training-free and don't require gradient-based optimization.
AI.result: The training-free embeddings preserve complementary aspects of graph organization and perform competitively with classic and recent methods across node-, edge-, and graph-level tasks. They require substantially less computation, offering favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. Combining both embedding types further improves inference quality for some tasks.
AI.conclusion: Informative graph embeddings can emerge from carefully chosen topological transformations before any learning operation is applied, suggesting that embedding quality may depend more on underlying graph structure transformations than on sophisticated model learning.

title: A Data-Driven Framework for Identifying and Prioritizing RPA Opportunities in Healthcare Processes
summary: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) is widely used to reduce administrative burden in United States hospitals, yet an estimated 30-50% of RPA initiatives underperform because processes are selected informally, without a repeatable method to catalogue candidates, prioritize them, match each to an automation tier -- a Python bot, an open-source orchestrator such as n8n, or an enterprise platform such as UiPath -- and forecast financial return before committing resources. We propose a four-module, data-driven framework unifying these decisions: a Process Taxonomy of twenty recurring hospital processes across five value streams; a Prioritization module deriving an Automation Suitability Index from an Analytic Hierarchy Process matrix with an explicit consistency check; a Tool-Tier Selection module recommending the least-cost technology sufficient for a process complexity, integration, and compliance profile; and a Return-on-Investment module quantifying labor savings, error-cost avoidance, payback, and net present value. Applied to a synthetic portfolio spanning all twenty processes, plus a reference data-flow architecture linking it to hospital EHR/payer/ERP systems: 12 of 20 clear the prioritization threshold; the ranking is robust to +/-20% weight perturbation (Spearman correlation 0.83, top-5 set preserved 97.7%, 2,000 Monte Carlo trials); an Automation Risk Index flags four qualifying processes as Critical risk; a budget-constrained portfolio optimization shows diminishing marginal NPV as spend scales from $400K to $1.03M; and a second Monte Carlo analysis shows portfolio NPV stays positive at its 5th percentile. The framework is a conceptual synthesis of the literature rather than an instrument calibrated on primary hospital data; we discuss HIPAA governance and a research agenda for empirical validation. A supplementary Python implementation accompanies the paper.

AI.tldr: A data-driven framework for selecting, prioritizing, and implementing RPA in hospitals through four modules that guide automation decisions and forecast financial returns.
AI.motivation: 30-50% of RPA initiatives in US hospitals underperform due to informal process selection without systematic methods for cataloging, prioritizing, matching automation tiers, or forecasting ROI before committing resources.
AI.method: Four-module data-driven framework: 1) Process Taxonomy of 20 recurring hospital processes across 5 value streams, 2) Prioritization module using Analytic Hierarchy Process with Automation Suitability Index, 3) Tool-Tier Selection module matching automation technology to process requirements, 4) ROI module quantifying savings, error avoidance, payback, and NPV. Tested on synthetic portfolio with Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.result: 12 of 20 processes cleared prioritization threshold; ranking robust to weight perturbations (Spearman 0.83); identified 4 processes as Critical risk via Automation Risk Index; portfolio optimization showed diminishing marginal NPV; portfolio remained positive at 5th percentile in Monte Carlo analysis.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides systematic approach to hospital RPA decisions, but is conceptual synthesis needing empirical validation. Includes HIPAA governance discussion and research agenda for real-world testing. Python implementation provided.

title: Geodesic-informed Generative Diffusion Model For Topology-preserved Image Video Generation
summary: Generative diffusion models have emerged as a class of powerful techniques for various imaging applications, including but not limited to synthesis, reconstruction, and segmentation. Despite their success, current generative models pose two key limitations. First, they primarily rely on image intensity and texture information, with limited attention to underlying object geometry. As a result, they do not guarantee geometric or topological consistency during the generation process, which is a crucial requirement for high-stakes domains such as computational anatomy, biology, and robotics, where preserving object structure is critical. Second, existing models fail to explicitly learn or represent shape changes in the generative process. Such deformation dynamics remain occluded within network parameters; hence leaving the transformation process uninterpretable and physically uninformed. To address these challenges, we introduce IGG (Image Generation informed by Geodesic dynamics), a novel framework that integrates topology-preserving geodesic principles into the diffusion-based generative process. In contrast to conventional methods that operate in image intensity space, IGG learns and synthesizes diverse samples within geodesic deformation spaces, where geometric object changes are learned as smooth and invertible smooth mappings from a given template/source image. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/nellie689/IGG.

AI.tldr: IGG integrates geodesic principles into diffusion models to ensure topological consistency and interpretable shape deformation during image generation.
AI.motivation: Current generative diffusion models rely primarily on image intensity/texture without attention to underlying geometry, failing to guarantee geometric or topological consistency. They also don't explicitly learn or represent shape changes, leaving deformation dynamics uninterpretable and physically uninformed - a critical issue for domains like computational anatomy, biology, and robotics where preserving object structure is essential.
AI.method: IGG (Image Generation informed by Geodesic dynamics) integrates topology-preserving geodesic principles into diffusion-based generative processes. Instead of operating in image intensity space, it learns and synthesizes samples within geodesic deformation spaces, where geometric object changes are learned as smooth and invertible smooth mappings from a given template/source image.
AI.result: The framework enables generation of diverse samples while maintaining geometric consistency and providing interpretable deformation dynamics through geodesic principles, addressing the limitations of conventional diffusion models regarding topological preservation and shape representation.
AI.conclusion: IGG represents a significant advancement in generative modeling by incorporating geometric constraints and interpretable deformation dynamics through geodesic principles, making it particularly suitable for high-stakes applications requiring topological consistency and physically-informed shape transformations.

title: SIM: Subspace Interaction-based Method for Token-Level Text Anomaly Detection
summary: Token-level text anomaly detection, as an emerging trend of text anomaly detection, moves beyond coarse-grained document-level detection by localizing anomalous tokens within text. By providing fine-grained abnormality prediction, token-level text anomaly detection plays a critical role in various real-world applications, such as spam filtering and fake news detection. However, existing methods still rely on the global distance calculation for scoring, during which the local anomaly signals are severely diluted by numerous redundant normal feature dimensions. Moreover, pre-trained language models used in these methods inevitably smooth out surface anomalies, further limiting their effectiveness in token-level anomaly detection. To address these limitations, we propose a Subspace Interaction-based Method (SIM for short) for token-level text anomaly detection. To prevent local signal dilution, SIM adopts a subspace interaction-based anomaly detector, which decouples high-dimensional token embeddings into multiple low-dimensional ones, amplifying localized anomaly signals hidden within specific dimensions. To counteract the over-smoothing effect, we design a hard pseudo-anomaly generation module to construct pseudo-anomalous tokens, simulating the subtle anomalies obscured by semantic smoothing. Also, a probabilistic boundary loss is developed to standardize anomaly scores into statistical distances, effectively enforcing anomalous instances to deviate significantly from the normal distribution center. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of SIM and demonstrate its remarkable efficiency, robustness, and interpretability. The source code is available at: https://github.com/yankehan/SIM-TAD.

AI.tldr: SIM is a token-level text anomaly detection method that uses subspace interaction to amplify local anomaly signals, generates hard pseudo-anomalies to counter semantic smoothing, and employs probabilistic boundary loss for better separation of anomalous from normal instances.
AI.motivation: Existing token-level text anomaly detection methods have two major limitations: 1) they use global distance calculations that dilute local anomaly signals among many normal dimensions, and 2) pre-trained language models smooth out surface anomalies, making subtle anomalies harder to detect despite the need for fine-grained anomaly localization in applications like spam filtering and fake news detection.
AI.method: The Subspace Interaction-based Method (SIM) consists of three key components: 1) a subspace interaction-based anomaly detector that decouples high-dimensional token embeddings into multiple low-dimensional subspaces to amplify localized anomaly signals, 2) a hard pseudo-anomaly generation module that creates simulated anomalous tokens to counteract the over-smoothing effect of language models, and 3) a probabilistic boundary loss that standardizes anomaly scores into statistical distances to enforce clear separation between normal and anomalous instances.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that SIM is effective, remarkably efficient, robust, and interpretable. The method shows significant improvements over existing approaches in token-level anomaly detection tasks.
AI.conclusion: SIM successfully addresses the limitations of existing token-level text anomaly detection methods by amplifying local anomaly signals through subspace decomposition and counteracting semantic smoothing through pseudo-anomaly generation, providing a more effective solution for fine-grained text anomaly detection in real-world applications.

title: Convergence issues in Relational Concept Analysis based on AOC-posets
summary: Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) is an approach for conceptual classification building and rule discovery from a binary table describing a set of objects by a set of attributes. Extensions have been proposed to deal with non-binary and more complex data, such as Relational Concept Analysis (RCA) for multi-relational data. RCA aims to highlight groups of objects characterized by their relationships with other groups of objects. The richer and more complex nature of the underlying data allows RCA to produce richer results than FCA, at the expense of higher computational and interpretive complexity. The most commonly used conceptual classification structure in FCA is the concept lattice. However, in many applications, concept lattice substructures, such as AOC-posets, are preferred over the full lattice, either to mitigate combinatorial blow-up or to focus on the most informative parts of the structure. Indeed, in an AOC-poset, only concepts introducing an object or an attribute are represented, which makes AOC-posets smaller and easier to compute and use than concept lattices. Although RCA was originally defined on concept lattices, it can also be instantiated on AOC-posets. RCA is iterative and its convergence is guaranteed in the lattice-based setting, but this guarantee is lost when using AOC-posets. In this paper, we investigate this loss of convergence in detail. We show why convergence is no longer guaranteed in the general case, identify conditions under which it can still be ensured, and discuss how a dataset can be transformed to recover convergence. We also propose a convergent variant of the process, which preserves the AOC-poset structure: relational attributes, once created, are never removed, which guarantees convergence at the price of attributes that may refer to concepts absent from the final structures.

AI.tldr: RCA on AOC-posets loses convergence guarantees; this paper analyzes why, identifies conditions for convergence, proposes dataset transformations, and introduces a convergent variant.
AI.motivation: While RCA produces richer results from multi-relational data than FCA, it faces computational complexity. AOC-posets offer smaller, more manageable structures than full concept lattices, but RCA's convergence guarantee is lost when applied to AOC-posets instead of lattices.
AI.method: Investigates why convergence is lost in RCA on AOC-posets, identifies conditions that can ensure convergence, discusses dataset transformations to recover convergence, and proposes a new convergent variant of the process that preserves AOC-poset structure by never removing relational attributes once created.
AI.result: Shows why general convergence is not guaranteed with AOC-posets, identifies specific conditions under which convergence can be ensured, provides methods to transform datasets to achieve convergence, and demonstrates a convergent variant of RCA that maintains AOC-poset structure at the cost of potentially retaining references to absent concepts.
AI.conclusion: While RCA on AOC-posets loses the convergence guarantee of lattice-based RCA, this paper provides both theoretical understanding and practical solutions - identifying convergence conditions, transformation methods, and proposing a convergent variant - making RCA more applicable to AOC-posets while preserving their computational advantages.

title: CUNO: Curriculum and Preference Optimization for Stable Graph Unlearning under Mass Deletion
summary: Graph unlearning removes the influence of designated training data from a trained graph model without retraining from scratch. However, existing methods suffer a sharp drop in model utility under large deletion ratios (mass deletion), a phenomenon we refer to as catastrophic unlearning. We find that a key cause is the uniform treatment of all deleted samples, which is particularly damaging in graph learning: structural dependencies cause different nodes to play vastly different roles in the learned model, yet existing methods apply the same forgetting operation to the entire forget set. Based on this insight, we propose CUNO, a curriculum-based graph unlearning framework that removes the forget set progressively, ordering samples by their estimated unlearning difficulty across multiple stages. CUNO further employs a distribution-level negative preference optimization (NPO) objective at each curriculum stage that steers the model away from its original behavior on the current forget subset while preserving retained performance. Our theoretical analysis shows that the curriculum design is most beneficial when the forget set spans a wide range of unlearning difficulty, a condition naturally satisfied under mass deletion. Comprehensive experiments confirm that CUNO consistently mitigates catastrophic unlearning: at 20% deletion, it retains 74% of the original utility compared to 26-53% for existing methods, and maintains more than half the original utility even at 50% deletion. Our code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/cuno-D4FF.

AI.tldr: CUNO introduces a curriculum-based graph unlearning framework that progressively removes training data based on estimated unlearning difficulty to mitigate catastrophic unlearning under mass deletion scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing graph unlearning methods suffer from catastrophic unlearning (sharp utility drop) under large deletion ratios due to uniform treatment of all deleted samples, ignoring that different nodes play vastly different roles in graph models due to structural dependencies.
AI.method: CUNO employs a curriculum-based framework that removes forget sets progressively, ordering samples by estimated unlearning difficulty across multiple stages, and uses distribution-level negative preference optimization (NPO) at each stage to steer the model away from original behavior on current forget subsets while preserving retained performance.
AI.result: At 20% deletion, CUNO retains 74% of original utility compared to 26-53% for existing methods, and maintains more than half original utility even at 50% deletion, consistently mitigating catastrophic unlearning across comprehensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: The curriculum design is most beneficial when forget sets span wide ranges of unlearning difficulty, a condition naturally satisfied under mass deletion, making CUNO an effective solution for catastrophic unlearning in graph models.

title: Neural Symbollic Regression Using Deep Learning and Sparse Modelling
comment: 11 pages, 5 tables, 5 figures, contains detailed mathematics behind the algorithm
summary: Symbolic Regression (SR) seeks to find succinct mathematical expressions that represent the fundamental relationships within data, providing interpretability and scientific understanding that exceeds that of black-box models. Nevertheless, traditional methods like Genetic Programming face challenges with scalability and are highly sensitive to noise, while sparse regression techniques such as SINDy rely significantly on predetermined feature libraries. In this work, we present a Neural Symbolic Regression (NSR) framework that treats neural networks as functional preconditioners for symbolic discovery. Our approach uses a decoupled pipeline: a neural network first learns a smooth, noise-robust approximation of the target function in an interaction- aware nonlinear feature space. LASSO is then applied to extract sparse, interpretable closed-form expressions. To improve predictive accuracy and symbolic fidelity by integrating distributed hyperparameter optimization with Ray Tune and ASHA scheduling. Experiments on the Nguyen benchmark suite show that our approach consistently outperforms SINDy and non-tuned neural baselines in RMSE, noise robustness, and out-of-distribution generalization. Ablation studies confirm the significance of feature interactions, neural depth, and tuning strategies. In general, this study presents a scalable and understandable neural-symbolic framework, creating a solid link between neural approximation and the discovery of sparse equations for scientific machine learning.

AI.tldr: A neural symbolic regression framework that uses neural networks as functional preconditioners to learn smooth approximations, then applies LASSO to extract interpretable symbolic expressions, outperforming traditional methods in accuracy and robustness.
AI.motivation: Traditional symbolic regression methods face challenges: Genetic Programming struggles with scalability and noise sensitivity, while sparse regression techniques like SINDy depend heavily on predetermined feature libraries, limiting their flexibility and effectiveness.
AI.method: The NSR framework uses a decoupled pipeline: 1) a neural network learns smooth, noise-robust approximations in an interaction-aware nonlinear feature space, 2) LASSO extracts sparse, interpretable closed-form expressions from these features, with distributed hyperparameter optimization using Ray Tune and ASHA scheduling for improved accuracy.
AI.result: On the Nguyen benchmark suite, the approach consistently outperforms SINDy and non-tuned neural baselines in RMSE, noise robustness, and out-of-distribution generalization. Ablation studies confirm the importance of feature interactions, neural depth, and tuning strategies.
AI.conclusion: The study presents a scalable and interpretable neural-symbolic framework that bridges neural approximation with sparse equation discovery, creating a solid foundation for scientific machine learning applications that require both accuracy and interpretability.

title: Revisiting Spectral Representations in Generative Diffusion Models
summary: Diffusion models have shown remarkable performance on diverse generation tasks. Recent work finds that imposing representation alignment on the hidden states of diffusion networks can both facilitate training convergence and enhance sampling quality, yet the mechanism driving this synergy remains insufficiently understood. In this paper, we investigate the connection between self-supervised spectral representation learning and diffusion generative models through a shared perspective on perturbation kernels. On the diffusion side, samples (e.g., images, videos) are produced by reversing a stochastic noise-injection process specified by Gaussian kernels; on the spectral representation side, spectral embeddings emerge from contrasting positive and negative relations induced by random perturbation kernels. Motivated by this, we propose a self-supervised spectral representation alignment method to facilitate diffusion model training. In addition, we clarify how joint spectral learning can benefit diffusion training from a geometric perspective. Furthermore, we find that the optimization of the spectral alignment objective is in an equivalent form of diffusion score distillation in the representation space. Building on these findings, we integrate a spectral regularizer into diffusion training objectives to improve the performance of diffusion models on multiple datasets. Experiments across images and 3D point clouds show consistent gains in generation quality. Code is released at https://github.com/yuehaowang/spectral-reg-diffusion.

AI.tldr: Spectral representation alignment improves diffusion models by revealing connections between self-supervised spectral learning and diffusion processes through shared perturbation kernel perspectives.
AI.motivation: Recent work shows representation alignment improves diffusion training but the mechanism is not well understood. The authors identify that both diffusion models (using Gaussian noise kernels) and spectral representation learning (using perturbation kernels) share a common mathematical foundation through perturbation kernels, suggesting potential synergy.
AI.method: Propose self-supervised spectral representation alignment method for diffusion training. Show optimization of spectral alignment is equivalent to diffusion score distillation in representation space. Integrate spectral regularizer into diffusion training objectives to improve performance.
AI.result: Experiments across images and 3D point clouds show consistent gains in generation quality, demonstrating improved diffusion model performance on multiple datasets.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified perspective connecting spectral representation learning and diffusion models through perturbation kernels, and shows that spectral alignment regularization can effectively improve diffusion model training and generation quality across different data modalities.

title: TC-Next: Zero-Shot Multimodal Cyclone Forecasting
summary: We present TropicalCycloneNext (TC-Next), a multimodal deep learning model that forecasts tropical cyclone track and intensity at $6$-$24$ h leads by leveraging a foundation model's forecast fields of atmospheric kinematic and thermodynamic fields and GridSat infrared satellite imagery. Trained only on GraphCast forecasts over the Western Pacific (WP), yet reliant only on generic atmospheric variables, TC-Next on GraphCast lowers track error by $15$-$44\%$ and intensity error by a factor of $3$-$6$ relative to a conventional, rule-based tracker, TempestExtremes; applied without retraining to the forecast fields of Pangu-Weather and IFS HRES, it stays ahead of TempestExtremes on both. Applied zero-shot to the generic weather fields of WeatherNext Cyclones on the 2025 WP season, TC-Next attains lower intensity error at every lead time, and lower or comparable track error, compared to that model's specialized direct tracker in a deterministic comparison. Our ablation studies show that our multimodal model is able to utilize the additional modality to improve performance in tracking errors at every lead time and in intensity prediction at longer lead times.

AI.tldr: TC-Next is a multimodal deep learning model that improves tropical cyclone track and intensity forecasting at 6-24 hour leads by combining atmospheric forecast fields with satellite imagery.
AI.motivation: Current tropical cyclone forecasting methods using rule-based trackers like TempestExtremes have limitations in accuracy. There's a need for more accurate track and intensity predictions, especially at short to medium ranges (6-24 hours), to improve disaster preparedness and response.
AI.method: The authors developed TC-Next, a multimodal deep learning model that leverages both atmospheric forecast fields (kinematic and thermodynamic variables from foundation weather models like GraphCast) and GridSat infrared satellite imagery. The model is trained on Western Pacific data but designed to work with generic atmospheric variables for transferability.
AI.result: TC-Next achieves significant improvements: 15-44% lower track error and 3-6 times lower intensity error compared to TempestExtremes when using GraphCast forecasts. It maintains superiority when applied to Pangu-Weather and IFS HRES forecasts without retraining. In zero-shot testing on WeatherNext Cyclones for 2025 WP season, it outperforms specialized direct trackers in intensity prediction and matches or exceeds track accuracy. Ablation studies confirm the multimodal approach improves tracking and long-lead intensity prediction.
AI.conclusion: TC-Next demonstrates that multimodal deep learning combining atmospheric forecast fields with satellite imagery can significantly improve tropical cyclone forecasting accuracy. The model shows strong generalization capabilities across different weather forecasting systems and maintains performance without retraining, offering a promising approach for operational tropical cyclone prediction.

title: Synergistic Fusion of Topological Structure and Temporal Semantics of Mobility for Urban Region Embedding
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
summary: Urban region embeddings have shown promising results in diverse urban sensing tasks such as crime, income, and service-call prediction. Recent methods improve representation quality by integrating mobility data with auxiliary modalities, using cross-view attention or contrastive objectives to align heterogeneous features into a unified region representation. However, leveraging the temporal dynamics of human mobility remains under-explored. Regional inflow and outflow fluctuate throughout the day, and inter-region connections emerge, persist, and dissolve over time. Moreover, prevailing fusion strategies combine views additively and miss the joint signal that emerges only when views co-occur. To address these gaps, we propose Mobility Stream-Structure Synergy (MoSS), which derives complementary views from mobility data: a Sequence view that preserves each region's hourly inflow/outflow profile, and a Structure view based on zigzag persistence diagrams that capture how regional connectivity emerges, persists, and dissolves over time. A synergy module then extracts emergent representations from the co-occurrence of these views through multi-degree interactions, explicitly capturing higher-order signal across views. Extensive experiments on New York City and Chicago show that MoSS achieves state-of-the-art performance across three downstream tasks using mobility data alone, outperforming baselines that rely on auxiliary modalities.

AI.tldr: MoSS is a novel urban region embedding method that captures temporal mobility dynamics through sequence and structure views, using a synergy module for higher-order cross-view interactions to achieve state-of-the-art performance without auxiliary data.
AI.motivation: Current urban region embedding methods inadequately leverage temporal dynamics of human mobility, treating inflow/outflow as static and missing how inter-region connections evolve over time. Additionally, existing fusion strategies combine views additively and fail to capture joint signals that only emerge when views co-occur.
AI.method: MoSS extracts two complementary views from mobility data: 1) Sequence view capturing each region's hourly inflow/outflow profiles, and 2) Structure view based on zigzag persistence diagrams that capture how regional connectivity emerges, persists, and dissolves over time. A synergy module then extracts emergent representations through multi-degree interactions between these views.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on New York City and Chicago show MoSS achieves state-of-the-art performance across three downstream urban sensing tasks using only mobility data, outperforming baselines that rely on auxiliary modalities.
AI.conclusion: MoSS demonstrates that effectively capturing temporal mobility dynamics through sequence-structure synergy enables superior urban region representations without needing auxiliary data, advancing the field of mobility-aware urban sensing.

title: ProToMEx: Rapid, Interpretable Explanations via Structured Representations
summary: Existing post-hoc explainers for machine learning classifiers primarily focus on feature attribution, assigning importance scores to individual features. While valuable, this approach struggles to articulate the complex, combinatorial patterns that often drive a model's decision-making process. To overcome this limitation, we introduce ProToMEx, a new paradigm for explainability that leverages Probabilistic Topic Models (PTMs). Our model-agnostic framework learns latent ''topics'' that represent distinct, high-level reasons for a classification, moving beyond simple feature importance to reveal underlying semantic structures. ProToMEx naturally provides both global explanations of a model's overall behaviour and local explanations that can disentangle multiple co-existing reasons for a specific prediction. We demonstrate empirically that ProToMEx not only produces explanations of comparable fidelity to popular methods like SHAP and LIME but also drastically reduces the amortised computational cost of generating local explanations, making it highly suitable for real-time applications. Specifically, we show that ProToMEx is ~30-40x faster than SHAP and LIME over standardised tabular datasets and synthetic datasets.

AI.tldr: ProToMEx introduces a new explainability paradigm using Probabilistic Topic Models to reveal high-level semantic reasons for classifications, offering faster and more interpretable explanations than traditional feature attribution methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional post-hoc explainers focus on feature attribution but struggle to articulate complex combinatorial patterns that drive model decisions, limiting interpretability and understanding of underlying semantic structures.
