AI.conclusion: OPL demonstrates that architectural and representation-learning inductive biases can achieve competitive adversarial robustness without computationally expensive adversarial training or test-time purification, offering a promising alternative approach to robust deep learning.

title: HOPE: Heterophily-Aware Open-Set Node Classification with Pseudo-Extrapolation
summary: Standard open-set node classification methods rely on the homophily assumption, where connected nodes share labels. However, real-world graphs are often heterophilic, exposing the limitations of current methods and posing new challenges to open-set node classification. On the one hand, cross-class connectivity causes representations from different known or unknown classes to become intertwined after aggregation, undermining their discriminative capacity. On the other hand, structural mixture invalidates threshold-based open-set methods and cross-class feature interpolation, leading to unreliable unknown-class rejection. To address these challenges, we propose HOPE, a Heterophily-aware Open-set node classification method with Pseudo-Extrapolation. To adapt open-set graph neural networks (GNNs) to heterophilic scenarios, HOPE uses a structure-augmented feature initialization layer to capture multi-hop structural patterns. Meanwhile, we design a trustworthy neighborhood aggregation mechanism for standard GNNs to dynamically filter noisy cross-class neighbors. To enhance unknown-class rejection, we introduce a heterophily-guided pseudo-extrapolation strategy. It dynamically maintains known-class centers and extrapolates along cross-class neighborhood displacement directions, synthesizing pseudo-unknown proxies near structurally ambiguous regions. Finally, we optimize the network with joint classification and logit margin regularization, routing synthetic proxies into a dedicated rejection slot without imposing geometric margin constraints in the representation space. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets show that HOPE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models, validating its effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency.

AI.tldr: HOPE is a heterophily-aware open-set node classification method that addresses challenges in heterophilic graphs through structure-augmented features, trustworthy neighborhood aggregation, pseudo-unknown proxy synthesis, and joint optimization.
AI.motivation: Current open-set node classification methods rely on homophily assumption (connected nodes share labels), but real-world graphs are often heterophilic. Cross-class connectivity causes representations to become intertwined, undermining discriminative capacity. Structural mixture invalidates threshold-based methods and cross-class feature interpolation, leading to unreliable unknown-class rejection.
AI.method: 1) Structure-augmented feature initialization layer to capture multi-hop structural patterns; 2) Trustworthy neighborhood aggregation mechanism to dynamically filter noisy cross-class neighbors; 3) Heterophily-guided pseudo-extrapolation strategy that maintains known-class centers and extrapolates along cross-class neighborhood displacement directions to synthesize pseudo-unknown proxies; 4) Joint optimization with classification and logit margin regularization that routes synthetic proxies to rejection slot without geometric margin constraints.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple datasets show HOPE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models, validating its effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency in heterophilic open-set node classification.
AI.conclusion: HOPE successfully addresses the challenges of open-set node classification in heterophilic graphs through its innovative combination of structure-aware feature engineering, adaptive neighbor filtering, pseudo-unknown proxy synthesis, and margin-based optimization, demonstrating superior performance over existing methods.

title: Hyperparameter Scaling Laws Across MoE Sparsity
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models expand model capacity without a proportional increase in training compute, but increasing sparsity makes reliable hyperparameter transfer challenging. In this work, we show that conventional hyperparameter scaling laws are insufficient for ultra-sparse MoEs: the optimal learning rate and batch size vary with activation ratio, and these shifts cannot be explained by either total or activated parameter count alone. To characterize this dependence, we conduct 1,800 pre-training runs spanning six activated-parameter scales and models with up to 6B total non-embedding parameters, processing approximately 20 trillion tokens at a cost of 200,000 equivalent H800 GPU-hours. Our results reconcile conflicting findings in prior work by revealing two scaling regimes. At fixed sparsity, the optimal batch size follows a power-law relationship with training tokens $D$, whereas the optimal learning rate scales with training compute $C$ and remains robust to the allocation between model size and data. Across sparsity levels, the activation ratio $A$ enters both relationships as an additional multiplicative power-law factor. These observations lead to unified hyperparameter scaling laws that transfer across MoE sparsity levels. Large-scale evaluation shows that the scaling form outperforms alternative functional forms. On a held-out ultra-sparse MoE with 12B total parameters and only 1/64 of its experts activated, the predicted hyperparameters remain close to the observed optima, supporting joint extrapolation across model scale and sparsity. Further experiments demonstrate transfer across expert granularities and isolate the effect of activation ratio from that of total expert count.

AI.tldr: MoE hyperparameter scaling laws differ from dense models: optimal learning rate and batch size vary with activation ratio, not just total or activated parameters, requiring new scaling formulations.
AI.motivation: Conventional hyperparameter scaling laws fail for ultra-sparse MoE models - they don't account for how optimal hyperparameters shift with activation ratio, leading to unreliable hyperparameter transfer across different sparsity levels.
AI.method: Conducted 1,800 pre-training runs spanning six activated-parameter scales up to 6B total non-embedding parameters (processing ~20T tokens). Analyzed how optimal batch size and learning rate scale with training tokens, compute, and activation ratio across different sparsity levels.
AI.result: Revealed two scaling regimes: at fixed sparsity, optimal batch size scales with training tokens D, while optimal learning rate scales with training compute C. Activation ratio A enters both as multiplicative power-law factor. Unified scaling laws transfer across MoE sparsity levels and outperform alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Proposed hyperparameter scaling laws enable reliable transfer across MoE sparsity levels, validated by successful extrapolation to ultra-sparse 12B parameter MoE with 1/64 activation ratio. Laws also transfer across expert granularities and isolate activation ratio effects from total expert count.

title: Chimaera: A Mixture-of-Graph-Experts Architecture for Cross-Task and Cross-Dataset Graph Learning
summary: Designing foundation models for graphs is challenging due to the irregular structure of graphs and the different sizes and characteristics of embeddings. Chimaera integrates mixture-of-experts with graph foundation models (GFM). It integrates different GFM architectures, such as graph prompts and linear GNN models. Large language models are used to generate embeddings, and experts can be trained and combined following different strategies, GFMs, embeddings, etc. Furthermore, Chimaera extends existing linear GNNs to support link-level and graph-level tasks in addition to node-level tasks. Empirical analyses are performed on same-task and cross-task experiments with node, link, and graph classification tasks using six benchmark text-attributed graph datasets. The experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Chimaera and its capabilities for transfer across tasks and datasets. Further insights include the need to use both large and small language models to generate embeddings for the experts, a strong cross-task transferability of simple but effective linear GNNs, and using few samples only to provide strong results.

AI.tldr: Chimaera is a graph foundation model framework that integrates mixture-of-experts with various GFM architectures, extends linear GNNs to support multiple task levels, and leverages LLMs for embeddings, demonstrating strong cross-task transferability with minimal samples.
AI.motivation: Foundation models for graphs are challenging due to irregular graph structures, varying embedding sizes, and different characteristics. There's a need for a unified framework that can handle node-level, link-level, and graph-level tasks while being transferable across different datasets and tasks.
AI.method: Chimaera integrates mixture-of-experts with graph foundation models, combining different GFM architectures (graph prompts, linear GNN models). It uses large language models to generate embeddings, trains experts following different strategies, and extends existing linear GNNs to support link-level and graph-level tasks in addition to node-level tasks.
AI.result: Empirical analyses on six benchmark text-attributed graph datasets show Chimaera's effectiveness in same-task and cross-task experiments (node, link, graph classification). Results demonstrate strong cross-task transferability, the benefit of using both large and small language models for embeddings, and that few samples can provide strong results.
AI.conclusion: Chimaera successfully addresses the challenges of graph foundation models by providing a flexible mixture-of-experts framework that supports multiple task levels and demonstrates strong transfer learning capabilities across tasks and datasets with efficient use of limited samples.

title: BAFF: Bid-Aware Filter Family for Mitigating Training Data Interference in RTB A/B Tests
comment: Accepted as a poster presentation at the OARS Workshop @RecSys 2026. 9 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables
summary: In online A/B tests for real-time bidding (RTB), control and treatment models are typically trained on a shared serving log that includes data generated by the counterpart model. This shared-log training biases each model's training data through two channels: the counterpart model may have selected a different ad from the ad-candidate pool (ad-ranking disagreement) and may have bid a different price (bid-pricing disagreement), potentially distorting the A/B test outcome. Log-splitting eliminates the bias but sacrifices training data; log-sharing retains all data but leaves the bias unaddressed. We formalize the Bid-Aware Filter Family (BAFF), a class of (k,l)-parameterized hard filters that controls tolerance to each channel independently, providing a structured search space between these two extremes. We further propose a three-stage online measurement protocol that enables evaluating data-sharing strategies by their deviation from an interference-free reference model in production. In offline simulation, a (k,l) sweep surfaces operating points with smaller deviation from the interference-free reference model than both log-sharing and log-splitting. In a live RTB deployment on a demand-side platform (DSP), filter-based variants preserve the reference model's business metrics (e.g., CPC, CTR) more closely than both baselines. The best operating point is setting-dependent, underscoring the practical value of the search space itself.

AI.tldr: A framework for managing training data bias in online A/B tests for real-time bidding systems by balancing between log-splitting and log-sharing through parameterized filters.
AI.motivation: In RTB A/B tests, control and treatment models share serving logs that contain data generated by the counterpart model, creating bias through ad-ranking disagreement and bid-pricing disagreement. This distorts A/B test outcomes, but existing solutions either eliminate bias by sacrificing data (log-splitting) or keep all data but leave bias unaddressed (log-sharing).
AI.method: The paper proposes the Bid-Aware Filter Family (BAFF), a class of (k,l)-parameterized hard filters that independently control tolerance to ad-ranking and bid-pricing disagreement channels. It also introduces a three-stage online measurement protocol to evaluate data-sharing strategies by comparing them to an interference-free reference model in production.
AI.result: In offline simulation, BAFF surfaces operating points with smaller deviation from the interference-free reference model than both log-sharing and log-splitting. In live RTB deployment on a DSP, filter-based variants preserve the reference model's business metrics (CPC, CTR) more closely than both baselines. The best operating point depends on specific settings.
AI.conclusion: The BAFF framework provides a structured search space between log-splitting and log-sharing extremes, enabling better trade-offs between bias reduction and data utilization in RTB A/B tests. The practical value lies in having the search space itself, as optimal settings are context-dependent.

title: PAC-Bayesian Bounds for Learning Partially Observed Stochastic Linear Time-Invariant State-Space Systems with Inputs and Sub-Gaussian Noise
summary: In this paper we derive a Probably Approximately Correct (PAC)-Bayesian error bound for partially observed linear time-invariant (LTI) stochastic dynamical systems in state-space form with inputs and sub-Gaussian noise. Such bounds are widespread in machine learning, and they are useful for characterizing the predictive power of models learned from finitely many data points. The bound derived in this paper relates the expectation of prediction errors with the prediction error generated by the model on the data used for learning. In addition, we show that it can also be used to derive bounds for the parameter estimation error. In turn, this allows us to provide finite-sample error bounds for the prediction error and parameter estimation error for a wide class of system identification algorithms. Furthermore, as LTI systems are a sub-class of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), these error bounds could be a first step towards PAC-Bayesian bounds for RNNs.

AI.tldr: PAC-Bayesian error bounds for partially observed LTI stochastic dynamical systems with inputs and sub-Gaussian noise, applicable to system identification algorithms and potentially extendable to RNNs.
AI.motivation: Need finite-sample error bounds for system identification algorithms to characterize predictive power of models learned from limited data, especially for linear time-invariant stochastic systems which are important in control and time series analysis.
AI.method: Derive a Probably Approximately Correct (PAC)-Bayesian error bound specifically for partially observed LTI stochastic dynamical systems in state-space form with inputs and sub-Gaussian noise, relating expected prediction errors to empirical errors.
AI.result: Developed PAC-Bayesian bounds that connect expected prediction errors with empirical errors on training data, enabling derivation of finite-sample error bounds for both prediction error and parameter estimation error for various system identification algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The derived PAC-Bayesian bounds provide rigorous finite-sample guarantees for system identification of LTI systems, and since LTI systems are sub-classes of RNNs, these results could serve as foundation for developing similar bounds for recurrent neural networks.

title: Adaptive Anisotropic Attention for Axis-Structured Signals
summary: Dense self-attention treats all token pairs as equally plausible before learning, an interaction-isotropic prior that can be mismatched to structured signals. For structured, low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) signals such as EEG, dependencies are organized along the electrode and time axes, and this uniform prior exposes each token to many irrelevant interactions. We introduce Adaptive Anisotropic Attention (AAA), which splits attention into two paths: a temporal path, where each token attends to the tokens of its own electrode across time, and a spatial path, where it attends to the tokens of the other electrodes at the same time step. A small gate predicts, for every token, a convex combination of the two path outputs: two non-negative weights that sum to one. On six EEG downstream tasks, the resulting model, AXON (AXis-factorized Operator Network), improves mean balanced accuracy over a dense baseline under both linear probing and full fine-tuning. We show that both paths (temporal and spatial) are necessary and that the weighted sum beats a hard choice of one path; most of the benefit comes from the gate learning a different temporal/spatial balance at each layer of the network. Controlled audio spectrogram experiments show that axis factorization transfers beyond EEG. These results suggest that aligning attention with the natural axes of structured signals provides a useful inductive bias.

AI.tldr: AXON introduces Adaptive Anisotropic Attention (AAA) which splits attention into temporal and spatial paths with adaptive gating, improving EEG signal processing by aligning attention with structured signal axes.
AI.motivation: Dense self-attention treats all token pairs equally, creating an interaction-isotropic prior that mismatches structured, low SNR signals like EEG where dependencies are organized along electrode (spatial) and time (temporal) axes. This uniform prior exposes tokens to many irrelevant interactions.
AI.method: Introduced Adaptive Anisotropic Attention (AAA) that splits attention into two paths: temporal path (each token attends to tokens of its own electrode across time) and spatial path (each token attends to tokens of other electrodes at same time step). A small gate predicts convex combination weights for each token's path outputs.
AI.result: On six EEG downstream tasks, AXON improves mean balanced accuracy over dense baseline under both linear probing and full fine-tuning. Both paths are necessary, weighted sum beats hard path choice, and most benefit comes from gate learning different temporal/spatial balance at each layer. Controlled audio experiments show transfer beyond EEG.
AI.conclusion: Aligning attention with the natural axes of structured signals provides a useful inductive bias for processing low SNR structured signals like EEG, with potential applications to other structured signal domains.

title: Eliciting Weak-to-Strong Generalization with On-Policy Reverse Distillation
summary: Weak-to-strong generalization asks whether stronger models can learn from weaker supervisors and surpass them. This question is particularly important for successive model generations and multi-domain consolidation, where repeating frontier-scale post-training from scratch can be prohibitively expensive. Yet conventional distillation treats the weak teacher as an optimization target, potentially imposing its capacity ceiling on the student. We introduce On-Policy Reverse Distillation (OPRD), which evaluates the teacher's policy shift relative to its reference policy on student rollouts and amplifies the component of the student's verifier-driven policy gradient along that direction. By rescaling only verifier-supported updates, OPRD preserves the stationary points of policy optimization while accelerating learning beyond the teacher. In both successive model transfer and multi-teacher distillation, OPRD achieves higher performance with fewer student updates than existing RL and distillation approaches. Response-style analysis shows that OPRD students remain closer to models trained with verifier-based RL alone than to their weak teachers, suggesting that teacher guidance accelerates rather than redirects the student's own optimization. Results in conventional strong-to-weak distillation further demonstrate that OPRD effectively combines verifier-driven policy optimization with teacher guidance regardless of capacity ordering.

AI.tldr: OPRD is a novel distillation method that uses weak teacher models to accelerate student learning without limiting the student's ultimate capacity, achieving better performance with fewer updates than traditional approaches.
AI.motivation: Current distillation methods treat weak teachers as optimization targets, which can impose the teacher's capacity ceiling on students. This is problematic for successive model generations and multi-domain consolidation where repeated frontier-scale training is too expensive.
AI.method: On-Policy Reverse Distillation (OPRD) evaluates the teacher's policy shift relative to its reference policy on student rollouts and amplifies the component of the student's verifier-driven policy gradient along that direction. It rescales only verifier-supported updates to preserve policy optimization stationary points.
AI.result: OPRD achieves higher performance with fewer student updates than existing RL and distillation approaches in both successive model transfer and multi-teacher distillation. Response-style analysis shows OPRD students remain closer to models trained with verifier-based RL alone than to their weak teachers.
AI.conclusion: OPRD effectively combines verifier-driven policy optimization with teacher guidance regardless of capacity ordering, with teacher guidance accelerating rather than redirecting the student's own optimization.

title: Length Generalization for Transformers via Compression
summary: Recent advancements in transformer length generalization theory enable us to reliably predict when a transformer can learn to solve a task. In particular, the C-RASP hypothesis (a formalized version of the so-called RASP-l conjecture) posits that transformers length-generalize on a task if and only if a solution is expressible in the C-RASP language. While this hypothesis has strong empirical validation, theoretical problems arise from the fact that no computable length generalization bounds exist for C-RASP, alongside the discovery of seemingly contradictory experiments. To address these problems, we refine the C-RASP hypothesis utilizing the recently-proposed fragments C-RASP+ and C-RASP1. These fragments have computable length generalization bounds, though in the worst case requiring an extremely large (double exponential) sample size. It is an open question whether these sample size bounds are tight. In this paper, we resolve this open question by providing an exponentially tighter bound. In doing so, we show a polynomial length generalization bound for transformers if we adopt compressed strings, via a novel connection to power words. As an application, we show how this yields a fine-grained analysis of the C-RASP conjecture that resolves contradicting experimental evidence against it.

AI.tldr: The paper refines the C-RASP hypothesis about transformer length generalization by providing exponentially tighter bounds using compressed strings and power words connections, resolving contradictory experimental evidence.
AI.motivation: The C-RASP hypothesis predicts transformer length generalization but faces theoretical problems: no computable length generalization bounds exist, and there are seemingly contradictory experimental findings. Existing fragments C-RASP+ and C-RASP1 have bounds but require extremely large (double exponential) sample sizes, making their tightness an open question.
AI.method: The paper refines the C-RASP hypothesis by establishing a novel connection to power words and using compressed strings to achieve polynomial length generalization bounds. This involves providing exponentially tighter sample size bounds than previous double exponential requirements.
AI.result: The paper resolves the open question by showing polynomial length generalization bounds for transformers when using compressed strings. This yields a fine-grained analysis of the C-RASP conjecture that resolves the contradictory experimental evidence against it.
AI.conclusion: By providing exponentially tighter bounds through compressed strings and power words connections, the paper successfully refines the C-RASP hypothesis, addresses its theoretical problems, and reconciles contradictory experimental evidence, advancing transformer length generalization theory.

title: Earth System World Model for What-If Simulations: A Case Study for Terrestrial Ecosystems
summary: Machine learning emulators have become essential for accelerating expensive Earth-system simulations, but most existing approaches remain passive forecasters: they reproduce simulator trajectories under prescribed forcings without an explicit interaction mechanism for user-specified interventions. This limits their use in interactive scientific workflows and Earth-system digital twins, where users often need to explore how a system would respond if selected state components were changed. We propose an action-conditioned world-modeling framework for Earth-system emulation that reformulates simulator trajectories as supervision for controllable state-transition learning. The key idea is transition-action pretraining: naturally observed state changes are treated as label-free action supervision, allowing the model to learn both prescribed dynamics and action-conditioned responses without manually annotated interventions. We further introduce masked response learning to infer unobserved variables under partial state edits and learn coupled system dependencies. We test this framework on ecosystem dynamics across six global regions and multiple stand ages. Experiments show that the model preserves competitive long-horizon emulation accuracy while enabling controllable structural interventions and coherent responses in coupled ecosystem-cycle variables. These results suggest a practical route from passive Earth-system emulators toward interactive, intervention-aware scientific surrogates.

AI.tldr: Proposes an action-conditioned world-modeling framework for Earth-system emulation that enables controllable interventions, moving beyond passive forecasting to interactive scientific surrogates.
AI.motivation: Current machine learning emulators for Earth-system simulations are passive forecasters that can't handle user-specified interventions, limiting their use in interactive scientific workflows and digital twins where users need to explore system responses to targeted state changes.
AI.method: Action-conditioned world-modeling framework that reformulates simulator trajectories as supervision for controllable state-transition learning. Uses transition-action pretraining (treating observed state changes as label-free action supervision) and masked response learning to infer unobserved variables under partial state edits and learn coupled system dependencies.
AI.result: Tested on ecosystem dynamics across six global regions and multiple stand ages. The model preserves competitive long-horizon emulation accuracy while enabling controllable structural interventions and coherent responses in coupled ecosystem-cycle variables.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a practical route from passive Earth-system emulators toward interactive, intervention-aware scientific surrogates, addressing limitations of existing approaches for interactive scientific workflows.

title: The BatchNorm Illusion: Diagnosing Normalization Artifacts in Machine Unlearning Evaluation
summary: Approximate machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training data from a trained model without retraining from scratch. We identify a previously undocumented confound in how unlearning is evaluated on BatchNorm-based architectures: a single forward pass over retain data, an operation that modifies no weight, can deterministically rewrite the model's normalization state and reverse the apparent surface-metric forgetting. We formalize this operation as a weight-preserving fixed-point operator and prove that any pre-versus-post gap it induces is provably attributable to BN running statistics rather than to any modification the unlearning method made to the weights. This attribution claim cleanly separates measurement failure (BN artifact) from encoder failure (residual weight-encoded information, recently documented in concurrent work), and the same operator framework yields a unique decomposition of linear-probe elevation into BN-measurement-bias and encoder-geometry components. Empirically, the artifact reverses headline forget accuracy by up to 78 pp across nine evaluated methods on standard benchmarks; an attacker with as few as 10 unlabeled images recovers most of the masked accuracy; and a strict GroupNorm control reduces the artifact to zero across all methods. The tested membership-inference attacks change little under recalibration, locating the observed evaluation failure in forget accuracy and linear probing.

AI.tldr: BatchNorm normalization statistics cause misleading unlearning evaluation metrics; forward passes can reverse apparent forgetting, revealing measurement artifacts rather than true unlearning.
AI.motivation: Current approximate machine unlearning evaluations on BatchNorm-based architectures may produce misleading results due to normalization statistic artifacts rather than actual weight modifications.
AI.method: Formalize forward pass operation as weight-preserving fixed-point operator, prove BN statistics attribution, decompose linear-probe elevation into measurement bias vs encoder geometry, empirically test across nine methods with GroupNorm controls.
AI.result: Single forward pass can reverse up to 78 pp of headline forget accuracy, attackers with 10 unlabeled images recover most masked accuracy, GroupNorm eliminates artifact, membership inference attacks unaffected.
AI.conclusion: BatchNorm creates evaluation artifacts that can be misinterpreted as successful unlearning; proper measurement requires separating normalization artifacts from actual weight modification effects.

title: GraphFAS: A Distributed System for Automated Graph Feature Generation and Selection in Industrial Transaction Networks
summary: Industrial fraud detection often relies on costly expert-crafted features that overlook graph-structured relational signals, while GNNs often do not meet the interpretability and deployment requirements of financial risk control. We propose GraphFAS (Graph Feature Automated Selection), a distributed feature selection procedure based on Boruta that bridges this gap through: (1) a non-parametric graph feature generation module that constructs explicit, interpretable structural features via multi-hop subgraph extraction and multi-scale aggregation without learned parameters; and (2) an automated distributed feature selection algorithm extending Boruta with median-based aggregation across partitions to robustly identify informative features at scale with minimal domain expertise. Compared with end-to-end GNN pipelines, GraphFAS decouples feature aggregation from model training, enabling direct integration with tabular models and direct compatibility with TreeSHAPbased explanations. Deployed in Alipay, GraphFAS delivers orderof-magnitude improvements in engineering efficiency while showing strong performance against expert-driven and graph-learning baselines on large-scale graphs.

AI.tldr: GraphFAS is a graph feature automated selection framework that bridges GNNs and industrial fraud detection needs by generating interpretable structural features without learned parameters and performing distributed feature selection.
AI.motivation: Industrial fraud detection relies on costly expert-crafted features that miss graph-structured signals, while GNNs lack the interpretability and deployment requirements needed for financial risk control systems.
AI.method: GraphFAS consists of: (1) a non-parametric graph feature generation module that creates explicit, interpretable structural features through multi-hop subgraph extraction and multi-scale aggregation without learned parameters; (2) an automated distributed feature selection algorithm extending Boruta with median-based aggregation across partitions to identify informative features at scale.
AI.result: Deployed in Alipay, GraphFAS delivers order-of-magnitude improvements in engineering efficiency while showing strong performance against expert-driven and graph-learning baselines on large-scale graphs.
AI.conclusion: GraphFAS successfully bridges the gap between graph learning and industrial fraud detection by decoupling feature aggregation from model training, enabling direct integration with tabular models and TreeSHAP-based explanations while maintaining scalability and interpretability.

title: Transformers as In-Context Samplers: From Closed-Form Diffusion to Estimation-Free Sampling
summary:
A growing body of work establishes that large language models are not mere statistical memorizers, but are capable of in-context learning: performing inference at test time using only examples provided in the prompt, without any parameter updates. Prior theoretical work has shown that this capability extends to supervised learning tasks such as linear regression. We prove that in-context learning extends further to \emph{data generation}: frozen transformers can simulate iterative generative samplers from in-context samples. We first show that transformers can realize closed-form and smoothed closed-form diffusion samplers. The construction identifies a concrete generative role for softmax attention: it computes responsibility weights and weighted empirical averages, while feedforward layers implement Euler updates.
  To empirically relate these constructions to pretrained language models, we study \emph{semantic-topic sampling}: prompts consisting of words drawn from a common semantic category, such as animals, foods, or cities. Across transformer layers, the normalized hidden states exhibit a two-stage geometry: they move toward a uniform spherical reference in intermediate layers and then return to structured, topic-dependent representations near the output. We further measure an interacting-particle energy on these hidden-state clouds and observe the same U-shape pattern. We then prove that transformers can approximate an energy-based sampler, constructing the same U-shape energy across the layers.

AI.tldr: Transformers can perform in-context data generation by approximating iterative generative samplers, with attention computing responsibility weights and feedforward layers implementing Euler updates, evidenced by empirical observations of two-stage geometry in hidden states.
AI.motivation: To understand the generative capabilities of frozen transformers beyond supervised in-context learning, specifically investigating whether they can simulate iterative generative samplers from in-context samples, moving beyond mere statistical memorization.
AI.method: Theoretical construction showing transformers can realize closed-form and smoothed closed-form diffusion samplers, with attention computing responsibility weights and feedforward layers implementing Euler updates. Empirical study of semantic-topic sampling using prompts from common semantic categories, analyzing hidden state geometry across transformer layers and measuring interacting-particle energy.
AI.result: Transformers can approximate energy-based samplers, constructing the same U-shape energy across layers observed empirically. Hidden states exhibit two-stage geometry: moving toward uniform spherical reference in intermediate layers then returning to structured topic-dependent representations near output, with interacting-particle energy showing the same U-shape pattern.
AI.conclusion: Frozen transformers are capable of in-context data generation by simulating iterative generative samplers, revealing that attention mechanisms serve a concrete generative role in computing responsibility weights while feedforward layers handle Euler updates, demonstrating broader generative capabilities beyond supervised learning.

title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning for False Ventricular Tachycardia Alarm Reduction in the ICU
summary: False ventricular tachycardia (VT) alarms are a leading contributor to alarm fatigue in intensive care units. We propose a deep learning framework combining a 1D SE-ResNet with ICU-realistic data augmentations and a physics-informed auxiliary reconstruction task based on the three-element Windkessel hemodynamic model, implemented as a differentiable forward simulation. By requiring the network's latent representation to produce physiologically plausible arterial pressure waveforms, artifact-driven ECG patterns are penalized while true VT remains coherent across modalities. Evaluated on the VTaC benchmark under a strict real-time protocol (10-second pre-alarm window), our method achieves a 5-point Challenge Score improvement over prior state-of-the-art. Ablation studies confirm that the physics-informed objective is the primary performance driver, providing gains in accuracy, 2x label efficiency, and more localized and clinically meaningful ECG segments.

AI.tldr: A deep learning framework combining 1D SE-ResNet with ICU-realistic data augmentations and physics-informed reconstruction using Windkessel hemodynamic model significantly reduces false VT alarms and outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: False ventricular tachycardia (VT) alarms are a leading cause of alarm fatigue in intensive care units, creating a critical need for more accurate alarm management systems to reduce unnecessary alerts while maintaining patient safety.
AI.method: Proposes a deep learning framework with: 1) 1D SE-ResNet architecture, 2) ICU-realistic data augmentations, and 3) physics-informed auxiliary reconstruction task using a differentiable forward simulation of the three-element Windkessel hemodynamic model. The network's latent representation is constrained to produce physiologically plausible arterial pressure waveforms, penalizing artifact-driven ECG patterns while preserving true VT patterns across modalities.
AI.result: Achieves a 5-point Challenge Score improvement over prior state-of-the-art on the VTaC benchmark under strict real-time protocol (10-second pre-alarm window). Ablation studies show the physics-informed objective drives performance gains, improving accuracy, providing 2x label efficiency, and producing more localized and clinically meaningful ECG segments.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed deep learning frameworks combining physiological modeling with neural networks are highly effective for reducing false VT alarms in ICU settings, offering superior performance, label efficiency, and clinically interpretable results compared to purely data-driven approaches.

title: Let It Go or Learn to Self-Correct: Continuous Diffusion for Constrained Discrete Tasks
comment: Preprint. The main results of this work were obtained by May 2026
summary: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) generate samples by starting from noise and repeatedly denoising while keeping each update close to the current noisy state. This behavior is effective in many continuous domains, but its role is less clear for globally constrained discrete tasks, such as Sudoku, graph connectivity, Latin squares, and N-queens. In such settings, early discrete errors can be difficult to undo. As a result, standard diffusion sampling may preserve early mistakes, even when the model's clean predictions are informative. We compare standard samplers to sampling directly from the model's clean prediction. Without retraining, this single change improves Sudoku validity from 31% to 95%, with consistent gains across the other discrete tasks. We hypothesize that staying close to the current noisy state is harmful because the reverse trajectory can drift off the forward noising distribution the model was trained on. To reduce this train-test mismatch, we further introduce self-correction training, which exposes the model to its own predictions, improving robustness to errors that arise during inference. This substantially improves the performance of standard samplers. Our results suggest that continuous diffusion models can learn nontrivial global constraints, but discrete reasoning tasks require better alignment between training and inference: either through samplers that reduce commitment to early decisions, or through training that teaches the model to correct its own inference-time errors.

AI.tldr: Directly sampling from the model's clean prediction instead of following standard diffusion sampling significantly improves performance on discrete constraint tasks like Sudoku, from 31% to 95% validity, by reducing commitment to early mistakes and addressing train-test mismatch.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates why standard diffusion sampling performs poorly on globally constrained discrete tasks (Sudoku, graph connectivity, Latin squares, N-queens). The authors observe that standard diffusion's requirement to stay close to current noisy states makes it difficult to correct early discrete errors, leading to preserved mistakes even when the model's clean predictions are informative.
AI.method: Two main approaches: (1) Direct sampling from the model's clean prediction instead of following standard diffusion sampling trajectory, and (2) Self-correction training that exposes the model to its own predictions during training to improve robustness to inference-time errors.
AI.result: Direct sampling dramatically improves Sudoku validity from 31% to 95% without retraining. Self-correction training further improves performance of standard samplers. Consistent gains observed across all tested discrete tasks.
AI.conclusion: Continuous diffusion models can learn non-trivial global constraints, but discrete reasoning tasks require better alignment between training and inference through either (1) samplers that reduce commitment to early decisions, or (2) training that teaches models to correct their own inference-time errors.

title: Do Reasoning Representations Help Humans Evaluate LLM Outputs?
summary: Reasoning representations are increasingly used as explanations for large language model outputs. Yet they are typically evaluated with model-centric criteria, such as answer accuracy and faithfulness, leaving it unclear whether they help people evaluate model responses. In this work, we study reasoning representations as human-facing interfaces rather than proxies for model reasoning ability. We conduct a controlled human study of six reasoning formats across tasks of varying complexity, supported by a web-based framework that randomizes task domains, problem instances, and representation order. The study collects fine-grained judgments of structural understanding, error detection and localization, and trust calibration. Our study shows a mismatch between perceived preference and support for human evaluation. Participants prefer planning- and decomposition-based representations, but simpler chain-of-thought traces better support verification, trust, and interpretability. Preferred representations also introduce calibration risks, with more false alarms on correct traces and high trust despite low willingness to verify.

AI.tldr: There's a mismatch between preferred reasoning formats and their actual utility: people prefer planning/decomposition formats, but simpler chain-of-thought better supports verification, trust, and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of reasoning representations focuses on model-centric metrics (accuracy, faithfulness) rather than assessing whether they actually help humans evaluate model responses. The paper aims to study reasoning formats as human-facing interfaces rather than proxies for model reasoning ability.
AI.method: Conducted controlled human study with six reasoning formats across tasks of varying complexity. Used web-based framework that randomized task domains, problem instances, and representation order. Collected fine-grained judgments on structural understanding, error detection/localization, and trust calibration.
AI.result: Found mismatch between preference and utility: participants preferred planning- and decomposition-based representations, but simpler chain-of-thought traces better supported verification, trust, and interpretability. Preferred representations also introduced calibration risks - more false alarms on correct traces and high trust despite low willingness to verify.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning representation design should prioritize human evaluation support over aesthetic preference, and simpler chain-of-thought representations may be more effective for practical human-model interaction despite being less preferred.

title: Training-Free Task Vectors for LLM Behavioral Control
summary: Task vectors enable post-training model editing by identifying semantically meaningful directions in weight space, typically computed as the difference between a fine-tuned model and its pretrained initialization. However, this reliance on fine-tuning makes discovering such directions costly and limits the practicality of post-training model editing. To address this limitation, we introduce Training-Free Task Vectors (TFTVs), a novel method to compute task-vector-like directions without requiring fine-tuning. Our method maps activation steering vectors to rank-one weight-space edits using only forward-pass statistics, while satisfying arithmetic properties that directly support learning via addition, forgetting via subtraction, and the composition of multiple edits. Empirically, we evaluate TFTVs on large language model behavioral control tasks and show that they consistently amplify, suppress, and compose target behaviors while preserving general knowledge and problem-solving skills. We also validate our method against other editing and steering baselines, experimentally demonstrating that TFTVs achieve stronger trait control with better or competitive utility preservation. We hope our work opens new directions for the community in post-training model editing and broader training-free model control. Code is available on the project website: tftv-llm.github.io.

AI.tldr: TFTVs (Training-Free Task Vectors) enable post-training model editing without fine-tuning by mapping activation steering vectors to rank-one weight-space edits using only forward-pass statistics.
AI.motivation: Traditional task vectors require costly fine-tuning to discover semantically meaningful directions in weight space, limiting the practicality of post-training model editing. This creates a need for more efficient, training-free alternatives.
AI.method: The authors introduce Training-Free Task Vectors (TFTVs) that compute task-vector-like directions without fine-tuning by mapping activation steering vectors to rank-one weight-space edits using only forward-pass statistics.
AI.result: TFTVs effectively amplify, suppress, and compose target behaviors while preserving general knowledge and problem-solving skills in large language models. They achieve stronger trait control with better or competitive utility preservation compared to other editing and steering baselines.
AI.conclusion: TFTVs represent a novel training-free approach to post-training model editing that opens new directions for model control, offering a practical alternative to fine-tuning-based methods while maintaining arithmetic properties for learning, forgetting, and composition of edits.

title: PlayTrain: An Efficient Reinforcement Learning Framework for LLM-Generated Adaptable JavaScript Games
summary: While many video-game environments (VGEs) have played crucial roles in advancing reinforcement learning (RL), developing novel VGEs or modifying existing ones to support new features, has been a laborious process requiring extensive hand-coding. Here we present PlayTrain, an RL framework that combines the abilities of large language models (LLMs) to robustly generate JavaScript (JS) games from a minimal human prompt, and an efficient pipeline that can run any JS game in a standard 'gym' environment. Not only are recent LLMs particularly good at writing JS code, but the JS format also allows users to easily play generated VGEs, while PlayTrain enables us to train RL agents on the exact same games. We demonstrate multiple use cases of PlayTrain, including cloning well-known Atari and ProcGen games in simple JS, where PlayTrain trains pixel-based agents end-to-end at over 1M agent-decisions per second on a single GPU node; and creating modified versions thereof (e.g., that support novel test sets, procedural generation logics, or game dynamics). Through PlayTrain, we reimagine RL VGE development: all we need is a single JS file, generated and modified through an LLM. We discuss promising future RL research directions that PlayTrain unlocks.

AI.tldr: PlayTrain is an RL framework that uses LLMs to generate JavaScript games from minimal prompts and provides an efficient pipeline to run any JS game in a standard gym environment, enabling rapid VGE development and agent training.
AI.motivation: Current video-game environment development for RL research requires extensive hand-coding, which is laborious and slows down experimentation. There's a need for a more efficient way to create, modify, and train on VGEs.
AI.method: Combines LLMs' ability to generate JavaScript games from minimal human prompts with an efficient pipeline that runs JS games in standard gym environments. LLMs generate JS code (which they're particularly good at), and PlayTrain enables training RL agents on the same generated games.
AI.result: Demonstrated multiple use cases: cloning Atari and ProcGen games in simple JS with PlayTrain training pixel-based agents at over 1M decisions per second on a single GPU; creating modified versions with novel test sets, procedural generation logics, or game dynamics.
AI.conclusion: PlayTrain reimagines RL VGE development by reducing it to a single JS file generated and modified through LLMs, unlocking promising future RL research directions with minimal manual coding effort.

title: Multi-Task Learning for Sparsely-Labeled Time Series: A Case Study on Cold-Hardiness Modeling
summary: We present a real-world case study of multi-task learning (MTL) for temporal process modeling from limited data with temporally sparse labels. Specifically, we investigate multi-task learning for the important agricultural problem of predicting grape cold hardiness, which is the temperature at which lethal freezing occurs. Cold hardiness changes in response to weather and is difficult to measure directly in the field. Thus, growers rely on predictions to decide when to apply costly frost mitigation measures. We apply recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for daily cold-hardiness prediction from time series weather data. A major challenge is that the cold hardiness response varies across plant cultivars and ground-truth data for each cultivar is temporally sparse and limited. To address this challenge, we investigate multi-task learning (MTL) approaches for combining data, where different tasks correspond to different cultivars. We develop a variety of MTL architectures and evaluate them in both MTL and transfer learning settings. Our results show significant differences between architectures and that certain architectures are able to consistently outperform single-task learning and state-of-the-art scientific models. Additionally, we show similar results for the qualitatively different, but related, task of budbreak prediction. Further, improved accuracy for budbreak and cold hardiness is achieved by a single MTL model that simultaneously learns both tasks.

AI.tldr: Multi-task learning RNNs outperform single-task models and scientific baselines for predicting grape cold hardiness and budbreak from weather data, addressing sparse temporal labels across cultivars.
AI.motivation: Predicting grape cold hardiness is crucial for frost protection decisions, but ground-truth measurements are temporally sparse and limited across different cultivars, making it difficult to build accurate prediction models.
AI.method: Used recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for daily cold-hardiness prediction from weather time series, with multi-task learning approaches where different tasks correspond to different grape cultivars. Developed various MTL architectures evaluated in both MTL and transfer learning settings, and extended to budbreak prediction.
AI.result: Certain MTL architectures consistently outperformed single-task learning and state-of-the-art scientific models. Similar improvements were shown for budbreak prediction. Best accuracy was achieved by a single MTL model that simultaneously learns both cold hardiness and budbreak prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: Multi-task learning with RNNs effectively addresses the challenge of limited, temporally sparse data in agricultural process modeling, providing practical improvements for cold hardiness and budbreak prediction that can help growers make better frost mitigation decisions.

title: ThinkPrior: Zero-Rollout Difficulty Priors for Cold-Start Prompt Selection in RLVR
summary: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trained with group relative policy optimization (GRPO), the KL-free reward-advantage term studied here depends on within-group reward variation. If all rollouts in a group are correct or all are wrong, their group-relative advantages are identically zero; these zero-advantage silent groups provide no reward-advantage gradient, yet uniform sampling spends 39% of a run's rollouts on them. History-based prompt selection must first spend target-policy rollouts to estimate difficulty, creating a cold start with rollout waste; ThinkPrior instead uses an external anchor in one offline pass to construct a zero-rollout difficulty prior before the first target-policy rollout. The verifier-scored anchor pass rate supplies an external-anchor initialization for a Beta posterior; ThinkPrior selects by expected learnability and then updates from training outcomes, changing neither the loss nor the optimizer. On Qwen2.5-Math-7B across sixteen seeds, ThinkPrior more than halves early silent groups and cuts wasted rollouts through step 30 by nearly a fifth, while we detect no difference in final accuracy. On this 250-prompt pool the fixed-budget result is a reallocation rather than a net saving. The measured ThinkPrior+DAPO composition reduces generated rollouts by 10.6% while both arms retain the same 3840-rollout update budget. The prior requires no target-policy rollout before the first selection, but the posterior thereafter uses target-policy outcomes.

AI.tldr: ThinkPrior improves RLVR with GRPO by using an external anchor to create a zero-rollout difficulty prior, reducing wasted rollouts on silent groups without affecting final accuracy.
AI.motivation: In RLVR with GRPO, 39% of rollouts are wasted on "silent groups" (groups with all correct or all wrong rollouts) that provide no reward-advantage gradient. Current history-based prompt selection methods require wasting target-policy rollouts to estimate difficulty, creating a cold start problem with significant rollout waste.
AI.method: ThinkPrior uses an external anchor in one offline pass to construct a zero-rollout difficulty prior before any target-policy rollout. It initializes a Beta posterior using verifier-scored anchor pass rates, selects prompts by expected learnability, and updates from training outcomes without changing the loss or optimizer. The method combines external anchor initialization with target-policy outcome updates.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5-Math-7B across sixteen seeds, ThinkPrior more than halves early silent groups and reduces wasted rollouts through step 30 by nearly a fifth. In combination with DAPO, it reduces generated rollouts by 10.6% while maintaining the same 3840-rollout update budget. No difference in final accuracy was detected.
AI.conclusion: ThinkPrior effectively addresses the cold start problem in RLVR with GRPO by leveraging external anchor information to reduce rollout waste on silent groups, achieving better rollout efficiency without compromising final performance. The method represents an efficient reallocation of rollouts rather than a net reduction, demonstrating the value of prior information in prompt selection strategies.

title: Curriculum Learning as Transport: Understanding Curricula with Wasserstein Geodesics
summary: Curriculum learning is governed by several coupled design choices---how difficulty is defined, how examples are ordered, how much exposure each level receives, and how quickly training moves across levels---making it hard to isolate what actually helps. We present Wasserstein curriculum paths, a simple transport-based framework that decouples these factors by representing curricula as trajectories of training distributions over discrete difficulty levels. Across a calibrated synthetic suite with 12 tasks and 33 difficulty axes, we use this framework to isolate the effects of ordering, matched exposure, endpoint smoothness, and pacing under fixed training budgets. We find that curriculum effects are strongly context-dependent: no single strategy dominates across tasks, difficulty axes, and budgets, and curricula mainly change where a fixed budget is spent most effectively. Within this framework, easy-to-hard ordering improves hard-level performance relative to exposure-matched static sampling, showing that the benefit is not explained by cumulative exposure alone. We further show that endpoint smoothness and pacing substantially affect where along the difficulty spectrum a curriculum is effective. Finally, we show that the same transport view naturally supports extensions to learned pacing through geometry and to structured difficulty spaces beyond one-dimensional orderings.

AI.tldr: A transport-based framework called Wasserstein curriculum paths decouples curriculum design choices, enabling systematic analysis of ordering, exposure, smoothness, and pacing effects across difficulty levels, revealing context-dependent benefits rather than universal strategies.
AI.motivation: Curriculum learning involves multiple coupled design choices (difficulty definition, example ordering, exposure levels, pacing) that make it difficult to isolate what actually works. Current approaches don't allow systematic disentanglement of these factors.
AI.method: Propose Wasserstein curriculum paths - a transport-based framework representing curricula as trajectories of training distributions over discrete difficulty levels. Test across synthetic suite with 12 tasks and 33 difficulty axes to isolate effects of ordering, matched exposure, endpoint smoothness, and pacing under fixed budgets.
AI.result: Curriculum effects are strongly context-dependent: no single strategy dominates across tasks, difficulty axes, and budgets. Easy-to-hard ordering improves hard-level performance relative to exposure-matched static sampling, showing benefit beyond cumulative exposure alone. Endpoint smoothness and pacing substantially affect where along difficulty spectrum curriculum is effective.
AI.conclusion: The transport view provides a systematic framework to analyze curriculum learning components, showing that curriculum design is context-dependent and primarily changes where fixed training budgets are spent most effectively. The framework naturally extends to learned pacing and structured difficulty spaces beyond one-dimensional orderings.

title: When Does Scale-Invariant Optimization Become Unstable? An Exact Schedule Law with Weight Decay
summary:
Normalization renders large parts of neural networks effectively scale invariant, inducing a hidden feedback loop in which learning-rate schedules and weight decay interact through the parameter norm to control the effective step taken by the optimizer. We show that this interaction is governed by an exact discrete-time law: a single scalar quantity captures all schedule and decay forcing, while norm growth induces an opposing geometric self-quenching effect. This yields a sharp boundary that cleanly separates contraction- and expansion-dominated effective learning rate regimes. To understand the underlying mechanism, we provide exact analysis of a fully solved normalized regression model where the dynamics reduce to two dimensions and show that the balance point is intrinsically unstable, implying that constant learning rate with weight decay cannot stably maintain an interior equilibrium and instead produces recurrent behavior driven by discrete-time Jacobian structure. We further extend this perspective across optimizers through unified homogeneous-optimizer framework that reveals a structural dichotomy in self-quenching strength, providing a first-principles explanation for why adaptive methods exhibit systematically weaker stabilization under normalization.
  Across dynamical systems and neural networks (MLP, CNN, GPT2 / MNIST, CIFAR, wikiText, OpenWebText), the predicted law holds with high precision and enables direct control of training via the identified scalar, with performance peaking sharply at the predicted boundary. Together, these results isolate a single governing quantity for scale-invariant optimization, providing a precise and actionable lens on training dynamics, optimizer behavior, and schedule design in modern deep learning. Code is available in https://github.com/shasanamin/normalized-optimization-dynamics.

AI.tldr: Normalization in neural networks creates a hidden feedback loop where learning rate schedules and weight decay interact through parameter norms, governed by a single scalar quantity that separates contraction- and expansion-dominated regimes, revealing optimizer behavior and enabling better training control.
AI.motivation: To understand the complex interaction between normalization, learning rate schedules, and weight decay in neural networks, which creates a hidden feedback loop that affects training dynamics and optimization stability.
AI.method: 1) Derived an exact discrete-time law capturing schedule/decay forcing and norm growth effects. 2) Analyzed a fully solved normalized regression model reducing dynamics to 2D. 3) Developed unified homogeneous-optimizer framework to compare optimizers. 4) Validated across dynamical systems and neural networks (MLP, CNN, GPT2 on MNIST, CIFAR, wikiText, OpenWebText).
AI.result: 1) A single scalar quantity captures all schedule and decay forcing, with norm growth inducing geometric self-quenching. 2) Identified a sharp boundary separating contraction- and expansion-dominated effective learning rate regimes. 3) Found that constant learning rate with weight decay cannot maintain stable equilibrium due to intrinsic instability, producing recurrent behavior. 4) Adaptive methods show systematically weaker stabilization under normalization. 5) The law holds with high precision across experiments, with performance peaking sharply at the predicted boundary.
AI.conclusion: The paper isolates a single governing quantity for scale-invariant optimization, providing a precise and actionable lens on training dynamics, optimizer behavior, and schedule design in modern deep learning, with practical implications for controlling training and understanding optimizer stabilization.

title: Nearly Tight Rademacher Bounds for Sparsely Activated Neural Networks
summary: An input may activate few hidden units even when different inputs collectively use an entire network. We study the statistical complexity of this input-dependent sparsity in the one-hidden-layer ReLU model of Awasthi et al. (COLT 2024). For width $s$, at most $k$ active units per input, and effective weight and bias bounds $W,B$, every size-$m$ sample in the class's fixed radius-$R$ input domain satisfies $\mathcal{R}(S)\le CWR\min\{k,\sqrt{sk/m}\log^{3/2}(2m)\}+kB/\sqrt m$. A support-preserving cover and a single normalized chaining argument remove the previous explicit dimension factor, up to logarithms. Lower bounds on appropriate i.i.d. marginals match up to those logarithms, showing how changing active units across inputs retains a width dependence. The input domain matters: zero-bias networks sparse on the entire ball have at most $2k$ nonzero units and complexity $O(kWR/\sqrt m)$, whereas bias bounds comparable to $WR$ restore the worst-case rate on that same domain in only logarithmic dimension. A spherical-cap construction proves the latter claim without assuming sparsity merely on the sampling support. For a specified normalized bounded loss and biases comparable to $WR$, we also obtain agnostic minimax excess-risk bounds of order $\min\{1,\sqrt{s/(km)}\}$ up to logarithms.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes statistical complexity bounds for input-dependent sparsity in ReLU networks, showing how active units per input affect learning rates, with matching lower bounds proving tightness up to logarithmic factors.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates how input-dependent sparsity in neural networks affects statistical learning complexity. When different inputs collectively use all hidden units but individual inputs activate only a subset, the effective complexity should be lower than worst-case. The authors aim to characterize this phenomenon formally for ReLU networks.
AI.method: The authors analyze one-hidden-layer ReLU networks with width s, at most k active units per input, and bounded weights/biases. They develop theoretical bounds using: (1) support-preserving covers that maintain activation patterns, (2) single normalized chaining arguments to remove explicit dimension factors, (3) lower bound constructions via appropriate i.i.d. marginals, and (4) spherical-cap constructions to prove domain-dependent results.
AI.result: Main results: (1) Rademacher complexity bound of CWR min{k,√(sk/m)log³/²(2m)} + kB/√m; (2) Input domain matters significantly - zero-bias networks sparse on entire ball have complexity O(kWR/√m) whereas comparable bias bounds restore worst-case rate with only logarithmic dimension dependence; (3) Lower bounds match upper bounds up to logarithmic factors; (4) Agnostic minimax excess-risk bounds of order min{1,√[s/(km)]} up to logarithms for normalized bounded loss with biases comparable to WR.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that input-dependent sparsity in ReLU networks reduces statistical complexity compared to worst-case bounds, but width dependence remains due to changing active units across inputs. The interplay between sparsity, bias magnitude, and input domain crucially affects learning rates, with formal characterization up to logarithmic factors.

title: Entropy-Regularized Rank-Masked Policy Optimization for Test-Time Reinforcement Learning in Code Generation
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. 15 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables
summary: Existing methods for test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) derive rewards from answer-level self-voting on unlabeled test-time tasks with canonical answers, but this breaks down for code generation because programs cannot be compared by surface form and therefore do not directly provide a usable training signal. To make TTRL applicable to code generation, we propose probe-driven TTRL, which constructs output-free probe inputs from the problem statement, executes candidate programs on these probes, and defines a Probe Consensus Reward (PCR) from the resulting behavioral agreement. PCR provides a behavioral training signal for open-vocabulary programs, but it is not a fully reliable verifier and remains susceptible to reward hacking through spurious consensus. We therefore introduce Entropy-Regularized Rank-Masked Policy Optimization (ERPO), which converts low PCR into conservative negative updates through rank masking and controls policy drift with an entropy ceiling. On coding benchmarks, ERPO substantially improves pass@1 and pass@k in both in-domain adaptation and zero-shot transfer.

AI.tldr: Probe-driven test-time RL for code generation uses behavioral consensus on probe inputs to create training signals, with entropy-regularized policy optimization to prevent reward hacking.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time RL methods rely on answer-level self-voting, which doesn't work for code generation because programs can't be compared by surface form and don't provide direct training signals.
AI.method: Probe-driven TTRL constructs output-free probe inputs from problem statements, executes candidate programs on these probes, and defines Probe Consensus Reward (PCR) from behavioral agreement. To address PCR's unreliability and reward hacking risks, they introduce Entropy-Regularized Rank-Masked Policy Optimization (ERPO) which converts low PCR into conservative negative updates via rank masking and controls policy drift with entropy ceiling.
AI.result: On coding benchmarks, ERPO substantially improves pass@1 and pass@k performance in both in-domain adaptation and zero-shot transfer scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Probe-driven TTRL with ERPO successfully extends test-time reinforcement learning to code generation by creating behavioral training signals from program execution rather than surface-level comparisons, while effectively mitigating reward hacking through careful regularization techniques.

title: NOAH: Learning the Full Patient Journey. A Longitudinal Multimodal Time-Aware Model for Representation and Forecasting
summary: The digitization of healthcare has generated vast, longitudinal, and multimodal patient records over a lifetime, yet fully exploiting these data to represent and predict patient state trajectories remains a critical challenge. Current AI models often struggle to capture the complex, irregular temporal dynamics and inherent stochasticity of real-world multimodal patient data. Existing AI approaches for modeling longitudinal patient records are predominantly discriminative, limited to a few modalities, constrained by closed categorical vocabularies, treating time as a monotonic inductive bias, or they are limited in forecasting future patient states. We introduce NOAH, a time-aware, task-agnostic, generative transformer model representing and forecasting the full multimodal patient journey. NOAH features a novel bidirectional time integration and a variational latent space to capture the continuous evolution of patient states and the stochasticity of clinical trajectories. Built from over 559 million clinical events from 431,000 hospital visits of 299,000 patients across the MIMIC dataset family, NOAH natively processes medical images, time-series and numeric signals, categorical events, as well as structured and unstructured clinical records. NOAH is the first truly holistic generative model in its field, enabling autoregressive forecasting with optional time control, zero-shot classification, and counterfactual intervention simulation. It generates highly informative and predictive patient state representations that demonstrate strong performance in probing for clinical outcomes, 15 ICD chapters, and 29 comorbidities, as well as in time-to-event prediction. Seamlessly handling diverse modalities and complex temporal dynamics, NOAH provides a versatile, task-agnostic, scalable foundation for intelligent predictive systems in personalized clinical care and digital medicine.

AI.tldr: NOAH is a time-aware, task-agnostic generative transformer that represents and forecasts multimodal patient journeys, handling diverse data types and complex temporal dynamics.
AI.motivation: Current AI models struggle with complex, irregular temporal dynamics and stochasticity of real-world multimodal patient data, and existing approaches have limitations like being predominantly discriminative, limited modalities, constrained vocabularies, poor time handling, or limited forecasting capabilities.
AI.method: Introduces NOAH, a generative transformer with novel bidirectional time integration and variational latent space to capture continuous patient state evolution and clinical stochasticity. Built on MIMIC data with 559M events from 299K patients, it natively processes medical images, time-series signals, categorical events, and structured/unstructured records.
AI.result: Generates highly informative and predictive patient state representations with strong performance in clinical outcome probing, 15 ICD chapters, 29 comorbidities, and time-to-event prediction. Enables autoregressive forecasting with time control, zero-shot classification, and counterfactual intervention simulation.
AI.conclusion: NOAH provides a versatile, task-agnostic, scalable foundation for intelligent predictive systems in personalized clinical care and digital medicine, being the first truly holistic generative model in this field.

title: Learning Length-Extrapolatable Recurrent Models
summary: Recurrent models provide a natural path to long-context modeling, yet models trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT) often fail beyond their training horizon. Classical analyses emphasize gradients that vanish or explode along temporal paths. However, dense per-token losses can still train a shared recurrent rule despite severe decay, showing that decay alone does not determine whether learning fails. We instead study state credit: the signal through which future losses reach earlier recurrent states before contributing to parameter updates. Accordingly, we intervene directly on state credit and propose Credit Stabilization through Time (CST). During backward propagation, CST locally rescales the state-credit signal to stabilize its norm without rotating the component being corrected, while leaving the forward computation unchanged. Because controlled synthetic tasks and real data exhibit different credit dynamics, we specialize CST to each regime. In both settings, CST improves performance beyond the training horizon, with gains observed at up to 128x the training length.

AI.tldr: CST (Credit Stabilization through Time) addresses the failure of recurrent models beyond training horizon by stabilizing state credit signals during backward propagation, enabling learning up to 128x training length.
AI.motivation: Recurrent models trained with BPTT often fail beyond their training horizon despite dense per-token losses showing that gradient decay alone doesn't explain learning failure. The paper identifies "state credit" - the signal through which future losses reach earlier recurrent states - as the key limitation.
AI.method: Proposed Credit Stabilization through Time (CST) intervenes directly on state credit during backward propagation. It locally rescales the state-credit signal to stabilize its norm without rotating the component being corrected, while leaving forward computation unchanged. The approach is specialized for different regimes (synthetic tasks vs real data).
AI.result: CST improves performance beyond the training horizon in both controlled synthetic tasks and real data settings. Gains are observed at up to 128x the training length, demonstrating significant improvement over standard BPTT training.
AI.conclusion: The failure of recurrent models beyond training horizon is better explained by state credit dynamics rather than gradient decay alone. CST provides an effective solution by stabilizing state credit signals, enabling recurrent models to learn effectively at much longer time horizons than they were trained on.
